The RDA with automatic forward selection showed that the fish community structure in the constructed wetlands was significantly correlated with the wetland area, \( H' \) of aquatic macrophytes, concentrations of DO, SS, TP, and COD, and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (\( p < 0.1 \), Monte Carlo permutation with 999 permutations; Table 7). Seven variables explained 46.4% of the total variation in abundances of four dominant fish species (\( F = 5.57, df = 6 \) and 44, \( p = 0.0010 \), Monte Carlo permutation test with 999 permutations; Table 8). The RDA plot showed that goldfish, tilapia, and topmouth gudgeon were more abundant in treatment cells with a larger area, higher concentrations of SS and COD, and a low density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 5). The blue gourami was more abundant in treatment cells with a higher \( H' \) value of macrophytes and TP concentrations (Fig. 5). For the distribution of aquatic macroinvertebrates, the RDA using automatic forward selection retained seven variables: fish species richness, richness and cover of aquatic macrophytes, water temperature, and values of conductivity, pH, and DO (\( p < 0.1 \), Monte Carlo permutation with 999 permutations; Table 7). The first four axes in the RDA model explained 21.3% of the total variation in abundance of the 13 most dominant aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa, 94.1% of which was significantly related to the measured variables (\( F = 3.80, df = 6 \) and 89, \( p = 0.0010 \), Monte Carlo permutation test with 999 permutations; Table 8). The RDA ordination plot indicated that narrow-winged damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Diplonychus sp.) and leaf beetle larvae (Chrysomelidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Apple snails (Pomacea canaliculata) and mayflies (Cloeon sp.) were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 6). Dipteran species such as mosquitoes (Culex spp.), brine flies (Ephydridae), and non-biting midges (Chironomidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high values of conductivity and low values of DO (Fig. 6). 4. Discussion 4.1. Performance of pollutant removal The construction of wetlands is an alternative measure to conventional water treatment, which provides a potentially more environmentally friendly and economical treatment system to mitigate the negative effects of domestic wastewater and urban runoff (Scholz et al., 2007). Our study showed that the two constructed wetlands were effective in nutrient removal, although the performances varied between the constructed wetlands and also among nutrients. Wetland design, water quality, hydraulics, soil chem- istry, microbial communities, macroinvertebrates, and vegetation each may greatly affect the performance of constructed wetlands. The main removal mechanisms of BOD and COD include microbial degradation and settling of colloidal particles (Vymazal et al., 1998). Nitrogen is primarily removed through microbial nitrification and denitrification in most constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998). Phosphorus removal in constructed wetlands occurs from absorption and precipitation by soil particles (Vymazal, 2010). The amount of nutrients such as phosphorus removed by plant uptake generally accounts for a small fraction of total nutrients removed in constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998), and may be released back into the water after plants decay (Vymazal, 2010). Small and deep wetlands increase phosphorus retention by increasing particle sedimentation, while large surface areas may maximize nitrogen removal (Hansson et al., 2005; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The removal rates in this study were similar compared to nearby constructed wetlands (Fan et al., 2009). 4.2. Biodiversity of constructed wetlands Along with treating wastewater, there is an increasing trend in designing constructed wetlands to restore degraded habitats for wildlife. However, different ecological functions of wetland systems are thought to be conflicting. High nutrient loadings that surpass a critical level may cause dramatic shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning (Verhoeven et al., 2006). Some potential problems, including bioaccumulation of toxic materials, transmission of disease, and environmental hazards, might result from the use of wetlands for wastewater treatment (Knight, 1992). Benyamine et al. (2004) indicated that the typical single-objective focus of scientific studies has led to contradictions in recommendations for the design and management of constructed wetlands for multiple uses. Nevertheless, this study combined with others (e.g., Knight, 1997; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006) suggest that constructed wetlands can provide attractive habitats for various kinds of wildlife. Meanwhile, after reviewing the North American Treatment Wetland (NADB) Database, Knight et al. (2001) indicated that there were no detrimental effects on wildlife caused by the pollution-cleansing function of treatment wetlands. Due to a lack of data in nearby freshwater habitats, the contribution of constructed wetlands to landscape biodiversity could not be determined in this study. Nevertheless, in addition to water quality improvement, this study suggests that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. This study further demonstrated that the biodiversity of different taxonomic groups in constructed wetlands is governed by various factors. 4.3. Factors affecting wetland biodiversity Our results suggest a positive relationship between the area of a constructed wetland and the biodiversity and abundance of birds, which is in accordance with other studies on wetlands (Zedler, 2003; Hansson et al., 2005). In addition to wetland area, bird biodiversity was found to be affected by adjacent and regional land uses, such as road density and connectedness (Whited et al., 2000). Ordination results suggested that bird communities were mainly determined by seasonal patterns, as well as food availability and nesting requirements for brood rearing. Bird species such as the Dusky Thrush, Teal, and Yellow Wagtail were winter visitors (Shiu et al., 2005), and, therefore, were negatively correlated with water temperature. Members of the Ardeidae such as Little Egrets and Black-crowned Night Herons, and the Recurvirostridae like Black-winged Stilts were found to be associated with the species richness and abundance of fishes (Fig. 4). A number of studies indicated that they feed on a wide variety of prey types but mainly on fish (Fasola, 1994; Kazantzidis and Goutner, 2005). The association of White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) with aquatic macrophytes can be attributed to nest-site selection for brood rearing (Gopakumar and Kaimal, 2008). Aquatic invertebrates are primary food resources for many wintering waterbirds. Wallau et al. (2010) indicated that the Common Moorhen feeds on pieces of aquatic macrophytes and removes macrophytes to search for invertebrates which utilize macrophytes as habitats. The Cattle Egret was found to rely heavily on various invertebrates as their main food sources (Lombardini et al., 2001), and its number was positively correlated with the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 4). Teal and Spot-billed Duck (Anatidae) may also compete with fish for the same food resources (invertebrates) and are thus found in lower densities at wetlands with fish compared to those without fish (e.g., Eriksson, 1979). Our study showed that fish biodiversity was low in these young (<5 years) constructed wetlands. Hansson et al. (2005) also found similar results and indicated that natural wetlands aged more than 100 years showed considerably higher fish species richness than young constructed wetlands. In constructed wetlands, possible sources of the fish are limited to those from nearby streams during floods and mercy releases, and, therefore, the biodiversity of fish is unlikely to increase over a short time period. This study showed that a wetland’s area is also important in determining the species richness of fishes. All treatment cells in our study were <2 ha (Fig. 2). Søndergaard et al. (2005) found that fish species richness was low, typically 1–3 species, in Danish ponds and lakes with areas of <1 ha, and gradually increased with lake size. Scheffer et al. (2006) proposed that fish are rare in small, isolated lakes, probably as a result of a higher likelihood of fish kills combined with their low colonizing ability. Moreover, fish biodiversity appeared to be most affected by the water quality in constructed wetlands. Fish species found in constructed wetlands appeared to be tolerant of high nutrient levels and low DO conditions. Blue gourami is an obligate air-breathing fish (Burggren, 1979), which means that it can adapt to changing DO levels in constructed wetlands. The dominant blue gourami and tilapia in constructed wetlands are exotics, but not the goldfish. Tilapia (Cichlidae) are among the most widely distributed exotic fishes in the world (Canonico et al., 2005). Studies found that they are able to respond to environmental changes by rapidly altering their life history characteristic and trophic levels (Bowen and Allanson, 1982), which may benefit their invasion into new environments (Holway and Suarez, 1999). The exotic species introduced to these wetlands either on purpose or accidentally may also threaten populations of native species. Our results suggest close relationships of the richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates with the coverage of aquatic macrophytes. The abundance and diversity of aquatic invertebrates were found to be associated with the vegetated area of wetlands (Gee et al., 1997). The presence of aquatic macrophytes might affect the distributions of aquatic macroinvertebrates and thus their biodiversity in several ways. Submerged vegetation in aquatic ecosystems forms complex structures, which may be used as habitats (Gee et al., 1997) or as refuges to reduce the foraging efficiency of predators (Diehl, 1992). Because there is more space for food attachment and collection, aquatic macrophytes provide additional resources such as epiphytes to the macroinvertebrate community, especially for grazers and thus may indirectly favor detritivores and predators (Diehl, 1992). Positive relationships between the abundance of aquatic macroinvertebrates and cover of aquatic macrophytes were reported elsewhere (de Szalay and Resh, 2000). In constructed wetlands, excessive nutrient loadings, high toxic pollutant levels, and anaerobic conditions often prevent aquatic macroinvertebrates from using wetlands as habitats (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Hence, our results indicated a negative relationship of COD with the taxon richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates. Decreases in richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates were shown to be related to changes in water quality in various aquatic ecosystems (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Jurado et al., 2010). The community structure of aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands was influenced by the presence of predators and suitable habitats. Fish are often the top predators in wetland ecosystems and can impact aquatic macroinvertebrates in terms of species richness, density, diversity, and community structure (Diehl, 1992). Ordination analyses indicated that the major dipteran taxa in these constructed wetlands, such as non-biting midges (Chironomidae), mosquitoes (Culicidae), and brine flies (Ephydridae), were negatively associated with the species richness of fish and dissolved oxygen. Most of the fish species in our study sites rely on aquatic invertebrates as their main food sources. The diet of the blue gourami mainly consists of aquatic invertebrates and algae-based foods (Syarifuddin and Kramer, 1996). Although goldfish predominantly eat non-animal food, studies showed that they also feed on a wide range of food resources, including various zooplankton and aquatic insects (e.g., Peterson et al., 2005). Numerous studies demonstrated that the presence of fish may reduce the density and biomass of certain taxa of aquatic invertebrates (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000) and change the community structure of aquatic invertebrates in wetlands (Tarr et al., 2005). Moreover, many species of these dipteran families are tolerant of low DO and polluted water (Courtney et al., 1996). Relationships of damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Belostomatidae), and leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) with the cover of aquatic macrophytes suggest that the vegetation is used as food and perch sites (Cloarec, 1990; Gibbons et al., 2002; Fernandez and Hilker, 2007). The amount of unexplained variation in our models suggests that some other unmeasured variables play certain roles in regulating communities in these constructed wetlands. Keddy and Fraser (2000) suggested that variations in water depth were the most important factor governing communities in shoreline wetlands. Increases in habitat heterogeneity or complexity (Hansson et al., 2005) and age (Fairchild et al., 2000) may increase the biodiversity of wetlands. In addition, the richness of aquatic invertebrates increases with the hydroperiod, i.e., the length of time that a wetland holds water (Tarr et al., 2005). In highly connected wetlands, aquatic invertebrate richness may also increase through dispersal from areas with different environmental conditions (e.g., Cottenie and De Meester, 2003). These factors could be constructed and manipulated through proper design and management of constructed wetlands, and can therefore be used to increase biodiversity. 4.4. Implications for the design and management of constructed wetlands Previous studies examined the impacts of environmental factors on biodiversity across various taxonomic groups in lentic ecosystems (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Results from those studies as well as ours reveal that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. In order to maximize biodiversity in constructed wetlands, the factors involved in each taxonomic group should be taken into consideration in wetland design and management from a holistic view. According to our results, wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes appeared to be the two most important factors affecting biodiversity in the constructed wetlands. A wetland constructed with the aim of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Findlay and Houlahan (1997) found that species richness of all taxa in their study, including birds, mammals, herptiles and plants, increased with wetland area. Whatever other considerations may be taken into the wetland design, from a biodiversity conservation perspective, bigger is indeed better, although the maximum richness of some taxa might be encountered at a certain area (e.g., 4–5 ha for birds, Hansson et al., 2005). Changes in macrophyte composition and cover are among the most important ecological successions in constructed wetlands (Mitsch et al., 2005). Although high macrophyte cover may increase taxa richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates, problems can arise as a result of the presence of dense vegetation in wetlands such as consumption of DO and contribution to nutrient loadings as plants decompose (Sartoris et al., 2000). For wastewater treatment, a high cover of aquatic macrophytes was designed as one of the important factors facilitating N retention (Thiere et al., 2011). For wildlife management, a 50:50 ratio of open water to emergent vegetation, i.e., hemi-marshes, was recommended to attract wildlife (Murkin et al., 1997). de Szalay and Resh (2000) indicated that the cover of aquatic macrophytes increased the abundances of some dipteran taxa, which might cause serious nuisance problems in wetlands. Our results also show that taxa responded differently to changes in the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Since the vegetation has both positive and negative effects on the performance of constructed wetland for wastewater treatment, a proper vegetation balance is needed for optimal treatment performance through vegetation management (Thullen et al., 2005). It is widely accepted that created wetlands, whether for wastewater treatment or not, may never express the full range of ecological variability found in natural wetlands (Brooks et al., 2005). However, as water quality improves due to sequential purification along the treatment cells, the last ponds in a constructed wetland may be capable of supporting biodiversity similar to that of natural wetlands (Jurado et al., 2010). 5. Conclusions Although characterized by high nutrient loadings, constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment are able to support various wildlife and enhance biodiversity. This study indicated that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. The richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with the wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentration. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Therefore, a wetland constructed with the aims of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Our results imply that ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands, used primarily for wastewater treatment or created for new wetland areas, can be managed to enhance biodiversity. Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison E. Einola,1 M. Rantakari,2 P. Kankaala,3 P. Kortelainen,2 A. Ojala,4 H. Pajunen,5 S. Mäkelä,1 and L. Arvola1 Received 23 December 2010; revised 6 May 2011; accepted 18 May 2011; published 27 July 2011. [1] Lakes play an important role in catchment carbon (C) balances. However, the role of lakes in landscape C cycling in changing climate is highly uncertain. We studied C pools in a chain of five boreal lakes and compared the C fluxes during a wet and a dry year. The included pools were dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) in lake water, as well as C pools in littoral macrophytes and lake sediments. The estimated C fluxes consisted of hydrological input and output of DIC and TOC, emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere, DIC incorporated as organic carbon in primary production of phytoplankton and littoral macrophytes, and sedimentation of C. The riverine input of C into the lakes increased remarkably (40–210%) in the year with high precipitation. Simultaneously, there was a clear increase in the flux of CO2 to the atmosphere from the three small uppermost lakes, whereas in two large lowland lakes the CO2 fluxes were higher during the warm dry year. On the landscape scale, the role of small lakes (area <1 km2) was emphasized in net C accumulation, whereas the large lowland lakes released more CO2 to the atmosphere. In parallel, the concentration of TOC in the water column decreased downstream the lake chain whereas DIC increased. The largest pool of C (>98%) in all the lakes was in the sediment. Sediment C store, calculated relative to the lake area, was positively correlated with lake water TOC (r2 = 0.93, P < 0.05) and Fe (r2 = 0.96, P < 0.05) concentrations. Lake water Fe content was also a good predictor for the long-term accumulation (r2 = 0.99, P < 0.01), as well as gross sedimentation rate of organic carbon (r2 = 0.48, P < 0.01). Citation: Einola, E., M. Rantakari, P. Kankaala, P. Kortelainen, A. Ojala, H. Pajunen, S. Mäkelä, and L. Arvola (2011), Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison, J. Geophys. Res., 116, G03009, doi:10.1029/2010JG001636. 1. Introduction [2] Although freshwater lakes and rivers cover a small area of the earth’s surface, their role in regional carbon (C) budgets and also in global C cycling is much more pronounced than expected only by their area. Rivers and lakes transport, mineralize and accumulate significant amounts of terrestrially fixed C and exchange inorganic C between water-air interfaces [e.g., del Giorgio and Peters, 1994; Kortelainen et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Downing, 2010]. [3] The riverine transport of organic carbon plays an important role in functioning of boreal lakes; e.g., in humic lakes, common in the Boreal Zone, terrestrial carbon input can be much higher than in-lake production [Sarvala et al., 1981; Arvola et al., 1990; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the majority of lakes and rivers are net heterotrophic, i.e., the biological C mineralization exceeds primary production [Alin and Johnson, 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009]. Moreover, the recent trend of increasing concentrations of colored organic substances in many northern lakes and rivers [e.g., Monteith et al., 2007; Lepistö et al., 2008] may further strengthen heterotrophy in these freshwater ecosystems because of decreasing light availability for primary producers. [4] In the Boreal Zone, the concentration of total organic carbon (TOC) in lakes and the export of TOC from catchments are strongly related to the coverage of peatlands [Kortelainen, 1993; Kortelainen et al., 2006a] and coniferous forests in the catchment area [Mattsson et al., 2003; Humborg et al., 2004]. Most (>80%) of the organic matter exported from the catchments is in dissolved form [Wetzel, 2001]. A small proportion of the dissolved organic matter (DOM) may aggregate with metals (amorphous iron and aluminum) [Jonsson, 1997] and/or flocculate with bacteria [von Wachenfeldt et al., 2009], contributing to C accumulation in bottom sediments. In small boreal headwater streams as well as large rivers flowing to the Figure 1. Map of the study area showing the study lakes, the rivers connecting them, and the vegetation type and land use of each study lake. Thick arrows indicate the main inlets of rivers running to and from the study lakes. Baltic Sea, the proportion of particulate organic carbon (POC) of TOC is <5% [Kortelainen et al., 2006a; Mattsson et al., 2005]. The contribution of living material is low especially in running waters, where bacteria, algae, protozoa and larger zooplankton may comprise only about 1% of the TOC [Arvola and Nurmesniemi, 2000]. [5] Most lakes in the Boreal Zone are connected by streams as chains that can differ considerably in their morphology and physical and chemical characteristics. The residence time of water in each basin, defined by the catchment setting and lake morphology, together with the average annual runoff, may be crucial for biogeochemical processing of the organic matter [cf. Algesten et al., 2004], i.e., for microbial decomposition in the water column and in the sediment as well as ultraviolet (UV) irradiance-induced breakdown in the uppermost water layer [Vähätalo et al., 2000; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the residence time influences the quantity and quality of organic matter flowing downstream, and the proportion of organic C released as carbon dioxide (CO_2) and methane (CH_4), or stored in the bottom sediments. Mattsson et al. [2005] showed that proportion of lake area in the upper catchment significantly reduced TOC transport by the large Finnish rivers to the coast. Thus, upstream lakes may be intensive sites for DOM processing, which decreases the export of C downstream [Rasmussen et al., 1989; Kortelainen, 1993; Larson et al., 2007]. [6] Climate change scenarios predict increasing precipitation and temperature for many areas in the Boreal Zone, resulting in major changes in seasonal runoff patterns in northern catchments [e.g., Andréasson et al., 2004], including increasing frequency of extreme weather conditions and thus also extremes in hydrology [e.g., Christensen and Christensen, 2003]. Since hydrology is a major driver of the variability of water C concentrations on the catchment scale [e.g., Erlandsson et al., 2008], the interannual variations in C budgets of individual lakes may be considerable [Arvola et al., 1990]. Although carbon budgets for single lakes [e.g., Arvola et al., 1990; Sobek et al., 2006] and also for a chain of hard-water lakes [Finlay et al., 2010] have been studied, C budgets for a chain of boreal lakes in climatically different years have remained unknown. [7] The aim of our study was to (1) estimate C pools (store in the sediment and in the water column and biomass of primary producers) in a chain of five boreal lakes consisting of one small headwater lake, two small drainage lakes, and two large downstream lakes and to (2) compare C fluxes (net primary production, inflow, outflow, sedimentation, and atmospheric efflux) between a dry and a rainy year within this Table 1. Material and Methods [8] The five study lakes (areal range 0.036–44 km2), situated in the southern Boreal Zone in Finland were numbered by their order in the chain: (1) Valkea-Kotinen, (2) Alinen Rautjärvi, (3) Ekojärvi, (4) Kuohijärvi, and (5) Kukkia (Figure 1). The area deglaciated about 11,500 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. The uppermost and the smallest lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), was isolated immediately after deglaciation, while the other lakes were submerged by waters of the ancient Baltic Sea. Since the postglacial land uplift was more rapid than the rise of sea level, the land area expanded and new lakes became isolated. Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) was isolated about 11,400 years ago, Lake Ekojärvi (3) about 9800 years ago and the largest lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) about 9700 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. [9] The Precambrian bedrock in the area consists of veined gneiss with granodiorite occurring around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and close to Lake Kuohijärvi (4). The soil is mostly moraine but there is gravel and sand around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and the river draining it, while clay areas partly surround lakes Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5). Coniferous forests with Norway Spruce (Picea abies [L.] H. Karst.) and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) cover 65–80% and peatlands less than 20% of the catchment areas of each lake (Figure 1). Except for the first lake of the chain, Valkea-Kotinen, which is situated in a nature reserve area, the human impact on the catchments has been quite intense, because of a >150 year long history of forestry and related activities, including draining of wetlands. Some agriculture is also practiced, predominantly in the lowland areas, but the proportion of agricultural land in the catchment does not exceed 5% around any of the studied lakes. The local names suggest that historically the local people have utilized lake iron (e.g., Alinen Rautjärvi = Lower Iron Lake). The lakes vary in their morphological characteristics (Table 1), and the lake area to catchment area ratio (LA/CA) is significantly higher in the two largest lowland lakes than in the first three lakes in the chain. The concentrations of TOC, total phosphorus, total nitrogen and chlorophyll \( a \) are higher in the small upstream lakes than in the largest lowland lakes (Table 2). In the uppermost lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), the hypolimnion is anoxic during winter and summer stratification. In Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3), the hypolimnetic anoxia during the stratification periods is occasional, whereas in Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) the entire water column is oxic throughout the year. The larger lakes are covered by ice usually from late November to late April and the smaller ones from late October or early November to early May. [10] The annual long-term (1987–2007) average precipitation in the area is 632 mm (Finnish Meteorological Institute). The highest runoff peaks are generally observed in spring after snowmelt. The runoff can also peak during autumn, when precipitation is generally higher than in summer and the evapotranspiration is small. However, high runoffs can also occur during summer, as in 1998, if the precipitation is high and the antecedent soil conditions are wet. [11] The annual precipitation during 1997 was 5% lower and during 1998 22% higher than the average (Table 3), with the most distinguishable difference in the precipitation patterns observed in summer: in 1997 the summer precipitation was 10% lower than the long-term average, while in 1998 it was 70% higher than the average. The differences in precipitation were reflected in the water residence time of the lakes. There was also a difference of almost 2°C between the daily average air temperatures during the two summers (Table 3). For the fifth lake in the chain (Kukkia) the data set was not sufficient for budget calculations. [13] In the three small uppermost lakes the sediment volume was estimated on the basis of coring and survey on site. The interface between organic sediment (gyttja, clay gyttja or gyttja clay) and the underlying mineral soil (till, sand, silt or clay) was interpreted to indicate lake isolation. The thickness of the lake sediment bed was determined at seven sites in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), 35 sites in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and 48 sites in Lake Ekojärvi (3). In the largest lowland lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), echo sounding was used to estimate the volume of the lake sediment bed with survey transects of 15 and 31 km, respectively. In these transects the proportion of accumulation bottom was measured. This proportion and the total lake area were used to estimate the accumulation area, which was multiplied with the average thickness to obtain the sediment volume. For the analysis of sediment density and C content, a sediment core was collected from each lake. The cores extended from the surface of the sediment bed to the depth of lake isolation. In the laboratory the cores were opened and their stratigraphy determined. The cores were divided into samples and a total of 104 samples were analyzed. The sample treatment and laboratory methods are thoroughly described by Pajunen et al. [2000]. The amount of total dry matter is based on sediment volume and average density and the amount of C on the amount of total dry matter and average C content. The average C store (g C m⁻²) was divided by the age of the lake to obtain the average Holocene accumulation rates (g C m⁻² yr⁻¹). [14] The gross sedimentation rate was measured only in the uppermost lake as part of a long-term monitoring program [cf. Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Sedimenting material was collected with three acrylic plastic tubes (length 45 cm, diameter 5 cm) placed below the epilimnion at a depth of 4 m. During the ice-free period, material settled in the tubes was removed every 2 weeks, dried, weighed and analyzed for C content with a high-temperature combustion method [Salonen, 1979]. For annual estimates of gross sedimentation we used the results from the under ice measurements, conducted in 1995 and 1996 with exactly the same methods as during the open water period but using a 3 week collection period. In addition to C, the Fe content of the gross sedimentation was measured during one open water season (in 2000) with a Varian AAS (Varian Inc. Palo Alto, Calif., United States). [15] The samples for TOC and DIC analyses of the water column were taken at 0.2–05 m depth in rivers and at 1 m depth in the lakes. The sampling frequency in the rivers was primarily once a month during the open water season (May–November) and once in winter (early April). The uppermost lake (Valkea-Kotinen) was sampled 24 times during the both years. The other lakes in the chain were sampled 1–4 times in 1997 and four times in 1998 (late winter, spring, summer, and autumnal mixing). For the missing data for spring 1997 in Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Kukkia (5), and for winter, spring and autumn 1997 in Kuohijärvi (4) the values for the corresponding season of 1998 were used. [16] The TOC concentration of the water was analyzed with a Shimadzu TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corp. Kyoto, Japan). For some occasions (about half of the river samples), water color values (platinum reference) were available instead of TOC. However, TOC was linearly related to water color in the samples taken from the study rivers and the lakes, and the missing TOC values were estimated with the regression equation: TOC [mg C L⁻¹] = 0.0408 * water color [mg Pt L⁻¹] + 5.29 (r² = 0.84, P < 0.05, n = 110). The DIC concentrations were estimated from the measured alkalinity values with the regression equation DIC [μmol L⁻¹] = 0.996 * Alkalinity [μeq L⁻¹] + 19.3, r² = 0.95, n = 874, obtained from measurements in randomly selected Finnish soft water lakes with similar range of alkalinity [Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. Temperature and oxygen concentration in the water column of the lakes was measured with YSI 55 (Yellow Springs Instruments) combined probe (accuracy ±0.3°C, ±0.3 mg O₂ L⁻¹). [17] The discharge from each subcatchment was estimated using measured daily runoff data for the years 1997 and 1998 (Finnish Environment Institute, OIVA service on environment and geographic information, 17 March 2010) from the rivers Mustajoki and Haarajoki, both situated less than 30 km from the study sites and having land use characteristics very similar to the study lakes, assuming that the discharge from each subcatchment was related to its area. The TOC and DIC input and output were calculated by multiplying the monthly discharge (the sum of measured daily values) at the inflows and outflows with the TOC and DIC concentration during the respective period in the rivers between the lakes. The min-max range of the annual TOC and DIC loads to lakes were estimated by multiplying monthly discharge with minimum concentration (annual mean – SD) as well as maximum concentration (annual mean + SD) of TOC and DIC of both Table 4. For the uppermost lake in the chain, the input of TOC and DIC from the catchment was estimated using the values of small brooks having similar catchments with no upstream lakes. We assumed that the input of C by groundwater was insignificant to the C fluxes in this flat landscape. [18] Emissions of CO\(_2\) from the lakes were calculated using the equation by Cole and Caraco [1998], in which the CO\(_2\) saturation in the surface water was compared with the equilibrium value. The CO\(_2\) concentrations were calculated from the available open water DIC and pH results of each lakes, with correction for water temperature [Stumm and Morgan, 1970; Butler, 1982; Kling et al., 1992]. Partial pressure of CO\(_2\) (\(p\)CO\(_2\)) was calculated from the CO\(_2\) concentrations, using Henry’s law constants corrected for temperature and atmospheric pressure [Plummer and Busenberg, 1982]. The equilibrium CO\(_2\) concentration in the lake water was calculated using the elevation of the lake and Henry’s law constants, assuming an atmospheric mixing ratio of 361 ppm by volume (ppmv) for 1996 and an annual increase of 1.5 ppmv y\(^{-1}\) by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [2001], equaling the values measured in Finland [e.g., Kulmala et al., 2000]. The piston velocity of CO\(_2\) was obtained by first determining the piston velocity of SF\(_6\), using the empirical relationship between the piston velocity of SF\(_6\) normalized to a Schmidt number of 600 and the wind speed at a height of 10 m [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and then calculating the Schmidt number for CO\(_2\), using empirical third-order polynomial fits to temperature [Jähne et al., 1987]. The wind speed was assumed to be 3 m s\(^{-1}\), which is the average long-term open water period wind speed for inland measurement stations in Finland [Leinonen, 2000]. All the equations for calculations of the CO\(_2\) emissions are presented by Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005]. Additional data for the range of CO\(_2\) emissions from the lakes, estimated for the year 2000 (annual precipitation 634 mm, summer precipitation 266 mm) on the basis of four measurements in three of the lakes, are also presented in the Table 6. The emissions of CH\(_4\) from some of the study lakes were minor compared to CO\(_2\) efflux and have been presented elsewhere [Kankaala et al., 2005, 2006; Bergström et al., 2007]. The measured atmospheric deposition of C in the area was 1 g C m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\) [Kortelainen et al., 2006a]. [19] The annual production of phytoplankton in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) was measured weekly during the open water season in situ using the \(^{14}\)C method [Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Since the incubation time was 24 h, the measurements resulted in net primary productivity values (NPP). For the other lakes, the range of NPP of phytoplankton was estimated using data obtained in previous measurements in neighboring lakes [Ilmavirta and Kotimaa, 1974; Arvola 1983, 1984; Arvola et al., 1999], with the same types of trophic status and chemical and physical properties as in the study lakes. The areas covered by different macrophyte species were mapped in 1997–2000. The macrophyte C pool was estimated as a seasonal maximum biomass (g dry weight (DW) m\(^{-2}\)) converted to C by a factor 0.38 [Duarte, 1992], obtained from the data for stands of the dominant species in the three uppermost lakes [Keskitalo and Heitto, 1996; Kankaala et al., 2003, 2005]. The NPP of macrophytes was estimated to be twofold the seasonal maximum biomass of all the stands [Westlake, 1982]. [20] We also made a regional, landscape-scale estimate of CO\(_2\) emissions and sediment net C accumulation of all the lakes in the cumulative catchment area of the lake chain. The results of the five lakes studied were upscaled for the respective lake size classes (area <0.1, 0.1–1, 1–10 and 10–50 km\(^2\)) throughout the area. The areal results (g C m\(^{-2}\)) of the largest size class were also applied to the size class 1–10 km, because none of the lakes in the chain studied belonged to that size class. [21] The statistical relationships between the different variables in the data set were calculated as Pearson’s linear correlations (Pearson’s r). The variables with skewed distributions were first log-transformed to approach normality. The analyses were done with PASW (SPSS) Statistics 17.0 software. 3. Results 3.1. Carbon Pools [22] In all the lakes, >98% of C was in the sediments (Table 4). The proportion of organic matter (Table 4) in the sediments decreased, while the density of the lake sediment bed increased downstream of the lake chain. In Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), the average sediment density was 0.056 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) 0.14 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lakes Ekojärvi (3) and Kuohijärvi (4) about 0.25 g cm\(^{-3}\) and in Lake Kukkia (5) 0.35 g cm\(^{-3}\). In the uppermost lake, the average thickness of the sediment bed (computed for the entire lake area) was 1.6 m, while in the succeeding three lakes the bed was around 2 m thick and in the lowermost lake only 1.2 m thick. [23] The water column TOC, including phytoplankton, constituted 95% of the lake water C pool in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) (Table 4). The proportion of TOC decreased along the lake chain to 68% in Kuohijärvi (4) and to 67% in Kukkia (5) while the proportion of DIC increased from 5% in Valkea-Kotinen to 33% in Kukkia. Accordingly, the annual maximum biomass of littoral macrophytes during late summer varied from 13% to 4% of the total C pool in the first three lakes, but in the larger lowland lakes the percentage of macrophytes was almost insignificant (Table 4). [24] The areal sediment C store correlated positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment and lake water TOC and Fe concentrations but negatively with lake area and the ratio between lake area to catchment area (LA/CA) (Table 7). The TOC concentration of the water correlated negatively with the size of the lakes and with LA/CA, and positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment. 3.2. Carbon Fluxes [25] The annual TOC loads into the lakes increased by 40–210% in the wet year 1998 compared with the dry year 1997 (Figure 2). The increased runoff in 1998 (average runoff in 1998 and 1997 was 9.03 L s⁻¹ km⁻² and 5.04 L s⁻¹ km⁻², respectively) was the main determinant for the higher loads, whereas the higher concentrations of TOC in river water in summer 1998 (average 14.7 mg C L⁻¹) compared with those in 1997 (average 10.8 mg C L⁻¹) played a minor role. During the wet year TOC inflow was higher than outflow in all the lakes, but during the dry year in the two uppermost lakes TOC loss by outflow exceeded that coming by inflow. The DIC loads were also higher in the wet year but the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year in all the lakes (average in the dry year 0.22 and in the wet year 0.14). [26] The annual input of C by the net production of macrophytes was always small compared with the C input to the lake by runoff. The net production of macrophytes was lower than the estimated net primary production by phytoplankton in each lake (Table 6). With the exception of the uppermost headwater lake during the dry year, C input from the catchment exceeded the autochthonously produced C in the lakes (Figure 4). [27] The high summer precipitation generally increased the C fluxes in the lakes (Figure 2 and Table 6). Hydrological import and export of TOC dominated the carbon fluxes especially in the two small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios (Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3)) in the middle of the chain (Table 6 and Figure 4). Atmospheric emissions were highest in the three uppermost lakes during the wet year (79–86 g C m⁻² a⁻¹). However, throughout the lake chain, the efflux of CO₂ into the atmosphere was not significantly correlated with the TOC input (Table 7). [28] In the uppermost headwater lake (Valkea-Kotinen (1)) the average long-term sediment deposition rate was 0.14 mm yr⁻¹ while in the small drainage lakes (Alinen Rautjärvi (2), Ekojärvi (3)) and in the large Kuohijärvi (4) the average deposition rate was higher, about 0.20 mm yr⁻¹. In Lake Kukkia (5) the average long-term deposition rate was the lowest, 0.12 mm yr⁻¹. In the uppermost lake the gross sedimentation rate of C was 7, eightfold compared with the average long-term accumulation rate in the sediment. The short-term gross sedimentation rates of C and Fe were positively correlated in the uppermost lake (Figure 3a). Throughout the lake chain the long-term net sedimentation of C was also positively correlated with Fe and TOC concentrations of the water column (Figure 3b). The proportion of net sedimentation was low in the lake C budgets; in the uppermost lake it was 3–5% of the annual C output and in the other lakes the proportion was 1–2% (Figure 4). [29] On the landscape scale, the small lakes (area <1 km²) were important in the net accumulation of carbon in the sediments, since they were responsible for 56% of the net C accumulation in all the lakes although they formed only 14% of the entire lake area (Table 8). On the other hand, the large lowland lakes (size class 10–50 km²) played a more important role in the CO₂ emissions. In the dry year, the emissions from these lakes made up 60% of the total C effluxes from all lakes in the area, and during the wet year the proportion was 47%. 4. Discussion [30] In the typical boreal lake chain C fluxes were dominated by the input of allochthonous organic matter from the catchment, especially in small drainage lakes with low LA/CA ratio (Figure 4). Although the sediments formed the most important carbon pool (>98%) in the lakes of all size classes, the average Holocene net accumulation rate of C was very small compared with that evaded as CO₂ to atmosphere. This indicates effective mineralization of the organic C within the lake chain. On the landscape scale, small lakes played more important role in long-term C accumulation in the sediments than the large ones, which were more important as emitters of atmospheric CO₂. As hypothesized, the hydrological conditions were important drivers of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year (Table 6 and Figure 4). Influence of Lake Size, Position, and Catchment Characteristics [31] In the uppermost lake the mean long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment was only about 13–14% of the recent annual gross sedimentation rate, indicating that the bulk of the organic C produced in the lake and received from the catchment is mineralized in sediment respiration. In a time series of varved sediments from a lake in Sweden, Gälman et al. [2008] observed that 20% of the annually deposited C in the sediment was lost within 5 years, after which the C loss rate decreased. Sobek et al. [2009] showed that C burial efficiency in lake sediments is negatively related to oxygen exposure time. In our study lakes, the lowest areal pools of C in the sediment were found in the two largest lakes (Table 4), in which the water column is oxic throughout the year. [32] In our study the sediment C pool estimates represent average accumulation during the whole Holocene period, which presumably underestimates the recent net accumulation rates; increasing human impact in the catchments generally results in increasing accumulation rates [e.g., Einsele et al., 2001]. In our study lakes, the human impact has been modest in the two uppermost lakes and more intensive in the catchments of the large lakes. Agriculture in the catchment promotes erosion, leading to increased mass accumulation rates, but to lower organic matter content [Kortelainen et al., 2004], as also found in the studied lake chain. The proportion of TOC in the lake water C pool decreased along the lake chain, while the proportion of DIC increased indicating mineralization of allochthonous C within the lake chain. This is also attributable to the increasing proportion of agriculture in the catchments. The proportion of DIC in the lake water total C is typically greater in lakes surrounded by agricultural land than in lakes in forested or peatland-rich areas [Oh and Raymond, 2006; Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. [33] We found that the lake water Fe content was a very good predictor for the pool and long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment. Although we used mean chemical composition of the lake water during the recent 20 years, the differences in the analyzed Fe contents of the lake waters (Table 2) presumably do not reflect only the recent Fe leaching from the catchment. Our observation of the significant correlation between gross sedimentation of POC and Fe in Valkea-Kotinen is in accordance with the results of Jonsson [1997] from the humic lake Örträsket (northern Sweden), where the gross sedimentation of organic C and amorphous Fe oxides were strongly correlated. [34] Lakes with long residence times (>1 year) and high LA/CA ratios typically showed lower TOC and DIC inputs from the catchment and atmospheric emissions formed the greatest output pathway for C, irrespective of the lake size or its position in the chain (Table 6 and Figure 4). The riverine inflow and outflow remarkably influenced the annual C budget of the two middlemost, relatively small drainage lakes with large catchments generating short residence times of only a few months. [35] Upstream lakes decrease the quantity of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in streams [Larson et al., 2007] and lakes [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993; Rantakari et al., 2004] and also decrease riverine TOC loads [e.g., Mattsson et al., 2005]. In our study, the proportion of lakes in the catchments did not affect the in-lake TOC concentrations, but decreased both the TOC inflow and the outflow (Table 7). In our study lakes the TOC concentrations correlated negatively with the lake area and the LA/CA ratio, but positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchments; the latter has been shown in several studies in the Boreal Zone [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993]. [36] The size of the lake also affects the emissions as the annual evasion of CO₂ increases toward the smaller size classes. In 177 randomly selected lakes in Finland the average value of CO₂ emissions varied from 37 g C m⁻² in the largest lakes (between 10 and 100 km²) to 102 g C m⁻² in the smallest lakes (<0.1 km²) [Kortelainen et al., 2006b]. The two middlemost lakes in our lake chain showed emission of the same range, while the emissions of both the uppermost and the lowest lakes were lower than the average size class values in the study by Kortelainen et al. [2006b]. [37] The partition and the actual values of different C pools and fluxes in the three smallest lakes of the chain mostly agreed with the ones reported from the small, boreal, humic Lake Friksjön [Sobek et al., 2006], with the most noticeable difference being the smaller role of macrophytes in our lakes. The areal sediment C pool in Lake Friksjön was lower than that in our small lakes, but remarkably higher than that of the two large lakes in our study. The C pools of large lakes also differed from Lake Friksjön in having higher proportions of DIC in the water column. Our results on the riverine C influx as the major regulator of the lake chain C budget might represent various vegetation zones and soils, since Finlay et al. [2010] had similar results in the hard water lake chain. Although inorganic C accounted for the highest proportion of the C budget in the hard water lake chain and the total C sedimentation was higher, the bulk density of the sediments as well as the total C content were similar in both studies. On the landscape scale, our study emphasizes not only the role of small lakes (<1 km²) in C accumulation in the sediments, as also observed by Kortelainen et al. [2004], but also the role of large lakes (>10 km²) as intensive sites of organic C mineralization and emitters as atmospheric CO₂. 4.2. Influence of Hydrological Conditions [38] The hydrology was an important driver of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year. This situation was comparable to tundra ponds, where the hydrological pathways acted as biogeochemical pathways for C during periods of high runoff [Macrae et al., 2004]. In addition to the rapid transport of C out of the catchments, the TOC concentrations in the lakes were also higher in the rainy year, the pattern which was shown in Lake Valkeakotinen by Arvola et al. [2010]. The C budgets of the lakes were negative in the dry year (1997), presumably indicating losses of C that had been formerly accumulated in the lakes. During the wet year, the three lakes along the chain acted as sinks of C, probably replacing the lake water C pool that had been decreasing during the preceding dry year. The output of C in the uppermost lake clearly dominated over the input, as was also noted in a small nearby lake by Arvola et al. [1990]. This may have been due to the difficulties in determining the amount of the C input from the catchment in the small lakes, and especially in lakes without inlets. Thus, our presumption of groundwater being an insignificant source of C may also have been wrong in Lake Valkeakotinen, since a strong groundwater signature in aquatic \( pCO_2 \) has been found in many lakes and streams in Sweden [Humborg et al., 2010]. [39] During the rainy year, the CO₂ emissions were higher than during the dry year in the three smallest upstream lakes. Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005] also found a close connection between annual CO₂ emission and precipitation in large Finnish lakes, and suggested that during periods of high precipitation more organic C produced in the terrestrial ecosystem is transported to the lakes and decomposed. They also emphasized the importance of the weather conditions of the previous autumn contributing to the delay between heavy rainfall in the autumn and increasing CO₂ concentrations in the large lakes in winter. This may have influenced our largest study lakes, Kuhohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), which have long residence times and large water volume. In these two lakes, the CO₂ emissions were higher during the dry year. On the other hand, the water temperatures of all the study lakes were higher during the dry year (Table 3), which may also have impacted the CO₂ fluxes to the atmosphere. Kosten et al. [2010] found that the \( pCO_2 \) closely followed the temperature in 82 South American lakes with wide ranges in DOC concentrations, suggesting an increase in temperature-dependent mineralization of DOC and larger lacustrine CO₂ emissions due to climate warming. The in-lake processes presumably had greater influence on the C fluxes in the large lakes of our study, while in the small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios, the allochthonous matter dominated. In the river input to all our lakes the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year. Thus the higher increase in concentrations of inorganic compared with organic C during the dry year was a characteristic of the allochthonous input. Not all the CO₂ in the lake results from the in-lake processes, since part of the DIC transported from the catchment is emitted directly from the lake to the atmosphere [Ojala et al., 2011]. Overall, the retention of C in the study lakes ((sedimentation + atmospheric emission)/C input) was more efficient in the dry year. This was presumably related to the longer hydraulic residence time during the dry year, providing longer time periods for sedimentation as well as for the biogeochemical and physical mineralization processes. [40] The increasing frequency of heavy precipitation events and wet/dry periods may further strengthen the variability in timing and magnitude of C loads [e.g., Hongve et al., 2004; Erlandsson et al., 2008]. Naden et al. [2010] showed that the future projection (for years 2071–2100) for the Mustajoki River, situated close the study area, includes a 7% increase in annual mean DOC concentrations and a 16% increase in annual mean DOC load. Our results emphasize the role of terrestrial signals and underline climate as the major driver of ecosystem C balances. Peatland C sequestration rates are highly sensitive even to minor climatic fluctuations [Yu et al., 2003], with wet periods correlating rapidly with peat accumulation. Similarly, the soil organic C pool in Nordic forest soils increases with both mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation [Callesen et al., 2003]. There will presumably be variation in the response of lakes to climatic drivers, depending on the characteristics of the lakes (e.g., size, morphology and LA/CA ratios) as well as on the properties of their catchments. 5. Conclusions [41] Boreal lakes are important conduits of terrestrially fixed C to the atmosphere. Over the long-term and on the landscape scale, they are also important sinks of C. The sediments of the uppermost headwater lakes are important storages of organic C, and in our boreal lakes Fe played an important role in C accumulation. [42] The lakes in the chain may play different roles in C transport, processing and storage. In the upstream lakes with low LA/CA ratios, the C budget is strongly controlled by TOC inflow and outflow. In the large lowland lakes the partition can be different between the components of the C budget: while the impact of riverine transport is lower, the emissions to the atmosphere play greater role in the C budget. [43] We have also shown that freshwater C budgets, including all major pools and fluxes, show highly variable patterns during dry and wet years. In our study, precipitation was an important driver for C balance in all these boreal lakes. Changing climate can thus greatly modify the role of lakes in landscape C balances. [44] Acknowledgments. Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison E. Einola,1 M. Rantakari,2 P. Kankaala,3 P. Kortelainen,2 A. Ojala,4 H. Pajunen,5 S. Mäkelä,1 and L. Arvola1 Received 23 December 2010; revised 6 May 2011; accepted 18 May 2011; published 27 July 2011. [1] Lakes play an important role in catchment carbon (C) balances. However, the role of lakes in landscape C cycling in changing climate is highly uncertain. We studied C pools in a chain of five boreal lakes and compared the C fluxes during a wet and a dry year. The included pools were dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) in lake water, as well as C pools in littoral macrophytes and lake sediments. The estimated C fluxes consisted of hydrological input and output of DIC and TOC, emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere, DIC incorporated as organic carbon in primary production of phytoplankton and littoral macrophytes, and sedimentation of C. The riverine input of C into the lakes increased remarkably (40–210%) in the year with high precipitation. Simultaneously, there was a clear increase in the flux of CO2 to the atmosphere from the three small uppermost lakes, whereas in two large lowland lakes the CO2 fluxes were higher during the warm dry year. On the landscape scale, the role of small lakes (area <1 km2) was emphasized in net C accumulation, whereas the large lowland lakes released more CO2 to the atmosphere. In parallel, the concentration of TOC in the water column decreased downstream the lake chain whereas DIC increased. The largest pool of C (>98%) in all the lakes was in the sediment. Sediment C store, calculated relative to the lake area, was positively correlated with lake water TOC (r2 = 0.93, P < 0.05) and Fe (r2 = 0.96, P < 0.05) concentrations. Lake water Fe content was also a good predictor for the long-term accumulation (r2 = 0.99, P < 0.01), as well as gross sedimentation rate of organic carbon (r2 = 0.48, P < 0.01). Citation: Einola, E., M. Rantakari, P. Kankaala, P. Kortelainen, A. Ojala, H. Pajunen, S. Mäkelä, and L. Arvola (2011), Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison, J. Geophys. Res., 116, G03009, doi:10.1029/2010JG001636. 1. Introduction [2] Although freshwater lakes and rivers cover a small area of the earth’s surface, their role in regional carbon (C) budgets and also in global C cycling is much more pronounced than expected only by their area. Rivers and lakes transport, mineralize and accumulate significant amounts of terrestrially fixed C and exchange inorganic C between water-air interfaces [e.g., del Giorgio and Peters, 1994; Kortelainen et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Downing, 2010]. [3] The riverine transport of organic carbon plays an important role in functioning of boreal lakes; e.g., in humic lakes, common in the Boreal Zone, terrestrial carbon input can be much higher than in-lake production [Sarvala et al., 1981; Arvola et al., 1990; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the majority of lakes and rivers are net heterotrophic, i.e., the biological C mineralization exceeds primary production [Alin and Johnson, 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009]. Moreover, the recent trend of increasing concentrations of colored organic substances in many northern lakes and rivers [e.g., Monteith et al., 2007; Lepistö et al., 2008] may further strengthen heterotrophy in these freshwater ecosystems because of decreasing light availability for primary producers. [4] In the Boreal Zone, the concentration of total organic carbon (TOC) in lakes and the export of TOC from catchments are strongly related to the coverage of peatlands [Kortelainen, 1993; Kortelainen et al., 2006a] and coniferous forests in the catchment area [Mattsson et al., 2003; Humborg et al., 2004]. Most (>80%) of the organic matter exported from the catchments is in dissolved form [Wetzel, 2001]. A small proportion of the dissolved organic matter (DOM) may aggregate with metals (amorphous iron and aluminum) [Jonsson, 1997] and/or flocculate with bacteria [von Wachenfeldt et al., 2009], contributing to C accumulation in bottom sediments. In small boreal headwater streams as well as large rivers flowing to the Figure 1. Map of the study area showing the study lakes, the rivers connecting them, and the vegetation type and land use of each study lake. Thick arrows indicate the main inlets of rivers running to and from the study lakes. Baltic Sea, the proportion of particulate organic carbon (POC) of TOC is <5% [Kortelainen et al., 2006a; Mattsson et al., 2005]. The contribution of living material is low especially in running waters, where bacteria, algae, protozoa and larger zooplankton may comprise only about 1% of the TOC [Arvola and Nurmesniemi, 2000]. [5] Most lakes in the Boreal Zone are connected by streams as chains that can differ considerably in their morphology and physical and chemical characteristics. The residence time of water in each basin, defined by the catchment setting and lake morphology, together with the average annual runoff, may be crucial for biogeochemical processing of the organic matter [cf. Algesten et al., 2004], i.e., for microbial decomposition in the water column and in the sediment as well as ultraviolet (UV) irradiance-induced breakdown in the uppermost water layer [Vähätalo et al., 2000; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the residence time influences the quantity and quality of organic matter flowing downstream, and the proportion of organic C released as carbon dioxide (CO_2) and methane (CH_4), or stored in the bottom sediments. Mattsson et al. [2005] showed that proportion of lake area in the upper catchment significantly reduced TOC transport by the large Finnish rivers to the coast. Thus, upstream lakes may be intensive sites for DOM processing, which decreases the export of C downstream [Rasmussen et al., 1989; Kortelainen, 1993; Larson et al., 2007]. [6] Climate change scenarios predict increasing precipitation and temperature for many areas in the Boreal Zone, resulting in major changes in seasonal runoff patterns in northern catchments [e.g., Andréasson et al., 2004], including increasing frequency of extreme weather conditions and thus also extremes in hydrology [e.g., Christensen and Christensen, 2003]. Since hydrology is a major driver of the variability of water C concentrations on the catchment scale [e.g., Erlandsson et al., 2008], the interannual variations in C budgets of individual lakes may be considerable [Arvola et al., 1990]. Although carbon budgets for single lakes [e.g., Arvola et al., 1990; Sobek et al., 2006] and also for a chain of hard-water lakes [Finlay et al., 2010] have been studied, C budgets for a chain of boreal lakes in climatically different years have remained unknown. [7] The aim of our study was to (1) estimate C pools (store in the sediment and in the water column and biomass of primary producers) in a chain of five boreal lakes consisting of one small headwater lake, two small drainage lakes, and two large downstream lakes and to (2) compare C fluxes (net primary production, inflow, outflow, sedimentation, and atmospheric efflux) between a dry and a rainy year within this Table 1. Material and Methods [8] The five study lakes (areal range 0.036–44 km2), situated in the southern Boreal Zone in Finland were numbered by their order in the chain: (1) Valkea-Kotinen, (2) Alinen Rautjärvi, (3) Ekojärvi, (4) Kuohijärvi, and (5) Kukkia (Figure 1). The area deglaciated about 11,500 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. The uppermost and the smallest lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), was isolated immediately after deglaciation, while the other lakes were submerged by waters of the ancient Baltic Sea. Since the postglacial land uplift was more rapid than the rise of sea level, the land area expanded and new lakes became isolated. Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) was isolated about 11,400 years ago, Lake Ekojärvi (3) about 9800 years ago and the largest lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) about 9700 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. [9] The Precambrian bedrock in the area consists of veined gneiss with granodiorite occurring around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and close to Lake Kuohijärvi (4). The soil is mostly moraine but there is gravel and sand around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and the river draining it, while clay areas partly surround lakes Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5). Coniferous forests with Norway Spruce (Picea abies [L.] H. Karst.) and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) cover 65–80% and peatlands less than 20% of the catchment areas of each lake (Figure 1). Except for the first lake of the chain, Valkea-Kotinen, which is situated in a nature reserve area, the human impact on the catchments has been quite intense, because of a >150 year long history of forestry and related activities, including draining of wetlands. Some agriculture is also practiced, predominantly in the lowland areas, but the proportion of agricultural land in the catchment does not exceed 5% around any of the studied lakes. The local names suggest that historically the local people have utilized lake iron (e.g., Alinen Rautjärvi = Lower Iron Lake). The lakes vary in their morphological characteristics (Table 1), and the lake area to catchment area ratio (LA/CA) is significantly higher in the two largest lowland lakes than in the first three lakes in the chain. The concentrations of TOC, total phosphorus, total nitrogen and chlorophyll \( a \) are higher in the small upstream lakes than in the largest lowland lakes (Table 2). In the uppermost lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), the hypolimnion is anoxic during winter and summer stratification. In Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3), the hypolimnetic anoxia during the stratification periods is occasional, whereas in Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) the entire water column is oxic throughout the year. The larger lakes are covered by ice usually from late November to late April and the smaller ones from late October or early November to early May. [10] The annual long-term (1987–2007) average precipitation in the area is 632 mm (Finnish Meteorological Institute). The highest runoff peaks are generally observed in spring after snowmelt. The runoff can also peak during autumn, when precipitation is generally higher than in summer and the evapotranspiration is small. However, high runoffs can also occur during summer, as in 1998, if the precipitation is high and the antecedent soil conditions are wet. [11] The annual precipitation during 1997 was 5% lower and during 1998 22% higher than the average (Table 3), with the most distinguishable difference in the precipitation patterns observed in summer: in 1997 the summer precipitation was 10% lower than the long-term average, while in 1998 it was 70% higher than the average. The differences in precipitation were reflected in the water residence time of the lakes. There was also a difference of almost 2°C between the daily average air temperatures during the two summers (Table 3). For the fifth lake in the chain (Kukkia) the data set was not sufficient for budget calculations. [13] In the three small uppermost lakes the sediment volume was estimated on the basis of coring and survey on site. The interface between organic sediment (gyttja, clay gyttja or gyttja clay) and the underlying mineral soil (till, sand, silt or clay) was interpreted to indicate lake isolation. The thickness of the lake sediment bed was determined at seven sites in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), 35 sites in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and 48 sites in Lake Ekojärvi (3). In the largest lowland lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), echo sounding was used to estimate the volume of the lake sediment bed with survey transects of 15 and 31 km, respectively. In these transects the proportion of accumulation bottom was measured. This proportion and the total lake area were used to estimate the accumulation area, which was multiplied with the average thickness to obtain the sediment volume. For the analysis of sediment density and C content, a sediment core was collected from each lake. The cores extended from the surface of the sediment bed to the depth of lake isolation. In the laboratory the cores were opened and their stratigraphy determined. The cores were divided into samples and a total of 104 samples were analyzed. The sample treatment and laboratory methods are thoroughly described by Pajunen et al. [2000]. The amount of total dry matter is based on sediment volume and average density and the amount of C on the amount of total dry matter and average C content. The average C store (g C m⁻²) was divided by the age of the lake to obtain the average Holocene accumulation rates (g C m⁻² yr⁻¹). [14] The gross sedimentation rate was measured only in the uppermost lake as part of a long-term monitoring program [cf. Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Sedimenting material was collected with three acrylic plastic tubes (length 45 cm, diameter 5 cm) placed below the epilimnion at a depth of 4 m. During the ice-free period, material settled in the tubes was removed every 2 weeks, dried, weighed and analyzed for C content with a high-temperature combustion method [Salonen, 1979]. For annual estimates of gross sedimentation we used the results from the under ice measurements, conducted in 1995 and 1996 with exactly the same methods as during the open water period but using a 3 week collection period. In addition to C, the Fe content of the gross sedimentation was measured during one open water season (in 2000) with a Varian AAS (Varian Inc. Palo Alto, Calif., United States). [15] The samples for TOC and DIC analyses of the water column were taken at 0.2–05 m depth in rivers and at 1 m depth in the lakes. The sampling frequency in the rivers was primarily once a month during the open water season (May–November) and once in winter (early April). The uppermost lake (Valkea-Kotinen) was sampled 24 times during the both years. The other lakes in the chain were sampled 1–4 times in 1997 and four times in 1998 (late winter, spring, summer, and autumnal mixing). For the missing data for spring 1997 in Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Kukkia (5), and for winter, spring and autumn 1997 in Kuohijärvi (4) the values for the corresponding season of 1998 were used. [16] The TOC concentration of the water was analyzed with a Shimadzu TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corp. Kyoto, Japan). For some occasions (about half of the river samples), water color values (platinum reference) were available instead of TOC. However, TOC was linearly related to water color in the samples taken from the study rivers and the lakes, and the missing TOC values were estimated with the regression equation: TOC [mg C L⁻¹] = 0.0408 * water color [mg Pt L⁻¹] + 5.29 (r² = 0.84, P < 0.05, n = 110). The DIC concentrations were estimated from the measured alkalinity values with the regression equation DIC [μmol L⁻¹] = 0.996 * Alkalinity [μeq L⁻¹] + 19.3, r² = 0.95, n = 874, obtained from measurements in randomly selected Finnish soft water lakes with similar range of alkalinity [Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. Temperature and oxygen concentration in the water column of the lakes was measured with YSI 55 (Yellow Springs Instruments) combined probe (accuracy ±0.3°C, ±0.3 mg O₂ L⁻¹). [17] The discharge from each subcatchment was estimated using measured daily runoff data for the years 1997 and 1998 (Finnish Environment Institute, OIVA service on environment and geographic information, 17 March 2010) from the rivers Mustajoki and Haarajoki, both situated less than 30 km from the study sites and having land use characteristics very similar to the study lakes, assuming that the discharge from each subcatchment was related to its area. The TOC and DIC input and output were calculated by multiplying the monthly discharge (the sum of measured daily values) at the inflows and outflows with the TOC and DIC concentration during the respective period in the rivers between the lakes. We assumed that the input of C by groundwater was insignificant to the C fluxes in this flat landscape. [18] Emissions of CO\(_2\) from the lakes were calculated using the equation by Cole and Caraco [1998], in which the CO\(_2\) saturation in the surface water was compared with the equilibrium value. The CO\(_2\) concentrations were calculated from the available open water DIC and pH results of each lakes, with correction for water temperature [Stumm and Morgan, 1970; Butler, 1982; Kling et al., 1992]. Partial pressure of CO\(_2\) (\(p\)CO\(_2\)) was calculated from the CO\(_2\) concentrations, using Henry’s law constants corrected for temperature and atmospheric pressure [Plummer and Busenberg, 1982]. The equilibrium CO\(_2\) concentration in the lake water was calculated using the elevation of the lake and Henry’s law constants, assuming an atmospheric mixing ratio of 361 ppm by volume (ppmv) for 1996 and an annual increase of 1.5 ppmv y\(^{-1}\) by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [2001], equaling the values measured in Finland [e.g., Kulmala et al., 2000]. The piston velocity of CO\(_2\) was obtained by first determining the piston velocity of SF\(_6\), using the empirical relationship between the piston velocity of SF\(_6\) normalized to a Schmidt number of 600 and the wind speed at a height of 10 m [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and then calculating the Schmidt number for CO\(_2\), using empirical third-order polynomial fits to temperature [Jähne et al., 1987]. The wind speed was assumed to be 3 m s\(^{-1}\), which is the average long-term open water period wind speed for inland measurement stations in Finland [Leinonen, 2000]. All the equations for calculations of the CO\(_2\) emissions are presented by Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005]. Additional data for the range of CO\(_2\) emissions from the lakes, estimated for the year 2000 (annual precipitation 634 mm, summer precipitation 266 mm) on the basis of four measurements in three of the lakes, are also presented in the Table 6. The emissions of CH\(_4\) from some of the study lakes were minor compared to CO\(_2\) efflux and have been presented elsewhere [Kankaala et al., 2005, 2006; Bergström et al., 2007]. The measured atmospheric deposition of C in the area was 1 g C m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\) [Kortelainen et al., 2006a]. [19] The annual production of phytoplankton in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) was measured weekly during the open water season in situ using the \(^{14}\)C method [Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Since the incubation time was 24 h, the measurements resulted in net primary productivity values (NPP). For the other lakes, the range of NPP of phytoplankton was estimated using data obtained in previous measurements in neighboring lakes [Ilmavirta and Kotimaa, 1974; Arvola 1983, 1984; Arvola et al., 1999], with the same types of trophic status and chemical and physical properties as in the study lakes. The areas covered by different macrophyte species were mapped in 1997–2000. The macrophyte C pool was estimated as a seasonal maximum biomass (g dry weight (DW) m\(^{-2}\)) converted to C by a factor 0.38 [Duarte, 1992], obtained from the data for stands of the dominant species in the three uppermost lakes [Keskitalo and Heitto, 1996; Kankaala et al., 2003, 2005]. The NPP of macrophytes was estimated to be twofold the seasonal maximum biomass of all the stands [Westlake, 1982]. [20] We also made a regional, landscape-scale estimate of CO\(_2\) emissions and sediment net C accumulation of all the lakes in the cumulative catchment area of the lake chain. The results of the five lakes studied were upscaled for the respective lake size classes (area <0.1, 0.1–1, 1–10 and 10–50 km\(^2\)) throughout the area. The areal results (g C m\(^{-2}\)) of the largest size class were also applied to the size class 1–10 km, because none of the lakes in the chain studied belonged to that size class. [21] The statistical relationships between the different variables in the data set were calculated as Pearson’s linear correlations (Pearson’s r). The variables with skewed distributions were first log-transformed to approach normality. The analyses were done with PASW (SPSS) Statistics 17.0 software. 3. Results 3.1. Carbon Pools [22] In all the lakes, >98% of C was in the sediments (Table 4). The proportion of organic matter (Table 4) in the sediments decreased, while the density of the lake sediment bed increased downstream of the lake chain. In Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), the average sediment density was 0.056 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) 0.14 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lakes Ekojärvi (3) and Kuohijärvi (4) about 0.25 g cm\(^{-3}\) and in Lake Kukkia (5) 0.35 g cm\(^{-3}\). In the uppermost lake, the average thickness of the sediment bed (computed for the entire lake area) was 1.6 m, while in the succeeding three lakes the bed was around 2 m thick and in the lowermost lake only 1.2 m thick. [23] The water column TOC, including phytoplankton, constituted 95% of the lake water C pool in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) (Table 4). The proportion of TOC decreased along the lake chain to 68% in Kuohijärvi (4) and to 67% in Kukkia (5) while the proportion of DIC increased from 5% in Valkea-Kotinen to 33% in Kukkia.
