Accordingly, the annual maximum biomass of littoral macrophytes during late summer varied from 13% to 4% of the total C pool in the first three lakes, but in the larger lowland lakes the percentage of macrophytes was almost insignificant (Table 4). [24] The areal sediment C store correlated positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment and lake water TOC and Fe concentrations but negatively with lake area and the ratio between lake area to catchment area (LA/CA) (Table 7). The TOC concentration of the water correlated negatively with the size of the lakes and with LA/CA, and positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment. 3.2. Carbon Fluxes [25] The annual TOC loads into the lakes increased by 40–210% in the wet year 1998 compared with the dry year 1997 (Figure 2). The increased runoff in 1998 (average runoff in 1998 and 1997 was 9.03 L s⁻¹ km⁻² and 5.04 L s⁻¹ km⁻², respectively) was the main determinant for the higher loads, whereas the higher concentrations of TOC in river water in summer 1998 (average 14.7 mg C L⁻¹) compared with those in 1997 (average 10.8 mg C L⁻¹) played a minor role. During the wet year TOC inflow was higher than outflow in all the lakes, but during the dry year in the two uppermost lakes TOC loss by outflow exceeded that coming by inflow. The DIC loads were also higher in the wet year but the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year in all the lakes (average in the dry year 0.22 and in the wet year 0.14). [26] The annual input of C by the net production of macrophytes was always small compared with the C input to the lake by runoff. The net production of macrophytes was lower than the estimated net primary production by phytoplankton in each lake (Table 6). With the exception of the uppermost headwater lake during the dry year, C input from the catchment exceeded the autochthonously produced C in the lakes (Figure 4). [27] The high summer precipitation generally increased the C fluxes in the lakes (Figure 2 and Table 6). Hydrological import and export of TOC dominated the carbon fluxes especially in the two small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios (Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3)) in the middle of the chain (Table 6 and Figure 4). Atmospheric emissions were highest in the three uppermost lakes during the wet year (79–86 g C m⁻² a⁻¹). However, throughout the lake chain, the efflux of CO₂ into the atmosphere was not significantly correlated with the TOC input (Table 7). [28] In the uppermost headwater lake (Valkea-Kotinen (1)) the average long-term sediment deposition rate was 0.14 mm yr⁻¹ while in the small drainage lakes (Alinen Rautjärvi (2), Ekojärvi (3)) and in the large Kuohijärvi (4) the average deposition rate was higher, about 0.20 mm yr⁻¹. In Lake Kukkia (5) the average long-term deposition rate was the lowest, 0.12 mm yr⁻¹. In the uppermost lake the gross sedimentation rate of C was 7, eightfold compared with the average long-term accumulation rate in the sediment. The short-term gross sedimentation rates of C and Fe were positively correlated in the uppermost lake (Figure 3a). Throughout the lake chain the long-term net sedimentation of C was also positively correlated with Fe and TOC concentrations of the water column (Figure 3b). The proportion of net sedimentation was low in the lake C budgets; in the uppermost lake it was 3–5% of the annual C output and in the other lakes the proportion was 1–2% (Figure 4). [29] On the landscape scale, the small lakes (area <1 km²) were important in the net accumulation of carbon in the sediments, since they were responsible for 56% of the net C accumulation in all the lakes although they formed only 14% of the entire lake area (Table 8). On the other hand, the large lowland lakes (size class 10–50 km²) played a more important role in the CO₂ emissions. In the dry year, the emissions from these lakes made up 60% of the total C effluxes from all lakes in the area, and during the wet year the proportion was 47%. 4. Discussion [30] In the typical boreal lake chain C fluxes were dominated by the input of allochthonous organic matter from the catchment, especially in small drainage lakes with low LA/CA ratio (Figure 4). Although the sediments formed the most important carbon pool (>98%) in the lakes of all size classes, the average Holocene net accumulation rate of C was very small compared with that evaded as CO₂ to atmosphere. This indicates effective mineralization of the organic C within the lake chain. On the landscape scale, small lakes played more important role in long-term C accumulation in the sediments than the large ones, which were more important as emitters of atmospheric CO₂. As hypothesized, the hydrological conditions were important drivers of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year (Table 6 and Figure 4). Influence of Lake Size, Position, and Catchment Characteristics [31] In the uppermost lake the mean long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment was only about 13–14% of the recent annual gross sedimentation rate, indicating that the bulk of the organic C produced in the lake and received from the catchment is mineralized in sediment respiration. In a time series of varved sediments from a lake in Sweden, Gälman et al. [2008] observed that 20% of the annually deposited C in the sediment was lost within 5 years, after which the C loss rate decreased. Sobek et al. [2009] showed that C burial efficiency in lake sediments is negatively related to oxygen exposure time. In our study lakes, the lowest areal pools of C in the sediment were found in the two largest lakes (Table 4), in which the water column is oxic throughout the year. [32] In our study the sediment C pool estimates represent average accumulation during the whole Holocene period, which presumably underestimates the recent net accumulation rates; increasing human impact in the catchments generally results in increasing accumulation rates [e.g., Einsele et al., 2001]. In our study lakes, the human impact has been modest in the two uppermost lakes and more intensive in the catchments of the large lakes. Agriculture in the catchment promotes erosion, leading to increased mass accumulation rates, but to lower organic matter content [Kortelainen et al., 2004], as also found in the studied lake chain. The proportion of TOC in the lake water C pool decreased along the lake chain, while the proportion of DIC increased indicating mineralization of allochthonous C within the lake chain. This is also attributable to the increasing proportion of agriculture in the catchments. The proportion of DIC in the lake water total C is typically greater in lakes surrounded by agricultural land than in lakes in forested or peatland-rich areas [Oh and Raymond, 2006; Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. [33] We found that the lake water Fe content was a very good predictor for the pool and long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment. Although we used mean chemical composition of the lake water during the recent 20 years, the differences in the analyzed Fe contents of the lake waters (Table 2) presumably do not reflect only the recent Fe leaching from the catchment. [35] Upstream lakes decrease the quantity of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in streams [Larson et al., 2007] and lakes [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993; Rantakari et al., 2004] and also decrease riverine TOC loads [e.g., Mattsson et al., 2005]. In our study, the proportion of lakes in the catchments did not affect the in-lake TOC concentrations, but decreased both the TOC inflow and the outflow (Table 7). In our study lakes the TOC concentrations correlated negatively with the lake area and the LA/CA ratio, but positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchments; the latter has been shown in several studies in the Boreal Zone [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993]. [36] The size of the lake also affects the emissions as the annual evasion of CO₂ increases toward the smaller size classes. In 177 randomly selected lakes in Finland the average value of CO₂ emissions varied from 37 g C m⁻² in the largest lakes (between 10 and 100 km²) to 102 g C m⁻² in the smallest lakes (<0.1 km²) [Kortelainen et al., 2006b]. The two middlemost lakes in our lake chain showed emission of the same range, while the emissions of both the uppermost and the lowest lakes were lower than the average size class values in the study by Kortelainen et al. [2006b]. [37] The partition and the actual values of different C pools and fluxes in the three smallest lakes of the chain mostly agreed with the ones reported from the small, boreal, humic Lake Friksjön [Sobek et al., 2006], with the most noticeable difference being the smaller role of macrophytes in our lakes. The areal sediment C pool in Lake Friksjön was lower than that in our small lakes, but remarkably higher than that of the two large lakes in our study. The C pools of large lakes also differed from Lake Friksjön in having higher proportions of DIC in the water column. Our results on the riverine C influx as the major regulator of the lake chain C budget might represent various vegetation zones and soils, since Finlay et al. [2010] had similar results in the hard water lake chain. Although inorganic C accounted for the highest proportion of the C budget in the hard water lake chain and the total C sedimentation was higher, the bulk density of the sediments as well as the total C content were similar in both studies. On the landscape scale, our study emphasizes not only the role of small lakes (<1 km²) in C accumulation in the sediments, as also observed by Kortelainen et al. [2004], but also the role of large lakes (>10 km²) as intensive sites of organic C mineralization and emitters as atmospheric CO₂. 4.2. Influence of Hydrological Conditions [38] The hydrology was an important driver of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year. This situation was comparable to tundra ponds, where the hydrological pathways acted as biogeochemical pathways for C during periods of high runoff [Macrae et al., 2004]. In addition to the rapid transport of C out of the catchments, the TOC concentrations in the lakes were also higher in the rainy year, the pattern which was shown in Lake Valkeakotinen by Arvola et al. [2010]. The C budgets of the lakes were negative in the dry year (1997), presumably indicating losses of C that had been formerly accumulated in the lakes. During the wet year, the three lakes along the chain acted as sinks of C, probably replacing the lake water C pool that had been decreasing during the preceding dry year. The output of C in the uppermost lake clearly dominated over the input, as was also noted in a small nearby lake by Arvola et al. [1990]. This may have been due to the difficulties in determining the amount of the C input from the catchment in the small lakes, and especially in lakes without inlets. Thus, our presumption of groundwater being an insignificant source of C may also have been wrong in Lake Valkeakotinen, since a strong groundwater signature in aquatic \( pCO_2 \) has been found in many lakes and streams in Sweden [Humborg et al., 2010]. [39] During the rainy year, the CO₂ emissions were higher than during the dry year in the three smallest upstream lakes. Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005] also found a close connection between annual CO₂ emission and precipitation in large Finnish lakes, and suggested that during periods of high precipitation more organic C produced in the terrestrial ecosystem is transported to the lakes and decomposed. They also emphasized the importance of the weather conditions of the previous autumn contributing to the delay between heavy rainfall in the autumn and increasing CO₂ concentrations in the large lakes in winter. This may have influenced our largest study lakes, Kuhohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), which have long residence times and large water volume. In these two lakes, the CO₂ emissions were higher during the dry year. On the other hand, the water temperatures of all the study lakes were higher during the dry year (Table 3), which may also have impacted the CO₂ fluxes to the atmosphere. Kosten et al. [2010] found that the \( pCO_2 \) closely followed the temperature in 82 South American lakes with wide ranges in DOC concentrations, suggesting an increase in temperature-dependent mineralization of DOC and larger lacustrine CO₂ emissions due to climate warming. The in-lake processes presumably had greater influence on the C fluxes in the large lakes of our study, while in the small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios, the allochthonous matter dominated. In the river input to all our lakes the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year. Thus the higher increase in concentrations of inorganic compared with organic C during the dry year was a characteristic of the allochthonous input. Not all the CO₂ in the lake results from the in-lake processes, since part of the DIC transported from the catchment is emitted directly from the lake to the atmosphere [Ojala et al., 2011]. Overall, the retention of C in the study lakes ((sedimentation + atmospheric emission)/C input) was more efficient in the dry year. This was presumably related to the longer hydraulic residence time during the dry year, providing longer time periods for sedimentation as well as for the biogeochemical and physical mineralization processes. [40] The increasing frequency of heavy precipitation events and wet/dry periods may further strengthen the variability in timing and magnitude of C loads [e.g., Hongve et al., 2004; Erlandsson et al., 2008]. Naden et al. [2010] showed that the future projection (for years 2071–2100) for the Mustajoki River, situated close the study area, includes a 7% increase in annual mean DOC concentrations and a 16% increase in annual mean DOC load. Our results emphasize the role of terrestrial signals and underline climate as the major driver of ecosystem C balances. Peatland C sequestration rates are highly sensitive even to minor climatic fluctuations [Yu et al., 2003], with wet periods correlating rapidly with peat accumulation. Similarly, the soil organic C pool in Nordic forest soils increases with both mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation [Callesen et al., 2003]. There will presumably be variation in the response of lakes to climatic drivers, depending on the characteristics of the lakes (e.g., size, morphology and LA/CA ratios) as well as on the properties of their catchments. 5. Conclusions [41] Boreal lakes are important conduits of terrestrially fixed C to the atmosphere. Over the long-term and on the landscape scale, they are also important sinks of C. The sediments of the uppermost headwater lakes are important storages of organic C, and in our boreal lakes Fe played an important role in C accumulation. [42] The lakes in the chain may play different roles in C transport, processing and storage. In the upstream lakes with low LA/CA ratios, the C budget is strongly controlled by TOC inflow and outflow. In the large lowland lakes the partition can be different between the components of the C budget: while the impact of riverine transport is lower, the emissions to the atmosphere play greater role in the C budget. [43] We have also shown that freshwater C budgets, including all major pools and fluxes, show highly variable patterns during dry and wet years. In our study, precipitation was an important driver for C balance in all these boreal lakes. Changing climate can thus greatly modify the role of lakes in landscape C balances. [44] Acknowledgments. CRYPTIC TROPHIC CASCADE ALONG A GRADIENT OF LAKE SIZE ALAN J. TESSIER1 AND PAMELA WOODRUFF W. K. Kellogg Biological Station and Department of Zoology, Michigan State University, Hickory Corners, Michigan 49060 USA Abstract. Lake size and depth mediate the strength of interaction between fish and zooplankton. We test whether this variation in zooplanktivory indirectly affects the phytoplankton by comparing 19 lakes that represent two food webs resulting from the absence of piscivores in small, partial-winterkill lakes. Lakes with piscivorous fish are further distinguished by thermal stratification, which provides a refuge for zooplankton to avoid fish predation. We contrasted phytoplankton abundance in these three categories of lakes over six years, using both direct measures of concentration and a growth bioassay that measures phytoplankton from the perspective of a standard grazer (Daphnia). Contrary to expectations, phytoplankton abundance was largely unaffected by trophic structure or the presence of a deep-water refuge. However, grazer growth differed dramatically among the three categories of lakes. Consistent with trophic cascade, increased fish planktivory resulted in more phytoplankton food as measured from the grazer’s perspective. This effect was independent of lake productivity or total abundance and size of phytoplankton. Instead, variation in food quality for grazers was associated with compositional differences in phytoplankton. These results indicate that persistent trophic cascades are more dramatic in the plankton than previously realized but primarily influence composition, rather than biomass. Although cryptic, such top-down effects create functional variation in grazer–resource coupling. Key words: Daphnia growth bioassay; indirect effects; phytoplankton; species sorting; trophic compensation; winterkill; zooplankton refuge. INTRODUCTION Changes at the top of food webs can have cascading effects, but what determines the magnitude and persistence of those effects is poorly understood. Addressing the issue demands that we first define what is meant by “effect” (Schmitz et al. 2000). Recently, Polis et al. (2000) argued for separation of species- and community-level effects of trophic cascade. They reasoned that effects on traits of individual species (e.g., leaf damage) do not hold the same significance for ecosystem processes as changes in community composition or biomass. While a primary concern with community change is reasonable, important differences in food web or trophic interactions need not involve shifts in the distribution of trophic biomass. Nor is it clear that species turnover will serve as a useful estimate of trophic cascade, given that most species are relatively rare. In short, the strength of trophic coupling and food web function may not be predictable from relative changes in biomass or species composition. We suggest a need for studies of trophic effects that quantify the functional consequences of changes in community composition. Of particular interest to trophic cascade theory is whether variation in predation changes the nature of prey–resource coupling. In a three-trophic-level food chain, increased predation weakens the coupling of prey with their resources and typically increases resource biomass. From the perspective of prey, this higher resource availability should increase individual growth and reproductive rates (a functional change). In real food webs, compensatory responses within either the prey or resource trophic levels might mask the cascade effect when measured in terms of biomass. But does compensation of biomass mean that the functional effects on trophic coupling are also diluted? We address this question by quantifying the indirect effect of predators (fish planktivores) on the resources (phytoplankton) of their prey (zooplankton grazers) from two perspectives: biomass and prey growth rate. We rely on prior work (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000) showing that the growth response of a standard Daphnia to different phytoplankton assemblages is broadly representative of growth and reproductive responses of other suspension feeders, the dominant grazers. This allows us to quantify resource availability from the perspective of the grazers in short-term growth bioassays and to compare that to traditional measures of phytoplankton biomass. Our bioassay approach provides a common currency with which to quantify the trophic significance of compositional changes within the phytoplankton. We apply this approach to a study of trophic cascade effects in lakes that naturally differ in intensity of fish planktivory. Fish planktivory is typically stronger in

Large Daphnia that are effective grazers (Mazumder 1994) exist in deep stratified lakes, while smaller grazers dominate in shallow lakes (Tessier and Welser 1991). The significance of zooplankton body size and especially of large Daphnia to grazing impact on phytoplankton is well documented (Carpenter and Kitchell 1993). Therefore, we predicted that at the same level of system productivity shallow lakes should display higher phytoplankton levels than deep lakes. METHODS Lake basins and trophic coupling We chose lakes located in southwestern Michigan, USA, on the basis of size, depth, and thermal stratification so as to achieve a representative sample of two different food webs and three different levels of zooplanktivory (Fig. 1, Table 1). Lakes in our first category have small surface area relative to depth, so they thermally stratify in summer. Consequently, the zooplankton of these “deep-refuge” lakes is dominated by large-bodied Daphnia species that vertically migrate to feed on phytoplankton in the surface waters at night, but refuge in deep waters during the day to avoid fish. Centrarchids are the dominant fish in this and the next category of lake; bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) and pumpkinseed (L. gibbosus) sunfish are the main planktivores, and largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) is the major piscivore (Werner et al. 1977). Lakes in our second category have large surface area relative to their depth and do not thermally stratify in summer. These “shallow” lakes have no refuge for zooplankton to avoid daytime planktivory, so zooplankton suffer a greater risk of predation than in the deep lakes (Tessier et al. 1992, Leibold and Tessier 1998). While not measured in our lakes, biomass of fish (per cubic meter) is generally known to be greater in shallow than in deep lakes (Jeppesen et al. 1997). Consequently, the zooplankton of shallow lakes is composed of a lower biomass of smaller-sized taxa than the big Daphnia of deep lakes (Fig. 1). Lakes in our last category are both shallow and small in water volume. Low oxygen under the ice in winter is a recurring stress in these lakes and results in partial winterkills (Greenbank 1945), to which largemouth bass is particularly sensitive (Moore 1942). Hence, lakes in this category lack strong piscivory, and the fish community is composed of high densities of efficient planktivores (Tonn and Magnuson 1982). Reflecting this “high planktivory,” the grazer assemblage is dominated by the smallest of cladocerans and copepods, and rotifers dominate the zooplankton in these lakes (Hall and Ellinger 1989, Mittelbach et al. 1995; Fig. 1). Hence, the three categories of lakes represent a gradient of intensity of fish planktivory; lowest in the deep-refuge lakes, intermediate in the shallow lakes, and highest in the partial winterkill lakes. We examined seven deep-refuge lakes, six shallow lakes, and six high-planktivory lakes over a period of 6 yr (Table 1). Most lakes were sampled in multiple years (>2 yr per lake) and on multiple dates throughout the summer (June–September). We also sampled each lake during the spring turnover and collected pelagic water for determination of total phosphorus. Phytoplankton-eston abundance We collected water from the pelagic zone, ~0.5 m below the lake surface between 0900 and 1300. Sam- ples were screened through 62-μm Nitex (Tetko, Elmsford, New York, USA) and then filtered on GF/F glass fiber filters (Whatman, Clifton, New Jersey, USA) for analysis of chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate matter. Chlorophyll \( a \) was extracted overnight in cold, 95% ethanol and measured using narrow band fluorometry. Ash-free dry mass of the seston was determined after muffling at 500°C and converted to carbon using a calibration based on C analysis using a Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer (C. E. Instruments, Milan, Italy; A. J. Tessier, unpublished data). During summer of 1999 we sampled all lakes for a size-fractionation of chlorophyll \( a \) (<3, <15, <35, <62, <100 μm, and total) using Nitex screens except for the <3-μm fraction, which was achieved by filtration through Whatman GF/D glass fiber filters. Growth bioassay As a direct estimate of phytoplankton food value for zooplankton, we conducted growth rate bioassays on the same dates that we sampled chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon. The bioassays measured juvenile specific growth rate of a clone of *D. pulex-pulicaria* fed seston from the lake but under standard laboratory conditions. Bioassay results are representative of growth and reproduction responses of all common daphniid species in our region (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000). Bioassays start with neonates (<24 h) born to mothers that were raised under a standard, high-food environment (Tessier et al. 2000). Each bioassay used a minimum of 10 neonates per lake-seston treatment, with an additional 15 harvested for initial dry mass. On each day, individual animals were changed to freshly collected lake water (screened through 80-μm Nitex to remove other zooplankton) in separate beakers until age 4 d, at which point animals were harvested for measurement of dry mass (see Desmarais and Tessier 1999 for detailed methods). Water was collected from the pelagic zone as described above. We expressed growth rate as the difference between the natural log of initial and final dry mass (measured to the nearest 0.1 μg) of the average individual, divided by 4 d (units are per day). The full range of growth rates expressed by our bioassay *Daphnia* is −0.10 (starvation) to 0.65 d\(^{-1}\). Statistical models We averaged all data collected in the same summer and lake to create a single value for chlorophyll \( a \), particulate carbon, and bioassay growth rate, per lake, per summer. These values constitute the lowest level of replication for comparison of lake categories. We used two different statistical models to compare phytoplankton-seston abundance and bioassay growth among the three categories of planktivory, using log\(_{10}\)-transformed seston and phosphorus values to satisfy the requirement of homogeneous variances. We first ran a nested ANOVA in which the three categories of planktivory were the top-level effect, lakes were nested within each category, and observations from different years were nested within each lake. We used restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) in Proc Mixed (SAS 1999) to estimate variances and test for significance at each of the three sampling levels. Second, we ran an ANCOVA model, using total phosphorus in spring as a covariate, in order to compare categories of planktivory while controlling for productivity. To meet the assumption of equal slopes for the ANCOVA model, we restricted the range of lakes to those having <1 μmol/L total phosphorus (i.e., oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes), which only meant removing 4 eutrophic observations (out of 46). We used repeated MANOVA (profile analysis) to compare size-fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) among the three categories of planktivory. Phytoplankton composition During the summer of 1998, we preserved phytoplankton from the pelagic zone (~0.5 m depth) of 11 lakes (5 deep-refuge, 3 shallow, and 3 high-planktivory) with acid Lugol’s solution, concentrated by settling, and counted abundance of each algae taxon. Taxonomic diversity was great, so to facilitate a comparison across levels of planktivory we lumped taxa into seven ecological groups based on morphology, taxonomy, and resistance to digestion. We then performed a multidimensional scaling of the correlation matrix for the 11 lake samples. The ordination was constrained to a single dimension to simplify visual comparison of categories of planktivory. RESULTS Chlorophyll \( a \) was tightly correlated with particulate carbon (<62 μm; \( r_p = 0.82, n = 43, P < 0.0001 \)), and both were correlated with total phosphorus (chlorophyll \( a \), \( r_p = 0.85, n = 43 \); particulate carbon, \( r_p = 0.63, n = 44 \); both \( P < 0.0001 \)). However, most variation in these parameters was distributed among lakes within the same level of planktivory (87% for chlorophyll \( a \) and 92% for particulate carbon). Differences among levels of planktivory were minor, explaining only 13% and 8% of the variation in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, respectively. Moreover, ANCOVA (covariate = total phosphorus) revealed no difference among the three levels of planktivory for chlorophyll \( a \) (\( F = 0.97, \text{df} = 2, 34, P = 0.39 \)) or particulate carbon (\( F = 2.5, \text{df} = 2, 36, P = 0.09 \)). Hence, there was no evidence of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass. In marked contrast, the bioassay growth rates revealed large differences among the three levels of planktivory (Fig. 2). Across the 6 yr of observations, 85% of the variation in *Daphnia* growth was explained by level of planktivory. The magnitude of this growth variation was dramatic; mean rates were 0.1453 ± 0.009 d\(^{-1}\) (mean ± 1 SE) for deep-refuge lakes, 0.343 Fig. 2. Values are based on single estimates for each lake, plotted separately for each year and level of planktivory. Growth was not measured in shallow lakes in summer 1997 or in high-planktivory lakes in 1995 and 2000. Planktivory category explains 85.1% of the variance in growth rate. ± 0.0147 d^{-1} for shallow lakes, and 0.491 ± 0.030 d^{-1} for the high-planktivory lakes. Additionally, controlling for variation in productivity did not change this pattern (ANCOVA: differences among the three planktivory categories using total phosphorus as a covariate, \( F = 93.4, \text{df} = 2, 36, P < 0.0001 \)). Hence, increasing fish planktivory resulted in richer food resources for grazers, as measured by growth rate, independent of lake productivity. Growth rate was only weakly associated with phytoplankton abundance (chlorophyll \( a \) or particulate carbon) or lake productivity (Fig. 3), except for a few eutrophic ponds having both high growth rates and high seston abundance. Over a range of productivity that encompassed oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes, variation in grazer growth was only marginally correlated with chlorophyll \( a \) (\( r_p = 0.41, n = 38, P < 0.06 \)) and independent of particulate carbon (\( r_p = -0.21, n = 40, P = 0.69 \)). Further, concentrations of particulate carbon were typically >300 \( \mu \)g/L, which exceeds the satiation level for most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998), including the bioassay animals. Size fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) revealed no difference among the three categories of planktivory (Fig. 4). Small particles dominated; picoplankton (<3 \( \mu \)m) made up ~20% of the chlorophyll \( a \), 60% was <15 \( \mu \)m, and ~75% was <35 \( \mu \)m. Since neither biomass nor size of phytoplankton explained the higher growth rate of grazers with increased planktivory, we examined the composition of phytoplankton. A multidimensional scaling of samples from 11 of the lakes explained 94% of the variation in relative abundance of seven ecological groups of phytoplankton as a single axis that reflected a gradient in resistance of phytoplankton to grazing (Fig. 5). Digestion-resistant taxa (including numerous Chlorococcales distinguished by thick cell walls or gelatinous sheaths) were positively associated with this axis. In contrast, small flagellates and unicells were negatively correlated with this axis. Lakes sorted out along this axis on the basis of level of planktivory (ANOVA \( F = 25.4, \text{df} = 2, 8, P < 0.001 \)). Deep-refuge lakes had relatively low abundances of easily digested flagellates and unicells, but higher abundances of digestion-resistant forms. Fig. 3. Relationships between resource quality for grazers (bioassay growth rates, d^{-1}) and chlorophyll \( a \), particulate carbon, and lake productivity (spring total phosphorus) across all six years of the study. Symbols and ellipses (means and 1 SD) indicate lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. DISCUSSION Based on differences in the strength of planktivory and the body size and biomass of grazers, we expected Fig. 4. Cumulative size-frequency distribution of chlorophyll \( a \) in lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. Values indicate means and among-lake SE for the proportion of total chlorophyll \( a \) smaller than various mesh sizes. Frequency profiles are not significantly different (\( F = 0.86, \) df = 2, 17, \( P = 0.44 \), size \( \times \) planktivory interaction Pillai Trace \( F = 0.54, \) df = 8, 30, \( P = 0.82 \)). to find more phytoplankton in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes than in the deep-refuge lakes. This was clearly not the case. However, a strong cascade effect on phytoplankton was apparent when measured in terms of growth rate of a representative grazer. The magnitude of this effect and its consistency across lakes and years is remarkable. Perhaps most surprising is that these large differences in grazer growth rates were fairly independent of phytoplankton biomass. Deep-refuge lakes varied in productivity (0.15–1.0 \( \mu \)mol/L total P) and in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, but exhibited little variation in food resources for *Daphnia* across all six summers of observations. Typical concentrations of particulate carbon in these lakes were 300–700 \( \mu \)g/L, and three-fourths of that was able to pass a 35-\( \mu \)m screen. These concentrations of edible seston suggest that food quantity was not limiting to most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998). Grazers in our lakes were apparently limited by food quality. Our study demonstrates a positive link between the strength of top-down planktivory and the food quality of phytoplankton for grazers. We further show that this relationship between phytoplankton food quality and level of planktivory is associated with changes in the composition of the phytoplankton. When grouped ecologically on the basis of defenses against grazing, (size, cell wall thickness, gelatinous sheaths, etc.), the phytoplankton assemblages illustrate a gradient from well-defended forms that dominate in the deep-refuge lakes to highly vulnerable forms that dominate in the high-planktivory lakes. This compositional change in phytoplankton along a gradient of top-down planktivory suggests a reasonable explanation for the variation in growth rates observed in our *Daphnia* bioassays. We acknowledge that categorization of phytoplankton with respect to digestion resistance is somewhat subjective. However, we have conducted experiments in deep and shallow lakes to quantify phytoplankton vulnerability to a standard grazer and found large differences consistent with our interpretation of Fig. 5 (A. J. Tessier and E. V. Bizina, *unpublished data*). These findings indicate that while compensation within the grazer or phytoplankton assemblage may dissipate the magnitude of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass, a functional effect on grazer growth rates is strong and persistent. Increased zoo-planktivory in shallower lakes eliminates the large-sized, effective grazers and allows the proliferation of less-defended phytoplankton species, resulting in higher resource quality for the remaining grazers. The pattern of a biomass cascade is not seen, but the process of cascading trophic interactions is revealed in the composition of the phytoplankton and the growth rates of the grazers. Explanations for why trophic biomass cascades are variable have focused on trophic heterogeneity and compensatory responses to top-down influences (Strong 1992, Leibold 1999). Some have argued that high diversity of plants and herbivores in terrestrial ecosystems limits wholesale cascades of trophic biomass compared to aquatic systems (Polis et al. 2000, Halaj and Wise 2001). Ecological diversity in predator defense and resource exploitation within a trophic level Fig. 5. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) of 11 lake samples based on composition of summer phytoplankton. Lengths of horizontal bars indicate Pearson correlations (vertical line = 0, scale between 1 and −1 on MDS axis) between the ordination axis and the abundance of each of the seven ecological groups of phytoplankton. Circles represent deep-refuge lakes, diamonds represent shallow lakes, and stars represent high-planktivory lakes. should dilute top-down influences but it is not apparent that such diversity will map directly on to taxonomic diversity or that aquatic systems harbor any less such diversity (Chase 2000). Further, compensation can occur at the level of individuals (Beckerman et al. 1997). For example, grazers in our deep lakes undergo diel vertical migration, which should restrict their foraging time on epilimnetic phytoplankton compared to grazers in shallow lakes. While we did not explicitly examine mechanisms of compensation, we did observe a systematic shift in the phytoplankton among the three lake types. Ecological diversity within phytoplankton is quite large; in particular, taxa greatly differ in vulnerability to grazers. There is strong evidence that traits that confer resistance to mortality from grazers (e.g., cell wall thickness) also decrease algal growth rates (Agrawal 1998). In the presence of large, effective grazers such as big Daphnia in deep-refuge lakes, selection for resistance to grazing seems a logical priority. But when planktivory is strong (i.e., shallow or small lakes) and the zooplankton are small in size and number, phytoplankton priorities may shift to competitive ability or rates of growth. Theoretical models that view phytoplankton assemblages as expressing a trade-off between grazer resistance and growth-competitive ability often predict that decreased mortality on the grazers (e.g., lower planktivory) should select for phytoplankton that are better defended against grazers (Grover 1995, Leibold 1996, Grover and Holt 1998). Changes in the species composition of phytoplankton along a gradient of grazer mortality could compensate for changes in grazing rate and result in little net change in phytoplankton biomass. However, from the perspective of a grazer, these models make the prediction that the food quality of the phytoplankton assemblage should increase with increased grazer mortality and that there might be little relationship between total phytoplankton abundance and grazer growth rate. Our bioassay growth approach provides a first test and confirmation of these theoretical predictions. Of course, it would be naïve to imagine that trophic cascade is the only mechanism contributing to compositional changes in phytoplankton across this large a lake size gradient. Obvious alternative mechanisms involve nutrient recycling. As basin size is decreased the opportunity for benthic-pelagic coupling is enhanced, resulting in faster recycling of nutrients. This may select for different forms of algae independent of top-down effects. Similarly, nutrient release by fish may also be higher in the high-planktivory lakes and so directly shape phytoplankton composition (Vanni and Findlay 1990). However, increased nutrient recycling alone cannot easily explain our results. In the absence of increased planktivory, grazer populations should increase in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes and ultimately select for better-defended algae. In fact, when we excluded fish from large enclosures in shallow and high-planktivory lakes, the grazers rapidly reduce phytoplankton abundance (A. J. Tessier and M. E. Matta, unpublished data). Still, we caution that experimental manipulation of planktivores and grazers across the lake size gradient is needed to quantify the relative significance of top-down planktivory vs. bottom-up productivity influences. In summary, we show that increased strength of fish planktivory in shallow and small lakes has a strong, indirect effect on phytoplankton as perceived by grazers. This cascade effect is hidden when measured in terms of biomass or size structure of phytoplankton, but is associated with shifts in composition of the phytoplankton. While trophic cascade is unlikely to be the only causal mechanism underlying shifts in phytoplankton composition along a gradient of lake size and depth, it is naturally confounded with other mechanisms, creating a general environmental gradient (Jeppesen et al. 1997, Moss et al. 1997). From a food web perspective, this suggests a major shift in the functional coupling of grazers and phytoplankton across this lake size/depth gradient. From an evolutionary perspective, grazers should perceive this as a correlated selection gradient of food quality and planktivory risk. We suspect that evidence of joint top-down; bottom-up selection will be found in the life histories of the grazers that exist along this gradient. CRYPTIC TROPHIC CASCADE ALONG A GRADIENT OF LAKE SIZE ALAN J. TESSIER1 AND PAMELA WOODRUFF W. K. Kellogg Biological Station and Department of Zoology, Michigan State University, Hickory Corners, Michigan 49060 USA Abstract. Lake size and depth mediate the strength of interaction between fish and zooplankton. We test whether this variation in zooplanktivory indirectly affects the phytoplankton by comparing 19 lakes that represent two food webs resulting from the absence of piscivores in small, partial-winterkill lakes. Lakes with piscivorous fish are further distinguished by thermal stratification, which provides a refuge for zooplankton to avoid fish predation. We contrasted phytoplankton abundance in these three categories of lakes over six years, using both direct measures of concentration and a growth bioassay that measures phytoplankton from the perspective of a standard grazer (Daphnia). Contrary to expectations, phytoplankton abundance was largely unaffected by trophic structure or the presence of a deep-water refuge. However, grazer growth differed dramatically among the three categories of lakes. Consistent with trophic cascade, increased fish planktivory resulted in more phytoplankton food as measured from the grazer’s perspective. This effect was independent of lake productivity or total abundance and size of phytoplankton. Instead, variation in food quality for grazers was associated with compositional differences in phytoplankton. These results indicate that persistent trophic cascades are more dramatic in the plankton than previously realized but primarily influence composition, rather than biomass. Although cryptic, such top-down effects create functional variation in grazer–resource coupling. Key words: Daphnia growth bioassay; indirect effects; phytoplankton; species sorting; trophic compensation; winterkill; zooplankton refuge. INTRODUCTION Changes at the top of food webs can have cascading effects, but what determines the magnitude and persistence of those effects is poorly understood. Addressing the issue demands that we first define what is meant by “effect” (Schmitz et al. 2000). Recently, Polis et al. (2000) argued for separation of species- and community-level effects of trophic cascade. They reasoned that effects on traits of individual species (e.g., leaf damage) do not hold the same significance for ecosystem processes as changes in community composition or biomass. While a primary concern with community change is reasonable, important differences in food web or trophic interactions need not involve shifts in the distribution of trophic biomass. Nor is it clear that species turnover will serve as a useful estimate of trophic cascade, given that most species are relatively rare. In short, the strength of trophic coupling and food web function may not be predictable from relative changes in biomass or species composition. We suggest a need for studies of trophic effects that quantify the functional consequences of changes in community composition. Of particular interest to trophic cascade theory is whether variation in predation changes the nature of prey–resource coupling. In a three-trophic-level food chain, increased predation weakens the coupling of prey with their resources and typically increases resource biomass. From the perspective of prey, this higher resource availability should increase individual growth and reproductive rates (a functional change). In real food webs, compensatory responses within either the prey or resource trophic levels might mask the cascade effect when measured in terms of biomass. But does compensation of biomass mean that the functional effects on trophic coupling are also diluted? We address this question by quantifying the indirect effect of predators (fish planktivores) on the resources (phytoplankton) of their prey (zooplankton grazers) from two perspectives: biomass and prey growth rate. We rely on prior work (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000) showing that the growth response of a standard Daphnia to different phytoplankton assemblages is broadly representative of growth and reproductive responses of other suspension feeders, the dominant grazers. This allows us to quantify resource availability from the perspective of the grazers in short-term growth bioassays and to compare that to traditional measures of phytoplankton biomass. Our bioassay approach provides a common currency with which to quantify the trophic significance of compositional changes within the phytoplankton. Consequently, the zooplankton of these “deep-refuge” lakes is dominated by large-bodied Daphnia species that vertically migrate to feed on phytoplankton in the surface waters at night, but refuge in deep waters during the day to avoid fish. Centrarchids are the dominant fish in this and the next category of lake; bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) and pumpkinseed (L. gibbosus) sunfish are the main planktivores, and largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) is the major piscivore (Werner et al. 1977). Lakes in our second category have large surface area relative to their depth and do not thermally stratify in summer. These “shallow” lakes have no refuge for zooplankton to avoid daytime planktivory, so zooplankton suffer a greater risk of predation than in the deep lakes (Tessier et al. 1992, Leibold and Tessier 1998). While not measured in our lakes, biomass of fish (per cubic meter) is generally known to be greater in shallow than in deep lakes (Jeppesen et al. 1997). Consequently, the zooplankton of shallow lakes is composed of a lower biomass of smaller-sized taxa than the big Daphnia of deep lakes (Fig. 1). Lakes in our last category are both shallow and small in water volume. Low oxygen under the ice in winter is a recurring stress in these lakes and results in partial winterkills (Greenbank 1945), to which largemouth bass is particularly sensitive (Moore 1942). Hence, lakes in this category lack strong piscivory, and the fish community is composed of high densities of efficient planktivores (Tonn and Magnuson 1982). Reflecting this “high planktivory,” the grazer assemblage is dominated by the smallest of cladocerans and copepods, and rotifers dominate the zooplankton in these lakes (Hall and Ellinger 1989, Mittelbach et al. 1995; Fig. 1). Hence, the three categories of lakes represent a gradient of intensity of fish planktivory; lowest in the deep-refuge lakes, intermediate in the shallow lakes, and highest in the partial winterkill lakes. We examined seven deep-refuge lakes, six shallow lakes, and six high-planktivory lakes over a period of 6 yr (Table 1). Most lakes were sampled in multiple years (>2 yr per lake) and on multiple dates throughout the summer (June–September). We also sampled each lake during the spring turnover and collected pelagic water for determination of total phosphorus. Phytoplankton-eston abundance We collected water from the pelagic zone, ~0.5 m below the lake surface between 0900 and 1300. Sam- ples were screened through 62-μm Nitex (Tetko, Elmsford, New York, USA) and then filtered on GF/F glass fiber filters (Whatman, Clifton, New Jersey, USA) for analysis of chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate matter. Chlorophyll \( a \) was extracted overnight in cold, 95% ethanol and measured using narrow band fluorometry. Ash-free dry mass of the seston was determined after muffling at 500°C and converted to carbon using a calibration based on C analysis using a Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer (C. E. Instruments, Milan, Italy; A. J. Tessier, unpublished data). During summer of 1999 we sampled all lakes for a size-fractionation of chlorophyll \( a \) (<3, <15, <35, <62, <100 μm, and total) using Nitex screens except for the <3-μm fraction, which was achieved by filtration through Whatman GF/D glass fiber filters. Growth bioassay As a direct estimate of phytoplankton food value for zooplankton, we conducted growth rate bioassays on the same dates that we sampled chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon. The bioassays measured juvenile specific growth rate of a clone of *D. pulex-pulicaria* fed seston from the lake but under standard laboratory conditions. Bioassay results are representative of growth and reproduction responses of all common daphniid species in our region (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000). Bioassays start with neonates (<24 h) born to mothers that were raised under a standard, high-food environment (Tessier et al. 2000). Each bioassay used a minimum of 10 neonates per lake-seston treatment, with an additional 15 harvested for initial dry mass. On each day, individual animals were changed to freshly collected lake water (screened through 80-μm Nitex to remove other zooplankton) in separate beakers until age 4 d, at which point animals were harvested for measurement of dry mass (see Desmarais and Tessier 1999 for detailed methods). Water was collected from the pelagic zone as described above. We expressed growth rate as the difference between the natural log of initial and final dry mass (measured to the nearest 0.1 μg) of the average individual, divided by 4 d (units are per day). The full range of growth rates expressed by our bioassay *Daphnia* is −0.10 (starvation) to 0.65 d\(^{-1}\). Statistical models We averaged all data collected in the same summer and lake to create a single value for chlorophyll \( a \), particulate carbon, and bioassay growth rate, per lake, per summer. These values constitute the lowest level of replication for comparison of lake categories. We used two different statistical models to compare phytoplankton-seston abundance and bioassay growth among the three categories of planktivory, using log\(_{10}\)-transformed seston and phosphorus values to satisfy the requirement of homogeneous variances. We first ran a nested ANOVA in which the three categories of planktivory were the top-level effect, lakes were nested within each category, and observations from different years were nested within each lake. We used restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) in Proc Mixed (SAS 1999) to estimate variances and test for significance at each of the three sampling levels. Second, we ran an ANCOVA model, using total phosphorus in spring as a covariate, in order to compare categories of planktivory while controlling for productivity. To meet the assumption of equal slopes for the ANCOVA model, we restricted the range of lakes to those having <1 μmol/L total phosphorus (i.e., oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes), which only meant removing 4 eutrophic observations (out of 46). We used repeated MANOVA (profile analysis) to compare size-fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) among the three categories of planktivory. Phytoplankton composition During the summer of 1998, we preserved phytoplankton from the pelagic zone (~0.5 m depth) of 11 lakes (5 deep-refuge, 3 shallow, and 3 high-planktivory) with acid Lugol’s solution, concentrated by settling, and counted abundance of each algae taxon. Taxonomic diversity was great, so to facilitate a comparison across levels of planktivory we lumped taxa into seven ecological groups based on morphology, taxonomy, and resistance to digestion. We then performed a multidimensional scaling of the correlation matrix for the 11 lake samples. The ordination was constrained to a single dimension to simplify visual comparison of categories of planktivory. RESULTS Chlorophyll \( a \) was tightly correlated with particulate carbon (<62 μm; \( r_p = 0.82, n = 43, P < 0.0001 \)), and both were correlated with total phosphorus (chlorophyll \( a \), \( r_p = 0.85, n = 43 \); particulate carbon, \( r_p = 0.63, n = 44 \); both \( P < 0.0001 \)). However, most variation in these parameters was distributed among lakes within the same level of planktivory (87% for chlorophyll \( a \) and 92% for particulate carbon). Differences among levels of planktivory were minor, explaining only 13% and 8% of the variation in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, respectively. Moreover, ANCOVA (covariate = total phosphorus) revealed no difference among the three levels of planktivory for chlorophyll \( a \) (\( F = 0.97, \text{df} = 2, 34, P = 0.39 \)) or particulate carbon (\( F = 2.5, \text{df} = 2, 36, P = 0.09 \)). Hence, there was no evidence of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass. In marked contrast, the bioassay growth rates revealed large differences among the three levels of planktivory (Fig. 2). Across the 6 yr of observations, 85% of the variation in *Daphnia* growth was explained by level of planktivory. The magnitude of this growth variation was dramatic; mean rates were 0.1453 ± 0.009 d\(^{-1}\) (mean ± 1 SE) for deep-refuge lakes, 0.343 Fig. 2. Bioassay growth rates (resource quality, d^{-1}) of a standard Daphnia-fed lake seston under uniform laboratory conditions (means ± 1 SE, among lakes). Values are based on single estimates for each lake, plotted separately for each year and level of planktivory. Growth was not measured in shallow lakes in summer 1997 or in high-planktivory lakes in 1995 and 2000. Planktivory category explains 85.1% of the variance in growth rate. ± 0.0147 d^{-1} for shallow lakes, and 0.491 ± 0.030 d^{-1} for the high-planktivory lakes. Additionally, controlling for variation in productivity did not change this pattern (ANCOVA: differences among the three planktivory categories using total phosphorus as a covariate, \( F = 93.4, \text{df} = 2, 36, P < 0.0001 \)). Hence, increasing fish planktivory resulted in richer food resources for grazers, as measured by growth rate, independent of lake productivity. Growth rate was only weakly associated with phytoplankton abundance (chlorophyll \( a \) or particulate carbon) or lake productivity (Fig. 3), except for a few eutrophic ponds having both high growth rates and high seston abundance. Over a range of productivity that encompassed oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes, variation in grazer growth was only marginally correlated with chlorophyll \( a \) (\( r_p = 0.41, n = 38, P < 0.06 \)) and independent of particulate carbon (\( r_p = -0.21, n = 40, P = 0.69 \)). Further, concentrations of particulate carbon were typically >300 \( \mu \)g/L, which exceeds the satiation level for most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998), including the bioassay animals. Size fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) revealed no difference among the three categories of planktivory (Fig. 4). Small particles dominated; picoplankton (<3 \( \mu \)m) made up ~20% of the chlorophyll \( a \), 60% was <15 \( \mu \)m, and ~75% was <35 \( \mu \)m. Since neither biomass nor size of phytoplankton explained the higher growth rate of grazers with increased planktivory, we examined the composition of phytoplankton. A multidimensional scaling of samples from 11 of the lakes explained 94% of the variation in relative abundance of seven ecological groups of phytoplankton as a single axis that reflected a gradient in resistance of phytoplankton to grazing (Fig. 5). Digestion-resistant taxa (including numerous Chlorococcales distinguished by thick cell walls or gelatinous sheaths) were positively associated with this axis. In contrast, small flagellates and unicells were negatively correlated with this axis. Lakes sorted out along this axis on the basis of level of planktivory (ANOVA \( F = 25.4, \text{df} = 2, 8, P < 0.001 \)). Deep-refuge lakes had relatively low abundances of easily digested flagellates and unicells, but higher abundances of digestion-resistant forms. Fig. 3. Relationships between resource quality for grazers (bioassay growth rates, d^{-1}) and chlorophyll \( a \), particulate carbon, and lake productivity (spring total phosphorus) across all six years of the study. Symbols and ellipses (means and 1 SD) indicate lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. DISCUSSION Based on differences in the strength of planktivory and the body size and biomass of grazers, we expected Fig. 4. Cumulative size-frequency distribution of chlorophyll \( a \) in lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. Values indicate means and among-lake SE for the proportion of total chlorophyll \( a \) smaller than various mesh sizes. Frequency profiles are not significantly different (\( F = 0.86, \) df = 2, 17, \( P = 0.44 \), size \( \times \) planktivory interaction Pillai Trace \( F = 0.54, \) df = 8, 30, \( P = 0.82 \)). to find more phytoplankton in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes than in the deep-refuge lakes. This was clearly not the case. However, a strong cascade effect on phytoplankton was apparent when measured in terms of growth rate of a representative grazer. The magnitude of this effect and its consistency across lakes and years is remarkable. Perhaps most surprising is that these large differences in grazer growth rates were fairly independent of phytoplankton biomass. Deep-refuge lakes varied in productivity (0.15–1.0 \( \mu \)mol/L total P) and in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, but exhibited little variation in food resources for *Daphnia* across all six summers of observations. Typical concentrations of particulate carbon in these lakes were 300–700 \( \mu \)g/L, and three-fourths of that was able to pass a 35-\( \mu \)m screen. These concentrations of edible seston suggest that food quantity was not limiting to most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998). Grazers in our lakes were apparently limited by food quality. Our study demonstrates a positive link between the strength of top-down planktivory and the food quality of phytoplankton for grazers. We further show that this relationship between phytoplankton food quality and level of planktivory is associated with changes in the composition of the phytoplankton. When grouped ecologically on the basis of defenses against grazing, (size, cell wall thickness, gelatinous sheaths, etc.), the phytoplankton assemblages illustrate a gradient from well-defended forms that dominate in the deep-refuge lakes to highly vulnerable forms that dominate in the high-planktivory lakes. This compositional change in phytoplankton along a gradient of top-down planktivory suggests a reasonable explanation for the variation in growth rates observed in our *Daphnia* bioassays. We acknowledge that categorization of phytoplankton with respect to digestion resistance is somewhat subjective. However, we have conducted experiments in deep and shallow lakes to quantify phytoplankton vulnerability to a standard grazer and found large differences consistent with our interpretation of Fig. 5 (A. J. Tessier and E. V. Bizina, *unpublished data*). These findings indicate that while compensation within the grazer or phytoplankton assemblage may dissipate the magnitude of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass, a functional effect on grazer growth rates is strong and persistent. Increased zoo-planktivory in shallower lakes eliminates the large-sized, effective grazers and allows the proliferation of less-defended phytoplankton species, resulting in higher resource quality for the remaining grazers. The pattern of a biomass cascade is not seen, but the process of cascading trophic interactions is revealed in the composition of the phytoplankton and the growth rates of the grazers. Explanations for why trophic biomass cascades are variable have focused on trophic heterogeneity and compensatory responses to top-down influences (Strong 1992, Leibold 1999). Some have argued that high diversity of plants and herbivores in terrestrial ecosystems limits wholesale cascades of trophic biomass compared to aquatic systems (Polis et al. 2000, Halaj and Wise 2001). Ecological diversity in predator defense and resource exploitation within a trophic level Fig. 5. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) of 11 lake samples based on composition of summer phytoplankton. Lengths of horizontal bars indicate Pearson correlations (vertical line = 0, scale between 1 and −1 on MDS axis) between the ordination axis and the abundance of each of the seven ecological groups of phytoplankton. Circles represent deep-refuge lakes, diamonds represent shallow lakes, and stars represent high-planktivory lakes. should dilute top-down influences but it is not apparent that such diversity will map directly on to taxonomic diversity or that aquatic systems harbor any less such diversity (Chase 2000). Further, compensation can occur at the level of individuals (Beckerman et al. 1997). For example, grazers in our deep lakes undergo diel vertical migration, which should restrict their foraging time on epilimnetic phytoplankton compared to grazers in shallow lakes. While we did not explicitly examine mechanisms of compensation, we did observe a systematic shift in the phytoplankton among the three lake types. Ecological diversity within phytoplankton is quite large; in particular, taxa greatly differ in vulnerability to grazers. There is strong evidence that traits that confer resistance to mortality from grazers (e.g., cell wall thickness) also decrease algal growth rates (Agrawal 1998). In the presence of large, effective grazers such as big Daphnia in deep-refuge lakes, selection for resistance to grazing seems a logical priority. But when planktivory is strong (i.e., shallow or small lakes) and the zooplankton are small in size and number, phytoplankton priorities may shift to competitive ability or rates of growth. Theoretical models that view phytoplankton assemblages as expressing a trade-off between grazer resistance and growth-competitive ability often predict that decreased mortality on the grazers (e.g., lower planktivory) should select for phytoplankton that are better defended against grazers (Grover 1995, Leibold 1996, Grover and Holt 1998). Changes in the species composition of phytoplankton along a gradient of grazer mortality could compensate for changes in grazing rate and result in little net change in phytoplankton biomass. However, from the perspective of a grazer, these models make the prediction that the food quality of the phytoplankton assemblage should increase with increased grazer mortality and that there might be little relationship between total phytoplankton abundance and grazer growth rate. Our bioassay growth approach provides a first test and confirmation of these theoretical predictions. Of course, it would be naïve to imagine that trophic cascade is the only mechanism contributing to compositional changes in phytoplankton across this large a lake size gradient. Obvious alternative mechanisms involve nutrient recycling. As basin size is decreased the opportunity for benthic-pelagic coupling is enhanced, resulting in faster recycling of nutrients. This may select for different forms of algae independent of top-down effects. Similarly, nutrient release by fish may also be higher in the high-planktivory lakes and so directly shape phytoplankton composition (Vanni and Findlay 1990). However, increased nutrient recycling alone cannot easily explain our results. In the absence of increased planktivory, grazer populations should increase in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes and ultimately select for better-defended algae. In fact, when we excluded fish from large enclosures in shallow and high-planktivory lakes, the grazers rapidly reduce phytoplankton abundance (A. J. Tessier and M. E. Matta, unpublished data). Still, we caution that experimental manipulation of planktivores and grazers across the lake size gradient is needed to quantify the relative significance of top-down planktivory vs. bottom-up productivity influences. In summary, we show that increased strength of fish planktivory in shallow and small lakes has a strong, indirect effect on phytoplankton as perceived by grazers. This cascade effect is hidden when measured in terms of biomass or size structure of phytoplankton, but is associated with shifts in composition of the phytoplankton. While trophic cascade is unlikely to be the only causal mechanism underlying shifts in phytoplankton composition along a gradient of lake size and depth, it is naturally confounded with other mechanisms, creating a general environmental gradient (Jeppesen et al. 1997, Moss et al. 1997). From a food web perspective, this suggests a major shift in the functional coupling of grazers and phytoplankton across this lake size/depth gradient. From an evolutionary perspective, grazers should perceive this as a correlated selection gradient of food quality and planktivory risk. We suspect that evidence of joint top-down; bottom-up selection will be found in the life histories of the grazers that exist along this gradient. Determinants of biodiversity in subtropical shallow lakes (Atlantic coast, Uruguay) CARLA KRUK*,†, LORENA RODRÍGUEZ-GALLEGRO*, MARIANA MEERHOFF‡,§, FEDERICO QUINTANS*, GISELL LACEROT*†, NÉSTOR MAZZEO†, FLAVIO SCASSO†, JUAN C. PAGGI**, EDWIN T. H. M. PEETERS† AND SCHEFFER MARTEN† *Sección Limnología, Departamento de Ecología, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de la República, Montevideo, Uruguay †Aquatic Ecology and Water Quality Management Group, Department of Environmental Sciences, Wageningen University, Wageningen, The Netherlands ‡Grupo de Ecología y Rehabilitación de Sistemas Acuáticos, Departamento de Ecología, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de la República, Montevideo, Uruguay §National Environmental Research Institute, University of Aarhus, Silkeborg, Denmark *Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo, Montevideo, Uruguay **Instituto Nacional de Limnología, Universidad Nacional Del Litoral, Santa Fe, Argentina SUMMARY 1. Shallow lakes and ponds contribute disproportionally to species richness relative to other aquatic ecosystems. In-lake conditions (e.g. presence of submerged plants) seem to play a key role in determining diversity, as has been demonstrated for temperate lakes. When water quality deteriorates and turbidity increases, conditions in such lakes are affected drastically resulting in a loss of diversity. However, it is not clear whether subtropical lakes show the same pattern and whether the richness of all groups reacts similarly to environmental changes. 2. Our aim was to analyse the main factors explaining patterns of species richness in plankton, fish and submerged macrophyte assemblages in both turbid and clear subtropical shallow lakes. We analysed abiotic and biotic features of 18 subtropical, small- to medium-sized, shallow lakes along the Uruguayan coast. We compared both turbid and clear ecosystem states and evaluated the relative variance explained by the factors measured. 3. Variables describing lake and catchment morphology, as well as the percentage of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes (%PVI) and water turbidity, had strong effects on taxon richness. Interestingly, individual biotic groups had dissimilar richness patterns. Macrophyte %PVI decreased with increasing lake area, while fish species richness showed the opposite pattern. Phytoplankton species richness increased with macrophyte %PVI, while the zooplankton richness pattern varied depending on the taxonomic group considered. 4. Overall, our results indicate that, as found for temperate lakes, a greater submerged plant cover promotes higher species richness in several groups, and that this may overwhelm the otherwise expected positive effect of lake size on species richness. On the other hand, small-bodied zooplankton predominated in lakes with high plant abundance. Our findings concur with recent studies, indicating that refuge capacity of aquatic plants might be weaker in (sub)tropical than in temperate shallow lakes. 5. The extremely high plant cover, frequently observed in warm lakes, could potentially lead to different richness patterns in some groups. This conclusion has important consequences for local managers and conservationists. Keywords: fish, lake area, plankton, species richness, submerged macrophytes Introduction Shallow lakes are crucial for the conservation of local and global biodiversity (Moss, 2000). These systems vary considerably in species richness, but at a regional level they may contribute more to diversity than other freshwater ecosystems, such as streams, ditches and temporary ponds (Williams et al., 2003). Most shallow lakes occur in lowland areas, often with high human population densities, and as a consequence their environmental and socioeconomic value is being dramatically affected (De Meester & Declerck, 2005). Rather surprisingly, studies on species richness patterns in shallow lakes are underrepresented and largely ignored in monitoring and protection strategies (Waide et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2003). Furthermore, studies analysing the determinants of biodiversity in subtropical or tropical lakes are even more scarce (Havens et al., 1996; Yuma et al., 2006). The application of the theory of island biogeography (Macarthur & Wilson, 1967; Debinski & Holt, 2000) to aquatic systems, would predict higher species richness in larger, deeper and less isolated lakes than in smaller, more isolated systems. However, in temperate small shallow lakes and ponds without obvious surface connections to other waterbodies, different factors driving biodiversity (from those described in such theory) might explain their disproportionally high number of species (Williams et al., 2003). Thus, the effects of in-lake processes may outweigh the effects of lake area and connectivity (Scheffer et al., 2006). Local factors, such as productivity (often associated with a clear or turbid water state), are usually crucial in explaining patterns of species richness (Scheffer et al., 1993). The turbid state, dominated by phytoplankton, has poorer water quality and fewer species. The clear water state, often accompanied by dominance of submerged macrophytes, is usually more species rich (Jeppesen et al., 1997, 1998; Declerck et al., 2005). Aquatic vegetation may play a key role in those systems, modulating (i.e. by modifying habitat heterogeneity) ecological interactions and thus leading to a greater species richness than predicted by the theory of island biogeography (Scheffer et al., 2006). In particular, submerged vegetation and the associated high spatial heterogeneity have been shown to promote relatively high richness of aquatic birds, amphibians and invertebrates (Søndergaard, Jeppesen & Jensen, 2005; Scheffer et al., 2006). Recent research in subtropical ecosystems has shown that a much greater richness and density of fish, but not of invertebrates, is associated with beds of submerged plants in subtropical lakes than in similar temperate ones (Meerhoff et al., 2007a,b; Teixeira-de Mello et al., 2009). Several studies have analysed the relationship between biodiversity and potentially explanatory variables in temperate shallow lakes. However, most studies of species richness have focussed only on one or two communities (e.g. zooplankton or macrophytes) and few works have addressed the simultaneous response of several groups to environmental change (Allen et al., 1999; Jeppesen et al., 2000; Declerck et al., 2005; Beisner et al., 2006). Therefore, it is not clear whether the species richness of all parts of the community changes in the same way in response to environmental drivers (Declerck et al., 2005). Neither it is known how such patterns are affected by trophic interactions among the groups (Dyer & Letourneau, 2003). Body size might affect the relative effect of the different potential factors. For example, lake area and connectivity are expected to be important for relatively large organisms, such as zooplankton and fish (Hillebrand & Azovsky, 2001). The effects of these factors are less clear for phytoplankton, with some studies showing contradictory results (e.g. Declerck et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2005). The fact that the richness of different species groups may respond differently to the environment could necessitate specific management or conservation programmes for such lakes. Our objective was to analyse factors explaining richness patterns of several assemblages (phytoplankton, zooplankton, fish and submerged macrophytes) in subtropical shallow lakes. Therefore, we studied several abiotic and biotic variables from 18 shallow lakes along the Uruguayan Atlantic coast that varied in environmental state (clear or turbid water). Based on the theoretical framework from the temperate zone, we expected that clear and plant-dominated shallow lakes would generally have more diverse species assemblages than turbid ones (e.g. Scheffer et al., 1993), and that the in-lake attributes would be more important than area and connectivity (e.g. Scheffer et al., 2006). Methods Study area We studied 18 shallow lakes along the south-eastern coast of Uruguay during the 2003 Austral summer (Fig. 1). The lakes are classified as subtropical according to Salas & Martino (1990). Most of these lakes originated during marine transgressions in the Quaternary (García-Rodríguez et al., 2004) and are located at sea level. All systems are freshwater, shallow and small to medium-sized (matching their catchments) and show a gradient in cover of submerged macrophytes. Most of them are surrounded by wetlands and may be considered in a semi-pristine state. Only Pajarera Lake is artificial, whereas Cisne and Diario lakes have been dammed, and Blanca, Escondida and García lakes are used as drinking water reservoirs. Data collection All lakes were sampled once during summer (first half of January 2003) following the same procedure. We selected summer as the sampling season because it is the time of maximum biological activity for most, if not all, organisms and was therefore best suited to give a representative picture of the ecosystems. We analysed an extensive list of variables (Table 1). Lake and catchment variables were calculated using aerial photographs and GIS methodology (Table 1). We measured in-lake variables in situ at the deepest point in each lake (e.g. dissolved oxygen, temperature, conductivity, light, etc.; Table 1). We took samples for water chemistry (e.g. alkalinity, nutrients, etc.) and plankton (Table 1) from three randomly selected shore to shore transects (thus reaching the limits of the surrounding wetland area). We divided each transect into five equidistant points at which we took whole water-column samples with a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) tube (20-cm diameter, length adjusted to lake depth). We mixed the water from the five points into a bulk sample, each transect being a sampling replicate. At the same points, we collected, by scuba diving, three 5-cm deep sediment cores for nutrient analysis. We sampled fish using two techniques (Table 1). The littoral zone was sampled during sunset, by point sample electrofishing, applying a short burst of electricity (hereafter referred to as a ‘pulse’), to between 30 and 45 points in each lake, according to the lake perimeter. The fish abundance was estimated as CPUE (capture per unit effort), and calculated as the total number of individuals divided by the total number of electric ‘pulses’ applied (i.e. points sampled). The pelagic zone was sampled overnight (12 h) with three multi-mesh gill nets (Table 1). Pelagic abundance was estimated as CPUE, and calculated as the number of individuals divided by the net area and by the time of exposure.
