Factors influencing macroinvertebrate assemblages in artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan Sen-Her Shieh · Yao-Sheng Chi Received: 21 August 2009/Revised: 14 April 2010/Accepted: 17 April 2010/Published online: 2 May 2010 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2010 Abstract Macroinvertebrate assemblages and its association with environmental factors at the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan were examined using the multivariate analysis software STATICO. The aims of the study were to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed seasonally, to examine which environmental factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of maroinvertebrate assemblages, and to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of macroinvertebrates. Macroinvertebrates were collected seasonally by a corer and a sweep net in 2007, and 13 physical and chemical factors were measured at the same time. A total of 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were collected during the sampling period, and the most dominant taxa were Chironomidae (31.7% of total animal abundance) and Tubificidae (22.4%). STATICO identified pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, and altitude as the major abiotic factors and Bufo melanostictus (Amphibia) as the major biotic factor to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. These factors changed with seasonality. For example, the abundance of B. melanostictus was the most important factor during the spring but became much less important in other seasons. According to the spatial distribution patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages, macroinvertebrates could be split into two groups based on their dispersal. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were strongly associated with pond size and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, were strongly associated with the pond depth and/or sediment depth. The results of this study suggested that pond size might influence macroinvertebrate assemblages through their dispersal mechanisms and that the environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most changed with seasons in this study area. Keywords Pond size · Active dispersers · Passive dispersers · STATICO Introduction Ponds are rich and diverse habitats and play a key role in safeguarding aquatic biodiversity. They are defined as waterbodies between 1 m^2 and 2 ha in area which may be permanent or seasonal, including both artificial and natural waterbodies (Biggs et al., 2005). Despite their small surface area, they are exceptionally rich in biodiversity, as compared to streams and large lakes, and contribute significantly to regional freshwater biodiversity in many northern temperate regions (Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004), but our understanding of the relative biodiversity importance of ponds elsewhere remains limited. However, the ponds are threatened due to anthropogenic activities, such as eutrophication, chemical pollution, acid rain, physical destruction, and invasion of exotic species (Heath & Whitehead, 1992; Brönmark & Hansson, 2002; Boothby, 2003). While monitoring programs for freshwaters have been widely carried out in many countries, particularly for streams and lakes, these programs have largely failed to include ponds (Oertli et al., 2005). The macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are influenced by both abiotic and biotic factors. Abiotic factors, such as pond size (Rundle et al., 2002) and water chemistry (Friday, 1987), affect the number of taxa in the community. It has been suggested that large ponds support more macroinvertebrate taxa than small ones due to habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005). Biotic factors, such as the presence or absence of large predators (fish and amphibians) in a pond and the dispersal ability of macroinvertebrates, appear to be important in determining macroinvertebrate assemblages. Invertebrate biomass was found to be higher in fishless wetlands than in wetlands with fish (Zimmer et al., 2001). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that the taxon richness of active dispersal macroinvertebrates was positively correlate with pond size, whereas the taxon richness of passive macroinvertebrates did not correlated with environmental variables. Assessing these influences on macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are a key process to understand community structure and succession and to propose a man-made control before any pollution resulting from anthropogenic activities could occur. The relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate distributions in freshwaters have often been studied using principal component analysis (Hinden et al., 2005), canonical correspondence analysis (Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004; Carchini et al., 2005), multidimensional scaling (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009), or clustering (Collinson et al., 1995; Nicolet et al., 2004; Bilton et al., 2006). The main drawback of these methods is that they do not consider that both environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages vary temporally and that the former affects the latter. In order to overcome this problem, the STATICO (STATIS and CO-inertia) has been developed (Thioulouse et al., 2004). It is a multivariate method allowing simultaneous analysis of a sequence of paired ecological tables recorded through a series of sampling occasions. Thioulouse et al. (2004) pointed that STATICO is particularly suited to study the relationship between the environmental and taxonomic tables when both vary time. Since ponds are not uniform as revealed by their shape, shoreline, and size, and a clear seasonal dynamics has been observed for the difference macroinvertebrate assemblages (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007), STATICO is a well-suited statistical tool to get a clear representation of the spatial and temporal variation of the macroinvertebrates assemblages in ponds. Most studies which examined macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds were conducted in Europe (Oertli et al., 2009). There are still relatively few such studies in Asia, especially artificial ponds, where the biodiversity has been poorly investigated. Because of the complexity of pond systems affected spatially and temporally by various abiotic and biotic factors, we analyzed using STATICO the relationships between these factors and maroinvertebrate assemblages in the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan. The first aim of the study was to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed among these subtropical ponds where seasonality was insignificant. The second aim was to examine which abiotic and biotic factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of these macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. We assumed that the pond size and the presence and absence of large predators in ponds should be the most important factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds. Therefore, it was predicted that ponds which were large and/or without large predators should support more taxon richness than ponds which were small and/or with large predators. The final aim was to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of active and passive dispersers of macroinvertebrates. We assumed that the active dispersal macroinvertebrate should be more associated with pond size. Materials and methods Study area Sampling sites were established in the coastal area of west central Taiwan. The area represents one of the biotopes most severely threatened by human impacts since the main land use of the area is municipal and agricultural. The area is flat, has low altitude (<300 m.a.s.l.), and has the annual precipitation of about 1,405 mm between 1998 and 2007, with the perhumid season from April to September and the relative drought season from October to December. Annual mean air temperature is about 23.2°C. The dominant vegetation of the area is Panicum maximum (Poaceae) and Acacia confuse (Fabaceae). Because our aims were to assess the relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages among different ponds, 11 artificial ponds were selected in this area to insure that they were influenced by the same climate condition and land use. These ponds are situated in school grounds and located between the coordinates 24°6′N, 120°31′E and 24°24′N, 120°38′E. Sampling methods Macroinvertebrates samples were collected in January (winter), April (spring), July (summer), and October (autumn) 2007. Because different habitats and groups of macroinvertebrates require different sampling methods, the use of a single method for all habitats could yield misleading conclusion on macroinvertebrate richness. Therefore, two methods, e.g., the quantitative and qualitative methods (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007) were used in this study. A benthic corer sampler (diameter = 26 cm) was used as a quantitative method. During each sampling occasion, the longest transect of the pond was selected, and three benthic samples were taken at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of this transect. The benthic corer was pushed into the substrate until it reached an impermeable layer. The sediments within the corer were transferred by a hand with a cup to a bucket. Animals, organic matter, and remaining water in bucket were passed through a sieve with 0.8-mm apertures. These materials were preserved in 95% ethanol in the field. This procedure allowed us to sample benthic macroinvertebrates. For the qualitative method, ponds were sampled with a sweep net (with 20-cm D-frame and 200-μm mesh) at different microhabitats (such as emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation and pond margins) for 5 min (Batzer et al., 2004). This method allowed us to collect nekton macroinvertebrates and to get a representative sample from the system (Collinson et al., 1995). Sample sizes and sampling time were decided after a pilot study undertaken in these ponds. The main outcomes of this pilot study were that three corer samples and a total time of 5 min were good enough to have the representative taxa for these ponds. In the laboratory, all the samples were rinsed by tap water, and the animals were sorted and preserved in 75% ethanol for further analysis. The macroinvertebrate taxa were identified to the lowest taxonomic unit possible. Aquatic insects were identified according to Morse et al. (1994) and other macroinvertebrate taxa according to Dudgeon (1999) and Shy & Yu (1998). Members of Ostracoda were not identified further. Three vertebrate taxa were collected in this study, and they were common Asian toad (Bufo melanostictus), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), and paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis). Both B. melanostictus and G. affinis were almost found in each of the sampling ponds and were abundant, and so the two species were included in the following analyses. The physical and chemical factors were measured at each of the 11 ponds on each sampling occasion. Conductivity, pH value, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature were measured using WTW multi 340i. Water depth and sediment depth were measured using a graduated stick at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of the longest transect. The shoreline and area of ponds were assessed with a measuring tape by pacing in field. The shoreline development index (SDI) was calculated as follows: \[ \text{SDI} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{\pi A}} \] where \( L \) = the length of shoreline, and \( A \) = the area of pond (Wetzel, 2001). Finally, the percentage of plant cover at each sampling pond was measured by taking the pictures. The relative area of plant cover was estimated by ImageJ 1.42 software. Data analysis For each sampling occasion, three benthic corer samples were combined together as a sample unit and mean densities, taxon richness, Gastropoda richness, and Odonata richness were calculated as community parameters. Simple correlations between community parameters and environmental factors were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \). STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997). Results Environmental factors Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm). Macroinvertebrate communities In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals. At ponds 1, 2, 3, 7, and 11, the dominant taxa were Chironomidae, Tubificidae at ponds 5, 6, 8, and 10, Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul at pond 4, and Neocaridina denticulate at pond 9 (Table 2). There was a trend that the higher the mean water temperature, the higher the number of individuals and taxa (Table 3). The results were associated with the fact that the higher the temperature, the higher the number of gastropod and odonate taxa. In contrast, the number of individuals and taxa were negatively correlated with the altitudes of ponds. Interstructure The interstructure factor maps of the STATICO showed that the decrease of the eigenvalues was high between the first and second eigenvalues (59.3 and 16.3% of the total inertia, respectively) (Fig. 1A). This suggested that only the first axis might be chosen for the compromise analysis. The correlation circle showed all the sampling dates displaying same sign on the first interstructure factor (axis 1), indicating a positive correlation between the corresponding set of matrices (Fig. 1A). Such a uniform distribution on the first axis indicated a strong common structure of seasonality. The structure expressed through the first axis of the interstructure, therefore, corresponded to a community spatial pattern common to the different sampling dates. The second interstructure factor was characterized by the opposition between the sampling dates of winter and spring (positive correlation with axis 2) against the sampling dates of summer and autumn (negatively correlated with the axis). Compromise The contribution of the different sampling dates to the construction of the compromise table was similar (weights from 0.485 to 0.515) (Fig. 1D). Therefore, each of the four samplings played a similar role in the construction of the compromise table. Moreover, the fit of each of the tables to the compromise table (\( \cos^2 \)) was homogeneous (from 0.70 in autumn to 0.80 in winter). The share of the total variability accounted for by each of the first two axes of the compromise was 38.4 and 27.3%, respectively (Fig. 1B). Out of the 13 environmental factors taken into account, only a few were found to be correlated with the structure of macroinvertebrate assemblages (Fig. 1B). The first axis described a positive association with the sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies, and a negative association with the altitude. The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. Factors influencing macroinvertebrate assemblages in artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan Sen-Her Shieh · Yao-Sheng Chi Received: 21 August 2009/Revised: 14 April 2010/Accepted: 17 April 2010/Published online: 2 May 2010 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2010 Abstract Macroinvertebrate assemblages and its association with environmental factors at the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan were examined using the multivariate analysis software STATICO. The aims of the study were to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed seasonally, to examine which environmental factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of maroinvertebrate assemblages, and to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of macroinvertebrates. Macroinvertebrates were collected seasonally by a corer and a sweep net in 2007, and 13 physical and chemical factors were measured at the same time. A total of 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were collected during the sampling period, and the most dominant taxa were Chironomidae (31.7% of total animal abundance) and Tubificidae (22.4%). STATICO identified pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, and altitude as the major abiotic factors and Bufo melanostictus (Amphibia) as the major biotic factor to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. These factors changed with seasonality. For example, the abundance of B. melanostictus was the most important factor during the spring but became much less important in other seasons. According to the spatial distribution patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages, macroinvertebrates could be split into two groups based on their dispersal. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were strongly associated with pond size and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, were strongly associated with the pond depth and/or sediment depth. The results of this study suggested that pond size might influence macroinvertebrate assemblages through their dispersal mechanisms and that the environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most changed with seasons in this study area. Keywords Pond size · Active dispersers · Passive dispersers · STATICO Introduction Ponds are rich and diverse habitats and play a key role in safeguarding aquatic biodiversity. They are defined as waterbodies between 1 m^2 and 2 ha in area which may be permanent or seasonal, including both artificial and natural waterbodies (Biggs et al., 2005). Despite their small surface area, they are exceptionally rich in biodiversity, as compared to streams and large lakes, and contribute significantly to regional freshwater biodiversity in many northern temperate regions (Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004), but our understanding of the relative biodiversity importance of ponds elsewhere remains limited. However, the ponds are threatened due to anthropogenic activities, such as eutrophication, chemical pollution, acid rain, physical destruction, and invasion of exotic species (Heath & Whitehead, 1992; Brönmark & Hansson, 2002; Boothby, 2003). While monitoring programs for freshwaters have been widely carried out in many countries, particularly for streams and lakes, these programs have largely failed to include ponds (Oertli et al., 2005). The macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are influenced by both abiotic and biotic factors. Abiotic factors, such as pond size (Rundle et al., 2002) and water chemistry (Friday, 1987), affect the number of taxa in the community. It has been suggested that large ponds support more macroinvertebrate taxa than small ones due to habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005). Biotic factors, such as the presence or absence of large predators (fish and amphibians) in a pond and the dispersal ability of macroinvertebrates, appear to be important in determining macroinvertebrate assemblages. Invertebrate biomass was found to be higher in fishless wetlands than in wetlands with fish (Zimmer et al., 2001). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that the taxon richness of active dispersal macroinvertebrates was positively correlate with pond size, whereas the taxon richness of passive macroinvertebrates did not correlated with environmental variables. Assessing these influences on macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are a key process to understand community structure and succession and to propose a man-made control before any pollution resulting from anthropogenic activities could occur. The relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate distributions in freshwaters have often been studied using principal component analysis (Hinden et al., 2005), canonical correspondence analysis (Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004; Carchini et al., 2005), multidimensional scaling (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009), or clustering (Collinson et al., 1995; Nicolet et al., 2004; Bilton et al., 2006). The main drawback of these methods is that they do not consider that both environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages vary temporally and that the former affects the latter. In order to overcome this problem, the STATICO (STATIS and CO-inertia) has been developed (Thioulouse et al., 2004). It is a multivariate method allowing simultaneous analysis of a sequence of paired ecological tables recorded through a series of sampling occasions. Thioulouse et al. (2004) pointed that STATICO is particularly suited to study the relationship between the environmental and taxonomic tables when both vary time. Since ponds are not uniform as revealed by their shape, shoreline, and size, and a clear seasonal dynamics has been observed for the difference macroinvertebrate assemblages (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007), STATICO is a well-suited statistical tool to get a clear representation of the spatial and temporal variation of the macroinvertebrates assemblages in ponds. Most studies which examined macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds were conducted in Europe (Oertli et al., 2009). There are still relatively few such studies in Asia, especially artificial ponds, where the biodiversity has been poorly investigated. Because of the complexity of pond systems affected spatially and temporally by various abiotic and biotic factors, we analyzed using STATICO the relationships between these factors and maroinvertebrate assemblages in the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan. The first aim of the study was to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed among these subtropical ponds where seasonality was insignificant. The second aim was to examine which abiotic and biotic factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of these macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. We assumed that the pond size and the presence and absence of large predators in ponds should be the most important factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds. Therefore, it was predicted that ponds which were large and/or without large predators should support more taxon richness than ponds which were small and/or with large predators. The final aim was to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of active and passive dispersers of macroinvertebrates. We assumed that the active dispersal macroinvertebrate should be more associated with pond size. Materials and methods Study area Sampling sites were established in the coastal area of west central Taiwan. The area represents one of the biotopes most severely threatened by human impacts since the main land use of the area is municipal and agricultural. The area is flat, has low altitude (<300 m.a.s.l.), and has the annual precipitation of about 1,405 mm between 1998 and 2007, with the perhumid season from April to September and the relative drought season from October to December. Annual mean air temperature is about 23.2°C. The dominant vegetation of the area is Panicum maximum (Poaceae) and Acacia confuse (Fabaceae). Because our aims were to assess the relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages among different ponds, 11 artificial ponds were selected in this area to insure that they were influenced by the same climate condition and land use. These ponds are situated in school grounds and located between the coordinates 24°6′N, 120°31′E and 24°24′N, 120°38′E. Sampling methods Macroinvertebrates samples were collected in January (winter), April (spring), July (summer), and October (autumn) 2007. Because different habitats and groups of macroinvertebrates require different sampling methods, the use of a single method for all habitats could yield misleading conclusion on macroinvertebrate richness. Therefore, two methods, e.g., the quantitative and qualitative methods (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007) were used in this study. A benthic corer sampler (diameter = 26 cm) was used as a quantitative method. During each sampling occasion, the longest transect of the pond was selected, and three benthic samples were taken at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of this transect. The benthic corer was pushed into the substrate until it reached an impermeable layer. The sediments within the corer were transferred by a hand with a cup to a bucket. Animals, organic matter, and remaining water in bucket were passed through a sieve with 0.8-mm apertures. These materials were preserved in 95% ethanol in the field. This procedure allowed us to sample benthic macroinvertebrates. For the qualitative method, ponds were sampled with a sweep net (with 20-cm D-frame and 200-μm mesh) at different microhabitats (such as emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation and pond margins) for 5 min (Batzer et al., 2004). This method allowed us to collect nekton macroinvertebrates and to get a representative sample from the system (Collinson et al., 1995). Sample sizes and sampling time were decided after a pilot study undertaken in these ponds. The main outcomes of this pilot study were that three corer samples and a total time of 5 min were good enough to have the representative taxa for these ponds. In the laboratory, all the samples were rinsed by tap water, and the animals were sorted and preserved in 75% ethanol for further analysis. The macroinvertebrate taxa were identified to the lowest taxonomic unit possible. Aquatic insects were identified according to Morse et al. (1994) and other macroinvertebrate taxa according to Dudgeon (1999) and Shy & Yu (1998). Members of Ostracoda were not identified further. Three vertebrate taxa were collected in this study, and they were common Asian toad (Bufo melanostictus), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), and paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis). Both B. melanostictus and G. affinis were almost found in each of the sampling ponds and were abundant, and so the two species were included in the following analyses. The physical and chemical factors were measured at each of the 11 ponds on each sampling occasion. Conductivity, pH value, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature were measured using WTW multi 340i. Water depth and sediment depth were measured using a graduated stick at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of the longest transect. The shoreline and area of ponds were assessed with a measuring tape by pacing in field. The shoreline development index (SDI) was calculated as follows: \[ \text{SDI} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{\pi A}} \] where \( L \) = the length of shoreline, and \( A \) = the area of pond (Wetzel, 2001). Finally, the percentage of plant cover at each sampling pond was measured by taking the pictures. The relative area of plant cover was estimated by ImageJ 1.42 software. Data analysis For each sampling occasion, three benthic corer samples were combined together as a sample unit and mean densities, taxon richness, Gastropoda richness, and Odonata richness were calculated as community parameters. Simple correlations between community parameters and environmental factors were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \). STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997). Results Environmental factors Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm). Macroinvertebrate communities In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals. At ponds 1, 2, 3, 7, and 11, the dominant taxa were Chironomidae, Tubificidae at ponds 5, 6, 8, and 10, Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul at pond 4, and Neocaridina denticulate at pond 9 (Table 2). There was a trend that the higher the mean water temperature, the higher the number of individuals and taxa (Table 3). The results were associated with the fact that the higher the temperature, the higher the number of gastropod and odonate taxa. In contrast, the number of individuals and taxa were negatively correlated with the altitudes of ponds. Interstructure The interstructure factor maps of the STATICO showed that the decrease of the eigenvalues was high between the first and second eigenvalues (59.3 and 16.3% of the total inertia, respectively) (Fig. 1A). This suggested that only the first axis might be chosen for the compromise analysis. The correlation circle showed all the sampling dates displaying same sign on the first interstructure factor (axis 1), indicating a positive correlation between the corresponding set of matrices (Fig. 1A). Such a uniform distribution on the first axis indicated a strong common structure of seasonality. The structure expressed through the first axis of the interstructure, therefore, corresponded to a community spatial pattern common to the different sampling dates. The second interstructure factor was characterized by the opposition between the sampling dates of winter and spring (positive correlation with axis 2) against the sampling dates of summer and autumn (negatively correlated with the axis). Compromise The contribution of the different sampling dates to the construction of the compromise table was similar (weights from 0.485 to 0.515) (Fig. 1D). Therefore, each of the four samplings played a similar role in the construction of the compromise table. Moreover, the fit of each of the tables to the compromise table (\( \cos^2 \)) was homogeneous (from 0.70 in autumn to 0.80 in winter). The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 1 for the environmental abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_370_180_1407_1207.png) study, however, we found that the distributions of the chironomids and tubificids were mostly associated with the pond size and pond depth, respectively. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. Fish assemblages in floodplain lakes in a Neotropical river during the wet season (Magdalena River, Colombia) Carlos Granado-Lorencio*,†, Alejandra Gulfo†, Frank Alvarez†, Luz Fernanda Jiménez-Segura†, Juan David Carvajal-Quintero† and Andrés Hernández-Serna† * Department of Plant Biology and Ecology, Faculty of Biology, University of Sevilla, Box 1095, 41080 Sevilla, Spain † Ichthyology Group, Sciences Institute, University of Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia (Accepted 20 February 2012) Abstract: A number of studies have pointed out that abiotic factors and recolonization dynamics appear to be more important than biotic interactions in structuring river–fish assemblages. In this paper, we studied the fish assemblages in 27 floodplain lakes, with perennial connection to the river, in the middle section of the Magdalena River (Colombia), to examine spatial pattern in freshwater fish diversity in relation to some environmental parameters. Our objective was to examine relationships between floodplain-lake fish communities and environmental variables associated with lake morphology, water chemistry and river–floodplain connectivity in a large river–floodplain ecosystem. During the study, a total of 18 237 fish were caught from 50 species (regional richness; 17 were migrants and 33 residents). In the present study, the most diverse order was Characiformes with 20 species, followed by Siluriformes, with 19 species. Characidae and Loricariidae were the richest families. The range of species richness (local richness) varied between five and 39 species. Similarity of local assemblages (using the presence–absence data) depends on the distance between lakes. A positive relationship was observed between the Ln of the total abundance of each species and the number of lakes where they were found. Out of all the environmental parameters taken in the lakes, only the size (Log Area) and relative perimeter length are significantly related to local assemblage species richness. It has not been possible to demonstrate that the connectivity (distance) from lakes to the main river can be considered a predictor of the local richness. Key Words: distance decay, fish, floodplain lakes, local richness, river INTRODUCTION Patterns of species co-occurrence have been widely investigated by ecologists (Jackson et al. 1992, Peres-Neto 2004). Fish communities are structured by effects working at a regional scale, where abiotic factors limit the species distributions; and at a local scale, where biotic factors determine species survival within a system (Gaston 2000, Thompson 2009). However, in highly variable aquatic systems, abiotic factors appear to be more important with little or no influence of biotic factors (Fisher & Lindenmayer 2002, Granado-Lorencio et al. 2007, Snodgrass et al. 1995, Suárez et al. 2004, Taylor & Warren 2001). In large tropical rivers, rainfall-driven hydrology is a key factor in the seasonality of aquatic environments (Sanderson et al. 2005). The flood-pulse concept (FPC) identifies seasonal hydrology as the major force structuring stream–fish assemblages (Araújo et al. 2009, Junk et al. 1989). During the flood pulse, the majority of water bodies become interconnected (floodplains) and the fish are free to disperse throughout the floodplain (Godoy et al. 1999). Floodplain lakes connected with the river by channels are open systems (Saint-Paul et al. 2000), and are typical ecotopes of large lowland rivers (Schomaker & Wolter 2011). In Neotropical floodplains, the flood cycle (pulse) associated with alteration of dry and rainy seasons produces major changes in fish communities (Rodríguez & Lewis 1994), and it acts as an intermediate disturbance. Because of high environmental variability, species assemblage organization has been portrayed as highly stochastic, without any apparent overall organizational pattern (Lowe-McConnell 1987, Lowe et al. 2006). However, more recent studies have seemingly found non-random associations of fishes within the floodplain (Petry et al. 2003, Winemiller 1996). Studies on the structure and dynamics of fish assemblages of permanent water bodies in different floodplain river systems indicate that these assemblages are structured by a combination of environmental variables, as well as by the pool of species available during the period in which the water bodies are permanently connected to the river (Fernandes et al. 2010). Certain environmental variables (hypoxia, depth, transparency, local-scale habitat, size and drainage area) have been considered to be good predictors of the richness of local associations of fish, within the floodplain (Montaña & Winemiller 2010). A study of the factors that control species richness in floodplain lakes requires information about the taxonomy and distribution of the species. Information is more extensive on fish species from temperate rivers and big tropical rivers than on fish species of floodplain lakes. Therefore, the first aim of this study was to catalogue fish species (ichthyofauna survey) and examine the fish richness in tropical floodplain lakes, during the high-water season. For this study, we selected 27 lakes from the Magdalena river, which vary in morphological and limnological characteristics. The fish caught were identified taxonomically and the sampling data were used to calculate the total abundance. The second aim was to determine the main factors that control local species richness (lake community). We test the following hypotheses: (1) there is an relationship between abundance and regional occupancy (%) in fish species of the floodplain lakes, (2) the area is related to the species richness of the lake (species–area relationship, SAR), (3) the distance to the main river (connectivity) is a predictive variable of local richness, and (4) the geographical distance between lakes has a relationship to the similarity in fish assemblages found in them (community similarity decay). METHODS The Magdalena River is 1612 km long and drains a 257 438-km² basin. The principal tributaries are the Cauca, Sogamoso, San Jorge and César Rivers. The average precipitation for the valley measured in run-off is 2050 mm y⁻¹. The lowest values are recorded for the December–January and July–August periods, and the highest between April–May and October–November (twice-yearly peak flooding). The annual mean discharge (data for 1975–1995) from the Magdalena River in the locality of Calamar (112 km upstream of the estuary) is 7200 m³ s⁻¹ (Restrepo & Jerfve 2000). The physical structure of the system comprises a meandering river channel with numerous connected and isolated lakes (lakes vary in size and degree of connection). The main types of habitats in floodplain lakes are herbaceous vegetation (aquatic macrophytes) and open water. The relative proportion of the habitats varies both regionally and seasonally. The whole middle and lower Magdalena River is not fragmented by dams and is still characterized by highly variable hydrological conditions. While some floodplain lakes become permanently cut off from the main flow of the river and remain closed (isolated), others remain open with perennial connection with the river. Twenty-seven connected lakes were studied, all in the midsection of the Magdalena River basin, between the localities of Puerto Boyacá and Barrancabermeja (840.92 km; Figure 1). The study area is centred at 6°04′N–7°26′N, 73°57′W–74°31′W (GPS derived). The selection was based on lake surface area and permanent connectivity with the main river. These lakes were selected to represent a range of size (4–2300 ha) and degree of human impact (Table 1). Lakes were sampled during the wet season, because of its near-maximum species richness and stability in water level. Ten lakes were sampled at the beginning of November 2008 (Palagua, Samaria, El Encanto, Rio Viejo, Barbacoas, Chucurí, El Opón, Juan Esteban, Tabacurú, Bija) and the remaining 17 in 2010, at the same month, coinciding with the second peak flooding. The sampling method was the same for all the lakes. Water parameters were measured for 24 h every 4 h. At each fishing site, dissolved oxygen concentration (DO in mg L⁻¹), water temperature (T in °C) and conductivity (μS) were measured in situ. DO (dissolved oxygen) and temperature were measured in the water column every metre. The maximum depth (m) of lakes was determined by sonar. For each lake, the area and perimeter length were calculated for the period of high water level. An index used to quantify this is called the shoreline development (DI). This index compares the minimum possible circumference of the lake, given a specific surface area (i.e. a perfect circle), to the actual circumference of the lake and its surface area. A value of 1 for shoreline development is a perfect circle and a larger value means that the shoreline is highly dissected. Lakes with high shoreline development are often naturally productive relative to those with low shoreline development. The shortest distance between lakes and the river were measured on maps (1: 100 000) from Google Earth. We use the length of the channel (measured in the field) that links the lake to the main river as a measure of connectivity; Tockner et al. (1999) consider that this distance is a good predictor for this structural variable. Prior to statistical analyses, all variables except pH and temperature were logarithmically transformed in order to approximate normal distributions. The measurements for environmental variables were analysed using a one-way ANOVA with the aim of discovering differences between periods, as well as between habitats for each period (Bonferroni correction included). In order to estimate the total species richness, sampling was designed for each of the various existing habitats. In all the lakes, one sampling station was chosen within each of these four macrohabitats: littoral with trees, littoral without trees, open water, and the connecting channel between the lake and main river. All were sampled simultaneously. Because sampling effort was constant across samples, it was not necessary to adjust richness estimates using rarefaction or other techniques to account for different sampling techniques or sample sizes. The fish were collected using experimental multifilament gillnets, formed from panels measuring 100 × 3 m, in nine different sizes (from 2 to 10 cm stretched mesh). This kind of technique for capture has been used in the studies of associations of fish in oxbow lakes (Winemiller et al. 2000). The nets were set out for 24 h, and checked every 4 h, with the intention of avoiding phenomena such as predators and decomposition due to the high temperature of the water. Fishes were classified as sedentary or short-distance migrant species based on available regional information. Catch per site was standardized according to the length of bank fished and the catch per unit effort (CPUE) determined as fish caught per 100 m. The standardized fish densities were used to calculate basic fish-assemblage metrics, like relative abundance (%) of species and richness. In all analyses for a lake, only the abundances and richness of taxa present at that lake were used. We used the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to test the occupancy-abundance relationship. We define the richness of species in a lake as local richness (LR, \( \alpha \)-diversity), and the analysis of all the lakes taken together as regional richness (RR, \( \gamma \)-diversity). We analysed the similarities of assemblages using only presence–absence data. Previous studies have shown that taxonomic patterns may differ when using the presence–absence or abundance data (La Sorte & McKinney 2007). In order to analyse whether the geographical distance between lakes has any relationship to the similarity in associations of fishes found in them (community similarity decay; Nekola & White 1999), the Sørensen index was applied (\( S = C/\alpha \); where C represents common species and \( \alpha \) the average richness for the two lakes), and the Figure 2.
