Daily GPP and R rates (open circles) with 95% CI and NEP (filled circles) are shown Respiration-production coupling and baseline respiration During spring 2015, daily values of GPP and R were closely coupled in Lake 4 loc. A–C and Lake 5 loc. A. Slopes for R (y) vs. GPP (x) ranged from 0.88 to 0.93 for most locations with deeper water and high charophyte biomass to only 0.62 for the shallow location with low charophyte cover (Fig. 6, S2). While the slope differed, the 95% CI of the intercepts (R_{base}) were not significantly different from zero in Lake 4 loc. A–C, which implies that background respiration was negligible. Despite being significantly positive, background respiration was very low in Lake 5 loc. A. Analysis of all four lakes during 9–10 days in June 2016 confirmed the close coupling between R and GPP with a common slope of 0.90 and a low intercept (−1.48 g O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹), which was not significantly different from zero (Fig. 6). This finding is in agreement with the analysis for individual lakes. Thus, in these shallow charophyte lakes, respiration is closely coupled to lake production on the same day and background respiration is low or negligible. Discussion Submerged macrophytes and temperature gradients The present analysis confirmed that small, shallow lakes with dense macrophyte vegetation undergo extreme diel temperature cycles (Andersen et al. 2016). Large diel variations in surface water temperatures at about 15 °C are possible due to a shallow mixed surface layer and high light attenuation. The observed high diel temperature range is not uncommon among small lakes (Woolway et al. 2016). Steep vertical stratification also developed during the day as a result of high light absorption in the dense charophyte canopy, while cooling of surface waters during the evening and night induced convective mixing (Andersen et al. 2016). Although it has previously been shown that submerged macrophyte stands can induce large temperature gradients (Dale and Gillespie 1977), the magnitude of temperature gradients demonstrated here for such shallow water columns is much greater than anticipated and unprecedented in previous studies. Because of the high submerged macrophyte biomass, the stratification-mixing cycle is a recurring daily phenomenon. Only modest surface heating is required for daytime stratification to develop as wind induced turbulence is rapidly dissipated by the charophyte canopy (Andersen et al. 2016). Daytime stratification was only absent on very cold, windy or rainy days during spring–summer. Modeling ecosystem metabolism A consequence of diel stratification is that the oxygen signal recorded from surface waters only reflects processes in the mixed surface layer during the day, but the entire water column at night. This should not affect our estimate of GPP because light only penetrates few centimeters into the Fig. 6 Linear relationship of daily rates of R (g O$_2$ m$^{-3}$ day$^{-1}$) versus GPP (g O$_2$ m$^{-3}$ day$^{-1}$) in Lakes 4, 5 (2015) along with the four lakes studied during 2016 (*solid line*, standard major axis regression). Shown are 95% CI (*grey area*) and the 1:1 linear relationship (*dotted line*). Rates are per unit volume and normalized to 20 °C. Regression parameter estimates of intercept (R$_{base}$) and slope (β) with 95% CI in parenthesis are: Lake 4 loc. A: R$_{base}$ = 0.05 (−1.4–1.4) and β = 0.88 (0.82–0.95), Lake 5 loc. A: R$_{base}$ = 1.36 (0.29–2.39) and β = 0.90 (0.86–0.95) and Lakes 1, 2, 3 and 4 (2016): R$_{base}$ = −1.48 (−5.25–1.96) and β = 0.90 (0.82–0.98) ![Scatter plots showing the linear relationship between R and GPP for Lakes 4 and 5, and Lakes 1, 2, 3, and 4, with regression lines and 95% confidence intervals.](page_1042_180_1012_1682.png) charophyte canopy owing to high light attenuation, which is also the main driver of thermocline development. Oxygen produced by photosynthesis is released to the mixed surface layer, and production below the thermocline is negligible. Respiration is estimated at night when photosynthesis is zero and the water column is well mixed and thus should encompass all ecosystem components, seeing that the nocturnal convective mixing is quite efficient (Andersen et al. 2016). Overestimation of NEP could occur when respiratory processes in bottom waters do not influence the oxygen signal recorded in surface waters during stratification. In Lake 4 during 2016, water volume below the thermocline constituted only 8–14% of the total volume. Therefore, estimates of lake metabolism by the described procedure include the relevant major components and processes. This conclusion is supported by the close agreement between observed and modeled diel oxygen signals, with generally narrow 95% CI’s. The observed oxygen signal in surface waters was well predicted by using the applied model (Eqs. 2–7). On most days, uncertainty of metabolism estimates was well constrained by the bootstrap analysis. Variation between observed and modeled oxygen signals may arise from processes not included in the model (Eq. 2), such as advective mixing or respiratory substrate limitation (McNair et al. 2013). Modeling the gas transfer velocity as a function of wind may also introduce error due to the fact that near-surface turbulence in small lakes is influenced by convective mixing (Read et al. 2012). Convective mixing is driven by heat loss from surface waters and, with the high diel temperature range observed in the investigated lakes, convective mixing could contribute to near-surface turbulence (Holgerson et al. 2016; MacIntyre et al. 2010). However, the applied empirical model was the best available for use in small lakes within the size range investigated here; it was derived from previous measurements in Lake 4 (Andersen 2015). High rates of ecosystem metabolism The summer metabolic rates reported here are probably close to annual maximum rates because temperature and irradiance were both high. Volumetric metabolic rates estimated in this study are very high compared to values from other aquatic systems (Duarte and Agustí 1998; Solomon et al. 2013). The high volumetric metabolic rates are attributed to the high charophyte biomass, shallow photic zone and high light availability in the upper canopy. Fig. 7 Aquatic ecosystem metabolism showing GPP versus R during summer for a data compilation from different aquatic ecosystems (Hoellein et al. 2013). Filled circles are daily rates of metabolism from measurements on shallow charophyte lakes during May and June in the present study (n = 111). The data ranges in the different ecosystems are enclosed within the covered areas Metabolic rates normalized to area are also high compared to other aquatic ecosystems (Fig. 7), because of the high proportion of incident irradiance absorbed by photosynthetic pigments. Absorption in these clear lakes not owing to photosynthetic pigments is likely to stem from precipitated CaCO₃ as well as associated colored components on the surfaces of charophytes. The high volumetric rates of production result in high demands for dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) in surface waters. The charophyte lakes are located on calcareous rock and have average DIC concentrations of 0.7–2.7 mM mainly available for photosynthesis in the form of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Free CO₂ has been shown to be used five to six times more readily than HCO₃⁻ by the dominant charophyte species (Chara aspera) in the lakes (Van den Berg et al. 2002), which requires active ion-transport (Lucas and Berry 1985). Bicarbonate is present typically in 10- to 100-fold higher concentrations in the charophyte lakes, and is the most important and stable source of inorganic carbon to charophyte photosynthesis (Madsen and Sand-Jensen 1991). The continuously high GPP rates in the charophyte lakes are unlike those of deep lakes with seasonal stratification in which gradual epilimnetic depletion of nutrients and DIC increasingly limits primary production during summer (Brighenti et al. 2015; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). In the charophyte lakes, photosynthesis can be constrained by reduced DIC in the afternoon (Andersen 2015), but the DIC pool is re-established by nocturnal mixing because CaCO₃ is dissolved and organic matter is degraded in the bottom waters during the stratification period. Thus, regeneration of DIC and nutrients, mixing and reinjection of resources into surface waters are daily recurring phenomena, which can sustain high GPP rates. During the summer 2016, volumetric rates of GPP and R in Lake 2 averaged at 74 (range 50–92) and 65 (range 39–90) g O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹, respectively (Table 2). These values correspond to oxygen pool turnover times of only 3.4–3.8 h. Despite a shorter turnover time of the oxygen pool than the duration of the night (5.5–6 h summer 2016), Lake 2 did not turn anoxic, though nocturnal oxygen minima were low. The lack of anoxia was probably due to enhanced gas exchange as surface water oxygen decreased and respiratory substrate limitation as previously demonstrated by large nocturnal decline of ecosystem respiration in free-water measurements in Lake 4, and confirmed by charophyte respiration in bottle incubations (Andersen 2015). Net ecosystem production Positive NEP values imply that ecosystems are net autotrophic and have a production surplus which can be incorporated into additional charophyte biomass, or accumulated in the sediment as organic matter (Staehr et al. 2012). Solomon et al. (2013) found that mean summer NEP values in 25 globally distributed lakes ranged between −7.3 and 9.9 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹ [−7.0 and 1.5 for lakes with total-P < 20 L⁻¹, Hoellein et al. (2013)]. The charophyte lakes studied here have oligotrophic waters and most nutrients are incorporated into charophyte biomass and buried in the sediments (Christensen et al. 2013). From this analysis, it cannot be concluded whether these charophyte lakes are net autotrophic or net heterotrophic on an annual scale, but they are probably close to zero or slightly net autotrophic as shown previously for Lake 4 (Christensen et al. 2013). Only thin sediments have built up in the deeper parts during the lakes’ 30 years of existence, and it shows that storage of organic carbon and dead charophyte fragments within the systems are low. Allochthonous organic carbon would contribute to this storage, but is low due to the sparse terrestrial vegetation and the restricted water input. An earlier study of a charophyte lake on Räpplinge alvar also found that NEP was slightly positive during spring and early summer (0.2–1.4 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹), but negative during desiccation in mid-summer and positive again in August in the time of refilling (Christensen et al. 2013). For the period studied here, the water depth did not reach the critical threshold in the deeper charophyte lakes. NEP ranged between −0.8 and 4.8 g O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹, but was predominantly positive. However, as a result of desiccation, periods of negative NEP were observed in the shallow Lake 3 and the shallow location Lake 5 loc. B during summer 2015. Measurements show that sediment respiration is low in the charophyte lakes (Andersen 2015). The positive NEP is mainly utilized by the charophytes for growth. Converting previously measured sediment respiration from Lake 4 (Andersen 2015) at 15°C to diel mean temperature, applying a Q_{10} value of 2.0 for the summer 2016, revealed that sediment respiration (R_{sed}) constituted, on average, 12% of total ecosystem respiration during the period in Lake 4 (Fig. 5). Respiration in free water is negligible and the main driver of both GPP and R is the large charophyte biomass (Andersen 2015). Assuming that respiration is only a result of charophytes (R_{Chara}) and sediments (R_{sed}), the net charophyte production (NP_{Chara}) can be estimated as NP_{Chara} = NEP + R_{sed}. For the 2016 summer period, this yields mean NEP values of 1.8 and NP_{Chara} of 2.6 g O_2 m^{-2} day^{-1}. This surplus is at the same level as the possible daily increase of charophyte biomass in g organic dry matter m^{-2}, which is equivalent to a biomass accumulation of about 200–300 g organic dry matter m^{-2} over 4 months in agreement with the measured level of charophyte biomass. Similar levels were reported by Christensen et al. (2013). R-GPP coupling and baseline respiration By applying regression analysis, a close coupling of R and GPP daily estimates was found. This finding was supported by data from Lake 4 and 5 in spring 2015 as well as Lake 1, 2, 3 and 4 in summer 2016. The very low or zero background respiration implies that terrestrial contribution to ecosystem metabolism is low or negligible during the spring–summer periods in the five charophyte lakes. The pool of more recalcitrant organic matter would likely consist of particulate matter from the sparse terrestrial vegetation, but otherwise be dominated by detritus from dead charophytes. Tight R-GPP coupling has previously been shown in nutrient-poor lakes (Richardson et al. 2016; Sadro et al. 2011; Solomon et al. 2013), as well as in Spanish shallow lakes with high metabolic rates (Geertz-Hansen et al. 2011). As a result of the small lake sizes, low horizontal heterogeneity of metabolism estimates was expected. Previous studies in larger lakes have found substantial spatial variation of metabolism within lakes (Lauster et al. 2006; Van de Bogert et al. 2012), which suggests that the mixed surface layer is not necessarily well mixed horizontally, or that the rates of turbulence are low compared to the local differences of metabolism. The shallow location C in Lake 4 is different from location A, B and D by being susceptible to desiccation resulting in a less dense and shorter charophyte canopy. This difference could explain the high GPP relative to R at this location. When self-shading is low in the canopy it will require less respiration in order to sustain the lower biomass. Comparison of ecosystem metabolism across aquatic systems A recent comprehensive study compiled estimates of ecosystem metabolism in different aquatic systems (Hoellein et al. 2013), for which we have added metabolic rates from the present study of shallow vegetated lakes (Fig. 7). The small oligotrophic vegetated lakes studied here do not fit the expectation that GPP should increase along a gradient of total P concentration as observed in larger lakes (Hanson et al. 2008; Solomon et al. 2013). The very low phosphate levels measured in Lake 3 and 4 are likely characteristic for all the investigated lakes located within short distances on the nutrient-poor alvar. The pattern can be explained by the dominance of benthic primary producers in the small lakes in contrast to the dominance of pelagic production by phytoplankton in larger, deeper lakes (Kalff 2002). Daily GPP is positively related to daily incident light utilized by a high density of photosynthetic pigments. The biomass of phytoplankton communities is often nutrient limited and is much higher in eutrophic than oligotrophic lakes (Kalff 2002). Maximum rates of photosynthesis relative to absorbed light are, however, comparable for phytoplankton- and submerged macrophyte communities (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998). As a result, the same high areal rates of GPP can be reached in dense charophyte stands in shallow, oligotrophic lakes as in deeper phytoplankton-rich water columns of eutrophic lakes (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998). Previous studies have shown that small lakes are active sites of carbon processing and atmospheric carbon emission compared to medium-sized and large lakes (Holgerson and Raymond 2016; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Their role in global carbon budgets is open to debate because of the uncertainties associated with the estimation of the number and surface area of small lakes (Downing et al. 2006; Verpoorter et al. 2014). Using the areas for small lakes (<0.01 km^2) and larger lakes (>0.01 km^2) reported by Downing et al. (2006), and the median areal GPP and R reported in this study and the lakes compiled in Hoellein et al. (2013), show that 30 and 21% of the global lake GPP and R may take place in small lakes. The values of GPP in the small, shallow lakes dominated by submerged macrophytes are probably higher than for many small lakes devoid of macrophytes. Nonetheless, the evaluation supports the notion that small aquatic systems are very important components of global carbon processing. Large fractionations of C and H isotopes related to methane oxidation in Arctic lakes Sarah B. Cadieux a,*, Jeffrey R. White b, Peter E. Sauer a, Yongbo Peng a,1, Amy E. Goldman a,b,2, Lisa M. Pratt a a Department of Geological Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA b School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA Received 14 November 2015; accepted in revised form 3 May 2016; available online 9 May 2016 Abstract Microbial oxidation of methane (CH4) plays a central role in carbon cycling in Arctic lakes, reducing potential CH4 emissions associated with warming. Isotopic signatures of CH4 (δ13C and δ2H) are indicators of microbial oxidation, wherein the process strongly enriches 13C and 2H in residual CH4. We present δ13C and δ2H measurements obtained from sampling the water column and sediment for dissolved CH4 from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland under both open-water and ice-covered conditions from 2013 to 2014. Despite substantial variations in aquatic chemistry among the lakes, δ13C and δ2H of CH4 suggested that CH4 was produced predominantly by acetoclastic methanogenesis in the littoral sediments and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. Surprisingly large variations for both δ13C and δ2H of CH4 were observed, with δ13C extending from −72‰ to +7.4‰ and δ2H from −390‰ to +250‰. The CH4 isotopic values reported here were significantly more enriched (p < 0.0001) in both 13C and 2H than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments. As is characteristic of methanotrophy, the enrichment in 13C and 2H was associated with low CH4 concentrations. We suggest that the CH4 most enriched in 13C and 2H may reflect unusually efficient methanotrophic communities in Arctic ice-margin lakes. This study provides the first measurement of δ2H for CH4 in an Arctic freshwater environment at concentrations <10 μM. The extreme enrichment of 13C and 2H of CH4 from Arctic methanotrophy has significant implications for interpreting sources and sinks of CH4. Without knowledge of local geology, stable isotope values of CH4 higher than −30‰ for δ13C and −150‰ for δ2H could be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic origins. Given crystalline bedrock and the strong positive correlation between δ13C and δ2H throughout the water columns in three Arctic lakes confirms that CH4 heavily enriched in 13C and 2H is the result of methanotrophy. Keywords: Methane; Hydrogen isotopes; Carbon isotopes; Arctic; Lakes 1. INTRODUCTION Small lakes (<10 km^2) represent approximately half of the total area of surface water in Arctic environments (Abnizova et al., 2012) and emit more methane (CH4) per unit area than larger lakes (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009; Downing, 2010). Microbial oxidation of CH4 is an important process in freshwater ecosystems, reincorporating CH4 back into the biogeochemical carbon cycle rather than being released as CH4 into the atmosphere. In northern lakes, up to 88% of the CH4 produced by microbes is oxidized by methanotrophs (Kankaala et al., 2006, 2007; Bastviken et al., 2008; López Bellido et al., 2009), leaving low concentrations of CH4 in surface water of lakes. Due to the challenge of reliably measuring stable isotope abundances at very low concentrations, the effect of methanotrophic oxidation on isotopes of CH4 in Arctic lakes has not previously been reported. The combination of concentration and isotopic signature is vital for understanding biogeochemical cycling of CH4 on Earth and for assessing pathways for production and oxidation of CH4 on Mars where episodic plumes of CH4 at low concentrations have been detected remotely and measured by instruments on martian rovers. In anticipation of returning samples from Mars to Earth and with increasing interest in astronauts as explorers on Mars, it is urgent to assess geochemical and/or biological processes influencing rates of CH4 formation and destruction (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Kinetic isotope effects associated with enzymatic processes during methanogenesis and methanotrophy are well established terrestrial biomarkers and are potential martian biomarkers for subsurface life. Measuring CH4 concentrations and CH4 fluxes are useful to assess the magnitude of emissions, but alone are unable to be used to decipher active production and pathways. Stable isotopic analysis of carbon (δ13C) and hydrogen (δ2H) is a well-established method to delineate the origin of CH4 gas, allowing for the differentiation of CH4 produced by microbial and thermal processes as well as microbial production and oxidation (Schoell, 1980; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Despite a wide range of literature using 13C and 2H to interpret origin and thermal maturity of hydrocarbons in petroleum systems (Stahl and Carey, 1975; Schoell, 1980, 1988; Whiticar, 1989; Jackson et al., 2014), there has been limited work on δ13C and δ2H of CH4 in natural environments, most of which has been focused on wetlands (Martens et al., 1992; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Sugimoto and Fujita, 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). Biogenic CH4 in freshwater environments is produced predominantly within anoxic sediments and is exported into the water column by ebullition (bubbling) or diffusion (Strayer and Tiedje, 1978; Bastviken et al., 2008). Microbial CH4 is produced by methanogens, strictly anaerobic Archaea, who are responsible for 10–50% of overall carbon mineralization in freshwater lakes (Bastviken et al., 2008). In freshwater environments, there are two primary metabolic pathways for CH4 production, acetoclastic methanogenesis (AM) and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM), which have been demonstrated to vary spatially in permafrost-influenced ecosystems (Prater et al., 2007). Both AM and HM are associated with a kinetic isotope effect resulting in depletion of 13C in the product CH4 relative to the pre-cursor substrate (Whiticar et al., 1986; Balabane et al., 1987; Valentine et al., 2004a,b). However, the magnitude of the carbon isotope effect is different for the two primary methanogenic pathways, with AM resulting in δ13CCH4 ranging from −60‰ to −40‰, and HM ranging from −110‰ to −60‰ (Whiticar et al., 1986). Hydrogen isotopes of CH4 similarly become depleted in 2H during microbial CH4 production. The δ2H value of CH4 depends on the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is either from cleavage of H2O or acetate (Woltemate et al., 1984; Whiticar, 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Although this remains contentious, it is generally assumed that during HM, all 4 H atoms are supplied by formation water, whereas during AM, the transfer of the methyl group to CH4 supplies 3 H atoms, and the additional H atom is derived from formation water (Whiticar et al., 1986). As a result, the magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect of hydrogen is different for the two pathways, dependent on value of precursor δ2H, with AM resulting in δ2HCH4 ranging from −530‰ to −250‰, and HM ranging from −250‰ to −170‰ (Sugimoto and Wada, 1995). The isotope systematics of hydrogen for homoacetogenesis in competition with methanogenesis under substrate-limiting conditions and low temperatures of natural systems is not well known (Kotsyurbenko et al., 2001), although culture studies suggest that there is rapid hydrogen isotope exchange between H2 and H2O during homoacetogenesis (Valentine et al., 2004a,b). Methane oxidation (MOx) depends on both the availability of CH4 and dissolved oxygen (DO); high CH4 oxidation rates are usually found at the oxic/anoxic interface where both CH4 and DO are abundant (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) can also occur by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors in lieu of dissolved oxygen (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). High affinity methanotrophs are able to oxidize CH4 at or below atmospheric concentrations (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Isotope fractionation associated with microbial CH4 oxidation leads to systematic enrichment in both 13C and 2H of CH4 in the residual un-oxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). The enrichment in both 13C and 2H during oxidation results in values being increased by <1–30‰ for δ13CCH4 and 3–200‰ for δ2HCH4 (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Bastviken et al., 2002). In this study, we report values of δ13C and δ2H for CH4 collected from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland to assess seasonal sources and sinks of CH4. Lakes were sampled during open-water conditions in July 2013 and under ice-cover in April 2014 when the lakes had been ice-covered and isolated from the atmosphere for 7–8 months. The studied lakes show considerable variation in concentration and proportions of major ions despite being located along a 6 km segment of a narrow valley. Therefore, we hypothesize that due to chemical heterogeneity, sources and sinks of CH4 in each lake would vary lake-to-lake as well as seasonally. Hundreds of thousands of Holocene lakes dot the landscape in southwestern Greenland (Anderson et al., 2001; Anderson and Stedmon, 2007) and are underlain by continuous permafrost (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Deglaciation began in the region ~11,000 BP (Van Tatenhove and van der Meer, 1996; Leng et al., 2012), exposing Precambrian metamorphic crystalline bedrock, primarily felsic gneisses (Jensen et al., 2002). As a result, CH4 in these lakes has had little to no influence from buried ancient organic matter, allowing biogenic CH4 cycles to be studied in isolation. To our knowledge, this work provides the first coupled measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 under both open-water and ice-covered conditions in a relatively undisturbed, periglacial, lacustrine setting thereby filling critical knowledge gaps concerning biogeochemical cycles of CH4 within small Arctic lakes and isotope fractionation of CH4 in low concentration environments. 2. STUDY AREA Lakes in this study are located between the village of Kangerlussuaq, Greenland at the head of Søndre Strømfjord and the active terminus of the Russell Glacier (Fig. 1). During the last Glacial Maximum, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) covered the area. Retreat of the GIS likely resulted in formation of the lakes in glacially scoured hollows (Leng et al., 2012). Currently, the margin of the GIS is ~2 km away from the study lakes. The region has continuous permafrost <50 cm below the surface, extending down to 130 m at Kangerlussuaq and 500 m at the edge of the ice sheet (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Bedrock is predominantly garnet-grade, Archean gneisses with Quaternary glacial, fluvial and alluvial deposits present in low-lying areas. Mean annual air temperature at the Kangerlussuaq weather station from 1974 to 2012 was −6 °C. During warm months of late May to early September, mean temperatures often exceed +11 °C and peak to +20 °C in July. The cold season extends from November to late March, with mean daily temperature averaging −21 °C in February. Precipitation in the Kangerlussuaq area is minimal, with annual precipitation <150 mm yr−1, mostly from June to August (Ohmura and Reeh, 1991). Dwarf shrubs (Salix, Vaccinium and Betula), Sphagnum spp., and graminoids (Carex and Calamagrostis) dominate the tundra vegetation in the region. 2.1. Study lakes In this paper three, small adjacent lakes (surface area <3 ha, maximum depth <8 m) with a range of different morphometries and aquatic chemistries (Fig. 1; Table 1) are studied. Lake names used herein are informal names. The study lakes are part of a series of lakes within a narrow valley overlying a structural shear zone extending from the Russell Glacier to the Søndre Strømfjord (Fig. 1). The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (\( Z_{\text{max}} \)), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L\(^{-1}\)), pH, and specific conductivity (\( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column \( CH_4 \) collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and \( CH_4 \) was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved \( CH_4 \) in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment \( CH_4 \) Profundal sediment samples were taken from \( Z_{\text{max}} \) of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Sediment was collected in polycarbonate plastic barrels with an internal diameter of 6.7 cm. Dissolved gas in the sediment was sampled using an equilibrium gas stripping method similar to the water-column CH₄ (Section 3.1.2.1). Sediment cores were subsectioned into 6–10 cm intervals and put into 8 L Nalgene bottles, with lids altered to include two syringe ports connected to Luer-Lock fittings. Once the sediment was put into the bottle and the lid was shut, the bottle was evacuated using a hand pump connected to a lid port. After evacuation, zero-CH₄ water was injected to create a 4 L sediment–water slurry. The bottle was vigorously shaken for 5 min to displace gas from the sediment-slurry into the headspace. 3.1.4. Littoral sediment CH₄ Littoral sediment gas samples were collected during open-water conditions by physically disturbing the sediment in order to release entrained gas bubbles. Each sample was collected from a vegetated region where water depth was <0.5 m. Gas bubbles were collected using an inverted plastic funnel (28 cm diameter) with a gas-tight sampling tube and 3-way Luer-Lock valve attached to the neck. Gas in the funnel was transferred to a Cali-5-Bond bag using a plastic syringe. Note that we were unable to quantify the volume of sediment sampled. Consequently, concentrations of CH₄ in gas collected from littoral sediments cannot be converted into pool size of CH₄ in the littoral sediments. Rather, the samples were used to constrain the isotopic composition of CH₄ present in the littoral sediments (Chanton, 2005). 3.2. Laboratory methods 3.2.1. Concentration of CH₄ Concentration of water-column CH₄ and sediment CH₄ was measured using a Los Gatos Research (LGR) Methane Carbon Isotope Analyzer (MCIA) (LGR, Mountain View CA, USA) at the Kangerlussuaq International Science Support facility (KISS). The LGR MCIA is a portable, off-axis, integrated cavity output spectrometer that measures CH₄ without sample preparation. All samples were processed within 24 h of collection. For each analysis, 400–600 mL of gas sample was required. Calibration was repeated every 10 samples, with Scotty® gas standards of 50 and 100 ppmv CH₄. Samples were diluted with a known volume of zero-air in order to bring them within the range of the calibration gases. The total concentration of CH₄ in each sample was corrected for dilution and calculated from the sum of the measured headspace partial pressure and the dissolved CH₄ remaining after gas stripping, calculated according to Henry’s law using values after Lide and Fredrikse (1995). Instrumental uncertainty of CH₄ from the MCIA was ±0.5 ppmv, which is one standard deviation of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. Previously, concentrations of CH₄ from MCIA were analyzed on a Gas Chromatograph Flame Ionization Detector (GC-FID) to confirm validity (Appendix 2). Aliquots of each sample were transferred to pre-evacuated glass vials and returned to Indiana University, USA for carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄. 3.3. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄ Stable C and H isotopes of CH₄ were analyzed using two approaches. MCIA was used for C isotopic analysis on samples with CH₄ concentrations >50 ppmv, but the MCIA produces unreliable results at lower concentrations (Appendix 3). Therefore, stable isotope ratios of both carbon and hydrogen of CH₄ were measured using continuous-flow gas chromatography-oxidation/pyrolysis isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-ox/pyr-IRMS) with a laboratory-built gas pre-concentrator interfaced with a ThermoFinnigan GCC and Delta Plus XP IRMS at the Stable Isotope Research Facility (SIRF) at Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana. The pre-concentrator design was modeled after principles described by Merritt et al. (1995) and inlet system developed by Miller et al. (2002) for carbon isotope analysis and Brass and Rockmann (2010) for carbon and hydrogen isotopes. The gas sample containing CH₄ is first dried by passing through a cold trap and then passed into a stainless steel sample loop packed with HayeSep D and kept at −130 °C. After the CH₄ is extracted, the trap is warmed to −20 °C and the CH₄ is cryofocused at the head of Varian Porabond Q GC column. Carbon of CH₄ is converted to CO₂ at 950 °C and H is converted to H₂ in an alumina reactor at 1450 °C. Carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios are expressed in standard δ notation (δ¹³C and δ²H): \[ \delta = [(R_{\text{sample}} - R_{\text{standard}})/R_{\text{standard}}] \times 1000 = \%o \] where \( R \) is the molar ratio of heavy to light isotopes (¹³C/¹²C, ²H/¹H) for both sample and standard. Carbon isotope values are referenced to VPDB and hydrogen isotope values are referenced to VSMOW by comparison with pure CH₄ where the isotopic composition has been measured by off-line combustion (http://mypage.iu.edu/~aschimme/compounds.html). Instrumental uncertainty of δ¹³C and δ²H from the GC-C-IRMS was calculated as ±0.4‰ and as ±10‰ respectively, which is one standard deviation for repeated measures of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. 3.4. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were made using IBM SPSS Statistics. Combined concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic compositions for all study lakes during each season were assessed for normal distribution via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and were found to be non-normally distributed. Student’s t tests of unequal variance were used for testing statistically significant differences in concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic values of CH₄ between seasons and between study results and reported isotopic values from other natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude. Systematic changes in δ¹³C and δ²H were analyzed using linear regression, based upon the pathway of oxidation leading to systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of CH₄ in the residual unoxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). 4. RESULTS 4.1. Water-column CH₄ 4.1.1. Concentration of CH₄ Under open-water conditions, concentrations of CH₄ were strongly related to DO dynamics (Fig. 2). Dissolved CH₄ concentrations in the surface waters of the three lakes ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 µM (Fig. 3). Clinograde DO profiles were measured in EVV Upper and Potentilla lakes with DO saturated in surface water (9.5 and 11.0 mg L⁻¹ respectively), and decreasing with depth to anoxia (<0.5 mg L⁻¹; Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column with decreasing DO, with the maximum CH₄ observed in the anoxic water at the sediment–water interface (150 and 67 µM respectively). Teardrop lake was oxic to suboxic (DO > 1 mg L⁻¹) throughout the water column with an oxygen anomaly at 4.0 m, wherein DO drastically shifted from >10 mg L⁻¹ at 3.5 m to 1.8 mg L⁻¹ at 4 m, and then returned to 7 mg L⁻¹ at 4.5 m. Throughout the water column of Teardrop lake, there were low CH₄ concentrations (<8.1 µM; Fig. 3). In all three lakes, concentrations of CH₄ were significantly greater under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (n = 31, p = 0.0002). A downward increase in CH₄ concentration from below ice-cover to the sediment–water interface was measured in all three lakes under ice-covered conditions (Fig. 3). Potentilla lake was the only lake with measurable DO under ice-cover (Fig. 3). Consequently, CH₄ concentrations dynamically followed DO with highest concentrations (220 µM) observed within the anoxic bottom waters and decreasing concentrations tracking increasing dissolved DO upward through the water column until concentrations of CH₄ reached levels <1 µM immediately below the ice (Fig. 3). EVV Upper and Teardrop lakes were entirely anoxic below ice-cover with concentrations of CH₄ >50 µM throughout the water column (Fig. 3). 4.1.2. \( \delta^{13}C \) of water-column CH₄ Under open-water conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the three lakes ranged from −68.7‰ to +7.4‰ (Fig. 3). In both EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ was enriched in \( ^{13}C \) in the surface waters relative to the bottom waters (Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake, CH₄ became depleted in \( ^{13}C \) by 20‰ down the water column, with \( \delta^{13}C \) decreasing from −48.1‰ at the surface to −68.7‰ at 5.0 m depth. The depletion of CH₄ in \( ^{13}C \) in EVV Upper lake down the water column corresponded with an increase in CH₄ concentration (Fig. 3). In Teardrop lake, CH₄ in the surface water was more depleted in \( ^{13}C \) compared to bottom waters (Fig. 3). An overall enrichment of 10‰ was observed down the water column, with \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) increasing from −47.4‰ at the surface to −36.5‰ at 5.0 m. At 4.0 m depth, an anomalously heavy \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) value of +7.4‰ was observed (Fig. 3). In Potentilla lake, with the exception of 2.0 m, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) was stable from the surface down the water column to 6.0 m. From 4.0 m to 7.0 m, \( \delta^{13}C \) of CH₄ became enriched by 28‰, with \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) increasing from −52.6‰ to −24.5‰ (Fig. 3). From 7.0 m to 7.25 m, a depletion of 43‰ was observed, corresponding with a sharp increase in CH₄ concentration (Fig. 3). Under ice-covered conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) values ranged from −72.2‰ to −33.2‰ (Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) was stable throughout the water column, ranging from −72.2‰ to −71.3‰, corresponding with stable CH₄ concentrations. The \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in Teardrop lake was also relatively stable, ranging from −59.1‰ to −56.3‰. However, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column. Isotopic evidence of production pathways for CH4 in Greenlandic lakes Bedrock in the Kangerlussuaq region consists of tightly folded, felsic gneisses exposed to garnet-grade metamorphism and contains no measurable organic C, therefore we assume that all CH4 within the study lakes is biologically produced. To look at differences in microbial production of CH4, we focus our discussion on the sediment CH4 in the study lakes from open-water conditions. In order to distinguish AM and HM CH4 production pathways from each other isotopically, isotopic compositions of H2O, dissolved inorganic matter (DIC), and organic matter (OM) must be constant. If not, the variation in δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 reflect not only different production pathways, but also variation in environmental factors that affect isotopic composition of reactants. In the study lakes, δ2H2O in the water column slightly decreases with distance away from the margin of the GIS, from a median of −91.5‰ in EVV Upper lake to −97.4‰ in Potentilla lake. Despite the spatial variation in δ2H2O among the lakes, there is no significant relationship between δ2H2O from the water column and δ2HCH4 from sediments (Fig. 5), suggesting that δ2HCH4 is not a direct reflection of variation in 2H2O. In addition to differences in δ2H2O among the lakes, there are also variations in δ13CDIC from the water column among the lakes (Stern et al., 2014). However, there is not enough data to confirm or deny if δ13CCH4 is reflecting variation in δ13CDIC. Approximately a 5‰ difference in δ13COM of particulate OM from profundal sediments was observed lake-to-lake, ranging from −29.2‰ in EVV Upper lake to −24.5‰ (Table 1). Data suggest that the ~45‰ difference in δ13CCH4 of profundal sediment may reflect the δ13COM of precursor OM (Fig. 5b). However, the range in δ13COM is narrow compared to the overall range observed in aquatic chemistry and δ13CCH4 among the lakes. In both the profundal and littoral sediments of the study lakes, values of δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 are consistent with microbial CH4 production (Fig. 4) (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Profundal sediment CH4 is more depleted in 13C and enriched in 2H relative to littoral sediment CH4 (Table 2), suggesting different microbial production pathways, partial oxidation of the littoral sediments, or higher precursor δ13COM in the littoral sediments. However, δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 values from both profundal and littoral sediments plot primarily within the AM field (Fig. 4). The HM pathway field in the δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 classification diagram was determined from marine samples where δ2H2O is ~0‰ (Whiticar, 1999; Waldron et al., 1999b). As a result, the HM pathway field may not accurately represent Arctic waters where δ2H2O ≪ 0‰. Using the assumptions from Chanton et al. (2006), we can adjust the measured sediment δ2HCH4 for the δ2H2O of the water in the lake where the CH4 was formed using the following equation: \[ \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-measured}} - \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\text{ water}} = \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-adjusted}} \] In order to use this equation, δ2HCH4 in the sediments must reflect CH4 production without isotopic overprinting from oxidation. If CH4 in the sediments was subjected to oxidation then a positive correlation between δ13CCH4 and δ²HCH₄ would be observed (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). An inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ from sediments, confirming CH₄ in the sediments had not been oxidized (Fig. 4). The adjustment for δ²H₂O shifted δ²HCH₄ of profundal sediments into the HM pathways field, whereas the littoral sediment δ²HCH₄ remains primarily in the AM pathway field (Fig. 6). Without δ¹³COM in the littoral sediments of each lake, we are unable to assess if the variations between the sediments are the result of different microbial pathways, or if there is also variations in precursor OM. However, δ¹³COM and C/N ratios of littoral sediments from EVV Upper lake suggested OM is sourced from in-lake primary production (Thompson, 2015). The difference in CH₄ production pathway between the littoral and profundal sediments likely reflects the supply of labile organic compounds and δ¹³COM, which would influence CH₄ formation (Duc et al., 2010). In the littoral sediments, aquatic macrophytes and phytoplankton supply a source of labile OM, resulting in AM. Correspondingly, the lake with the highest CH₄ concentrations in the littoral sediments (EVV Upper lake) has the highest concentration of aquatic macrophytes, with the shoreline dominated by Hippuris vulgaris. In freshwater environments, CH₄ typically is produced by AM (Whiticar et al., 1986; Conrad, 1999) because plant root exudates and fresh OM provide a ready supply of labile OM to the bacteria. Previous theoretical values predict that HM accounts for ~30% of overall CH₄ production in freshwater lakes (Conrad, 1999). In high-latitude Sphagnum bogs, CH₄ production via HM is dominant because of an inhibition of the AM pathway, whereas AM is dominant in Carex-rich environments (Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Sphagnum spp. was a significant component of littoral communities of lakes in this study. In closed lake basins, OM from these areas may represent important carbon inputs, which could be influencing the HM pathway for CH₄ production in the profundal sediments. We were surprised to discover that despite significant variations in DOC, SO₄²⁻ and conductivity among the lakes, formation pathways of CH₄ in littoral and profundal sediments seem to be identical in all of the lakes. Competition for substrates (particularly acetate and H₂) favors sulfate reduction (SR), inhibiting CH₄ production (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Ward and Winfrey, 1985; Scholten et al., 2002). Methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased because SR can very effectively uptake both H₂ and acetate, maintaining H₂ and acetate concentrations too low for methanogens (Lovely and Klung, 1986). In the study lakes, EVV Upper lake has the highest SO₄²⁻ concentrations and is the only lake with detectable H₂S in the water column during open-water conditions (Table 1). The presence and accumulation of CH₄ in the sediments indicates that there is sufficient carbon to both fuel reduction of the SO₄²⁻ pool and support methanogenesis in EVV Upper lake. Given the current data, there is no way to assess if communities are spatially coexisting or separated by vertical stratification. However, EVV Upper lake does have the lowest concentration of CH₄ in the profundal sediments, which could be due to SR reducing methanogenesis. Isotopic evidence of consumption of CH₄ by methanotrophic oxidation Under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, concentrations of CH₄ are strongly related to dissolved oxygen dynamics, suggesting MOx is reducing water column CH₄. Methane can also be consumed under anoxic conditions, by AOM (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). However, the strong relationship between CH₄ and DO suggests that in the lakes here, aerobic MOx is the dominant pathway consuming CH₄. Oxidation of CH₄ leads to a systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of the residual un-oxidized CH₄ (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). In the profundal and littoral sediments of all of the lakes, an inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄, suggesting the CH₄ has not been fully oxidized. In the water column under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, a strong, positive correlation between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ is observed in all the lakes (\( n = 51, R = 0.93, p < 0.001 \); Fig. 2c), indicating CH₄ has been oxidized. In oxic waters, CH₄ is systematically enriched in both ¹³C and ²H, which is consistent with MOx (Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Happell et al., 1994; Whiticar, 1999; Bastviken et al., 2002; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). The slope of enrichment of ¹³C and 2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly. Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994): \[ f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000) \] where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx. The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014). 5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported. Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed. Large fractionations of C and H isotopes related to methane oxidation in Arctic lakes Sarah B. Cadieux a,*, Jeffrey R. White b, Peter E. Sauer a, Yongbo Peng a,1, Amy E. Goldman a,b,2, Lisa M. Pratt a a Department of Geological Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA b School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA Received 14 November 2015; accepted in revised form 3 May 2016; available online 9 May 2016 Abstract Microbial oxidation of methane (CH4) plays a central role in carbon cycling in Arctic lakes, reducing potential CH4 emissions associated with warming. Isotopic signatures of CH4 (δ13C and δ2H) are indicators of microbial oxidation, wherein the process strongly enriches 13C and 2H in residual CH4. We present δ13C and δ2H measurements obtained from sampling the water column and sediment for dissolved CH4 from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland under both open-water and ice-covered conditions from 2013 to 2014. Despite substantial variations in aquatic chemistry among the lakes, δ13C and δ2H of CH4 suggested that CH4 was produced predominantly by acetoclastic methanogenesis in the littoral sediments and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. Surprisingly large variations for both δ13C and δ2H of CH4 were observed, with δ13C extending from −72‰ to +7.4‰ and δ2H from −390‰ to +250‰. The CH4 isotopic values reported here were significantly more enriched (p < 0.0001) in both 13C and 2H than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments. As is characteristic of methanotrophy, the enrichment in 13C and 2H was associated with low CH4 concentrations. We suggest that the CH4 most enriched in 13C and 2H may reflect unusually efficient methanotrophic communities in Arctic ice-margin lakes. This study provides the first measurement of δ2H for CH4 in an Arctic freshwater environment at concentrations <10 μM. The extreme enrichment of 13C and 2H of CH4 from Arctic methanotrophy has significant implications for interpreting sources and sinks of CH4. Without knowledge of local geology, stable isotope values of CH4 higher than −30‰ for δ13C and −150‰ for δ2H could be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic origins. Given crystalline bedrock and the strong positive correlation between δ13C and δ2H throughout the water columns in three Arctic lakes confirms that CH4 heavily enriched in 13C and 2H is the result of methanotrophy. Keywords: Methane; Hydrogen isotopes; Carbon isotopes; Arctic; Lakes 1. INTRODUCTION Small lakes (<10 km^2) represent approximately half of the total area of surface water in Arctic environments (Abnizova et al., 2012) and emit more methane (CH4) per unit area than larger lakes (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009; Downing, 2010). Microbial oxidation of CH4 is an important process in freshwater ecosystems, reincorporating CH4 back into the biogeochemical carbon cycle rather than being released as CH4 into the atmosphere. In northern lakes, up to 88% of the CH4 produced by microbes is oxidized by methanotrophs (Kankaala et al., 2006, 2007; Bastviken et al., 2008; López Bellido et al., 2009), leaving low concentrations of CH4 in surface water of lakes. Due to the challenge of reliably measuring stable isotope abundances at very low concentrations, the effect of methanotrophic oxidation on isotopes of CH4 in Arctic lakes has not previously been reported. The combination of concentration and isotopic signature is vital for understanding biogeochemical cycling of CH4 on Earth and for assessing pathways for production and oxidation of CH4 on Mars where episodic plumes of CH4 at low concentrations have been detected remotely and measured by instruments on martian rovers. In anticipation of returning samples from Mars to Earth and with increasing interest in astronauts as explorers on Mars, it is urgent to assess geochemical and/or biological processes influencing rates of CH4 formation and destruction (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Kinetic isotope effects associated with enzymatic processes during methanogenesis and methanotrophy are well established terrestrial biomarkers and are potential martian biomarkers for subsurface life. Measuring CH4 concentrations and CH4 fluxes are useful to assess the magnitude of emissions, but alone are unable to be used to decipher active production and pathways. Stable isotopic analysis of carbon (δ13C) and hydrogen (δ2H) is a well-established method to delineate the origin of CH4 gas, allowing for the differentiation of CH4 produced by microbial and thermal processes as well as microbial production and oxidation (Schoell, 1980; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Despite a wide range of literature using 13C and 2H to interpret origin and thermal maturity of hydrocarbons in petroleum systems (Stahl and Carey, 1975; Schoell, 1980, 1988; Whiticar, 1989; Jackson et al., 2014), there has been limited work on δ13C and δ2H of CH4 in natural environments, most of which has been focused on wetlands (Martens et al., 1992; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Sugimoto and Fujita, 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). Biogenic CH4 in freshwater environments is produced predominantly within anoxic sediments and is exported into the water column by ebullition (bubbling) or diffusion (Strayer and Tiedje, 1978; Bastviken et al., 2008). Microbial CH4 is produced by methanogens, strictly anaerobic Archaea, who are responsible for 10–50% of overall carbon mineralization in freshwater lakes (Bastviken et al., 2008). In freshwater environments, there are two primary metabolic pathways for CH4 production, acetoclastic methanogenesis (AM) and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM), which have been demonstrated to vary spatially in permafrost-influenced ecosystems (Prater et al., 2007). Both AM and HM are associated with a kinetic isotope effect resulting in depletion of 13C in the product CH4 relative to the pre-cursor substrate (Whiticar et al., 1986; Balabane et al., 1987; Valentine et al., 2004a,b). However, the magnitude of the carbon isotope effect is different for the two primary methanogenic pathways, with AM resulting in δ13CCH4 ranging from −60‰ to −40‰, and HM ranging from −110‰ to −60‰ (Whiticar et al., 1986). Hydrogen isotopes of CH4 similarly become depleted in 2H during microbial CH4 production. The δ2H value of CH4 depends on the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is either from cleavage of H2O or acetate (Woltemate et al., 1984; Whiticar, 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Although this remains contentious, it is generally assumed that during HM, all 4 H atoms are supplied by formation water, whereas during AM, the transfer of the methyl group to CH4 supplies 3 H atoms, and the additional H atom is derived from formation water (Whiticar et al., 1986). As a result, the magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect of hydrogen is different for the two pathways, dependent on value of precursor δ2H, with AM resulting in δ2HCH4 ranging from −530‰ to −250‰, and HM ranging from −250‰ to −170‰ (Sugimoto and Wada, 1995). The isotope systematics of hydrogen for homoacetogenesis in competition with methanogenesis under substrate-limiting conditions and low temperatures of natural systems is not well known (Kotsyurbenko et al., 2001), although culture studies suggest that there is rapid hydrogen isotope exchange between H2 and H2O during homoacetogenesis (Valentine et al., 2004a,b). Methane oxidation (MOx) depends on both the availability of CH4 and dissolved oxygen (DO); high CH4 oxidation rates are usually found at the oxic/anoxic interface where both CH4 and DO are abundant (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) can also occur by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors in lieu of dissolved oxygen (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). High affinity methanotrophs are able to oxidize CH4 at or below atmospheric concentrations (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Isotope fractionation associated with microbial CH4 oxidation leads to systematic enrichment in both 13C and 2H of CH4 in the residual un-oxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). The enrichment in both 13C and 2H during oxidation results in values being increased by <1–30‰ for δ13CCH4 and 3–200‰ for δ2HCH4 (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Bastviken et al., 2002). In this study, we report values of δ13C and δ2H for CH4 collected from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland to assess seasonal sources and sinks of CH4. Lakes were sampled during open-water conditions in July 2013 and under ice-cover in April 2014 when the lakes had been ice-covered and isolated from the atmosphere for 7–8 months. The studied lakes show considerable variation in concentration and proportions of major ions despite being located along a 6 km segment of a narrow valley. Therefore, we hypothesize that due to chemical heterogeneity, sources and sinks of CH4 in each lake would vary lake-to-lake as well as seasonally. Hundreds of thousands of Holocene lakes dot the landscape in southwestern Greenland (Anderson et al., 2001; Anderson and Stedmon, 2007) and are underlain by continuous permafrost (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Deglaciation began in the region ~11,000 BP (Van Tatenhove and van der Meer, 1996; Leng et al., 2012), exposing Precambrian metamorphic crystalline bedrock, primarily felsic gneisses (Jensen et al., 2002). As a result, CH4 in these lakes has had little to no influence from buried ancient organic matter, allowing biogenic CH4 cycles to be studied in isolation. To our knowledge, this work provides the first coupled measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 under both open-water and ice-covered conditions in a relatively undisturbed, periglacial, lacustrine setting thereby filling critical knowledge gaps concerning biogeochemical cycles of CH4 within small Arctic lakes and isotope fractionation of CH4 in low concentration environments. 2. STUDY AREA Lakes in this study are located between the village of Kangerlussuaq, Greenland at the head of Søndre Strømfjord and the active terminus of the Russell Glacier (Fig. 1). During the last Glacial Maximum, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) covered the area. Retreat of the GIS likely resulted in formation of the lakes in glacially scoured hollows (Leng et al., 2012). Currently, the margin of the GIS is ~2 km away from the study lakes. The region has continuous permafrost <50 cm below the surface, extending down to 130 m at Kangerlussuaq and 500 m at the edge of the ice sheet (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Bedrock is predominantly garnet-grade, Archean gneisses with Quaternary glacial, fluvial and alluvial deposits present in low-lying areas. Mean annual air temperature at the Kangerlussuaq weather station from 1974 to 2012 was −6 °C. During warm months of late May to early September, mean temperatures often exceed +11 °C and peak to +20 °C in July. The cold season extends from November to late March, with mean daily temperature averaging −21 °C in February. Precipitation in the Kangerlussuaq area is minimal, with annual precipitation <150 mm yr−1, mostly from June to August (Ohmura and Reeh, 1991). Dwarf shrubs (Salix, Vaccinium and Betula), Sphagnum spp., and graminoids (Carex and Calamagrostis) dominate the tundra vegetation in the region. 2.1. Study lakes In this paper three, small adjacent lakes (surface area <3 ha, maximum depth <8 m) with a range of different morphometries and aquatic chemistries (Fig. 1; Table 1) are studied. Lake names used herein are informal names. The study lakes are part of a series of lakes within a narrow valley overlying a structural shear zone extending from the Russell Glacier to the Søndre Strømfjord (Fig. 1).
