The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (\( Z_{\text{max}} \)), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L\(^{-1}\)), pH, and specific conductivity (\( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column \( CH_4 \) collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and \( CH_4 \) was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved \( CH_4 \) in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment \( CH_4 \) Profundal sediment samples were taken from \( Z_{\text{max}} \) of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Sediment was collected in polycarbonate plastic barrels with an internal diameter of 6.7 cm. Dissolved gas in the sediment was sampled using an equilibrium gas stripping method similar to the water-column CH₄ (Section 3.1.2.1). Sediment cores were subsectioned into 6–10 cm intervals and put into 8 L Nalgene bottles, with lids altered to include two syringe ports connected to Luer-Lock fittings. Once the sediment was put into the bottle and the lid was shut, the bottle was evacuated using a hand pump connected to a lid port. After evacuation, zero-CH₄ water was injected to create a 4 L sediment–water slurry. The bottle was vigorously shaken for 5 min to displace gas from the sediment-slurry into the headspace. 3.1.4. Littoral sediment CH₄ Littoral sediment gas samples were collected during open-water conditions by physically disturbing the sediment in order to release entrained gas bubbles. Each sample was collected from a vegetated region where water depth was <0.5 m. Gas bubbles were collected using an inverted plastic funnel (28 cm diameter) with a gas-tight sampling tube and 3-way Luer-Lock valve attached to the neck. Gas in the funnel was transferred to a Cali-5-Bond bag using a plastic syringe. Note that we were unable to quantify the volume of sediment sampled. Consequently, concentrations of CH₄ in gas collected from littoral sediments cannot be converted into pool size of CH₄ in the littoral sediments. Rather, the samples were used to constrain the isotopic composition of CH₄ present in the littoral sediments (Chanton, 2005). 3.2. Laboratory methods 3.2.1. Concentration of CH₄ Concentration of water-column CH₄ and sediment CH₄ was measured using a Los Gatos Research (LGR) Methane Carbon Isotope Analyzer (MCIA) (LGR, Mountain View CA, USA) at the Kangerlussuaq International Science Support facility (KISS). The LGR MCIA is a portable, off-axis, integrated cavity output spectrometer that measures CH₄ without sample preparation. All samples were processed within 24 h of collection. For each analysis, 400–600 mL of gas sample was required. Calibration was repeated every 10 samples, with Scotty® gas standards of 50 and 100 ppmv CH₄. Samples were diluted with a known volume of zero-air in order to bring them within the range of the calibration gases. The total concentration of CH₄ in each sample was corrected for dilution and calculated from the sum of the measured headspace partial pressure and the dissolved CH₄ remaining after gas stripping, calculated according to Henry’s law using values after Lide and Fredrikse (1995). Instrumental uncertainty of CH₄ from the MCIA was ±0.5 ppmv, which is one standard deviation of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. Previously, concentrations of CH₄ from MCIA were analyzed on a Gas Chromatograph Flame Ionization Detector (GC-FID) to confirm validity (Appendix 2). Aliquots of each sample were transferred to pre-evacuated glass vials and returned to Indiana University, USA for carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄. 3.3. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄ Stable C and H isotopes of CH₄ were analyzed using two approaches. MCIA was used for C isotopic analysis on samples with CH₄ concentrations >50 ppmv, but the MCIA produces unreliable results at lower concentrations (Appendix 3). Therefore, stable isotope ratios of both carbon and hydrogen of CH₄ were measured using continuous-flow gas chromatography-oxidation/pyrolysis isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-ox/pyr-IRMS) with a laboratory-built gas pre-concentrator interfaced with a ThermoFinnigan GCC and Delta Plus XP IRMS at the Stable Isotope Research Facility (SIRF) at Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana. The pre-concentrator design was modeled after principles described by Merritt et al. (1995) and inlet system developed by Miller et al. (2002) for carbon isotope analysis and Brass and Rockmann (2010) for carbon and hydrogen isotopes. The gas sample containing CH₄ is first dried by passing through a cold trap and then passed into a stainless steel sample loop packed with HayeSep D and kept at −130 °C. After the CH₄ is extracted, the trap is warmed to −20 °C and the CH₄ is cryofocused at the head of Varian Porabond Q GC column. Carbon of CH₄ is converted to CO₂ at 950 °C and H is converted to H₂ in an alumina reactor at 1450 °C. Carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios are expressed in standard δ notation (δ¹³C and δ²H): \[ \delta = [(R_{\text{sample}} - R_{\text{standard}})/R_{\text{standard}}] \times 1000 = \%o \] where \( R \) is the molar ratio of heavy to light isotopes (¹³C/¹²C, ²H/¹H) for both sample and standard. Carbon isotope values are referenced to VPDB and hydrogen isotope values are referenced to VSMOW by comparison with pure CH₄ where the isotopic composition has been measured by off-line combustion (http://mypage.iu.edu/~aschimme/compounds.html). Instrumental uncertainty of δ¹³C and δ²H from the GC-C-IRMS was calculated as ±0.4‰ and as ±10‰ respectively, which is one standard deviation for repeated measures of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. 3.4. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were made using IBM SPSS Statistics. Combined concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic compositions for all study lakes during each season were assessed for normal distribution via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and were found to be non-normally distributed. Student’s t tests of unequal variance were used for testing statistically significant differences in concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic values of CH₄ between seasons and between study results and reported isotopic values from other natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude. Systematic changes in δ¹³C and δ²H were analyzed using linear regression, based upon the pathway of oxidation leading to systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of CH₄ in the residual unoxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). 4. RESULTS 4.1. Water-column CH₄ 4.1.1. Concentration of CH₄ Under open-water conditions, concentrations of CH₄ were strongly related to DO dynamics (Fig. 2). Dissolved CH₄ concentrations in the surface waters of the three lakes ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 µM (Fig. 3). Clinograde DO profiles were measured in EVV Upper and Potentilla lakes with DO saturated in surface water (9.5 and 11.0 mg L⁻¹ respectively), and decreasing with depth to anoxia (<0.5 mg L⁻¹; Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column with decreasing DO, with the maximum CH₄ observed in the anoxic water at the sediment–water interface (150 and 67 µM respectively). Teardrop lake was oxic to suboxic (DO > 1 mg L⁻¹) throughout the water column with an oxygen anomaly at 4.0 m, wherein DO drastically shifted from >10 mg L⁻¹ at 3.5 m to 1.8 mg L⁻¹ at 4 m, and then returned to 7 mg L⁻¹ at 4.5 m. Throughout the water column of Teardrop lake, there were low CH₄ concentrations (<8.1 µM; Fig. 3). In all three lakes, concentrations of CH₄ were significantly greater under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (n = 31, p = 0.0002). Isotopic evidence of production pathways for CH4 in Greenlandic lakes Bedrock in the Kangerlussuaq region consists of tightly folded, felsic gneisses exposed to garnet-grade metamorphism and contains no measurable organic C, therefore we assume that all CH4 within the study lakes is biologically produced. To look at differences in microbial production of CH4, we focus our discussion on the sediment CH4 in the study lakes from open-water conditions. In order to distinguish AM and HM CH4 production pathways from each other isotopically, isotopic compositions of H2O, dissolved inorganic matter (DIC), and organic matter (OM) must be constant. If not, the variation in δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 reflect not only different production pathways, but also variation in environmental factors that affect isotopic composition of reactants. In the study lakes, δ2H2O in the water column slightly decreases with distance away from the margin of the GIS, from a median of −91.5‰ in EVV Upper lake to −97.4‰ in Potentilla lake. Despite the spatial variation in δ2H2O among the lakes, there is no significant relationship between δ2H2O from the water column and δ2HCH4 from sediments (Fig. 5), suggesting that δ2HCH4 is not a direct reflection of variation in 2H2O. In addition to differences in δ2H2O among the lakes, there are also variations in δ13CDIC from the water column among the lakes (Stern et al., 2014). However, there is not enough data to confirm or deny if δ13CCH4 is reflecting variation in δ13CDIC. Approximately a 5‰ difference in δ13COM of particulate OM from profundal sediments was observed lake-to-lake, ranging from −29.2‰ in EVV Upper lake to −24.5‰ (Table 1). Data suggest that the ~45‰ difference in δ13CCH4 of profundal sediment may reflect the δ13COM of precursor OM (Fig. 5b). However, the range in δ13COM is narrow compared to the overall range observed in aquatic chemistry and δ13CCH4 among the lakes. In both the profundal and littoral sediments of the study lakes, values of δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 are consistent with microbial CH4 production (Fig. 4) (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Profundal sediment CH4 is more depleted in 13C and enriched in 2H relative to littoral sediment CH4 (Table 2), suggesting different microbial production pathways, partial oxidation of the littoral sediments, or higher precursor δ13COM in the littoral sediments. However, δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 values from both profundal and littoral sediments plot primarily within the AM field (Fig. 4). The HM pathway field in the δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 classification diagram was determined from marine samples where δ2H2O is ~0‰ (Whiticar, 1999; Waldron et al., 1999b). As a result, the HM pathway field may not accurately represent Arctic waters where δ2H2O ≪ 0‰. Using the assumptions from Chanton et al. (2006), we can adjust the measured sediment δ2HCH4 for the δ2H2O of the water in the lake where the CH4 was formed using the following equation: \[ \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-measured}} - \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\text{ water}} = \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-adjusted}} \] In order to use this equation, δ2HCH4 in the sediments must reflect CH4 production without isotopic overprinting from oxidation. If CH4 in the sediments was subjected to oxidation then a positive correlation between δ13CCH4 and δ²HCH₄ would be observed (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). An inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ from sediments, confirming CH₄ in the sediments had not been oxidized (Fig. 4). The adjustment for δ²H₂O shifted δ²HCH₄ of profundal sediments into the HM pathways field, whereas the littoral sediment δ²HCH₄ remains primarily in the AM pathway field (Fig. 6). Without δ¹³COM in the littoral sediments of each lake, we are unable to assess if the variations between the sediments are the result of different microbial pathways, or if there is also variations in precursor OM. However, δ¹³COM and C/N ratios of littoral sediments from EVV Upper lake suggested OM is sourced from in-lake primary production (Thompson, 2015). The difference in CH₄ production pathway between the littoral and profundal sediments likely reflects the supply of labile organic compounds and δ¹³COM, which would influence CH₄ formation (Duc et al., 2010). In the littoral sediments, aquatic macrophytes and phytoplankton supply a source of labile OM, resulting in AM. Correspondingly, the lake with the highest CH₄ concentrations in the littoral sediments (EVV Upper lake) has the highest concentration of aquatic macrophytes, with the shoreline dominated by Hippuris vulgaris. In freshwater environments, CH₄ typically is produced by AM (Whiticar et al., 1986; Conrad, 1999) because plant root exudates and fresh OM provide a ready supply of labile OM to the bacteria. Previous theoretical values predict that HM accounts for ~30% of overall CH₄ production in freshwater lakes (Conrad, 1999). In high-latitude Sphagnum bogs, CH₄ production via HM is dominant because of an inhibition of the AM pathway, whereas AM is dominant in Carex-rich environments (Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Sphagnum spp. was a significant component of littoral communities of lakes in this study. In closed lake basins, OM from these areas may represent important carbon inputs, which could be influencing the HM pathway for CH₄ production in the profundal sediments. We were surprised to discover that despite significant variations in DOC, SO₄²⁻ and conductivity among the lakes, formation pathways of CH₄ in littoral and profundal sediments seem to be identical in all of the lakes. Competition for substrates (particularly acetate and H₂) favors sulfate reduction (SR), inhibiting CH₄ production (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Ward and Winfrey, 1985; Scholten et al., 2002). Methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased because SR can very effectively uptake both H₂ and acetate, maintaining H₂ and acetate concentrations too low for methanogens (Lovely and Klung, 1986). In the study lakes, EVV Upper lake has the highest SO₄²⁻ concentrations and is the only lake with detectable H₂S in the water column during open-water conditions (Table 1). The presence and accumulation of CH₄ in the sediments indicates that there is sufficient carbon to both fuel reduction of the SO₄²⁻ pool and support methanogenesis in EVV Upper lake. Given the current data, there is no way to assess if communities are spatially coexisting or separated by vertical stratification. However, EVV Upper lake does have the lowest concentration of CH₄ in the profundal sediments, which could be due to SR reducing methanogenesis. Isotopic evidence of consumption of CH₄ by methanotrophic oxidation Under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, concentrations of CH₄ are strongly related to dissolved oxygen dynamics, suggesting MOx is reducing water column CH₄. Methane can also be consumed under anoxic conditions, by AOM (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). However, the strong relationship between CH₄ and DO suggests that in the lakes here, aerobic MOx is the dominant pathway consuming CH₄. Oxidation of CH₄ leads to a systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of the residual un-oxidized CH₄ (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). In the profundal and littoral sediments of all of the lakes, an inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄, suggesting the CH₄ has not been fully oxidized. In the water column under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, a strong, positive correlation between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ is observed in all the lakes (\( n = 51, R = 0.93, p < 0.001 \); Fig. 2c), indicating CH₄ has been oxidized. In oxic waters, CH₄ is systematically enriched in both ¹³C and ²H, which is consistent with MOx (Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Happell et al., 1994; Whiticar, 1999; Bastviken et al., 2002; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). The slope of enrichment of ¹³C and 2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly. Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994): \[ f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000) \] where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx. The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014). 5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported. Fig. 7. \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$ in this study (open diamonds; 55 data points) compared to natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude reported in the literature: Lake ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013) (closed squares; 155 data points), dissolved CH$_4$ in an Antarctic lake (Wand et al., 2006) (closed triangles; 6 data points) and wetlands (Woltemate et al., 1984; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011) (closed circles; 137 data points). The shaded area denotes the field of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) associated with microbial CH$_4$ production (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) 5.4. Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed. Life-cycle phenology of some aquatic insects: implications for pond conservation JÉRÔME CAYROU and RÉGIS CÉRÉGHINO* Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Hydrosystèmes, Université Paul Sabatier, Toulouse, France ABSTRACT 1. Life-cycles and growth patterns were determined for 21 dominant aquatic insect species in small permanent ponds in an arid, karstic region (SW France, site fr7300909 of the Natura 2000 conservation network). The species studied are widely distributed throughout Europe, but some life-cycle patterns are reported here for the first time. 2. The life-history patterns of the 21 species can be divided into five main types: (i) a semivoltine cycle spreading over 2 years; (ii) slow univoltine cycles; (iii) fast univoltine cycles; (iv) multivoltine life-cycles with a long winter generation and two or three summer generations per year; and (v) bivoltine life-cycles with two fast generations per year. Growth was either exponential over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or divided into two or three successive periods during each of which the growth rate was fairly constant. 3. Biodiversity estimates strongly depend on the temporal and spatial scale over which observations are made. Ponds thus provide useful models to show how life-history patterns enable many temporally segregated populations to utilize small ecosystems. Conservation frameworks should therefore carefully consider the time-frame needed to survey ponds, as many species with fast cycles could be overlooked. The spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats and thus preserve pond networks must be broadened, rather than attempting to target individual water bodies for particular management actions. Copyright © 2005 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. KEY WORDS: aquatic insects; wetlands; ponds; life-history; growth; temporal niche segregation; temperature; conservation INTRODUCTION The diversity of habitat types within wetlands allows them to be colonized by a wide range of specialist and generalist species (Masing et al., 2000). Wetlands are thus often considered as ‘hot spots’ of biodiversity within a region or a landscape (Gopal et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2004). However, wetlands and the biodiversity they support are threatened by human activity (e.g. agriculture, industry, urban development), though these ecosystems have significant ecological functions (Dugan, 1990) and recognized social and economic uses (Chapman et al., 2001). During the 20th century, wetland losses reached 40–90% in a number of north-western European countries (Hull, 1997), and in the United States more than 50% of these ecosystems have been destroyed by man (Tiner, 1984; Williams, 1990). Due to such large-scale habitat loss, many species are also endangered. This threat has prompted specific studies aimed at understanding the dynamics of wetland populations. Such an understanding is expected to help in planning conservation efforts such as the creation or restoration of ecosystems (Biggs et al., 1994). Although ponds have only recently started receiving some attention (Oertli, 1995; Hull, 1997; Angélbert et al., 2004), it is now well established that their management and conservation is closely linked to an understanding of the biodiversity and ecology of the biota they host (Gee et al., 1997; Gaston et al., 2005). Many of the models used to predict the consequences of future conservation strategies require life-history data (Rustigian et al., 2003). Therefore, information on the life-cycles of aquatic species is of fundamental importance for virtually all aspects of wetland conservation, including the conservation of ponds. Aquatic insects constitute an important part of animal production within wetlands (Oertli, 1993), and are tightly integrated into the structure and functioning of their habitats (e.g. organic matter processing, nutrient retention, food resources for vertebrates such as amphibians, fish, or birds). In a given area, the spatial and temporal variability of habitat types are key factors influencing the biodiversity of insect communities (Minshall, 1984; Hanquet et al., 2004), and are reflected in the ecological strategies and adaptation exhibited by species (Townsend, 1989; Townsend et al., 1997). In contrast to the large volume of studies in river ecology, very little research has addressed the population dynamics of pond insects. Most attention has instead been paid to patterns of biodiversity such as spatial variations in species richness (Oertli, 1995), or species diversity vs. area relationships (Oertli et al., 2002). Information on the life-history of pond insects is generally sparse, and usually available for a few, separately studied, species (e.g., Di Giovanni et al., 2000). However, there have been no previous attempts to gather – in a single investigation – detailed life-cycle and growth data on a large number of pond insects that are likely to coexist. Such an investigation would provide an overview of life-history traits and would consequently have significant implications for planning management and/or conservation actions in a particular area. In this investigation, the life-cycle phenologies, including growth patterns, of 21 aquatic insect species were determined in three small, permanent ponds in the arid, karstic region of the ‘Causses du Quercy’ (SW France). This area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and the results are discussed with reference to the implications for broader conservation strategies. STUDY AREA Located in south-western France, the ‘Causses du Quercy’ is a 2156 km\(^2\) limestone plateau. This arid area is affected by Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Continental climates, and this is reflected in its distinctive weather conditions and vegetation cover. The dominant plant species found in the area are *Quercus pubescens* Willd. and *Acer monspessulanum* L., while the moorland vegetation is principally composed of *Juniperus communis* L. The area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and is identified as site fr7300909. The plateau has no natural surface fresh water; however, it has more than 300 artificial ponds (typically permanent, rectangular in shape, and shallow, with a density of less than one pond per square kilometre). These ponds, bored into the calcareous rock, were created to hold rain water and support agricultural activities, and it is a technique that has been practised since the 12th century. Abandoned during the 1960s, the ponds are progressively filling with sediment and aquatic vegetation. Although they are now at various stages of natural succession, they support an aquatic vegetation community classified for conservation by the European Fauna-Flora-Habitat guideline 92/43/CEE: ‘22.12X22.44, oligo-mesotrophic calcareous waters with benthic vegetation of Characea’. This study was conducted from November 2000 to November 2001 in three such permanent ponds with a rocky substrate (hereafter called 1, 2 and 3). These three ponds are at different stages of natural succession; their main characteristics are shown in Table 1. A thorough study of their physical and chemical features (together with a fauna and flora species list) can be found in Angélibert et al. (2004). METHODS Sampling In each pond, samples were collected monthly from November 2000 to February 2001, then every 2 weeks from March to November 2001. Different techniques were used to obtain qualitative samples of aquatic insects within each pond. First, samples were randomly taken in each pond and at each sampling date by intensive sweeping of a hand net (mesh size = 250 μm) through the various habitats for 15–20 min. In order to maximize the number of available individuals on each sampling occasion, additional samples were specifically taken from the various substrate types (Table 1), each requiring a specific sampling technique (Oertli, 1993). Thin layers of mud (< 5 cm) deposited on the calcareous substrate and bryophytes were sampled using an air-lift sampler (Boulton, 1985) (sampling area 186 cm², mesh size of the net: 250 μm). Thick layers of mud (> 5 cm) were sampled using a plastic core sampler (sampling area: 28.2 cm²). Specific cores (40 cm high and 4.4 cm in diameter) were used to sample the submerged section of Typha stems. The aerial part of the plant was cut at water level, and the remaining submerged part was quickly enclosed in the core and cut at approximately 35 cm under the surface of the water. Chara beds at mid-depth were sampled by rapidly enclosing plants in a plastic box (7.5 × 16 × 11.5 cm). The Chara plants were then cut with shears. Table 1. Life-history and growth Twenty-one species were found in sufficient numbers throughout their developmental period to allow their life histories and growth patterns to be studied. All larvae were divided into size categories (0.1 mm) based either on head capsule width or tibia length of the third leg. Size–frequency plots for life-cycle determination were based on direct identification of larval instars (four species of Heteroptera, seven Coleoptera, five Diptera), or on head or tibia measurements when larval instars could not be easily identified (one species of Ephemeroptera, four Odonata). Sets of larvae (at least 10 individuals) from different size categories were dried at 60°C for 24 h and then weighed. Larval mean individual dry weights (\( W \), mg) were derived from linear regressions (\( \ln W = a + bL \) with 95% C.L.) between the natural log of weight (\( \ln W \)) and tibia length or head capsule width. Mean individual dry weights of cohorts from each site were natural log transformed to generate a series of subsegment linear regressions that represent a generation’s seasonal growth patterns over the year (see, for example, Figure 8). RESULTS Life-history patterns The life-history patterns of the 21 study species (Figures 1–7) can be divided into five main types. (1) The semivoltine life-cycle of Anax imperator began in summer (June–September). It lasted 2 years and ended in late spring (June). There was a large range of larval sizes throughout the year, with two overlapping generations. (2) Five species showed slow cycles with one generation per year. The eggs began to hatch in the spring (Coenagrion scitulum, Libellula depressa, Agabus nitidus, Haliplus lineatocollis) or late summer (Odontomyia ornata), and growth occurred over a long period (9–12 months) before spring or early summer emergences. (3) Ten species exhibited fast univoltine cycles (one generation per year), with hatching periods in late winter (Hygrotus inaequalis, Acilius sulcatus), spring (Chalcolestes viridis, Corixa punctata, Plea leachi, Hygrobia hermanni, Phaenobezzia sp.), or early summer (Haliplus mucronatus, Noterus clavicornis, Stratiomys potamida) with a short growth period (2–4 months), and were adult by spring, summer, or autumn. (4) Three species were multivoltine (two or three generations per year) with a long winter generation (September to May) and one (Culicoides sp., Dicrotendipes tritomus) or two (Cloeon dipterum) short summer generations (from July to August). It should be noted that two additional mayflies, Cloeon simile and Caenis luctuosa, occurred in pond 1 (but not in ponds 2 and 3). Their life-cycle patterns were previously described in Cayrou and Céréghino (2003): both species had a long winter and a short summer generation. (5) Two species were clearly bivoltine, with two short generations per year, i.e., in spring and summer (Naucoris maculatus), or both in spring (Notonecta maculata). DISCUSSION Compared with previous reports, some species seemed to exhibit flexible life histories. Cloeon dipterum occurs throughout much of Europe, and most authors have described univoltine and bivoltine (with a short summer generation) life-cycles (Clifford, 1982), whereas three generations per year were recorded in ponds 2 and 3 (see also Elliott et al., 1988). Libellula depressa was clearly univoltine in ponds 2 and 3. However, Di Giovanni et al. (2000) noted that Libellula depressa had a 2-yr life-cycle, although some more rapidly growing individuals were able to emerge after 1 yr. The data in the present study suggested that Anax imperator had a 2-yr life-cycle. However, in colder regions (e.g. Germany, United Kingdom), A. imperator shows larval cycles extending either over 1 or 2 yr (Corbet, 1955; Sternberg and Buchwald, 2000), even at a given locality (which remains likely in our study area). Corixa punctata is mostly univoltine, but a second generation was observed by Papáček and Bohoněk (1989). According to Svensson et al. (2000), Notonecta maculata has one generation per year in Sweden, with adult emergence in August (compared with two generations per year and emergence from May to July in this study). Acilius sulcatus grew from February to June in pond 2 (this study), but from May to June in Wisconsin, USA (Hilsenhoff, 1993). Finally, previously undescribed life-cycle and growth patterns were detailed for the following species: Naucoris maculatus, Haliplus lineatocollis, Haliplus mucronatus, Hygrotus inaequalis, Noterus clavicornis, Odontomyia ornata, Stratiomys potamida, Dicrotendipes tritomus – thus contributing further to an understanding of the population dynamics of wetland insects. As wetland habitats, ponds have only recently started receiving some attention, and most of the current research still focuses on assessing the biodiversity they support (Briers and Biggs, 2003; Angélbert et al., 2004) or are likely to host (Davies et al., 2004; Gaston et al., 2005). Among wetland inhabitants, aquatic insects have the potential to be relevant ecological indicators. Indeed, they are already widely used to reveal short- and long-term environmental changes in both running and still waters (Céréghino et al., 2003; Verneaux et al., 2004), most notably through the strong influence of human disturbance on the species richness of aquatic insects (Rosenberg and Resh, 1993). Such disturbances usually lead to losses of taxa (Compin and Céréghino, 2003). However, in a given area, biodiversity estimates (e.g. species richness, evenness, etc.) strongly depend on the spatial scale (type of habitat) and temporal scale (week, month, or season) over which observations are made. Water temperature is usually considered to be the major abiotic factor affecting the life-cycle phenology of aquatic invertebrates (Vannote and Sweeney, 1980; Sweeney et al., 1986), influencing the seasonality and development patterns of aquatic insects through growth, adult size, and fecundity (Lavandier, 1988; Giberson and Rosenberg, 1992; Pritchard and Zloty, 1994). This study suggested that the increased growth of those species with long generations (e.g., Cloeon dipterum) seemed to correspond to the rise in water temperature in spring (March), and that the warmest period (spring–summer) favoured the hatching and rapid development of short summer generations in most species. Whatever the biotic and/or abiotic factors controlling the life-cycle phenologies, and, subsequently, the temporal patterns of aquatic insect communities within ponds, this study clearly emphasizes the temporal dimension of biodiversity in small bodies of water. The seasonality of wetland-dependent insects in particular may influence the biodiversity ponds may support. Similar recommendations are already part of protocols for sampling and assessment of both riverine and wetland habitats, e.g. RIVPACS sampling for rivers (Wright et al., 2000), and UK National Pond Survey methods (Pond Action, 1989). Life-cycle attributes (e.g., reproduction, hatching and emergence periods) need to be carefully considered when restoring, managing and/or creating new ponds for conservation purposes (Ripley et al., 2004). Owing to the difficulty of pond creation in the study area (a limestone plateau), dredging the abandoned ponds is the only option for wetland restoration. Therefore, environmental managers should minimize the likelihood that dredging will eliminate populations (e.g., during the main growth or hatching periods). Theoretically, the acceptable period for dredging would be between adult emergence and egg-laying, i.e. during the flight and reproduction period. Given that most populations show a temporal sequence of species replacements (e.g. certain Coleoptera, Heteroptera), or have delayed life-cycle events (certain Odonata), defining an optimal period for dredging seems to be an impossible task. As an alternative, a plan of pond management should be envisaged over a large spatial scale to maintain the heterogeneity of pond networks in the area. Such a plan would imply promoting the conservation of all ponds, regardless of their successional stages. This is especially important when the density of ponds in the network is very sparse. Indeed, a recent study in the same area (Angélibert and Giani, 2003) on the dispersal capability of Odonata showed that dispersal phenomena were low because of the distance separating ponds. Thus, after dredging, species adapted to late succession ponds have little hope of finding suitable conditions in other ponds to ensure their development. The insects studied are widely distributed throughout Europe (see the Limnofauna Europaea (Illies, 1978)) and are regarded as having a low conservation priority. Broader conservation strategies should therefore ensure that such currently common organisms do not become the endangered species of the future (Rustigian et al., 2003). Ponds also provide useful models for studying how life-history patterns enable many populations to utilize small ecosystems, temporal segregation and/or differences in the size of coexisting nymphs certainly reducing interspecific competition for food and habitat resources (Svensson et al., 2000; Cayrou and Céréghino, 2003). Subsequently, interesting ideas and/or alternative strategies can be derived for conservation planning. Because the growth of most species is markedly seasonal and many species are temporally segregated, the spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats must be enlarged. Thus, when possible, pond networks should primarily be preserved rather than attempting to target some bodies of water for particular management actions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We wish to thank N. Life-cycle phenology of some aquatic insects: implications for pond conservation JÉRÔME CAYROU and RÉGIS CÉRÉGHINO* Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Hydrosystèmes, Université Paul Sabatier, Toulouse, France ABSTRACT 1. Life-cycles and growth patterns were determined for 21 dominant aquatic insect species in small permanent ponds in an arid, karstic region (SW France, site fr7300909 of the Natura 2000 conservation network). The species studied are widely distributed throughout Europe, but some life-cycle patterns are reported here for the first time. 2. The life-history patterns of the 21 species can be divided into five main types: (i) a semivoltine cycle spreading over 2 years; (ii) slow univoltine cycles; (iii) fast univoltine cycles; (iv) multivoltine life-cycles with a long winter generation and two or three summer generations per year; and (v) bivoltine life-cycles with two fast generations per year. Growth was either exponential over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or divided into two or three successive periods during each of which the growth rate was fairly constant. 3. Biodiversity estimates strongly depend on the temporal and spatial scale over which observations are made. Ponds thus provide useful models to show how life-history patterns enable many temporally segregated populations to utilize small ecosystems. Conservation frameworks should therefore carefully consider the time-frame needed to survey ponds, as many species with fast cycles could be overlooked. The spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats and thus preserve pond networks must be broadened, rather than attempting to target individual water bodies for particular management actions. KEY WORDS: aquatic insects; wetlands; ponds; life-history; growth; temporal niche segregation; temperature; conservation INTRODUCTION The diversity of habitat types within wetlands allows them to be colonized by a wide range of specialist and generalist species (Masing et al., 2000). Wetlands are thus often considered as ‘hot spots’ of biodiversity within a region or a landscape (Gopal et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2004). However, wetlands and the biodiversity they support are threatened by human activity (e.g. agriculture, industry, urban development), though these ecosystems have significant ecological functions (Dugan, 1990) and recognized social and economic uses (Chapman et al., 2001). During the 20th century, wetland losses reached 40–90% in a number of north-western European countries (Hull, 1997), and in the United States more than 50% of these ecosystems have been destroyed by man (Tiner, 1984; Williams, 1990). Due to such large-scale habitat loss, many species are also endangered. This threat has prompted specific studies aimed at understanding the dynamics of wetland populations. Such an understanding is expected to help in planning conservation efforts such as the creation or restoration of ecosystems (Biggs et al., 1994). Although ponds have only recently started receiving some attention (Oertli, 1995; Hull, 1997; Angélbert et al., 2004), it is now well established that their management and conservation is closely linked to an understanding of the biodiversity and ecology of the biota they host (Gee et al., 1997; Gaston et al., 2005). Many of the models used to predict the consequences of future conservation strategies require life-history data (Rustigian et al., 2003). Therefore, information on the life-cycles of aquatic species is of fundamental importance for virtually all aspects of wetland conservation, including the conservation of ponds. Aquatic insects constitute an important part of animal production within wetlands (Oertli, 1993), and are tightly integrated into the structure and functioning of their habitats (e.g. organic matter processing, nutrient retention, food resources for vertebrates such as amphibians, fish, or birds). In a given area, the spatial and temporal variability of habitat types are key factors influencing the biodiversity of insect communities (Minshall, 1984; Hanquet et al., 2004), and are reflected in the ecological strategies and adaptation exhibited by species (Townsend, 1989; Townsend et al., 1997). In contrast to the large volume of studies in river ecology, very little research has addressed the population dynamics of pond insects. Most attention has instead been paid to patterns of biodiversity such as spatial variations in species richness (Oertli, 1995), or species diversity vs. area relationships (Oertli et al., 2002). Information on the life-history of pond insects is generally sparse, and usually available for a few, separately studied, species (e.g., Di Giovanni et al., 2000). However, there have been no previous attempts to gather – in a single investigation – detailed life-cycle and growth data on a large number of pond insects that are likely to coexist. Such an investigation would provide an overview of life-history traits and would consequently have significant implications for planning management and/or conservation actions in a particular area. In this investigation, the life-cycle phenologies, including growth patterns, of 21 aquatic insect species were determined in three small, permanent ponds in the arid, karstic region of the ‘Causses du Quercy’ (SW France). This area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and the results are discussed with reference to the implications for broader conservation strategies. STUDY AREA Located in south-western France, the ‘Causses du Quercy’ is a 2156 km\(^2\) limestone plateau. This arid area is affected by Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Continental climates, and this is reflected in its distinctive weather conditions and vegetation cover. The dominant plant species found in the area are *Quercus pubescens* Willd. and *Acer monspessulanum* L., while the moorland vegetation is principally composed of *Juniperus communis* L. The area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and is identified as site fr7300909. The plateau has no natural surface fresh water; however, it has more than 300 artificial ponds (typically permanent, rectangular in shape, and shallow, with a density of less than one pond per square kilometre). These ponds, bored into the calcareous rock, were created to hold rain water and support agricultural activities, and it is a technique that has been practised since the 12th century. Abandoned during the 1960s, the ponds are progressively filling with sediment and aquatic vegetation. Although they are now at various stages of natural succession, they support an aquatic vegetation community classified for conservation by the European Fauna-Flora-Habitat guideline 92/43/CEE: ‘22.12X22.44, oligo-mesotrophic calcareous waters with benthic vegetation of Characea’. This study was conducted from November 2000 to November 2001 in three such permanent ponds with a rocky substrate (hereafter called 1, 2 and 3). These three ponds are at different stages of natural succession; their main characteristics are shown in Table 1. A thorough study of their physical and chemical features (together with a fauna and flora species list) can be found in Angélibert et al. (2004). METHODS Sampling In each pond, samples were collected monthly from November 2000 to February 2001, then every 2 weeks from March to November 2001. Different techniques were used to obtain qualitative samples of aquatic insects within each pond. First, samples were randomly taken in each pond and at each sampling date by intensive sweeping of a hand net (mesh size = 250 μm) through the various habitats for 15–20 min. In order to maximize the number of available individuals on each sampling occasion, additional samples were specifically taken from the various substrate types (Table 1), each requiring a specific sampling technique (Oertli, 1993). Thin layers of mud (< 5 cm) deposited on the calcareous substrate and bryophytes were sampled using an air-lift sampler (Boulton, 1985) (sampling area 186 cm², mesh size of the net: 250 μm). Thick layers of mud (> 5 cm) were sampled using a plastic core sampler (sampling area: 28.2 cm²). Specific cores (40 cm high and 4.4 cm in diameter) were used to sample the submerged section of Typha stems. The aerial part of the plant was cut at water level, and the remaining submerged part was quickly enclosed in the core and cut at approximately 35 cm under the surface of the water. Chara beds at mid-depth were sampled by rapidly enclosing plants in a plastic box (7.5 × 16 × 11.5 cm). The Chara plants were then cut with shears. Table 1. Invertebrates were preserved in the field in 5% formalin, identified in the laboratory and then preserved in 70% ethanol. Life-history and growth Twenty-one species were found in sufficient numbers throughout their developmental period to allow their life histories and growth patterns to be studied. All larvae were divided into size categories (0.1 mm) based either on head capsule width or tibia length of the third leg. Size–frequency plots for life-cycle determination were based on direct identification of larval instars (four species of Heteroptera, seven Coleoptera, five Diptera), or on head or tibia measurements when larval instars could not be easily identified (one species of Ephemeroptera, four Odonata). Sets of larvae (at least 10 individuals) from different size categories were dried at 60°C for 24 h and then weighed. Larval mean individual dry weights (\( W \), mg) were derived from linear regressions (\( \ln W = a + bL \) with 95% C.L.) between the natural log of weight (\( \ln W \)) and tibia length or head capsule width. Mean individual dry weights of cohorts from each site were natural log transformed to generate a series of subsegment linear regressions that represent a generation’s seasonal growth patterns over the year (see, for example, Figure 8). RESULTS Life-history patterns The life-history patterns of the 21 study species (Figures 1–7) can be divided into five main types. (1) The semivoltine life-cycle of Anax imperator began in summer (June–September). It lasted 2 years and ended in late spring (June). There was a large range of larval sizes throughout the year, with two overlapping generations. (2) Five species showed slow cycles with one generation per year. The eggs began to hatch in the spring (Coenagrion scitulum, Libellula depressa, Agabus nitidus, Haliplus lineatocollis) or late summer (Odontomyia ornata), and growth occurred over a long period (9–12 months) before spring or early summer emergences. (3) Ten species exhibited fast univoltine cycles (one generation per year), with hatching periods in late winter (Hygrotus inaequalis, Acilius sulcatus), spring (Chalcolestes viridis, Corixa punctata, Plea leachi, Hygrobia hermanni, Phaenobezzia sp.), or early summer (Haliplus mucronatus, Noterus clavicornis, Stratiomys potamida) with a short growth period (2–4 months), and were adult by spring, summer, or autumn. (4) Three species were multivoltine (two or three generations per year) with a long winter generation (September to May) and one (Culicoides sp., Dicrotendipes tritomus) or two (Cloeon dipterum) short summer generations (from July to August). It should be noted that two additional mayflies, Cloeon simile and Caenis luctuosa, occurred in pond 1 (but not in ponds 2 and 3). Their life-cycle patterns were previously described in Cayrou and Céréghino (2003): both species had a long winter and a short summer generation. (5) Two species were clearly bivoltine, with two short generations per year, i.e., in spring and summer (Naucoris maculatus), or both in spring (Notonecta maculata). Growth A simple regression (\( \ln W = a + bL \)) provided the best means for measuring the relationship between dry weight (\( W \)) and head width or tibia length (\( L \)). Table 2 presents values for constants a and b (\( \pm 95\% \) CL) obtained for the 21 species studied. The ‘\( r \)’ values ranged from 0.82 to 0.99, and were significant for each species (\( p < 0.05 \) or \( p < 0.01 \)). Growth was exponential either over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or over two or three successive periods during which the growth rate was fairly constant. Three cohort growth pattern types could be perceived (Figure 8): (I) growth occurred mainly in autumn and spring; it was low in winter; (II) growth was higher in summer and autumn than in winter and spring; and (III) all of the growth occurred continuously over 2–4 months in spring or summer. DISCUSSION Compared with previous reports, some species seemed to exhibit flexible life histories. Cloeon dipterum occurs throughout much of Europe, and most authors have described univoltine and bivoltine (with a short summer generation) life-cycles (Clifford, 1982), whereas three generations per year were recorded in ponds 2 and 3 (see also Elliott et al., 1988). Libellula depressa was clearly univoltine in ponds 2 and 3. However, Di Giovanni et al. (2000) noted that Libellula depressa had a 2-yr life-cycle, although some more rapidly growing individuals were able to emerge after 1 yr. The data in the present study suggested that Anax imperator had a 2-yr life-cycle. However, in colder regions (e.g. Germany, United Kingdom), A. imperator shows larval cycles extending either over 1 or 2 yr (Corbet, 1955; Sternberg and Buchwald, 2000), even at a given locality (which remains likely in our study area). Corixa punctata is mostly univoltine, but a second generation was observed by Papáček and Bohoněk (1989). According to Svensson et al. (2000), Notonecta maculata has one generation per year in Sweden, with adult emergence in August (compared with two generations per year and emergence from May to July in this study). Acilius sulcatus grew from February to June in pond 2 (this study), but from May to June in Wisconsin, USA (Hilsenhoff, 1993). Finally, previously undescribed life-cycle and growth patterns were detailed for the following species: Naucoris maculatus, Haliplus lineatocollis, Haliplus mucronatus, Hygrotus inaequalis, Noterus clavicornis, Odontomyia ornata, Stratiomys potamida, Dicrotendipes tritomus – thus contributing further to an understanding of the population dynamics of wetland insects. Figure 7. Life-history of Diptera species in pond 1 (Dicrotendipes tritomus) and 2 (other species). Frequency distribution of the various larval instars (I–IV) at each sampling date (November 2000–November 2001). See caption to Figure 1. As wetland habitats, ponds have only recently started receiving some attention, and most of the current research still focuses on assessing the biodiversity they support (Briers and Biggs, 2003; Angélbert et al., 2004) or are likely to host (Davies et al., 2004; Gaston et al., 2005). Among wetland inhabitants, aquatic insects have the potential to be relevant ecological indicators. Indeed, they are already widely used to reveal short- and long-term environmental changes in both running and still waters (Céréghino et al., 2003; Verneaux et al., 2004), most notably through the strong influence of human disturbance on the species richness of aquatic insects (Rosenberg and Resh, 1993). Such disturbances usually lead to losses of taxa (Compin and Céréghino, 2003). However, in a given area, biodiversity estimates (e.g. species richness, evenness, etc.) strongly depend on the spatial scale (type of habitat) and temporal scale (week, month, or season) over which observations are made. Water temperature is usually considered to be the major abiotic factor affecting the life-cycle phenology of aquatic invertebrates (Vannote and Sweeney, 1980; Sweeney et al., 1986), influencing the seasonality and development patterns of aquatic insects through growth, adult size, and fecundity (Lavandier, 1988; Giberson and Rosenberg, 1992; Pritchard and Zloty, 1994). This study suggested that the increased growth of those species with long generations (e.g., Cloeon dipterum) seemed to correspond to the rise in water temperature in spring (March), and that the warmest period (spring–summer) favoured the hatching and rapid development of short summer generations in most species. Whatever the biotic and/or abiotic factors controlling the life-cycle phenologies, and, subsequently, the temporal patterns of aquatic insect communities within ponds, this study clearly emphasizes the temporal dimension of biodiversity in small bodies of water. The seasonality of wetland-dependent insects in particular may influence the biodiversity ponds may support. Similar recommendations are already part of protocols for sampling and assessment of both riverine and wetland habitats, e.g. RIVPACS sampling for rivers (Wright et al., 2000), and UK National Pond Survey methods (Pond Action, 1989). Life-cycle attributes (e.g., reproduction, hatching and emergence periods) need to be carefully considered when restoring, managing and/or creating new ponds for conservation purposes (Ripley et al., 2004). Owing to the difficulty of pond creation in the study area (a limestone plateau), dredging the abandoned ponds is the only option for wetland restoration. Therefore, environmental managers should minimize the likelihood that dredging will eliminate populations (e.g., during the main growth or hatching periods). Theoretically, the acceptable period for dredging would be between adult emergence and egg-laying, i.e. during the flight and reproduction period. Given that most populations show a temporal sequence of species replacements (e.g. certain Coleoptera, Heteroptera), or have delayed life-cycle events (certain Odonata), defining an optimal period for dredging seems to be an impossible task. As an alternative, a plan of pond management should be envisaged over a large spatial scale to maintain the heterogeneity of pond networks in the area. Such a plan would imply promoting the conservation of all ponds, regardless of their successional stages. This is especially important when the density of ponds in the network is very sparse. Indeed, a recent study in the same area (Angélibert and Giani, 2003) on the dispersal capability of Odonata showed that dispersal phenomena were low because of the distance separating ponds. Thus, after dredging, species adapted to late succession ponds have little hope of finding suitable conditions in other ponds to ensure their development. The insects studied are widely distributed throughout Europe (see the Limnofauna Europaea (Illies, 1978)) and are regarded as having a low conservation priority. Broader conservation strategies should therefore ensure that such currently common organisms do not become the endangered species of the future (Rustigian et al., 2003). Ponds also provide useful models for studying how life-history patterns enable many populations to utilize small ecosystems, temporal segregation and/or differences in the size of coexisting nymphs certainly reducing interspecific competition for food and habitat resources (Svensson et al., 2000; Cayrou and Céréghino, 2003). Subsequently, interesting ideas and/or alternative strategies can be derived for conservation planning. Because the growth of most species is markedly seasonal and many species are temporally segregated, the spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats must be enlarged. Thus, when possible, pond networks should primarily be preserved rather than attempting to target some bodies of water for particular management actions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We wish to thank N. Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013).
