Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. For plotting purposes, the environmental vectors have been multiplied by factors of 2 and 0.5 for the sites and species biplots, respectively For example, despite being shallow, some of the study lakes were stratified at the time of sampling (mid-summer), with observed differences in water temperature of more than 10 °C across the water column (Mossocrop 2013). Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Specifically, decreases in the relative abundance of pelagic, Daphnia Fig. 5 Comparison of the relative abundances of the dominant cladoceran taxa in modern and pre-industrial sediments from 26 lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Modern and pre-industrial cladoceran relative abundances are shown as solid and open bars, respectively spp. that require more Ca were related to declines in lake water Ca concentrations, a finding supported by laboratory evidence (Ashforth and Yan 2008), field data (Cairns 2010), and other paleoecological studies in the Muskoka-Haliburton region (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2012a, b). Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Thus, while it is possible that climate may be an important factor influencing cladocerans in some lakes, we believe that it has played a less important role than long-term ![Boxplots comparing deep and shallow values for various water quality parameters: NO3/NO2, TP, Ca, Mg, SO4, spec. conductance, pH, DOC, surface area, and maximum depth.](page_0_0_2048_2048.png) Fig. 6 Box plots comparing ten physical or chemical variables in 30 shallow (this study) and 41 deeper (DeSellas et al. 2008) lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Specifically, decreases in the relative abundance of pelagic, Daphnia Fig. 5 Comparison of the relative abundances of the dominant cladoceran taxa in modern and pre-industrial sediments from 26 lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Modern and pre-industrial cladoceran relative abundances are shown as solid and open bars, respectively spp. that require more Ca were related to declines in lake water Ca concentrations, a finding supported by laboratory evidence (Ashforth and Yan 2008), field data (Cairns 2010), and other paleoecological studies in the Muskoka-Haliburton region (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2012a, b). Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Multiyear measurements of ebullitive methane flux from three subarctic lakes Martin Wik,1 Patrick M. Crill,1 Ruth K. Varner,2 and David Bastviken1,3 Received 24 April 2013; revised 29 July 2013; accepted 3 August 2013; published 20 September 2013. [1] Ebullition (bubbling) from small lakes and ponds at high latitudes is an important yet unconstrained source of atmospheric methane (CH4). Small water bodies are most abundant in permanently frozen peatlands, and it is speculated that their emissions will increase as the permafrost thaws. We made 6806 measurements of CH4 ebullition during four consecutive summers using a total of 40 bubble traps that were systematically distributed across the depth zones of three lakes in a sporadic permafrost landscape in northernmost Sweden. We identified significant spatial and temporal variations in ebullition and observed a large spread in the bubbles’ CH4 concentration, ranging from 0.04% to 98.6%. Ebullition followed lake temperatures, and releases were significantly larger during periods with decreasing atmospheric pressure. Although shallow zone ebullition dominated the seasonal bubble CH4 flux, we found a shift in the depth dependency towards higher fluxes from intermediate and deep zones in early fall. The average daily flux of 13.4 mg CH4 m−2 was lower than those measured in most other high-latitude lakes. Locally, however, our study lakes are a substantial CH4 source; we estimate that 350 kg of CH4 is released via ebullition during summer (June–September), which is approximately 40% of total whole year emissions from the nearby peatland. In order to capture the large variability and to accurately scale lake CH4 ebullition temporally and spatially, frequent measurements over long time periods are critical. Citation: Wik, M., P. M. Crill, R. K. Varner, and D. Bastviken (2013), Multiyear measurements of ebullitive methane flux from three subarctic lakes, J. Geophys. Res. Biogeosci., 118, 1307–1321, doi:10.1002/jgrg.20103. 1. Introduction [2] Lakes are common features of the terrestrial landscape and known sources of methane (CH4) [Bastviken et al., 2004], an important radiatively active trace gas in Earth’s atmosphere [Cicerone and Oremland, 1988; Reeburgh, 2003]. There is much uncertainty in the contributions of water bodies to atmospheric CH4 due to few measurements on even fewer lakes and because of large unknowns in the spatiotemporal variability in emission [Bastviken et al., 2004]. Particularly numerous small lakes and ponds are critical for improved understanding of the role of water bodies, both in the global carbon (C) cycle and in quantifying the global CH4 budget [Cole et al., 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009; Downing, 2010]. [3] Bastviken et al. [2011] have recently estimated global lake CH4 emissions of 72 ± 69 Tg yr−1, which is approximately 40% of the global contribution by wetlands, considered the single largest natural source of atmospheric CH4 [Denman et al., 2007]. Although reported global lake CH4 emissions are dominated by releases from temperate, subtropical, and tropical surface waters [Bastviken et al., 2011], lakes and ponds most frequently occur at higher latitudes, particularly in climate-sensitive permafrost landscapes [Lehner and Döll, 2004; Smith et al., 2007]. The available data sets for these high-latitude environments are limited, and therefore, they cannot be seen as fully representative. In a warming Arctic, permafrost degradation is likely to cause increased wetness and widespread formation of ponds and small lakes [Sannel and Kuhry, 2011]. Large amounts of labile organic C, currently stored in frozen peatlands, can potentially be mobilized following thaw and transported to anoxic lake sediments that favor CH4 production and release to the atmosphere [van Huissteden et al., 2011]. Hence, there is speculation that the source contribution of CH4 from high-latitude lakes will increase and be a positive feedback to projected future warming [Walter et al., 2006; Cole et al., 2007]. [4] Ebullition is a spatially and temporally complex, yet major, transport mode of CH4 from anoxic lake bottoms. It has been estimated to dominate over diffusional losses from the water column [Crill et al., 1988; Keller and Stallard, 1994; Bastviken et al., 2011]. The bubbles are gas mixtures that can be almost entirely CH4, but more often, they also Figure 1. Location of our study lakes within the Stordalen Mire, 11 km east of Abisko in northern Sweden (68°21'N, 19°02'E). Colored contours and solid white circles indicate water depth and bubble trap placement, respectively. Note that Lake Villasjön is evenly shallow around 1 m. The aerial infrared photograph was taken in July 2000 (available at the Abisko Scientific Research Station (ANS)). contain percent concentrations of nitrogen (N_2) and trace amounts of carbon dioxide (CO_2) and hydrogen (H_2) [Fendinger et al., 1992; Walter et al., 2008]. Methane formation in anoxic sediments is through both acetate fermentation and CO_2 reduction by H_2 and is controlled by heat energy and the availability of organic substrate [Zeikus and Winfrey, 1976; Kelly and Chynoweth, 1981; Duc et al., 2010]. Bubbling events are believed to occur when the pressure of the gas in the sediment exceeds the overlying hydrostatic loading [Fendinger et al., 1992]; negative changes in atmospheric pressure as well as decreasing water level have been found to coincide with gas eruptions from surface waters [Mattson and Likens, 1990; Varadharajan and Hemond, 2012]. [5] Observations suggest that bubbles are more frequently released in shallow zones close to lake margins [Keller and Stallard, 1994; Zimov et al., 1997; Bastviken et al., 2004]. Apart from a lower hydrostatic pressure, shallow areas often support plant growth, providing an autochthonous source of fresh organic C. Labile allochthonous organic loading is also likely to have a shorter residence time in the water column and a higher likelihood to be deposited to sediments in shallow zones. At depth, it eventually accumulates in a more decomposed state after a longer transit time and a prolonged period in the water column [Torres et al., 2010]. Shallow zones also favor bubble formation because they are generally warmer, which both stimulates methanogenesis [Duc et al., 2010] and makes CH_4 less soluble [Yamamoto et al., 1976]. After release, ebullitive CH_4 is largely unaffected by oxidation and dissolution in the water column because of the bubbles' buoyancy and rapid ascent to the surface [Chanton, 2005], although in deeper water bodies, exchange between the rising bubbles and the surrounding water occurs [McGinnis et al., 2006]. [6] A large amount of bubbles are emitted from point sources (seeps) in the sediment that are capable of more or less reoccurring releases [Walter et al., 2007; Wik et al., 2011]. Studies of Arctic lakes in permafrost regions in Alaska and Siberia report that seep ebullition can be persistent enough to maintain open holes (hot spots) in the ice during winter [e.g., Anthony et al., 2012]. Furthermore, Walter et al. [2007] argue that seeps in lake sediments are spatially fixed and that randomly dispersed measurements, or those that are not located directly over seeps, are likely to fail to capture large bubbling events and only monitor what they label as background ebullition, an overall smaller part of the total ebullitive flux. However, fluxes quantified irrespective of predetermined seep locations should not be neglected. Lake systems differ morphologically, and long-term spatially fixed seeps are likely absent in sediments that are not linked to deeper gas-rich structures or geological C-rich deposits such as coal seams [Etiope et al., 2009] and Table 1. Ice surveys of trapped bubbles on frozen high-latitude lakes indicate that seeps are often short-lived, emitting bubbles episodically during a limited time only [Wik et al., 2011]. [7] Bottom-up estimates and predictions of northern lake CH$_4$ emissions are limited not only by large uncertainties in the vulnerability and fate of permafrost [Hugelius et al., 2012] but also by the lack of long-term flux measurements that address highly heterogeneous emission pathways and large unknowns in release mechanisms [Bastviken et al., 2004; Tranvik et al., 2009]. This paper reports four years of seasonal (June–September) measurements of CH$_4$ ebullition from three lakes in subarctic Sweden that lie within a peatland underlain by sporadic permafrost. We identify the distribution of ebullition rates, bubble CH$_4$ concentrations, and fluxes with this unique data set. The core of this study focuses on determining the temporal and spatial variability of ebullition. We use analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare bubble CH$_4$ concentrations and fluxes among our study lakes and among sampling locations and different depth zones. Using the same approach, we also investigate annual, monthly, and daily variability among the four years, from June to September. Furthermore, the bubble CH$_4$ concentrations and fluxes are compared with those measured in previous studies on other northern lakes. We also compare the flux magnitudes with CH$_4$ emissions from the major subhabitats of the surrounding landscape, and we highlight the importance of long-term measurements and use cumulative fluxes when extrapolating seasonal fluxes across entire lake areas. 2. Note the different scales on the y axes. complex, a dynamic subarctic peatland 11 km east of Abisko in northern Sweden (68°21′N, 19°02′E; Figure 1). The mire is 350 m above sea level and underlain by sporadic permafrost visible as ombrotrophic palsas that rise above semiwet and wet minerotrophic fens, streams, and shallow lakes. The Abisko region has warmed 1.5°C in recent decades, from a mean annual temperature of −0.9°C in 1974 to 0.6°C in 2006 [Callaghan et al., 2010]. At the Stordalen Mire, warming above the 0°C threshold has caused substantial permafrost degradation, shallow water pool formation, and shorter ice-covered seasons [Christensen, 2004; Johansson et al., 2006]. Although the elevated parts of the mire experience permafrost degradation, there are limited erosional margins around the lakes. Instead, the lakes are mostly surrounded by wet fens (dominated by Eriophorum angustifolium, Carex rostrata, and Sphagnum spp.) and semiwet subalpine birch forest [Malmer et al., 2005]. [9] Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön are smaller but deeper lakes than Villasjön, which is overall shallow (Table 1) and bottom freezes during winter. Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön share water via Yttre Harrsjön, and during high flow, Villasjön drains into Inre Harrsjön through a fen and southwest into the continuously north flowing stream. Mellan Harrsjön receives the majority of its water from the same stream, and there is a small inflow feeding water into Villasjön from the east. Inre Harrsjön, on the other hand, lacks a comparable surface water source [Olefeldt et al., 2012]. Both Inre Harrsjön and Villasjön are considered partly spring fed; springs have been located north and south of Inre Harrsjön [Nilsson, 2006], and water upwelling has been observed in Villasjön. The lakes are usually ice free from mid-May to mid-October. [10] Little is known about the lake sediments. Radiocarbon dating of sediment sequences in Inre Harrsjön and Villasjön suggests that initial sedimentation began 2650 and 3400 calibrated years B.P., respectively [Kokfelt et al., 2010]. The organic layer in the central intermediately deep (3.5 m) part of Inre Harrsjön consists of 275 cm gyttja with a 40% C content [loss on ignition (LOI)] in the top meter. In the northeastern part of Villasjön, the organic layer measures 323 cm of peat-rich detritus gyttja with a C content of up to 80% (LOI) [Kokfelt et al., 2010]. The lakes have similar drainage basins and are shallow enough to have similar wind mixing and resuspension of surface sediments during storm events. Inre Harrsjön and Mellan Harrsjön are underlain by schist bedrock, whereas Villasjön is underlain by granite [Lindström et al., 1985]. 2.2. Ebullition Sampling [11] We measured lake CH4 ebullition during consecutive summers (June–September) of 2009–2012 at 40 locations using bubble traps. The trap design consisted of an inverted 50 cm wide circular funnel fitted with a closed scaled cylinder (10 ml polypropylene syringe and three-way stopcock; Figure 2). The narrow neck of the sampler was designed to limit the potential surface area that could promote diffusion of CH4 from the trap back into the water. Each funnel was stabilized by floating foam and three equally sized weights and attached to a separate float connected to a mooring, allowing it to roam in an area of 12 m². This ensured that the traps were not affected by their moorings. [12] In Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön, 13 and 17 bubble traps were distributed along transects that stretched over the entire lakes, covering different water depth zones (Figure 1). The transect locations were also chosen with respect to the distribution of trapped bubbles in the ice in winter reported by Wik et al. [2011]. We measured not only zones with high spatial density of clustered bubble morphologies but also areas where clusters were minimal. In shallow Villasjön, 10 traps were deployed across the southwestern part of the lake, a zone that stretches from the central peat plateau toward a rockier bottom with little aquatic vegetation. We estimated that the shallow, intermediate, and deep zones covered 19.2, 0.8, and 0.3 ha, respectively, using the depth contour map developed by Wik et al. [2011]. 3. Results 3.1. Overall Bubble Volume, CH4 Concentration, and Flux [18] Altogether, we measured 6806 headspace volumes from the bubble traps, of which 45% were greater than zero and 88% were sampled in periods of 24–72 h. Ebullition rates were on average 39.9 mL m−2 d−1 (10–90 percentile range: 0–103.6, n = 6806) and ranged from 0 to 2771.8 mL m−2 d−1. Bubble CH4 concentrations averaged 34.8% (SD = 25.2, n = 3763) and ranged from 0.04% to 98.6%. No relationship was found between CH4 concentration and corresponding headspace volume (R2 = 0.012, n = 3763). The calculated bubble fluxes were on average 13.4 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 (10–90 percentile range: 0–33.9, n = 6806) and ranged from 0 to 1682.5 mg CH4 m−2 d−1. Both the frequency distributions of ebullition rates and bubble CH4 fluxes followed a gamma distribution with a median close to zero (α = 0.14576 and 0.07663, β = 273.13 and 174.05; Figures 3a and 3c). The bubble CH4 concentrations were less positively skewed, following a Dagum distribution with a median close to the mean (k = 0.06023, α = 11.98, β = 80.883; Figure 3b). 3.2. Temporal Variability and Trends [19] Bubble CH4 concentrations and fluxes were highly variable among the four summer periods (p < 0.001, n = 3763 and 6806; Table 2). The average concentration was highest in 2010 and lowest in 2009, whereas the average flux was highest in 2009 and lowest in 2012. Monthly variations from June to September were larger than interannual variabilities (Table 3). We found a near twofold overall increase in bubble CH4 concentration during summer (p < 0.001, n = 3763; Table 2). Bubble CH4 flux magnitudes followed the heating and cooling of the lakes with a threefold overall increase from June to late August, after which they decreased in September (p < 0.001, n = 6806; Figure 4 and Table 2). [20] Ebullition was most variable on a daily basis (Table 3); average bubble fluxes (all 40 traps) ranged from 0 to 143.5 mg CH4 m−2 among the individual sampling periods. Days of peak ebullition often coincided with steep drops in atmospheric pressure and were observed as increased bubbling across the different depth zones (Figure 4). On average, the bubble CH4 flux was twofold higher and more variable during periods with an overall decreasing atmospheric pressure (p < 0.001, n = 6604; Figure 5). 3.3. Spatial and Depth-Dependent Variability [21] Bubble CH4 concentrations and fluxes were highly variable among and within the three lakes (p < 0.001, n = 3763 and 6806; Figure 6 and Table 2). Lake-specific averages were highest in Villasjön and lowest in Inre Harrsjön. Trap-specific averages ranged from 6.5% to 55.4% and from 0.4 to 52.8 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 and were lowest in the eastern shallow end of Inre Harrsjön (traps 1 and 2). Methane concentrations were highest in bubbles captured over the deep hole in Mellan Harrsjön (trap 20), and bubble CH4 fluxes were highest near the western shore of Villasjön (traps 31–34). [22] Altogether, bubble CH4 concentrations were similar among depth zones (p = 0.404, n = 3762).
