Furthermore, as discussed by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1999), a rise in high arctic annual average temperatures could potentially trigger an increase in ion content and nutrient levels leading to greater productivity. However, arctic environments are difficult to monitor on a frequent basis due to financial and logistical constraints (SMOL and DOUGLAS, 1996) and, as a result, relatively little ecological baseline data exist for many areas of the High Arctic (DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994). Earlier limnological analyses from other high latitude North American regions were published by, for example, FOGED (1958), LAMAR (1966), LIVINGSTONE (1967), HOBBIE (1980), SHEATH (1986), and DENYS and BEYENS (1987). The collection and analysis of North American arctic limnological data have continued with additional works: ALEXANDER et al. (1989), KLING et al. (1992), CORNWELL and BANAHAN (1992), GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) all in arctic Alaska; DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) on Cape Herschel, Ellesmere Island; LUDLAM (1996) on Cornwallis and Ellesmere Island, N.W.T.; PIENITZ et al. (1997 a, b) in the (a) Yukon and Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula, N.W.T., and (b) the Yellowknife region; RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998) on arctic treeline lakes in the central N.W.T., and ongoing research. Despite this recent surge of activity in the Arctic, we are still lacking even basic limnological data from many parts of the High Arctic, including the Bathurst Island region. Although some preliminary temperature records from a shallow pond have been published (DANKS, 1971), a more thorough documentation of the limnology of the lakes and ponds has yet to be completed. This information could eventually play a key role in the successful interpretation of paleolimnological data for climate change studies. Our study presents an overview of the water chemistry data of 38 lakes and ponds from eastern Bathurst Island, Nunavut (Fig. 1). This limnological information will also form part of a larger effort to create a limnological database of the Canadian High Arctic. 2. Site Description Bathurst Island (75°42' N, 97°21' W) is situated near the geographic center of the Canadian High Arctic (Fig. 1). The geology is similar to most other areas of the High Arctic in that it is covered by sedimentary Ordovician to Late Devonian rocks. The island is characterized geologically by its folded strata consisting mostly of limestone and siltstone (BUDKEWITSCH et al., 1996). The eastern-most segment of the Parry Islands Fold Belt is exposed on this island (HARRISON et al., 1991). The stratigraphic record in this area starts above the base of the Eleanor River Formation, which is a Lower to Middle Ordovician shelf carbonate unit (HARRISON et al., 1991). On Bathurst Island, the lithology and mineralogy encompasses shale, anhydrite, siltstone, sandstone, limestone, and dolostone (HODGSON, 1989). This underlying geology has resulted in low relief with few areas being more than 300 m asl; however, the island is also marked by areas of rugged topography with deeply incised streams and V-shaped valleys (KERR, 1981). Large portions of the island are also covered by felsenmeer or by glacial sands and gravels (KERR, 1981). The surficial geology is dominated by weathered and colluviated bedrock (HODGSON, 1989; TARNOCAI, 1976), and is highly alkaline (pH > 7.8) in the eastern portion of Bathurst Island (EDLUND, 1990). The texture of the surficial materials on the eastern side of Bathurst (where all the sampling took place for this study) usually have sufficient fines for the rooting of vascular plants (EDLUND, 1990). As with other high arctic sites, a continuous permafrost layer is prevalent throughout this study area. Low relief on eastern Bathurst Island has caused impeded drainage resulting in soils that are much more developed and wetter compared to other high arctic islands in the region. These soils are highly affected by cryogenic processes that have helped to rejuvinate soil surface nutrients by the continuous addition of new materials (TARNOCAI, 1976). Along the eastern side of the island, drainage characteristics range from poorly drained, highly saturated soils, to moderately to imperfectly drained slopes (EDLUND, 1990). This level of soil development directly affects vegetation, as Bathurst Island is much more lush than other nearby islands. This distinguishing characteristic is noteworthy given the similarity in short growing seasons and harsh winter conditions that Bathurst Island shares with its less vegetated, neighboring islands. Saxifraga oppositifolia, herbaceous plant communities, and a few local shrubs and sedges (EDLUND and ALT, 1989) characterize the vegetated areas in the eastern part of the island. Some eastern areas are also completely unvegetated and drain through highly alkaline (pH > 8.0) silt, sand, or gravel (EDLUND and ALT, 1989). The sandstone formations on Bathurst Island (Fig. 1, sections a, b, c, d) are commonly covered by green and black lichen, while the limestone and dolomite are nearly bare of any vegetation (KERR, 1974). Around the limnological sample sites, there were often abundant submerged mosses and grasses, which most likely affect the nutrient content of each water body. Mean annual temperature on Bathurst Island is −15.0 °C. The warmest summer month (July) has a mean temperature as high as 5.0 °C, although summer temperatures can, for short periods of time, rise to between 15 °C and 20 °C. Lakes and ponds begin to thaw in late June, whereas freeze-up and winter snows usually begin in late August or early September. 3. Materials and Methods 3.1. Sample Collection and Analysis A total of 38 lakes (>2 m deep) and ponds (<2 m deep) were sampled using a helicopter on Bathurst Island, Nunavut, Canada (Fig. 1) over the period of July 14–20, 1994. All lake and pond names are unofficial, and are given a designation of BC to BZ (B = Bathurst) and then BAA to BAN. A total of 39 limnological variables (both field and laboratory) were measured for each site. Latitudes and longitudes for all sites were recorded using a handheld Global Positioning System (GPS). These sites were selected in order to cover as wide an environmental gradient as possible (e.g. proximity to sea, altitude, size, drainage characteristics, vegetation, etc.). Sampling techniques for all abiotic and biotic components followed routine procedures as detailed by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) and PIENITZ et al. (1997a). Water temperature at approximately 0.3 m water depth was measured to the nearest 0.5 °C at each site using a handheld thermometer. Water samples for chemical analyses were collected from approximately 0.3 m water depth. At each site, pre-cleaned 250 ml Nalgene® bottles were rinsed three times with lake/pond water prior to water collection. Unfiltered samples for major and minor ion analysis were collected in these bottles. Similar samples were collected for trace metals. Unfiltered samples for total unfiltered phosphorus (TPU) were collected in pre-washed 250 ml glass bottles. A 1 L Nalgene® bottle was filled with lake/pond water that would be subsequently partitioned and prepared for future analysis of: total chlorophyll \( a \), particulate organic carbon (POC), particulate organic nitrogen (PON), further nutrient analysis, pH, and conductivity (COND) measurements. Upon return to base camp, unfiltered samples were measured for pH with a Hannah pH meter that was calibrated to buffers daily. Conductivity and salinity levels were measured using a Yellow Springs Instrument (YSI model 33) temperature/conductivity/salinity meter (readings accurate to better than ±5%). In preparation for subsequent nutrient analysis (i.e. total “dissolved” phosphorus (TPF), nitrite (NO\(_2\)), nitrate (NO\(_3\)), ammonia (NH\(_3\)), soluble reactive phosphate-phosphorus (SRP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), and total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN)), some water samples were filtered through 47 mm diameter cellulose acetate Sartorius filters (pore size = 0.45 \( \mu \)m), and the fil- trate was placed in acid rinsed 125 ml glass bottles. All water chemistry analyses were conducted by the National Water Research Institute (NWRI) in Burlington, Ontario, following standard methods (ENVIRONMENT CANADA, 1994a and b). In order to estimate biomass, on average 300 ml of each water sample were also filtered through glass microfiber filters for analysis of total chlorophyll (i.e. CHLAU and CHLAC; uncorrected and corrected for phaeophytin, respectively). Statistical Analysis The statistical analyses we used are summarized in Jongman (1987). Principal Components Analysis (PCA), using the computer program CANOCO v.3.15 (Ter Braak, 1990, 1997), was performed to ordinate the site and environmental data. From the 39 environmental variables measured, chemical concentrations that were recorded as being below the detection limit in more than half the study sites were eliminated from the active dataset (i.e. [Be^{2+}], [Cd^{2+}], [Co^{2+}], [Cr^{2+}], [Cu^{2+}], and [Pb^{2+}]). These variables were treated as passive elements in the statistical analyses. Therefore, the final environmental dataset comprised a total of 33 variables measured for each site (see Table 1 for a list of the active variables). A Pearson correlation matrix with Bonferroni adjustment (Table 2) was used to identify pairs of significantly (\( p \leq 0.05 \)) correlated environmental variables during data analysis. In order to check for skewness in the distribution of each environmental variable, CALIBRATE v.0.3 (Juggins and Ter Braak, 1992) was used. If necessary, the data were normalized through either a log (x), log (x + 1), or square root transformation. A list of each variable and the type of transformation performed is listed in Appendix 2 of Lim (1999). The PCA was performed using this transformed dataset. In an effort to identify trends and correlations in the nutrient relationships of the study sites, PON : POP (particulate organic phosphorus), TN : TPU, POC : POP, C : N : P and POC : CHLAU ratios were calculated (Table 1). A linear regression of CHLAU vs. TPU was also performed and compared to the Dillon and Rigler (1974) results. Finally, in order to discern differences in N-limitation amongst the sites, a series of separate CHLAU vs. TN linear regressions were performed for (1) all 38 sites, (2) sites with PON : POP \( \leq 10 : 1 \), and (3) sites with PON : POP \( > 10 : 1 \). 4. Results and Discussion 4.1. Physical Variables The 38 study sites, which ranged in elevation (ELEV) from sea level to a maximum of 335 m asl (mean ELEV = 93 m asl), included 23 shallow ponds, and 15 lakes that were deeper (see Table 1). Temperatures of all samples sites ranged from 2.5 \( ^\circ \)C to 19.5 \( ^\circ \)C. Not surprisingly, the shallow ponds were notably warmer than the deeper lakes. All shallower pond sites (n = 23) freeze solid to the bottom during the winter, and had an average July temperature of 12.2 \( ^\circ \)C, while the deeper lakes (n = 15) had an average temperature of 6.2 \( ^\circ \)C. Shallow sites have lower thermal capacities and will therefore heat up or cool down much faster than deeper lakes. The correlation matrix (Table 2) helped to identify correlations among several of the measured variables. Elevation (ELEV) was not correlated with temperature (TEMP). Therefore, temperature variation amongst sites during the week of sampling was most likely driven by the differences in thermal inertia and water volume/hydrological budget, and not the slight elevation gradient present on the island. 4.2. Overall, the concentrations (mg/L) of the major ions were relatively high (Table 1) compared to those of typical inland fresh waters (McNEELY et al., 1979). Ca^{2+}, Na^{+} and Mg^{2+} are the major cations, while CO_3^{-} (i.e. DIC), SO_4^{-} and Cl^{-} are the major anions. The major ion concentrations are relatively similar among all sites; however a gradient exists between the shallower vs. deeper sites with respect to ionic concentration, in that the deeper sites were more dilute relative to the shallower sites. The relative concentration of cations among sampled sites was Ca > Mg > Na > K (Table 1), with means of 30.8 mg/L, 5.6 mg/L, 3.1 mg/L, and 0.4 mg/L respectively. These ratios are similar to those of KLING et al. (1992), EILERS et al. (1993), DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994), PIENITZ et al. (1997a, b) (although Mg was not considered), RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998), and GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000). The relative concentration of the major anions among the sites was, on average, CO₃ > SO₄ > Cl. The dominance of calcium carbonate and bicarbonate ions reflects the calcium-carbonate rich limestone bedrock or dolostone tills in the drainage basins of all sample sites. Concentrations of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ were largely a function of proximity to the Arctic Ocean. From the correlation matrix (Table 2), it is apparent that elevation (ELEV) was negatively correlated with [Na], and [Cl]. More inland and higher elevation sites would be less subject to sea spray inputs carrying Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, and Ba²⁺ than sites closer to the ocean (Table 1). Varying concentrations of K⁺ might be related to the abundance of vascular plants in the catchment that are thought to leak out this cation (PRENTKI et al., 1980). Similar to the findings of DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994), those sites with abundant grasses, mosses and other vascular plants growing within the drainage basin had higher [K] (Table 1). SO₄ concentrations were usually relatively high, ranging from 0.60 mg/L (site BF)–22.0 mg/L (site BAI), with a mean concentration of 6.3 mg/L (Table 1). High SO₄ concentrations were also found in the PIENITZ et al. (1997a) study lakes that were in areas of prevalent limestone-dolomite, sandstone, siltstone, and conglomerate rock (i.e. bedrock similar to that of Bathurst Island). PIENITZ et al. (1997a) attributed the elevated SO₄ levels to weathering from this bedrock. There did not appear to be a link between SO₄ levels and proximity to the ocean in the Bathurst Island samples. The relationship between higher levels of pH, conductivity and major ions within the sample sites is similar to the findings of RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998) for their ‘Tundra’ sites in the central arctic mainland, and for those sites sampled by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) on Ellesmere Island. These similarities may point to a homogeneity within high arctic water bodies, however this must not be assumed given that so little of the geographic range of the High Arctic has been sampled and analyzed for limnological characteristics. 4.3. Nutrients: N and P Nutrient concentrations in all of the sampled sites were below the averages for uncontaminated surficial waters listed by McNEELY et al. (1979), which reflects the characteristic oligotrophic aquatic environments typical for high arctic regions. TKN was the most variable, with a range from 0.056 mg/L to 1.08 mg/L, and a mean of 0.334 mg/L. These values are similar to those reported by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) for the western arctic mainland of Canada, and GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) for arctic Alaska. The NO₂, NO₃–NO₂, and NH₃ values for the Bathurst Island sites are all near or below detection limits (<0.001 mg/L) (Table 1). Sites BAA and BAB were, however, exceptions to this with NO₃–NO₂ values well above the mean (Table 1). BAA was receiving ice and snow cover melt inputs at time of sampling, which may have caused a spike in the NO₃–NO₂ concentrations from the land. Furthermore, both BAA and BAB were surrounded by a large area of mud, through which run-off channels had been carved. These channels may have also contributed nitrate and nitrite inputs into these sites, hence elevating their concentrations relative to other lakes and ponds on Bathurst Island. Among the three phosphorus variables, TPU and TPF had the highest correlation with themselves (r = 0.51) (Table 2). TPU ranged from 3.2 µg/L–64.0 µg/L, and had an average of 12.7 µg/L, which is comparable to values reported by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) for their western arctic sites. TPF ranged from 1.7 µg/L–11.5 µg/L (mean = 6.1 µg/L), which is again comparable to those values reported by other limnological studies in arctic tundra regions (e.g. DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994; WHALEN and CORNWELL, 1985; McNEELY and GUMMER, 1984). Values for SRPF ranged from 0.9 µg/L–4.3 µg/L (mean = 1.5 µg/L), which is comparable to the results of PRENTKI et al. (1980) and PIENITZ et al. (1997a, b). These TPU levels may not necessarily indicate that phosphorus is the primary limiting nutrient for algae in the Bathurst Island sites. Patterns in the ratios of PON to particulate organic phosphorus (POP = TPU – TPF) (i.e. PON : POP), total nitrogen (TN = NO₃NO₂ + TKN + PON) to TPU (i.e. TN : TPU), and C : N : P were examined in order to identify sites which were potentially more P-limited than others. According to SAKAMOTO (1966) and SCHANZ and JUON (1983), ambient N : P ratios greater than approximately 20 : 1 are characteristic of significantly P-limited aquatic environments. If, however, the N : P ratio is less than 10 : 1, then the algae may be N-limited. Ratios between 10 : 1 and 20 : 1 may indicate limitation by either nutrient. However, these nutrient ratios are useful only in cases where the ambient concentrations are near growth-limiting concentrations (BORCHARDT, 1996). The oligotrophic Bathurst Island lakes and ponds appear to conform to this criterion. PON : POP ratios ranged from 1 : 1 (BF, BAH) to 90 : 1 (BT) (mean = 13 : 1). Overall, 63% of the sites had ratios of \( \leq 10 : 1 \), 13% had ratios of \( \geq 20 : 1 \), while 24% fell in the intermediate zone of 10 : 1 to 20 : 1. Sites BD, BF, BK, BP, BR, BU, BY, BZ, BAD, BAH, and BAJ, which have PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), all have [TPU] greater than the reported mean of 12.7 \( \mu \)g/L, and, according to our field notes, were characterized by a ‘greenish’ tinge. The elevated TPU values of these sites may be attributed to the large quantity of excrement left both in and around these watersheds by the local wildlife (e.g., caribou, lemmings, muskox, and arctic terns). Five of these sites (BK, BU, BY, BZ, BAD), in particular, are grouped along the TPU gradient on the Principal Components Analysis (PCA) ordination (Fig. 2). Some of the sites (i.e. BC, BG, BL, BM, BN, BS, BAB, BAC, BAI, BAK, BAL, BAM, BAN) with PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \) do have [TPU] below the mean. However with the exception of BAL and BAN, all of these sites also had PON values significantly below the mean (38.0 \( \mu \)g/L) (Table 1). The TPU and PON values for BAL (9.6 \( \mu \)g/L, 40.0 \( \mu \)g/L) and BAN (12.3 \( \mu \)g/L, 54.0 \( \mu \)g/L) deviated only slightly below and above from the respective means. Therefore, although both nutrient levels may be lower relative to other sites, nitrogen may still be the limiting factor to algal growth in these sites. Those sites with PON : POP ratios \( \geq 20 : 1 \), BE, BH, BT, BAE, and BAG, all had [TPU] below the mean, and were characterized by rocky drainage areas. Sites BH and BAE are larger, deeper lakes, which may also account for their more dilute concentrations of TPU relative to other sites. TN : TPU ratios ranged from 12 : 1 to 150 : 1, with a mean of 64 : 1. These ratios are comparable to those reported by SHORTREED and STOCKNER (1986) (i.e., 38 : 1 to 109 : 1) for 19 lakes in the Yukon Territory, PIENITZ et al. (1997a) (i.e., 13 : 1 to 103 : 1) for their 59 lakes along a southern Yukon to Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula transect, and by GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) (i.e., 3 : 1 to 124 : 1) for 51 lakes in arctic Alaska. Two-thirds of the sites which had PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), also had TN : TPU ratios below the mean for the Bathurst Island dataset (Table 1). This may indicate that, instead of being P-limited, algae may be limited to a greater degree by nitrogen. Nitrogen has been found to be the dominant limiting nutrient to phytoplankton growth in subarctic lakes when the lakes were P-fertilized (SMITH et al., 1984). The TN : TPU ratios reported for Bathurst Island, as well as by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) and by SHORTREED and STOCKNER (1986) for the western arctic mainland and the Yukon Territory respectively, are much higher than those reported by SMITH (1983) for lakes dominated by nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Moreover, in shallow ponds wind agitation of the sediment, as was demonstrated by ALEXANDER et al. (1989), may be the dominant source of pond water N. In larger lakes, N levels may be even lower, because the sediment recharge of N would be low due to the low rate of sedimentation, low water temperature, and year-round oxic conditions (ALEXANDER et al., 1989). Most of the Bathurst sites with TN : TPU ratios below the mean were either larger, deeper lakes (e.g. BC, BK) and/or they drained through snow-banks with diluted nutrient concentrations (e.g. BF, BAM) (LIM, 1999). This observation supports the findings of ALEXANDER et al. (1989), and suggests that these sites (a) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for 38 sites](page_184_180_627_496.png) (b) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for sites with PON : POP < 10 : 1](page_1012_180_627_496.png) (c) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for sites with PON : POP > 10 : 1](page_184_728_627_496.png) Figure 2. Finally, by comparing the average C : N : P ratios for the Bathurst Island sites to those of other studies, we can make an overall assessment of whether or not these sites are more N or P limited. The average C : N : P ratio for Bathurst Island is 107 : 6 : 1, which is lower than the ratio of 137 : 18 : 1 reported by Shortreed and Stockner (1986) for 19 Yukon lakes. Based on the average ratio for Bathurst Island, and in comparison to other reported values, we conclude that most of the sites may in fact be N-limited. However, it should be noted that the range of the C : N : P ratios was large, ranging from 29 : 1 : 1 for site BF to 1950 : 90 : 1 for site BT. Therefore, a few sites, as discussed earlier, are either severely or moderately P-limited. 4.4. Carbon DIC values ranged from 9.3 mg/L to 39.9 mg/L (mean = 20.1 mg/L). These values are comparable to the [DIC] from the Pienitz et al. (1997a) arctic study sites, and likely reflect similarities in bedrock geology. DOC concentrations were generally low to moderate on Bathurst Island, which is common in oligotrophic waters that are beyond the treeline. For example, average DOC concentrations in the PIENITZ et al. (1997a) study were lowest in unforested arctic tundra sites, whereas they were highest in boreal forest and forest-tundra sites. The [DOC] for Bathurst Island ranged from 1.1 mg/L to 11.2 mg/L (mean = 4.1 mg/L). PIENITZ et al. (1997a) found a significant correlation between watershed vegetation and DOC levels, an association which might account for the differences in our DOC concentrations. All of the sites with [DOC] greater than the mean drained through relatively lush vegetation such as grasses and mosses, and also supported abundant submerged mosses (LIM, 1999). Furthermore, the shallower pond sites on Bathurst Island were typically found in lush valley areas that supported various species of sedges and grasses, whereas deeper sites usually had more rocky drainage areas than the ponds. The increase in vegetation within these sites may have also provided ample substrate sources to support a rich diatom community, which would have also contributed to DOC levels through photosynthetic processes (McNEELY et al., 1979). Of course, deeper sites would also more likely dilute any terrestrial/detrital DOC. DOC levels play a critical role in controlling the depth of ultraviolet (UV) penetration into the lake or pond, which in turn has an impact on aquatic biota. Given the relatively low [DOC] in many Bathurst Island lakes, any slight changes in the environment that affect [DOC] may potentially have far reaching consequences (VINCENT and PIENITZ, 1996). 4.5. Chlorophyll a CHLAU concentrations for the 38 Bathurst Island sites ranged from below detection limits (<0.001 \( \mu \)g/L) to 3.4 \( \mu \)g/L (mean = 0.8 \( \mu \)g/L). In an effort to identify whether the POC in the water was mostly derived from either algal or terrestrial/detrital sources, POC : CHLAU ratios were calculated (Table 1). Furthermore, in order to compare this dataset to the DILLON and RIGLER (1974) linear regression of summer CHLA vs. TP, the slope and r-value for the linear regression of CHLAU vs. TPU for the Bathurst Island sites were calculated. Some POC : CHLAU ratios were not calculated, since CHLAU values were sometimes below the detection limit (n = 9). Those POC : CHLAU values that were available (n = 29) for calculation ranged from 11000 : 1 to 235 : 1, with a mean of 871 : 1. However, with the reduced sample size, this mean value should be treated cautiously. The range suggests significant variability in detrital input amongst the sites. Sites which drained through lush, vegetated areas where detrital material could be transported in the run-off, usually had POC : CHLAU ratios above the mean. However, it was surprising to find that sites such as BK, which have elevated [TPU] relative to other sites, would still have POC : CHLAU ratios far above the mean. One possible explanation is that site BK is N-limited rather than P-limited. Another possible explanation is that phosphorus can form strong bonds with Fe and DOC, making it inaccessible to algae. Site BK, in particular, had [Fe] and [DOC] levels (2.42 mg/L and 5.8 mg/L, respectively) above the reported means. This characteristic, coupled with a highly vegetated drainage basin, could drive the POC : CHLAU ratio up. According to DILLON and RIGLER (1974), sites which lie on or deviate only slightly from the CHLA-TP slope of 1.583 (derived from a linear regression of the SAKAMOTO (1966) dataset), will most likely be P-limited. However, those sites that have low N : P ratios would show much larger deviations from the overall trend. The CHLAU-TPU slope calculated for Bathurst Island was 3.784 (P > 0.01). Therefore, the Bathurst Island sites are, generally not severely P-limited. Instead, as has been documented throughout this study, the sites are most likely only partly P-limited or N-limited. The relationship between CHLAU and TN was also examined for all 38 sites. These two variables did not show a strong correlation (P > 0.01) (Fig. 2a). However, given that the relationship between CHLAU and TPU was also not significant, it is possible that nutrient factors other than N or P were playing a significant role in limiting algal growth. As stated earlier (see section 4.3), 63% of the sites are considered to be N-limited, having PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), while 37% of the sites had ratios \( > 10 : 1 \), and were considered to be either influenced by other nutrient factors or P-limited. Therefore, by running separate CHLAU vs TN regressions on those sites with (a) PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), and (b) PON : POP ratios \( > 10 : 1 \), differences in nutrient limiting factors among the sites were identified. From these regressions, it was apparent that the N-limited sites showed a significant correlation with the CHLAU values (\( r = 0.45; P \leq 0.01 \)) (Fig. 2b). Conversely, those sites that are most likely not N-limited were not significantly correlated with CHLAU (\( r = 0.10; P \geq 0.01 \)) (Fig. 2c). This also suggests that the prominent limitation for algal growth in approximately two thirds of the Bathurst Island sites may be nitrogen. Therefore, any disruptions to the nitrogen budget of these sites could cause a significant change in the algal biota. 4.6. PCA Axes 1 and 2 of the PCA accounted for 34.4% and 12.6%, respectively, of the variance (Table 3). Axes 3 and 4 collectively captured only 18.1% of the total cumulative percentage variance, and are therefore not discussed further here. Axes lengths were less than four standard deviations (SD), which indicates that the sites share many common attributes (JONGMAN et al., 1987). This is influenced by the similarity in local climate, and underlying bedrock at the sites. The dominant gradients identified in the PCA ordination (Fig. 3) of the measured limnological variables indicate that differences in: (a) major ion content, especially concentrations of calcium and magnesium; and (b) DOC levels along Axis 1; and (c) pH along Axis 2, mostly separate the distribution of the 38 lake and pond sites on the ordination. However, shallower pond sites tend to cluster separately from the deeper lakes. For example, eleven of the fifteen deeper sites are clustered in the two left quadrats of the PCA ordination. Conductivity (COND), [Ca], and [Mg] show a high positive correlation along the first axis of the PCA (Fig. 3). This relationship is also clear in the correlation matrix (Table 2), with positive correlations between COND and [Ca] and [Mg]. Those sites (e.g., BD, BE, BAJ) which have relatively elevated Ca and Mg levels, ordinate closely in relation to the gradient extremes of these environmental variables, located in the lower right quadrat of the PCA (Fig. 3). Aluminum, iron, and manganese also show high positive correlations with Axis 1 (Fig. 3), and share high correlations to each other (Table 2). This is to be expected, given that water containing elevated levels of calcium and magnesium salts are commonly associated with polyvalent metals such as iron, aluminum, and manganese (LIND, 1974). Sites BK, BU, BY, BZ and BAD, located in the upper right-hand quadrat of the PCA, all had high levels of these metals (Table 1). In acidic lakes, high levels aluminum have been correlated with pH (DIXIT et al., 1993). The results indicate that the dominant limnological gradients affecting variation among the lakes and ponds are: (a) major ion content, and (b) DOC levels along Axis 1, and pH along Axis 2. trations of Al were fairly similar and relatively low at the Bathurst sites (mean of 0.05 mg/L). This is to be expected given the similarity in catchment geology. The DOC gradient is most likely driving the differences between the shallower ponds and the deeper lakes (Fig. 3). Shallower pond sites (e.g., BD, BE, and BJ) are ordinated closely to the DOC gradient extremity, while deeper sites (e.g., BG, BH, and BO) are ordinated in the opposite quadrat. The projection of site scores onto environmental arrows allows for the detection of key patterns of variation in the limnological dataset, and for the inference of the chemical composition of any given site (JONGMAN et al., 1987). Therefore, we can infer that the shallower sites had higher organic matter concentrations relative to the deeper sites. Small oligotrophic water bodies such as shallow tundra ponds can receive significant amounts of dissolved organic carbon from the catchment vegetation and soils even in the absence of trees. Field observations indicated that the ponds tended to have more grasses and mosses in their catchments relative to the lake sites. The pH gradient is most closely related to Axis 2, but it also shares a relationship with the Ca–Mg and polyvalent metal gradients driving Axis 1 (Fig. 3). Those sites (e.g., BAI, BAJ, BAL) ordinated at the end of the pH arrow have higher alkalinity levels and elevated Ca and Mg levels (Table 1). Sites located in the upper left-hand quadrat (Fig. 3) (i.e., BF, BG, BH, BL, BN, BO, BS, BT, BAK) all have lower pH, Ca and Mg levels relative to other sample sites (Table 2). This pH trend is not correlated with size or elevation (ELEV). Indeed, given the short pH gradient length and the similarity in underlying bedrock at the sites, only slight differences exist in the levels of pH. 5. Conclusions Major ion concentrations of the Bathurst Island ponds and lakes were relatively high. This is consistent with the calcareous, limestone, and dolomite bedrock of the drainage basins at these sites. Differences in Na and Cl concentrations were primarily related to the proximity of each site to the sea. Overall, this limnological dataset was similar to those reported by other studies from similar geological settings in the subarctic and arctic regions of North America (see KLING et al., 1992; EILERS et al., 1993; DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994; PIENITZ et al., 1997a, b; RÜHLAND and SMOL, 1998; GREGORY-EAVES et al., 2000; Table 4). Nutrient concentrations at all sites were typical for high arctic, oligotrophic aquatic environments. TPU values were comparable to the reported values from other arctic sites (e.g., PIENITZ et al., 1997a). Examination of PON : POP, TN : TPU and REDFIELD (C : N : P) ratios showed that, although certain sites were P-limited, most of the Bathurst Island sites may have been N-limited. Comparison of the slope of the CHLA vs. TP linear regression for Bathurst Island to that calculated by DILLON and RIGLER (1974) for summer values also suggests that most of our sites are not highly P-limited, but rather range from partly P-limited to N-limited. Variance in [DOC] could be partially explained by differences in surrounding vegetation for each site, as well as the water volume of the sites. Sites with [DOC] greater than the mean were typically smaller ponds, which drained through prominently vegetated areas, where detrital material could be transported in the run-off. PCA eigenvalues showed that the first two axes of the ordination could explain most of the limnological variation among the sites. Conductivity, DOC, and variables related to water hardness, such as Ca-Mg ions and other polyvalent metals, contributed primarily to Axis 1, while Axis 2 was driven primarily by pH. Differences between the shallow vs. deeper sites were especially clear in their spread in the ordination relative to the DOC gradient. Future work on Bathurst Island should include a detailed limnological analysis of the western portion of the island. Surficial geological material on western Bathurst Island is much less alkaline (pH < 4.0) than in the east (EDLUND, 1990). A comparison of the water chemistry of the lakes and ponds in these two areas could help expand our understanding of the dominant limnological trends governing Bathurst Island. 6. Box 450 Station A, Ottawa, Ontario, K1N 6N5, Canada Physical and Chemical Limnological Characteristics of 38 Lakes and Ponds on Bathurst Island, Nunavut, Canadian High Arctic key words: limnology, high arctic, nitrogen, phosphorus, dissolved organic carbon Abstract The limnological features that characterize the shallow ponds (<2 m deep) and lakes (>2 m deep) on Bathurst Island, Nunavut, Canada were examined through chemical analyses and multivariate statistical methods as part of a larger on-going survey to document and monitor environmental changes in these remote and sensitive areas. All sites were relatively oligotrophic and alkaline. Nutrient ratios indicated that nitrogen could be limiting algal growth to a greater degree than phosphorus in over 63% of the sites. Principal components analysis (PCA) was used to explore the patterns of variation in the limnological dataset. The three dominant limnological gradients were: major ion content and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) levels along Axis 1; and pH along Axis 2. 1. Introduction The High Arctic is a critical area for environmental and climatic research, as the effects of hemispheric temperature trends are exacerbated in this region (Rouse et al., 1997). For example, warming in the central Arctic since 1976 has been in excess of 0.75 °C per decade, while mid-latitude increases are typically less than 0.5 °C per decade (Jones, 1988). Furthermore, over the 20th century, increases in average arctic temperatures have exceeded those recorded for the hemisphere as a whole (Overpeck et al., 1997). The prediction that Canada’s cold environments will be affected by greater climatic change than experienced elsewhere is also suggested by general circulation model simulations (Ledrew, 1993). These simulations predict temperature increases as great as 4 °C in the summer and 9 °C in the winter for a 2 × CO2 scenario (Rouse et al., 1997). It is known that the High Arctic is strongly tied to general circulation patterns due to its inherent role as an energy sink (Ledrew, 1993), and therefore the effects of arctic climate change will not be restricted to this extreme area of the globe. Instead, it is predicted that any changes to the high arctic’s climate will inevitably affect low latitude climate systems. For example, changes in river run-off affected by atmospheric temperature increases could alter global thermohaline circulation patterns (Overpeck et al., 1997). With the need to better understand the far reaching effects of high arctic climatic and environmental changes, comes the requirement for long-term monitoring of this region. Physical, chemical and biological limnic information from high arctic lakes and shallow ponds provides a means to monitor environmental change in this region. These systems are Figure 1. Furthermore, as discussed by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1999), a rise in high arctic annual average temperatures could potentially trigger an increase in ion content and nutrient levels leading to greater productivity. However, arctic environments are difficult to monitor on a frequent basis due to financial and logistical constraints (SMOL and DOUGLAS, 1996) and, as a result, relatively little ecological baseline data exist for many areas of the High Arctic (DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994). Earlier limnological analyses from other high latitude North American regions were published by, for example, FOGED (1958), LAMAR (1966), LIVINGSTONE (1967), HOBBIE (1980), SHEATH (1986), and DENYS and BEYENS (1987). The collection and analysis of North American arctic limnological data have continued with additional works: ALEXANDER et al. (1989), KLING et al. (1992), CORNWELL and BANAHAN (1992), GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) all in arctic Alaska; DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) on Cape Herschel, Ellesmere Island; LUDLAM (1996) on Cornwallis and Ellesmere Island, N.W.T.; PIENITZ et al. (1997 a, b) in the (a) Yukon and Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula, N.W.T., and (b) the Yellowknife region; RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998) on arctic treeline lakes in the central N.W.T., and ongoing research. Despite this recent surge of activity in the Arctic, we are still lacking even basic limnological data from many parts of the High Arctic, including the Bathurst Island region. Although some preliminary temperature records from a shallow pond have been published (DANKS, 1971), a more thorough documentation of the limnology of the lakes and ponds has yet to be completed. This information could eventually play a key role in the successful interpretation of paleolimnological data for climate change studies. Our study presents an overview of the water chemistry data of 38 lakes and ponds from eastern Bathurst Island, Nunavut (Fig. 1). This limnological information will also form part of a larger effort to create a limnological database of the Canadian High Arctic. 2. Site Description Bathurst Island (75°42' N, 97°21' W) is situated near the geographic center of the Canadian High Arctic (Fig. 1). The geology is similar to most other areas of the High Arctic in that it is covered by sedimentary Ordovician to Late Devonian rocks. The island is characterized geologically by its folded strata consisting mostly of limestone and siltstone (BUDKEWITSCH et al., 1996). The eastern-most segment of the Parry Islands Fold Belt is exposed on this island (HARRISON et al., 1991). The stratigraphic record in this area starts above the base of the Eleanor River Formation, which is a Lower to Middle Ordovician shelf carbonate unit (HARRISON et al., 1991). On Bathurst Island, the lithology and mineralogy encompasses shale, anhydrite, siltstone, sandstone, limestone, and dolostone (HODGSON, 1989). This underlying geology has resulted in low relief with few areas being more than 300 m asl; however, the island is also marked by areas of rugged topography with deeply incised streams and V-shaped valleys (KERR, 1981). Large portions of the island are also covered by felsenmeer or by glacial sands and gravels (KERR, 1981). The surficial geology is dominated by weathered and colluviated bedrock (HODGSON, 1989; TARNOCAI, 1976), and is highly alkaline (pH > 7.8) in the eastern portion of Bathurst Island (EDLUND, 1990). The texture of the surficial materials on the eastern side of Bathurst (where all the sampling took place for this study) usually have sufficient fines for the rooting of vascular plants (EDLUND, 1990). As with other high arctic sites, a continuous permafrost layer is prevalent throughout this study area. Low relief on eastern Bathurst Island has caused impeded drainage resulting in soils that are much more developed and wetter compared to other high arctic islands in the region. These soils are highly affected by cryogenic processes that have helped to rejuvinate soil surface nutrients by the continuous addition of new materials (TARNOCAI, 1976). Along the eastern side of the island, drainage characteristics range from poorly drained, highly saturated soils, to moderately to imperfectly drained slopes (EDLUND, 1990). This level of soil development directly affects vegetation, as Bathurst Island is much more lush than other nearby islands. This distinguishing characteristic is noteworthy given the similarity in short growing seasons and harsh winter conditions that Bathurst Island shares with its less vegetated, neighboring islands. Saxifraga oppositifolia, herbaceous plant communities, and a few local shrubs and sedges (EDLUND and ALT, 1989) characterize the vegetated areas in the eastern part of the island. Some eastern areas are also completely unvegetated and drain through highly alkaline (pH > 8.0) silt, sand, or gravel (EDLUND and ALT, 1989). The sandstone formations on Bathurst Island (Fig. 1, sections a, b, c, d) are commonly covered by green and black lichen, while the limestone and dolomite are nearly bare of any vegetation (KERR, 1974). Around the limnological sample sites, there were often abundant submerged mosses and grasses, which most likely affect the nutrient content of each water body. Mean annual temperature on Bathurst Island is −15.0 °C. The warmest summer month (July) has a mean temperature as high as 5.0 °C, although summer temperatures can, for short periods of time, rise to between 15 °C and 20 °C. Lakes and ponds begin to thaw in late June, whereas freeze-up and winter snows usually begin in late August or early September. 3. Materials and Methods 3.1. Sample Collection and Analysis A total of 38 lakes (>2 m deep) and ponds (<2 m deep) were sampled using a helicopter on Bathurst Island, Nunavut, Canada (Fig. 1) over the period of July 14–20, 1994. All lake and pond names are unofficial, and are given a designation of BC to BZ (B = Bathurst) and then BAA to BAN. A total of 39 limnological variables (both field and laboratory) were measured for each site. Latitudes and longitudes for all sites were recorded using a handheld Global Positioning System (GPS). These sites were selected in order to cover as wide an environmental gradient as possible (e.g. proximity to sea, altitude, size, drainage characteristics, vegetation, etc.). Sampling techniques for all abiotic and biotic components followed routine procedures as detailed by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) and PIENITZ et al. (1997a). Water temperature at approximately 0.3 m water depth was measured to the nearest 0.5 °C at each site using a handheld thermometer. Water samples for chemical analyses were collected from approximately 0.3 m water depth. At each site, pre-cleaned 250 ml Nalgene® bottles were rinsed three times with lake/pond water prior to water collection. Unfiltered samples for major and minor ion analysis were collected in these bottles. Similar samples were collected for trace metals. Unfiltered samples for total unfiltered phosphorus (TPU) were collected in pre-washed 250 ml glass bottles. A 1 L Nalgene® bottle was filled with lake/pond water that would be subsequently partitioned and prepared for future analysis of: total chlorophyll \( a \), particulate organic carbon (POC), particulate organic nitrogen (PON), further nutrient analysis, pH, and conductivity (COND) measurements. Upon return to base camp, unfiltered samples were measured for pH with a Hannah pH meter that was calibrated to buffers daily. Conductivity and salinity levels were measured using a Yellow Springs Instrument (YSI model 33) temperature/conductivity/salinity meter (readings accurate to better than ±5%). In preparation for subsequent nutrient analysis (i.e. total “dissolved” phosphorus (TPF), nitrite (NO\(_2\)), nitrate (NO\(_3\)), ammonia (NH\(_3\)), soluble reactive phosphate-phosphorus (SRP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), and total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN)), some water samples were filtered through 47 mm diameter cellulose acetate Sartorius filters (pore size = 0.45 \( \mu \)m), and the fil- trate was placed in acid rinsed 125 ml glass bottles. All water chemistry analyses were conducted by the National Water Research Institute (NWRI) in Burlington, Ontario, following standard methods (ENVIRONMENT CANADA, 1994a and b). In order to estimate biomass, on average 300 ml of each water sample were also filtered through glass microfiber filters for analysis of total chlorophyll (i.e. CHLAU and CHLAC; uncorrected and corrected for phaeophytin, respectively). All filtered and unfiltered samples were kept chilled and in the dark for the duration of the field period. Subsequently, samples were shipped to the National Water Research Institute (NWRI) (Burlington, Ontario) for nutrient and major ion analysis. 3.2. Statistical Analysis The statistical analyses we used are summarized in Jongman (1987). Principal Components Analysis (PCA), using the computer program CANOCO v.3.15 (Ter Braak, 1990, 1997), was performed to ordinate the site and environmental data. From the 39 environmental variables measured, chemical concentrations that were recorded as being below the detection limit in more than half the study sites were eliminated from the active dataset (i.e. [Be^{2+}], [Cd^{2+}], [Co^{2+}], [Cr^{2+}], [Cu^{2+}], and [Pb^{2+}]). These variables were treated as passive elements in the statistical analyses. Therefore, the final environmental dataset comprised a total of 33 variables measured for each site (see Table 1 for a list of the active variables). A Pearson correlation matrix with Bonferroni adjustment (Table 2) was used to identify pairs of significantly (\( p \leq 0.05 \)) correlated environmental variables during data analysis. In order to check for skewness in the distribution of each environmental variable, CALIBRATE v.0.3 (Juggins and Ter Braak, 1992) was used. If necessary, the data were normalized through either a log (x), log (x + 1), or square root transformation. A list of each variable and the type of transformation performed is listed in Appendix 2 of Lim (1999). The PCA was performed using this transformed dataset. In an effort to identify trends and correlations in the nutrient relationships of the study sites, PON : POP (particulate organic phosphorus), TN : TPU, POC : POP, C : N : P and POC : CHLAU ratios were calculated (Table 1). A linear regression of CHLAU vs. TPU was also performed and compared to the Dillon and Rigler (1974) results. Finally, in order to discern differences in N-limitation amongst the sites, a series of separate CHLAU vs. TN linear regressions were performed for (1) all 38 sites, (2) sites with PON : POP \( \leq 10 : 1 \), and (3) sites with PON : POP \( > 10 : 1 \). 4. Results and Discussion 4.1. Physical Variables The 38 study sites, which ranged in elevation (ELEV) from sea level to a maximum of 335 m asl (mean ELEV = 93 m asl), included 23 shallow ponds, and 15 lakes that were deeper (see Table 1). Temperatures of all samples sites ranged from 2.5 \( ^\circ \)C to 19.5 \( ^\circ \)C. Not surprisingly, the shallow ponds were notably warmer than the deeper lakes. All shallower pond sites (n = 23) freeze solid to the bottom during the winter, and had an average July temperature of 12.2 \( ^\circ \)C, while the deeper lakes (n = 15) had an average temperature of 6.2 \( ^\circ \)C. Shallow sites have lower thermal capacities and will therefore heat up or cool down much faster than deeper lakes. The correlation matrix (Table 2) helped to identify correlations among several of the measured variables. Elevation (ELEV) was not correlated with temperature (TEMP). Therefore, temperature variation amongst sites during the week of sampling was most likely driven by the differences in thermal inertia and water volume/hydrological budget, and not the slight elevation gradient present on the island. 4.2. Overall, the concentrations (mg/L) of the major ions were relatively high (Table 1) compared to those of typical inland fresh waters (McNEELY et al., 1979). Ca^{2+}, Na^{+} and Mg^{2+} are the major cations, while CO_3^{-} (i.e. DIC), SO_4^{-} and Cl^{-} are the major anions. The major ion concentrations are relatively similar among all sites; however a gradient exists between the shallower vs. deeper sites with respect to ionic concentration, in that the deeper sites were more dilute relative to the shallower sites. The relative concentration of cations among sampled sites was Ca > Mg > Na > K (Table 1), with means of 30.8 mg/L, 5.6 mg/L, 3.1 mg/L, and 0.4 mg/L respectively. These ratios are similar to those of KLING et al. (1992), EILERS et al. (1993), DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994), PIENITZ et al. (1997a, b) (although Mg was not considered), RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998), and GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000). The relative concentration of the major anions among the sites was, on average, CO₃ > SO₄ > Cl. The dominance of calcium carbonate and bicarbonate ions reflects the calcium-carbonate rich limestone bedrock or dolostone tills in the drainage basins of all sample sites. Concentrations of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ were largely a function of proximity to the Arctic Ocean. From the correlation matrix (Table 2), it is apparent that elevation (ELEV) was negatively correlated with [Na], and [Cl]. More inland and higher elevation sites would be less subject to sea spray inputs carrying Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, and Ba²⁺ than sites closer to the ocean (Table 1). Varying concentrations of K⁺ might be related to the abundance of vascular plants in the catchment that are thought to leak out this cation (PRENTKI et al., 1980). Similar to the findings of DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994), those sites with abundant grasses, mosses and other vascular plants growing within the drainage basin had higher [K] (Table 1). SO₄ concentrations were usually relatively high, ranging from 0.60 mg/L (site BF)–22.0 mg/L (site BAI), with a mean concentration of 6.3 mg/L (Table 1). High SO₄ concentrations were also found in the PIENITZ et al. (1997a) study lakes that were in areas of prevalent limestone-dolomite, sandstone, siltstone, and conglomerate rock (i.e. bedrock similar to that of Bathurst Island). PIENITZ et al. (1997a) attributed the elevated SO₄ levels to weathering from this bedrock. There did not appear to be a link between SO₄ levels and proximity to the ocean in the Bathurst Island samples. The relationship between higher levels of pH, conductivity and major ions within the sample sites is similar to the findings of RÜHLAND and SMOL (1998) for their ‘Tundra’ sites in the central arctic mainland, and for those sites sampled by DOUGLAS and SMOL (1994) on Ellesmere Island. These similarities may point to a homogeneity within high arctic water bodies, however this must not be assumed given that so little of the geographic range of the High Arctic has been sampled and analyzed for limnological characteristics. 4.3. Nutrients: N and P Nutrient concentrations in all of the sampled sites were below the averages for uncontaminated surficial waters listed by McNEELY et al. (1979), which reflects the characteristic oligotrophic aquatic environments typical for high arctic regions. TKN was the most variable, with a range from 0.056 mg/L to 1.08 mg/L, and a mean of 0.334 mg/L. These values are similar to those reported by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) for the western arctic mainland of Canada, and GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) for arctic Alaska. The NO₂, NO₃–NO₂, and NH₃ values for the Bathurst Island sites are all near or below detection limits (<0.001 mg/L) (Table 1). Sites BAA and BAB were, however, exceptions to this with NO₃–NO₂ values well above the mean (Table 1). BAA was receiving ice and snow cover melt inputs at time of sampling, which may have caused a spike in the NO₃–NO₂ concentrations from the land. Furthermore, both BAA and BAB were surrounded by a large area of mud, through which run-off channels had been carved. These channels may have also contributed nitrate and nitrite inputs into these sites, hence elevating their concentrations relative to other lakes and ponds on Bathurst Island. Among the three phosphorus variables, TPU and TPF had the highest correlation with themselves (r = 0.51) (Table 2). TPU ranged from 3.2 µg/L–64.0 µg/L, and had an average of 12.7 µg/L, which is comparable to values reported by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) for their western arctic sites. TPF ranged from 1.7 µg/L–11.5 µg/L (mean = 6.1 µg/L), which is again comparable to those values reported by other limnological studies in arctic tundra regions (e.g. DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994; WHALEN and CORNWELL, 1985; McNEELY and GUMMER, 1984). Values for SRPF ranged from 0.9 µg/L–4.3 µg/L (mean = 1.5 µg/L), which is comparable to the results of PRENTKI et al. (1980) and PIENITZ et al. (1997a, b). These TPU levels may not necessarily indicate that phosphorus is the primary limiting nutrient for algae in the Bathurst Island sites. Patterns in the ratios of PON to particulate organic phosphorus (POP = TPU – TPF) (i.e. PON : POP), total nitrogen (TN = NO₃NO₂ + TKN + PON) to TPU (i.e. TN : TPU), and C : N : P were examined in order to identify sites which were potentially more P-limited than others. According to SAKAMOTO (1966) and SCHANZ and JUON (1983), ambient N : P ratios greater than approximately 20 : 1 are characteristic of significantly P-limited aquatic environments. If, however, the N : P ratio is less than 10 : 1, then the algae may be N-limited. Ratios between 10 : 1 and 20 : 1 may indicate limitation by either nutrient. However, these nutrient ratios are useful only in cases where the ambient concentrations are near growth-limiting concentrations (BORCHARDT, 1996). The oligotrophic Bathurst Island lakes and ponds appear to conform to this criterion. PON : POP ratios ranged from 1 : 1 (BF, BAH) to 90 : 1 (BT) (mean = 13 : 1). Overall, 63% of the sites had ratios of \( \leq 10 : 1 \), 13% had ratios of \( \geq 20 : 1 \), while 24% fell in the intermediate zone of 10 : 1 to 20 : 1. Sites BD, BF, BK, BP, BR, BU, BY, BZ, BAD, BAH, and BAJ, which have PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), all have [TPU] greater than the reported mean of 12.7 \( \mu \)g/L, and, according to our field notes, were characterized by a ‘greenish’ tinge. The elevated TPU values of these sites may be attributed to the large quantity of excrement left both in and around these watersheds by the local wildlife (e.g., caribou, lemmings, muskox, and arctic terns). Five of these sites (BK, BU, BY, BZ, BAD), in particular, are grouped along the TPU gradient on the Principal Components Analysis (PCA) ordination (Fig. 2). Some of the sites (i.e. BC, BG, BL, BM, BN, BS, BAB, BAC, BAI, BAK, BAL, BAM, BAN) with PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \) do have [TPU] below the mean. However with the exception of BAL and BAN, all of these sites also had PON values significantly below the mean (38.0 \( \mu \)g/L) (Table 1). The TPU and PON values for BAL (9.6 \( \mu \)g/L, 40.0 \( \mu \)g/L) and BAN (12.3 \( \mu \)g/L, 54.0 \( \mu \)g/L) deviated only slightly below and above from the respective means. Therefore, although both nutrient levels may be lower relative to other sites, nitrogen may still be the limiting factor to algal growth in these sites. Those sites with PON : POP ratios \( \geq 20 : 1 \), BE, BH, BT, BAE, and BAG, all had [TPU] below the mean, and were characterized by rocky drainage areas. Sites BH and BAE are larger, deeper lakes, which may also account for their more dilute concentrations of TPU relative to other sites. TN : TPU ratios ranged from 12 : 1 to 150 : 1, with a mean of 64 : 1. These ratios are comparable to those reported by SHORTREED and STOCKNER (1986) (i.e., 38 : 1 to 109 : 1) for 19 lakes in the Yukon Territory, PIENITZ et al. (1997a) (i.e., 13 : 1 to 103 : 1) for their 59 lakes along a southern Yukon to Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula transect, and by GREGORY-EAVES et al. (2000) (i.e., 3 : 1 to 124 : 1) for 51 lakes in arctic Alaska. Two-thirds of the sites which had PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), also had TN : TPU ratios below the mean for the Bathurst Island dataset (Table 1). This may indicate that, instead of being P-limited, algae may be limited to a greater degree by nitrogen. Nitrogen has been found to be the dominant limiting nutrient to phytoplankton growth in subarctic lakes when the lakes were P-fertilized (SMITH et al., 1984). The TN : TPU ratios reported for Bathurst Island, as well as by PIENITZ et al. (1997a) and by SHORTREED and STOCKNER (1986) for the western arctic mainland and the Yukon Territory respectively, are much higher than those reported by SMITH (1983) for lakes dominated by nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. Moreover, in shallow ponds wind agitation of the sediment, as was demonstrated by ALEXANDER et al. (1989), may be the dominant source of pond water N. In larger lakes, N levels may be even lower, because the sediment recharge of N would be low due to the low rate of sedimentation, low water temperature, and year-round oxic conditions (ALEXANDER et al., 1989). Most of the Bathurst sites with TN : TPU ratios below the mean were either larger, deeper lakes (e.g. BC, BK) and/or they drained through snow-banks with diluted nutrient concentrations (e.g. BF, BAM) (LIM, 1999). This observation supports the findings of ALEXANDER et al. (1989), and suggests that these sites (a) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for 38 sites](page_184_180_627_496.png) (b) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for sites with PON : POP < 10 : 1](page_1012_180_627_496.png) (c) ![Linear regression analysis of CHLAU vs. TN for sites with PON : POP > 10 : 1](page_184_728_627_496.png) Figure 2. Finally, by comparing the average C : N : P ratios for the Bathurst Island sites to those of other studies, we can make an overall assessment of whether or not these sites are more N or P limited. The average C : N : P ratio for Bathurst Island is 107 : 6 : 1, which is lower than the ratio of 137 : 18 : 1 reported by Shortreed and Stockner (1986) for 19 Yukon lakes. Based on the average ratio for Bathurst Island, and in comparison to other reported values, we conclude that most of the sites may in fact be N-limited. However, it should be noted that the range of the C : N : P ratios was large, ranging from 29 : 1 : 1 for site BF to 1950 : 90 : 1 for site BT. Therefore, a few sites, as discussed earlier, are either severely or moderately P-limited. 4.4. Carbon DIC values ranged from 9.3 mg/L to 39.9 mg/L (mean = 20.1 mg/L). These values are comparable to the [DIC] from the Pienitz et al. (1997a) arctic study sites, and likely reflect similarities in bedrock geology. DOC concentrations were generally low to moderate on Bathurst Island, which is common in oligotrophic waters that are beyond the treeline. For example, average DOC concentrations in the PIENITZ et al. (1997a) study were lowest in unforested arctic tundra sites, whereas they were highest in boreal forest and forest-tundra sites. The [DOC] for Bathurst Island ranged from 1.1 mg/L to 11.2 mg/L (mean = 4.1 mg/L). PIENITZ et al. (1997a) found a significant correlation between watershed vegetation and DOC levels, an association which might account for the differences in our DOC concentrations. All of the sites with [DOC] greater than the mean drained through relatively lush vegetation such as grasses and mosses, and also supported abundant submerged mosses (LIM, 1999). Furthermore, the shallower pond sites on Bathurst Island were typically found in lush valley areas that supported various species of sedges and grasses, whereas deeper sites usually had more rocky drainage areas than the ponds. The increase in vegetation within these sites may have also provided ample substrate sources to support a rich diatom community, which would have also contributed to DOC levels through photosynthetic processes (McNEELY et al., 1979). Of course, deeper sites would also more likely dilute any terrestrial/detrital DOC. DOC levels play a critical role in controlling the depth of ultraviolet (UV) penetration into the lake or pond, which in turn has an impact on aquatic biota. Given the relatively low [DOC] in many Bathurst Island lakes, any slight changes in the environment that affect [DOC] may potentially have far reaching consequences (VINCENT and PIENITZ, 1996). 4.5. Chlorophyll a CHLAU concentrations for the 38 Bathurst Island sites ranged from below detection limits (<0.001 \( \mu \)g/L) to 3.4 \( \mu \)g/L (mean = 0.8 \( \mu \)g/L). In an effort to identify whether the POC in the water was mostly derived from either algal or terrestrial/detrital sources, POC : CHLAU ratios were calculated (Table 1). Furthermore, in order to compare this dataset to the DILLON and RIGLER (1974) linear regression of summer CHLA vs. TP, the slope and r-value for the linear regression of CHLAU vs. TPU for the Bathurst Island sites were calculated. Some POC : CHLAU ratios were not calculated, since CHLAU values were sometimes below the detection limit (n = 9). Those POC : CHLAU values that were available (n = 29) for calculation ranged from 11000 : 1 to 235 : 1, with a mean of 871 : 1. However, with the reduced sample size, this mean value should be treated cautiously. The range suggests significant variability in detrital input amongst the sites. Sites which drained through lush, vegetated areas where detrital material could be transported in the run-off, usually had POC : CHLAU ratios above the mean. However, it was surprising to find that sites such as BK, which have elevated [TPU] relative to other sites, would still have POC : CHLAU ratios far above the mean. One possible explanation is that site BK is N-limited rather than P-limited. Another possible explanation is that phosphorus can form strong bonds with Fe and DOC, making it inaccessible to algae. Site BK, in particular, had [Fe] and [DOC] levels (2.42 mg/L and 5.8 mg/L, respectively) above the reported means. This characteristic, coupled with a highly vegetated drainage basin, could drive the POC : CHLAU ratio up. According to DILLON and RIGLER (1974), sites which lie on or deviate only slightly from the CHLA-TP slope of 1.583 (derived from a linear regression of the SAKAMOTO (1966) dataset), will most likely be P-limited. However, those sites that have low N : P ratios would show much larger deviations from the overall trend. The CHLAU-TPU slope calculated for Bathurst Island was 3.784 (P > 0.01). Therefore, the Bathurst Island sites are, generally not severely P-limited. Instead, as has been documented throughout this study, the sites are most likely only partly P-limited or N-limited. The relationship between CHLAU and TN was also examined for all 38 sites. These two variables did not show a strong correlation (P > 0.01) (Fig. 2a). However, given that the relationship between CHLAU and TPU was also not significant, it is possible that nutrient factors other than N or P were playing a significant role in limiting algal growth. As stated earlier (see section 4.3), 63% of the sites are considered to be N-limited, having PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), while 37% of the sites had ratios \( > 10 : 1 \), and were considered to be either influenced by other nutrient factors or P-limited. Therefore, by running separate CHLAU vs TN regressions on those sites with (a) PON : POP ratios \( \leq 10 : 1 \), and (b) PON : POP ratios \( > 10 : 1 \), differences in nutrient limiting factors among the sites were identified. From these regressions, it was apparent that the N-limited sites showed a significant correlation with the CHLAU values (\( r = 0.45; P \leq 0.01 \)) (Fig. 2b). Conversely, those sites that are most likely not N-limited were not significantly correlated with CHLAU (\( r = 0.10; P \geq 0.01 \)) (Fig. 2c). This also suggests that the prominent limitation for algal growth in approximately two thirds of the Bathurst Island sites may be nitrogen. Therefore, any disruptions to the nitrogen budget of these sites could cause a significant change in the algal biota. 4.6. PCA Axes 1 and 2 of the PCA accounted for 34.4% and 12.6%, respectively, of the variance (Table 3). Axes 3 and 4 collectively captured only 18.1% of the total cumulative percentage variance, and are therefore not discussed further here. Axes lengths were less than four standard deviations (SD), which indicates that the sites share many common attributes (JONGMAN et al., 1987). This is influenced by the similarity in local climate, and underlying bedrock at the sites. The dominant gradients identified in the PCA ordination (Fig. 3) of the measured limnological variables indicate that differences in: (a) major ion content, especially concentrations of calcium and magnesium; and (b) DOC levels along Axis 1; and (c) pH along Axis 2, mostly separate the distribution of the 38 lake and pond sites on the ordination. However, shallower pond sites tend to cluster separately from the deeper lakes. For example, eleven of the fifteen deeper sites are clustered in the two left quadrats of the PCA ordination. Conductivity (COND), [Ca], and [Mg] show a high positive correlation along the first axis of the PCA (Fig. 3). This relationship is also clear in the correlation matrix (Table 2), with positive correlations between COND and [Ca] and [Mg]. Those sites (e.g., BD, BE, BAJ) which have relatively elevated Ca and Mg levels, ordinate closely in relation to the gradient extremes of these environmental variables, located in the lower right quadrat of the PCA (Fig. 3). Aluminum, iron, and manganese also show high positive correlations with Axis 1 (Fig. 3), and share high correlations to each other (Table 2). This is to be expected, given that water containing elevated levels of calcium and magnesium salts are commonly associated with polyvalent metals such as iron, aluminum, and manganese (LIND, 1974). Sites BK, BU, BY, BZ and BAD, located in the upper right-hand quadrat of the PCA, all had high levels of these metals (Table 1). In acidic lakes, high levels aluminum have been correlated with pH (DIXIT et al., 1993). Aluminum did not, however, have a significant correlation with pH in this study (Table 2), because the Bathurst Island sites are alkaline (\( \mathrm{pH} = 8.0-8.6 \)). Concen-

This is to be expected given the similarity in catchment geology. The DOC gradient is most likely driving the differences between the shallower ponds and the deeper lakes (Fig. 3). Shallower pond sites (e.g., BD, BE, and BJ) are ordinated closely to the DOC gradient extremity, while deeper sites (e.g., BG, BH, and BO) are ordinated in the opposite quadrat. Therefore, we can infer that the shallower sites had higher organic matter concentrations relative to the deeper sites. Small oligotrophic water bodies such as shallow tundra ponds can receive significant amounts of dissolved organic carbon from the catchment vegetation and soils even in the absence of trees. Field observations indicated that the ponds tended to have more grasses and mosses in their catchments relative to the lake sites. The pH gradient is most closely related to Axis 2, but it also shares a relationship with the Ca–Mg and polyvalent metal gradients driving Axis 1 (Fig. 3). Those sites (e.g., BAI, BAJ, BAL) ordinated at the end of the pH arrow have higher alkalinity levels and elevated Ca and Mg levels (Table 1). Sites located in the upper left-hand quadrat (Fig. 3) (i.e., BF, BG, BH, BL, BN, BO, BS, BT, BAK) all have lower pH, Ca and Mg levels relative to other sample sites (Table 2). This pH trend is not correlated with size or elevation (ELEV). Indeed, given the short pH gradient length and the similarity in underlying bedrock at the sites, only slight differences exist in the levels of pH. 5. Conclusions Major ion concentrations of the Bathurst Island ponds and lakes were relatively high. This is consistent with the calcareous, limestone, and dolomite bedrock of the drainage basins at these sites. Differences in Na and Cl concentrations were primarily related to the proximity of each site to the sea. Overall, this limnological dataset was similar to those reported by other studies from similar geological settings in the subarctic and arctic regions of North America (see KLING et al., 1992; EILERS et al., 1993; DOUGLAS and SMOL, 1994; PIENITZ et al., 1997a, b; RÜHLAND and SMOL, 1998; GREGORY-EAVES et al., 2000; Table 4). Nutrient concentrations at all sites were typical for high arctic, oligotrophic aquatic environments. TPU values were comparable to the reported values from other arctic sites (e.g., PIENITZ et al., 1997a). Examination of PON : POP, TN : TPU and REDFIELD (C : N : P) ratios showed that, although certain sites were P-limited, most of the Bathurst Island sites may have been N-limited. Comparison of the slope of the CHLA vs. TP linear regression for Bathurst Island to that calculated by DILLON and RIGLER (1974) for summer values also suggests that most of our sites are not highly P-limited, but rather range from partly P-limited to N-limited. Variance in [DOC] could be partially explained by differences in surrounding vegetation for each site, as well as the water volume of the sites. Sites with [DOC] greater than the mean were typically smaller ponds, which drained through prominently vegetated areas, where detrital material could be transported in the run-off. PCA eigenvalues showed that the first two axes of the ordination could explain most of the limnological variation among the sites. Conductivity, DOC, and variables related to water hardness, such as Ca-Mg ions and other polyvalent metals, contributed primarily to Axis 1, while Axis 2 was driven primarily by pH. Differences between the shallow vs. deeper sites were especially clear in their spread in the ordination relative to the DOC gradient. Future work on Bathurst Island should include a detailed limnological analysis of the western portion of the island. Surficial geological material on western Bathurst Island is much less alkaline (pH < 4.0) than in the east (EDLUND, 1990). A comparison of the water chemistry of the lakes and ponds in these two areas could help expand our understanding of the dominant limnological trends governing Bathurst Island. 6.
