OC accumulation in eutrophic, agricultural impoundments is high because they receive allochthonous OC through erosion, enhanced autochthonous OC through nutrient-driven primary productivity, and very high rates of preservation due to nearly continuous sediment anoxia. [22] These estimates are important for several reasons. First, they indicate that OC burial is likely to be much greater in moderately sized and large impoundments than previously believed, especially where landscapes are disturbed and nutrients abundant. If these data are representative of other regions where impoundments have been created, the average areal OC burial rate in impoundments between 0.01 and 100 km2 may not be quite as high as the rates we observed, but may average about 1000 g m−2 a−1, more than double the rate calculated in previous analyses [e.g., Dean and Gorham, 1998; Stallard, 1998]. Although extrapolation of these values to a world scale is speculative, if our analyses are representative, moderately sized impoundments may bury as much as 4 times as much carbon as the world’s oceans [Dean and Gorham, 1998]. Although this is a highly provisional estimate for the burial of OC by constructed lakes, the potentially great intensity of OC burial in these systems warrants further refinement and investigation. Appropriate upscaling of these estimates to a global scale will require much more knowledge about the rate of OC burial in aquatic ecosystems and the factors that control it. [23] Second, these analyses extend OC burial estimates to the smallest water bodies that dominate the area occupied a diversity of methods by a variety of U.S. government agencies so the accuracy of these data “varies greatly” [Dendy and Champion, 1978]. Our higher estimates of OC burial derive both from higher estimates of sediment accumulation rates and our direct measurements of dry bulk density and sediment organic matter content. Renwick et al. [2005] have also noted that the historic sediment deposition data [i.e., Dendy and Champion, 1978] seem to yield lower estimates than do modern estimates made with uniform technologies. Further, calculations of OC burial from historical deposition rates have been made with assumed average dry bulk densities instead of more appropriate site-specific values [Dendy and Champion, 1978] and with low values of sediment OC content extrapolated from other lakes [e.g., Ritchie, 1989]. Because we found that dry bulk density and organic matter content of sediments varied markedly, and were each often greater than assumed in previous studies (e.g., Table 1), this may account for the relatively high estimates of OC burial we found in these impoundments. [21] The rates of OC burial seen in these eutrophic impoundments were also large when compared to terrestrial OC accumulation. For example, Schlesinger [1997] reported OC burial rates in tundra and forests ranging from only 0.2 to 12 g m−2 a−1 (Table 2). We have only recently gained some understanding of the number and areal extent of the smallest aquatic ecosystems, especially small impoundments that may have very short lives. Small agricultural impoundments have been shown to occupy >75,000 km^2, globally, and are increasing in abundance [Downing et al., 2006]. If our data are representative of the order of magnitude of OC burial in these small impoundments, these impoundments may bury OC at an average rate of around 2000 g m^{-2} a^{-1}. If global estimates of farm pond abundance are accurate, these smallest impoundments, which have not been considered in prior OC burial estimates, may bury around 150 Tg of OC each year. This is in the range of 33% of all the carbon delivered to the ocean annually by the world’s rivers [Degens et al., 1991; Stallard, 1998] and is near to the estimated annual carbon burial in the world’s oceans [Meybeck, 1993; Sundquist, 2003], excluding marine vegetated habitats [Duarte et al., 2004]. Although such upscaling of rates to a global level makes broad assumptions about the prevalence of high-OC burial in small impoundments, it suggests that the role of such water bodies may have been underestimated in the past. The impoundments we studied may be unique in these high rates of apparent OC burial or they may be indicative of a site of global OC burial that had not been previously estimated. More detailed data on OC burial in small aquatic ecosystems are needed to more completely understand the global implications of these small yet carbon-active ecosystems. [24] Third, burial of OC in the sediments of impoundments includes autochthonous production and therefore may represent an active OC sink that has been heretofore underestimated. The negative relationship between the organic matter content of sediment and the relative size of the watershed to the impoundment area (Figure 5) suggests that the impoundments with the least allochthonous input have the highest sediment organic content. Further, the highest sediment accumulation rates per unit impoundment area were found in the smallest water bodies (equation (1)). Rather than simply being burial points for terrestrial OC, the high rates of primary production in eutrophic impoundments may be responsible for a substantial fraction of the OC burial. That these OC burial rates include both allochthonous and autochthonous inputs is illustrated by rates of annual primary production that rarely exceed 1000 g C m^{-2} a^{-1}, even under very eutrophic conditions [Kalf, 2001; Wetzel, 2001]. The partitioning of OC burial between allochthonous and autochthonous sources is an important question that may be complicated by the confounding of C:N:P stoichiometry in impoundments receiving divergent agricultural signals [Arbuckle and Downing, 2001] and the assumptions of stable isotope analyses where diverse amendments are applied [Post, 2002]. [25] Finally, although decreased delivery of sediments through improved farming practices have been seen elsewhere [Renwick and Andereck, 2006], there is no indication in the data that OC burial has changed as farm practice has been improved over the last century. Erosion control has been a hallmark of improved farming practice in this agricultural region [Cole et al., 1993], thus OC burial through soil erosion should have declined substantially over the analysis period. Although delays to conveyance of eroded agricultural sediment to lakes and the existence of a weak correlation between lake size and dates of surveys may impede the detection of the influence of improved soil conservation on organic carbon burial, the data do not suggest large differences between early and more recent OC burial. The lack of temporal correlation in OC burial rates suggests that impoundments do not only bury eroded terrestrial OC, but conserve a substantial proportion of atmospheric C fixation through autochthonous production driven by nutrient losses from intensively managed landscapes. Therefore the major agricultural improvement to practice in this region over the last century, i.e., decreased erosional losses [Yang et al., 2003], may not have led to decreased OC burial because OC burial is driven by both erosion and nutrient-enhanced aquatic eutrophication. [26] The sediments of eutrophic impoundments appear to be among the most active sites of C sequestration in the biosphere. Owing to the high rates of autochthonous production, the high rates of input of terrestrial carbon through erosion, and the long-term preservation of organic materials in anaerobic sedimentary environments promoted by high nutrient concentrations, areal rates of OC burial in eutrophic impoundments can be much larger than those observed anywhere else in the biosphere. This finding builds on previous studies showing that ponds and reservoirs can dominate the sediment budgets of large geographical areas [e.g., Renwick et al., 2005] and that erosion and sedimentation can be major OC sinks within the very large watersheds of major river systems [Smith et al., 2005]. Because these are constructed ecosystems, much of the OC sequestered in these lakes met a different fate prior to human development. A recent analysis [Downing et al., 2006] has suggested that impoundments, especially small, low-tech reservoirs, are growing in areal coverage from 1–6% annually in many agricultural regions around the world (e.g., Europe, India, and the United States). Their increasing area and their extreme ability to sequester OC suggest that they have a growing importance as sinks in the global C cycle. Notation A lake area, km^2. Jones¹*, Joshua J. Millspaugh¹, Robert J. Kremer², John A. Downing³ ¹ Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA ² USDA, Agricultural Research Service, Cropping Systems & Water Quality Research Unit and Department of Soil, Environment & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA ³ Department of Ecology, Evolution and Organismal Biology, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA * Corresponding author email: jonesj@missouri.edu Received 6 March 2012; accepted 1 December 2012; published 28 January 2013 Abstract Four small impoundments (5–25 ha) in the Glacial Plains of the Midwestern USA were intensively sampled to determine the concentration and spatial distribution of sediment organic carbon (OC; 31–40 cores per reservoir, averaging 2.7 samples per hectare). Burial rates for sediment OC varied from 183 to 279 g OC m⁻² a⁻¹ over the lifetime of these reservoirs (about 50 years). Organic carbon averaged 39.4 mg per gram dry sediment (n = 137) and mean values varied from 20.3 to 54.8 mg OC per gram dry sediment among the reservoirs; these concentrations are within the mid-range of values reported from other lakes and reservoirs. Spatial distribution of OC generally showed an increase from the inflow to the dam and in some cases lateral gradients that varied by a factor of 2. Based on simple random sampling, 10 core samples provide relative precision of around 25% and equate to a mean of 0.8 samples per hectare. This analysis of sampling effort will be useful for global up-scaling of carbon sequestration in small impoundments. Key words: carbon cycling, sediment organic carbon, sampling, Missouri reservoirs Introduction Freshwater lakes and impoundments are considered disproportionately active locations for carbon cycling relative to their areal extent on the continents (Downing et al. 2006, Cole et al. 2007). Carbon burial rates in the sediments of small, fertile impoundments are greater than either large reservoirs or natural lakes; one estimate suggests annual burial of organic carbon (OC) in the world’s farm ponds is similar to storage in ocean sediments (Downing et al. 2008). The number of small impoundments continues to increase globally with direct impact on carbon sequestration (Downing et al. 2006, 2008, Kastowski et al. 2011). An area of uncertainty in ecology and limnology, however, is knowledge to assure accurate and precise sampling protocols and calculations for carbon cycling from freshwater ecosystems to better constrain global estimates (Downing 2010). Several studies have assessed spatial distribution of sediments, sampling, and sample representativeness in natural lakes (Håkanson 1984, Rowan et al. 1995, Rippey et al. 2008), but there is a lack of similar information for impoundments (Abraham et al. 1999). Sampling protocols for reservoirs may differ greatly from those of lakes because of morphological and hydrodynamic differences between the 2 lake types. Reservoirs are typically constructed at the confluence of several tributaries with comparatively large watersheds and inputs of mineral turbidity; these characteristics cause them to rapidly accumulate sediment along a longitudinal gradient from inflow to outflow (Shotbolt et al. 2005, Vanni et al. 2011). In this study, we intensively sampled OC concentrations in the sediments of 4 small impoundments located in the Glacial Plains of northern Missouri (5–25 ha; Table 1). The objectives were to describe the spatial distribution of OC in recently deposited sediments in these basins and determine an optimal sampling strategy. Organic nitrogen was also measured, and values are presented to further characterize reservoir sediments in this region. Study sites The 4 study impoundments were selected because they were of near-equal age (about 50 years; constructed between 1957 and 1963), and concentrations of nutrients, algal chlorophyll, and suspended solids approximate the range of conditions found in reservoirs located in the Glacial Plains of northern Missouri (Table 1; Jones et al. 2008a, 2008b, Jones 2010). These reservoirs were constructed about a century after historic prairie and forest vegetation was altered for agriculture; as such, riverine nutrient and sediment loads from this landscape were in place prior to impoundment of these artificial lakes. The trophic state of these reservoirs is determined by land cover (a surrogate for nutrient loading), morphology, and hydraulic flushing, and there is no evidence that conditions have changed since construction (Jones et al. 2009). Methods From 31 to 40 cores were collected from each impoundment (n = 137; Table 1) using a modified Kajak-Brinkhurst sediment corer (with a 6.35 cm inner diameter and 70 cm tube; Pittman 2011). The sampling strategy consisted of collecting cores at equal distances along 2 parallel transects running the length of each basin to characterize longitudinal distribution and along 2 perpendicular transects in each basin to characterize lateral distribution (Pittman 2011). To determine how well individual cores represent local OC and N concentrations, 3 cores were collected within a 2 m radius (±1 m) from a location near the middle or near-dam in each reservoir. Our effort to characterize spatial distribution using transects and a grid pattern resulted in a sampling density averaging 2.7 samples per ha. This sampling effort is more intensive than previous collections from impoundments (Abraham 1998, ~1 sample per 50 ha; Abraham et al. 1999, ~1 sample per 26–480 ha; Downing et al. 2008, ~1 sample per 40 ha; Ritchie 1989, ~1 sample per 70–100 ha) and similar to the high-density sampling applied to several natural lakes (Anderson 1990, Rippey et al. 2008, ~2 samples per ha). Our collections, however, were less intensive than the studies by Bloemendal et al. (1979, 21 samples per ha) or Foster and Walling (1994, 5 samples per ha). Total OC and total nitrogen (N) concentrations were determined on 5 to 10 cm sections of these cores by dry combustion at 950 °C using an LECO Tru-Spec C/N analyzer (St. Joseph, MI) with methods after Nelson and Sommers (1996). Results are expressed as mg OC per gram dry sediment. Dry bulk density of the sediment (g dry mass cm\(^{-3}\)) was determined after Downing et al. (2008). Soft sediment thickness was measured after Brenner et al. (1999) at 6 to 11 locations along the midline and a lateral transect in each reservoir. Sediment thickness was divided by years since each reservoir was impounded as an estimate of sediment accumulation rate (cm a\(^{-1}\)). Burial rates for sediment OC were calculated based on mean OC concentration in individual cores, dry bulk density, and sediment accumulation rate (Pittman 2011). This approach assumes that little OC has been respired in the past 50 years due to low oxygen status in the sediment and does not account for possible compaction (Dean 1999, Heathcote and Downing 2012, Heathcote et al. 2012). Consistent with the goal of estimating recent carbon deposition in these reservoirs, analyses were based on OC concentrations in the 0–5 cm segment of the cores, unless noted otherwise. The universal kriging function of the geostatistical wizard tool in ArcMap 9.3.1 was used to predict the spatial distribution of sediment OC. Concentrations were classified by natural breaks (Jenks’ optimization) to separate data into classes based on natural groupings in the data distribution (ESRI 2011). Results and discussion Sediment averaged 39.6 mg OC per gram dry sediment (hereafter expressed as mg g\(^{-1}\), n = 137) with individual samples ranging from 6.5 to 79.2 mg g\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). Among the 4 reservoirs, mean concentrations varied from 20.3 to 55.4 mg g\(^{-1}\) (Table 1); within individual reservoirs the difference between minimum and maximum values ranged by 2-fold (Fayette) to 12-fold (Jamesport; Table 1). Overall, these OC concentrations are near the mid-range of values reported in similar studies (United States, Ritchie 1989; Iowa, Downing et al. 2008; Sweden, Rippey et al. 2008; New Zealand and China, Trolle et al. 2010; Ohio, Vanni et al. 2011). Moderate values are expected in impoundments because they are located in erosional topography, and high inorganic sedimentation dilutes organic materials and lowers OC values (Hyne 1978, Mulholland and Elwood 1982). The mean and range of sediment OC was the smallest in Fayette, the impoundment with the highest concentration of mineral turbidity in the water column and largest ratio of catchment area to reservoir surface area (Table 1). Surface sediment from Fayette also had the largest dry bulk density values of the study reservoirs (mean = 0.43 vs. 0.28–0.30 g dry mass cm\(^{-3}\)). Table 1. (2008a). Organic carbon and nitrogen are from the top 5 cm of sediment, measured in mg per gram dry sediment. Water content of sediment is percent. Sedimentation variables include sediment accumulation rate (SAR) and organic carbon burial rate (OC).

The cores averaged 28 cm long (from 5 to 55 cm, n = 137) and were collected at a mean water depth of 322 cm (from 60 to 620 cm). The OC concentration in the 0–5 cm segment of sediment was highly correlated with average OC in the entire core (r = 0.91, n = 137). The ratio of these 2 measurements was 1.3. Larger OC concentrations in the surface layer are expected because organics degrade over time in strata of greater depth and age (Trolle et al. 2010), but this ratio suggests sediment OC has not degraded substantially over the short life of these reservoirs. The water content of these surficial sediments (Table 1) varied from <50%, which characterizes coarse-grained materials, to >75%, which characterizes fine grain sediments (after Håkanson 1984). Within each reservoir there was a strong correlation between sediment water content and OC concentration (r = 0.85–0.93, \( p < 0.001 \)). Based on the depth of soft sediments in these impoundments, sediment accumulation rates since construction varied from 0.97 to 2.47 cm a\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). These estimates do not account for sediment compaction or surface diagenesis but are within the range of sediment ac- cumulation rates measured in reservoirs (Mulholland and Elwood 1982, Downing et al. 2008). Using these values, the top 5 cm of sediment is recently deposited material that has accumulated over about 3.5 years (from 2 years in Lick Creek to 5 years in Jamesport). The age of this top layer is consistent with our goal of characterizing OC in recently deposited sediments. Based on measurements of sediment deposition since construction and OC values in the cores, burial rates for sediment OC in these impoundments varied from 183 to 279 g OC m\(^{-2}\) a\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). These values fit the pattern with surface area for a broad range of eutrophic lakes shown by Downing et al. (2008; Fig. 1). Accumulation rates in the Missouri impoundments were somewhat less than those found in similar size lakes in agricultural watersheds in Iowa; this disparity is consistent with differences in ambient soil fertility and the intensity of crop production between the 2 regions (Jones et al. 2008b). The coefficient of variation among 3 cores collected within a 2 m radius near the middle or a near-dam location in each reservoir ranged from 1.6 to 3.7% for OC and 2.1 to 4.2% for N. This variability is low when compared with previous studies of replicate cores (Hargrave and Nielsen 1977, Slater and Boag 1978, Anderson et al. 1982, Downing and Rath1988) but matches the findings of others (Reynoldson and Hamilton 1982, Twinch and Peters 1984). This outcome suggests inter-core variation of OC, and N was modest in these impoundments. As such, individual samples represent local conditions on a scale of several meters and support use of these data to interpret spatial patterns. Analytical error was only ±2.2% (Nelson and Sommers 1996) and can be considered minor relative to spatial variation in OC. Similar to the pattern previously described for reservoirs (Shotbolt et al. 2005, Vanni et al. 2011), sediment OC concentrations increased from the inflow to the outflow in these basins (Fig. 2). Low values near the inflow are attributed to dilution by sedimentation of coarse inorganic matter (Hyne 1978, Shotbolt et al. 2005). The pattern of the down-reservoir increase in OC differed among reservoirs. In Jamesport, the most fertile reservoir sampled (Table 1), OC concentrations increased perpendicular to water flow forming an arched shaped fan of high sediment OC in front of the dam (Fig. 2a). In Fayette and Lick Creek reservoirs the down-reservoir pattern showed a modest, clockwise shift resulting from lateral differences in OC concentrations with high values along the westernmost shore of each basin (Fig. 2b and 2c). In Lick Creek (Fig. 2c), OC concentrations differed by about 2-fold across the mid-line, while lateral differences were much smaller in Fayette (Fig. 2b). In Worth County, neither the longitudinal nor lateral gradient was strongly defined; in this basin OC values were nearly homogenous beyond the inflow (Fig. 2d). These various patterns likely reflect differences in tributary inflows and wind mixing among basins. Collectively, the patterns (Fig. 2) are the best available characterization of the longitudinal and lateral spatial distribution of OC in small reservoirs on the Glacial Plains in Missouri. In each reservoir, distributions and gradients in sediment N were analogous to the OC pattern. There was a strong positive correlation between sediment OC and N across samples (r = 0.91, n = 137) with an average ratio of sediment N to OC of 1:10. To assess optimal sampling strategy of similar impoundments in the region, data from all 4 reservoirs were pooled to determine relative precision for OC (maximum acceptable error as a percent of the mean) against sample size, assuming simple random sampling (Fig. 3; Thompson 1992). Pooling was justified because these reservoirs represent the size and trophic state of many impoundments in the region (Table 1; Jones et al. 2008a, Jones 2010). The utility of stratified random sampling was evaluated but was not supported when compared with simple random sampling. The analysis suggests that with the collection of 10 random core samples the relative precision approximates 25% (Fig. 3). This equates to a mean of 0.8 samples per hectare in these reservoirs. Small ponds and lakes are more numerous than previously believed (Kastowski et al. 2011), and they sequester carbon at rates orders-of-magnitude greater than other global ecosystems (Downing 2010). Downing³ ¹ Department of Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA ² USDA, Agricultural Research Service, Cropping Systems & Water Quality Research Unit and Department of Soil, Environment & Atmospheric Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO, USA ³ Department of Ecology, Evolution and Organismal Biology, Iowa State University, Ames, IA, USA * Corresponding author email: jonesj@missouri.edu Received 6 March 2012; accepted 1 December 2012; published 28 January 2013 Abstract Four small impoundments (5–25 ha) in the Glacial Plains of the Midwestern USA were intensively sampled to determine the concentration and spatial distribution of sediment organic carbon (OC; 31–40 cores per reservoir, averaging 2.7 samples per hectare). Burial rates for sediment OC varied from 183 to 279 g OC m⁻² a⁻¹ over the lifetime of these reservoirs (about 50 years). Organic carbon averaged 39.4 mg per gram dry sediment (n = 137) and mean values varied from 20.3 to 54.8 mg OC per gram dry sediment among the reservoirs; these concentrations are within the mid-range of values reported from other lakes and reservoirs. Spatial distribution of OC generally showed an increase from the inflow to the dam and in some cases lateral gradients that varied by a factor of 2. Based on simple random sampling, 10 core samples provide relative precision of around 25% and equate to a mean of 0.8 samples per hectare. This analysis of sampling effort will be useful for global up-scaling of carbon sequestration in small impoundments. Key words: carbon cycling, sediment organic carbon, sampling, Missouri reservoirs Introduction Freshwater lakes and impoundments are considered disproportionately active locations for carbon cycling relative to their areal extent on the continents (Downing et al. 2006, Cole et al. 2007). Carbon burial rates in the sediments of small, fertile impoundments are greater than either large reservoirs or natural lakes; one estimate suggests annual burial of organic carbon (OC) in the world’s farm ponds is similar to storage in ocean sediments (Downing et al. 2008). The number of small impoundments continues to increase globally with direct impact on carbon sequestration (Downing et al. 2006, 2008, Kastowski et al. 2011). An area of uncertainty in ecology and limnology, however, is knowledge to assure accurate and precise sampling protocols and calculations for carbon cycling from freshwater ecosystems to better constrain global estimates (Downing 2010). Several studies have assessed spatial distribution of sediments, sampling, and sample representativeness in natural lakes (Håkanson 1984, Rowan et al. 1995, Rippey et al. 2008), but there is a lack of similar information for impoundments (Abraham et al. 1999). Sampling protocols for reservoirs may differ greatly from those of lakes because of morphological and hydrodynamic differences between the 2 lake types. Reservoirs are typically constructed at the confluence of several tributaries with comparatively large watersheds and inputs of mineral turbidity; these characteristics cause them to rapidly accumulate sediment along a longitudinal gradient from inflow to outflow (Shotbolt et al. 2005, Vanni et al. 2011). In this study, we intensively sampled OC concentrations in the sediments of 4 small impoundments located in the Glacial Plains of northern Missouri (5–25 ha; Table 1). The objectives were to describe the spatial distribution of OC in recently deposited sediments in these basins and determine an optimal sampling strategy. Organic nitrogen was also measured, and values are presented to further characterize reservoir sediments in this region. Study sites The 4 study impoundments were selected because they were of near-equal age (about 50 years; constructed between 1957 and 1963), and concentrations of nutrients, algal chlorophyll, and suspended solids approximate the range of conditions found in reservoirs located in the Glacial Plains of northern Missouri (Table 1; Jones et al. 2008a, 2008b, Jones 2010). These reservoirs were constructed about a century after historic prairie and forest vegetation was altered for agriculture; as such, riverine nutrient and sediment loads from this landscape were in place prior to impoundment of these artificial lakes. The trophic state of these reservoirs is determined by land cover (a surrogate for nutrient loading), morphology, and hydraulic flushing, and there is no evidence that conditions have changed since construction (Jones et al. 2009). Methods From 31 to 40 cores were collected from each impoundment (n = 137; Table 1) using a modified Kajak-Brinkhurst sediment corer (with a 6.35 cm inner diameter and 70 cm tube; Pittman 2011). The sampling strategy consisted of collecting cores at equal distances along 2 parallel transects running the length of each basin to characterize longitudinal distribution and along 2 perpendicular transects in each basin to characterize lateral distribution (Pittman 2011). To determine how well individual cores represent local OC and N concentrations, 3 cores were collected within a 2 m radius (±1 m) from a location near the middle or near-dam in each reservoir. Our effort to characterize spatial distribution using transects and a grid pattern resulted in a sampling density averaging 2.7 samples per ha. This sampling effort is more intensive than previous collections from impoundments (Abraham 1998, ~1 sample per 50 ha; Abraham et al. 1999, ~1 sample per 26–480 ha; Downing et al. 2008, ~1 sample per 40 ha; Ritchie 1989, ~1 sample per 70–100 ha) and similar to the high-density sampling applied to several natural lakes (Anderson 1990, Rippey et al. 2008, ~2 samples per ha). Our collections, however, were less intensive than the studies by Bloemendal et al. (1979, 21 samples per ha) or Foster and Walling (1994, 5 samples per ha). Total OC and total nitrogen (N) concentrations were determined on 5 to 10 cm sections of these cores by dry combustion at 950 °C using an LECO Tru-Spec C/N analyzer (St. Joseph, MI) with methods after Nelson and Sommers (1996). Results are expressed as mg OC per gram dry sediment. Dry bulk density of the sediment (g dry mass cm\(^{-3}\)) was determined after Downing et al. (2008). Soft sediment thickness was measured after Brenner et al. (1999) at 6 to 11 locations along the midline and a lateral transect in each reservoir. Sediment thickness was divided by years since each reservoir was impounded as an estimate of sediment accumulation rate (cm a\(^{-1}\)). Burial rates for sediment OC were calculated based on mean OC concentration in individual cores, dry bulk density, and sediment accumulation rate (Pittman 2011). This approach assumes that little OC has been respired in the past 50 years due to low oxygen status in the sediment and does not account for possible compaction (Dean 1999, Heathcote and Downing 2012, Heathcote et al. 2012). Consistent with the goal of estimating recent carbon deposition in these reservoirs, analyses were based on OC concentrations in the 0–5 cm segment of the cores, unless noted otherwise. The universal kriging function of the geostatistical wizard tool in ArcMap 9.3.1 was used to predict the spatial distribution of sediment OC. Concentrations were classified by natural breaks (Jenks’ optimization) to separate data into classes based on natural groupings in the data distribution (ESRI 2011). Results and discussion Sediment averaged 39.6 mg OC per gram dry sediment (hereafter expressed as mg g\(^{-1}\), n = 137) with individual samples ranging from 6.5 to 79.2 mg g\(^{-1}\) (Table 1). Among the 4 reservoirs, mean concentrations varied from 20.3 to 55.4 mg g\(^{-1}\) (Table 1); within individual reservoirs the difference between minimum and maximum values ranged by 2-fold (Fayette) to 12-fold (Jamesport; Table 1). Overall, these OC concentrations are near the mid-range of values reported in similar studies (United States, Ritchie 1989; Iowa, Downing et al. 2008; Sweden, Rippey et al. 2008; New Zealand and China, Trolle et al. 2010; Ohio, Vanni et al. 2011). Moderate values are expected in impoundments because they are located in erosional topography, and high inorganic sedimentation dilutes organic materials and lowers OC values (Hyne 1978, Mulholland and Elwood 1982). The mean and range of sediment OC was the smallest in Fayette, the impoundment with the highest concentration of mineral turbidity in the water column and largest ratio of catchment area to reservoir surface area (Table 1). Surface sediment from Fayette also had the largest dry bulk density values of the study reservoirs (mean = 0.43 vs. 0.28–0.30 g dry mass cm\(^{-3}\)). Table 1. Similar studies of small size-class impoundments and natural lakes in other geographic regions are needed to determine the generality of these findings and their importance for accurate and precise up-scaling of the role of these systems in the global carbon budget (Downing et al. 2008). Some Observations on Internal Recycling, Regeneration and Oscillation of Dissolved Nitrogen and Phosphorus in Shallow Self-contained Lakes By Jan Barica, Winnipeg With 15 figures and 3 tables in the text Abstract From the fluctuations in mass of nutrients in the water column of four productive shallow lakes in the Erickson area, southwest Manitoba, it is possible to assume that the decomposing plankton is an important source of ammonia and phosphate. The cycle of these nutrients appears to be essentially internal and periodically repeated. The nutrients were released from decomposing algae during totally or partially anoxic conditions in mid-winter under the ice and during short periods in the summer following the collapses of algal blooms. The ammonia and phosphate was subsequently assimilated by algae, transformed into particulate or dissolved organic form and released again. Oscillatory pattern of rates of chemical changes in the bloom-collapse period was demonstrated. Dissolved organic nitrogen and dissolved organic phosphorus were produced by both living and decomposing algae. The midwestern pothole winterkill lakes are small water bodies located in isolated depressions. They lack any permanent inflow or outflow, and depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for their water supply (Fig. 1). The lakes are usually shallow (2—3 m) with no pronounced thermal stratification. Some of the surrounding land is intensively farmed and the lakes have reached high degrees of eutrophy. Many of the lakes experience noxious algal blooms in the summer. In addition most of them also develop anoxic conditions during the 5—6 month long ice cover period. Hence the name "winterkill" lakes. In spite of this drawback, these lakes represent a great potential for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970). In this paper some observations on internal recycling of dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus are presented. They deal with four representative shallow self-contained lakes, with the objective of determining the mechanism and kinetics of chemical changes taking place during characteristic periods of the annual cycles of the lakes. This work presents a part of broader chemical-limnological studies, currently in progress as a part of the aquaculture program of the Freshwater Institute. Fig. 1. Aerial photograph of a group of pothole winterkill lakes. Lake 885 and surrounding lakes. Study Area and Methods The four lakes discussed in this paper are some of about 50 being used for experiments with rainbow trout farming in midwestern winterkill lakes. They are located near Erickson in southwestern Manitoba, south of the Riding Mountain National Park, at about 50° 30' N, 100° 10' W. The area is characterized by morainal deposits resulting from a series of glaciations during the Pleistocene. Many "potholes", formed by remaining blocks of ice after the general ice-sheet retreat, subsequently became small discrete lakes with neither inflow nor outflow. They depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for the maintenance of their water levels, which fluctuate significantly. Most of the area is cultivated with natural forest remaining on hillsides and lake shores (Sunde et al. 1970). The lakes vary significantly as far as their water quality is concerned: some lakes are clear with no apparent algal blooms in the summer, others experience water blooms without any radical changes in their quality. The most problematic group of lakes are those containing nearly pure cultures of Aphanizomenon flos aquae, reaching in mid-summer noxious levels of 0.5 to 2 ml/liter. The sudden dieoff and decomposition of the algal cells in the "summerkill" lakes can cause a complete depletion of dissolved oxygen (Barica 1973) and death of fish. The rationale for selection of representative lakes for this paper was as follows: 1. Lake 885: a representative example of the most extreme cases of summerkill lakes, with several consecutive blooms and collapses of Aphan. flos-aquae during the year. No fish stocks are able to survive the summer months. 2. Lake 154: a lake with less severe conditions of fish kills, having only one algal bloom collapse in late summer with a partial fish kill. 3. Lake 302: with blooms involving algae other than Aphan. flos-aquae. The collapse of the bloom does not cause a total oxygen depletion and subsequent fish mortalities. 4. Lake 255: A "good" lake in a fish farming and water quality sense, with algal populations evenly distributed throughout the summer and never reaching noxious blooms or bloom collapse conditions. All the above lakes are winterkill lakes, reaching anoxic conditions between December and February. They are re-stocked with fish every spring for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970; Sunde et al. 1970). Morphometry, chemistry and phytoplankton data characterizing selected lakes are presented in Tables 1—2. The lakes are small (2.4 to 17.3 hectares), shallow (2—5 m) and fairly saline (specific conductance 780 to 1750 \( \mu \)mhos/cm). Magnesium and sulphate are the predominant ions. The four lakes were under observation from the middle of summer 1971 until April 1973 with the frequency of sampling adjusted according to the advance of the algal blooms, more frequently in summer (1—7 days) than in winter (1—2 months). The lakes were sampled in the center in a vertical profile (usually 0, 1, 2, 3 m in the upper part and 25—50 cm near the bottom), using a Kemmerer or Friedinger sampling bottle. Dissolved oxygen (DO) was measured at 50 cm vertical intervals in before-noon hours using a Model 4 Y.S.I. oxygen meter which was regularly calibrated by the Winkler method (APHA Standard Methods 1971). Ammonia and phosphate, i.e., soluble reactive phosphate as defined by Strickland & Parsons (1968) expressed as PO\(_4\)-P, were determined spectrophotometrically in the field laboratory at Erickson on a Spectronic 88 colorimeter (Bausch and Lomb). The phenol-hypochlorite (Solórzano 1969) and acid-molybdate-ascorbic acid (Murphy & Riley 1962) methods, respectively, were used. Nitrate was determined by reduction to nitrite with a Cd-Cu couple (Wood et al. 1967). Water samples were filtered using GF/C filters in the field laboratory and analyzed in Winnipeg for particulate C, N and P (Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer for particulate C and N, ignition and acid digestion for particulate P). Part of the filtrate was irradiated by ultraviolet light and analyzed for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP) (Henriksen 1970). Concentrations of dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) and dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) were obtained by subtracting the inorganic forms from total dissolved N and P. Other major and minor constituents were determined by standard procedures of Freshwater Institute Analytical Laboratory (MS). N, D, J and S indicate the months; w - winter, s - summer. face area (1 m^2) to give a better comparison and assessment of the relative changes within the lake in time than a conventional weight per volume presentation. The values shown here were calculated on the basis of determinations for various depths as integrated values for each vertical profile \[ M = A \int_{z_0}^{z_{\text{max}}} C(z) \, dz \] where M = total mass of the substance in the water column, A = area of the water column (1 m^2) and C(z) = concentration of the substance at depth z. Computations were done for DON, NH_3-N, NO_3-N, DOP, PO_4-P and compared with dissolved oxygen and particulate CNP, i.e., the sum of particulate C + particulate N + particulate P, representing the total biomass. From Figs. 2—5 it seems quite obvious that the changes in both inorganic and organic N- and P-forms depend on biological processes in the ![Line graphs showing DON, NH3-N, NO3-N, DOP, PO4-P, DO, and Partic. CNP concentrations over time for L885, with labeled months and years.](page_184_1042_1207_1042.png) Fig. 2 ![Line graph showing DON, NH3-N, NO3-N, DOP, PO4-P, Partic. CNP, and DO concentrations in Lake 154 from 1971 to 1973.](page_246_180_1347_1042.png) Fig. 3 lakes, as indicated by DO and particulate CNP lines, and are much more pronounced in lakes which produced blooms than in Lake 255, which is a non-blooming lake. Fluctuations in total N and P contents occur chiefly in 3 characteristic periods: 1. during the ice cover, mainly in its last phase (February—March); 2. prior to and during the algal blooms; 3. during the die-off or sudden collapse of the algal blooms. In all four lakes presented here there is an obvious periodicity as far as increase or decrease (release or uptake) of the nutrients is concerned; in mid-winter there is an appreciable accumulation of dissolved N and P in the lakes as a result of anoxic bacterial decomposition of organic matter and subsequent regeneration of N and P in inorganic forms. This process is intensified by the substantially limited uptake by algae at this time of the year due to their minimum production (winter 1972). In this period nitrate, ammonia and phosphate reach their peak concentrations and represent a potential nutrient supply for the productive period ahead. Since there is no L 302 DON — NH₃-N — NO₃-N DOP — PO₄-P — Partic. CNP — DO — Fig. 4 significant input of nutrients from the basin during the winter, we can presume that all inorganic N and P present was regenerated from dead plankton produced the previous season. This is in accordance with the results of laboratory experiments performed by Krause (1961, 1964). However, dead phytoplankton play the major role in these lakes due to their relative abundance over zooplankton. The degree of mineralization of organic matter in the winter period is highest in the most productive lake (L. 885), where the reserve of DON and DOP sank to zero levels and was quantitatively transformed into inorganic forms. This process was clearly pronounced in the "normal" winter conditions of '71/'72, while the unusually mild winter in '72/'73 and the continuing primary production under the ice until Fig. 5 Seasonal variations in total content of ammonia, nitrate, and dissolved organic nitrogen; reactive phosphate and dissolved oxygen and plankton biomass (expressed as particulate C + N + P) in the lake water column below 1 m^2 of the lake surface at the site of maximum depth (integrated values). December and a new start from February left an appreciably higher amount of unmineralized DON and DOP in the lakes. The basic source of ammonia and phosphate is obviously DON and DOP, which is either directly excreted by living algae in the previous productive season (Fogg 1966; LEAN & NALEWAJKO 1973) or liberated from the dead cells by bacteria during their lysis. Mainly DON shows a proportional decrease in its content during the winter period with the increasing ammonia concentration, which indicates that ammonia is produced by deamination of DON. Deamination of various dissolved organic N-compounds reaches its maximum in anaerobic late winter conditions. This applies also to the increase in NO_3-N content at the same time, although there is no evidence that the increase in NO_3-N is not only due to the minimum uptake by algae and the continuous input from groundwater. However, nitrate concentration was usually only a small fraction of the total inorganic nitrogen, as compared with NH_3-N. From among all N- forms present in the systems, DON is the most abundant form (3—6 times higher than NH_3-N). This is quite characteristic for lakes with blue-green algae (Prescott 1959). Following the ice break-up and the first occurrence of algal blooms the spring reserves of ammonia, nitrate, and phosphate are reduced to undetectable limits. This is accompanied by their transformation into the particulate form (see the appropriate lines for particulate CNP) together with photosynthetic production of DO. This state remains unchanged as long as the bloom stays alive. Then, if either a sudden collapse of the bloom or its gradual die-off takes place, ammonia and phosphate are rapidly released again via bacterial decay of dead algae. This decomposition, accompanied by a release of ammonia and phosphate, takes place in both settled algae on the bottom as well as sinking algae passing through the water column. The peaks of ammonia and phosphate release in the bloom-collapse periods correspond always to a sudden decrease in seston concentrations (as particulate CNP) and to a nearly total depletion of DO, reaching anoxic conditions in the whole water column for several days. There is usually a certain time lag between the decrease of DO and responding changes in N, P and seston, varying from 1 to 4 days, however, in some instances the response is faster. This depends presumably on the multiplication rates of bacterial populations decomposing the dead plankton and depleting DO, and the time lag required to reach their exponential phase. This at the same time makes any statistical correlation between DO, seston and various organic and inorganic N and P forms impossible. The released ammonia and phosphate are subsequently taken up by the upcoming new algal blooms, which can occur for several times a year (L. 885). Lake 255, which had no blooms, shows steady conditions in the summer without any significant fluctuations in the discussed chemical parameters and shows an appreciable release of nutrients only under sub-ice anaerobic conditions in the mid-winter. It is noteworthy that the release of ammonia or phosphate occurs even during the relative decrease of DO concentrations and not necessarily its complete depletion to anoxic conditions. With the progressing primary production, DON and DOP gradually increase their content and reach their maxima during the algal bloom collapses. This indicates on the one hand that they are produced by phytoplankton itself and do not enter the lakes from allochtonous sources, and on the other hand that they are released additionally from the dying plankton prior to their deamination (peaks of DON in the summer bloom period precede those of NH_3-N by several days in the blooming lakes). If the chemical parameters are compared with the occurrence and duration of algal bloom periods and algal bloom collapses, with resulting anoxic conditions as shown on the baselines of graphs 2—5, it can be seen that the fluctuations in the nutrient content correspond to blooms and decomposition periods, whether they be in the winter or in the summer. Decrease in DO content indicates subsequent releases of N and P from dissolved or particulate organic matter back into the water column. This supports the classical theories on phosphate and ammonia release during the reductive conditions (see Discussion). As far as cycling in release or uptake of nutrients is concerned, there are two distinct patterns: 1. the major year-to-year cycle, characterized by an initial stage in January—March which represents the substantial part of the nutrient supply (additional supplementary input by spring run-off is negligible and limited to a very short period of time — currently under study). The source of this nutrient supply is primarily the decomposed plankton and the mineralized dissolved extracellular products. This amount, since the further surface input from the trainage basin practically does not exist, must meet the demand of algae for the whole ice-free season. Since this amount is extremely high, it is sufficient to support an excessive growth of algae in all lakes except L. 255, where the initial supply is much lower. The initial supply is exhausted sometimes in mid-May, when the first algal blooms reach their maxima (L. 885, 154 and 302). 2. At this point, a series of short-time "minor" cycles starts. The first non-Aphanizomenon blooms (Table 2) die off (gradually without a depletion of DO) and a part of the nutrients is released back into solution by bacterial decomposition of dead cells. The new succession usually favours occurrence of Aphanizomenon flos aquae (L. 885, 154), which takes over completely, soon reaching densities as high as 1—2 ml/liter in near-shore parts of the lakes. Collapse of this bloom is accompanied by a greater oxygen depletion than the previous time. In the case of aquaculture lakes, fish stocks are killed partially or totally, depending on the severity and duration of the DO depletion. In this stage a new release of ammonia and phosphate takes place, with about 30—60\% of the initial winter supply being released again. These "little" cycles can occur several times during the ice-free season, with the new fraction of nutrients being released again and subsequently taken up by new blooms. In the most productive lakes, the algal blooms can occur under the ice (L. 885, 154). Eventually, the cycles end with the death of the last bloom and its bacterial decomposition, and the release of a new initial supply in the winter which is available for the new algal blooms in the forthcoming ice-free season. Both patterns are schematically illustrated in Fig. 6. Vertical distribution of N and P concentrations From the absolute increases or decreases of nutrients in water column shown earlier it is possible to assume that the decomposing plankton is the Fig. 6. Schematic diagramm showing a year-to-year cycling of regenerated N and P in shallow self-contained winterkill lakes. 1 — basic "major" cycle in a lake without any algal blooms (L. 255); 2 — supplementary summer "minor" cycles in lakes experiencing algal die-offs and fish kills (L. 885). major source of ammonia and phosphate in the shallow self-contained lakes discussed above and that their cycle is essentially internal, with released N and P being assimilated by algae, transformed into dissolved organic or particulate form, sedimented and released again to serve as nutrients for new algal populations. Since there is little surface inflow and outflow and groundwater movement is probably negligible, this explanation seems to be credible. However, the integrated values for the whole depth of each lake, presented in Figs. 2—5 and affected by the maximum depth of each lake, do not present an adequate picture of an actual movement of nutrients in the whole profile as well as the actual concentrations in conventional units (\( \mu g/l \)). To eliminate this drawback as well as to enable mutual comparison of the lakes discussed here, some representative vertical profiles, covering typical phases of the "large" or "small" cycles, are shown in Figs. 7—10. They present a vertical distribution of the mentioned chemical parameters starting with an initial stage in winter 1972 and ending with a new starting point for the new season, including summer uptake maxima during the bloom periods and the maxima releases of P and N during the algal collapses. Regardless of the time cycling, which was discussed earlier, this form of data presentation shows that the starting base for the release of nutrients during the reducing condition (DO depletion) is the lake bottom, i.e., the decomposing sediments. Characteristic phases of the NH\(_3\)-N and PO\(_4\)-P feedback can be schematically presented as ![Schematic diagrams showing nutrient cycling and vertical distribution](page_180_180_1200_400.png) NH\(_3\)-N PO\(_4\)-P Fig. 7 Fig. 8 whereby the wind seems to accelerate substantially the diffusion and homogenization of the whole profile during the ice-free season. Distribution of particulate CNP and DO is a mirror image of the above curves: Part. CNP DO Fig. 9 Fig. 10 Fig. 7 — Lake 885 Fig. 8 — Lake 154 Fig. 9 — Lake 255 Fig. 10 — Lake 302 Characteristic vertical profiles showing various stages of lake evolution throughout a year. DON and DOP show the following pattern during the ice-free season: ![DON and DOP profile diagrams](page_420_222_420_120.png) DON DOP with the maxima near the bottom only (or both near the bottom and near the surface during the bloom peaks, which shows that they are produced by both living and dead sinking or already sunk algae during their decomposition. In all instances, a dependence of dissolved N and P forms, both inorganic and organic, on particulate forms and DO is obvious. As before, the non-blooming lake, 255, does not experience any summer fluctuations, and the release of ammonia and phosphate starts in early winter from near the bottom again and reaches the total homogeneity in the profile in mid-winter. Nutrient release or uptake rates: chemical oscillation Figs. 2—5 showed an internal recycling of N and P below the lake surface with decomposing plankton being their most important source on a short-term basis (year-to-year or month-to-month in the summer). In order to demonstrate kinetics of changes in total nutrient content the curves in Figs. 2—5 were differentiated as \[ \frac{dM}{dt} \approx M(x+1) - M(x) \] for \( dt \to 1 \) day where \( M(x) \) and \( M(x+1) \) are the total masses (\( g/m^2 \)) for two consecutive days and \( dM \) is a change in total mass over the time \( dt \). The transformed data are shown in Figs. 11—14 for each lake and chemical parameter separately. Thus, the positive \( dM \) values for ammonia and phosphate would represent nutrient release rates (\( g/day \) in water column of a \( 1 \ m^2 \) surface area), and the negative ones the uptake rates caused by algae. For DON and DOP the \( +dM \) values would represent rate of release by living or decomposing phytoplankton and the \( -dM \) values a bacterial uptake or mineralization rates respectively. For DO, \( +dM \) means a photosynthetic production, \( -dM \) on the other hand the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) rates (total oxygen uptake). In the case of seston (particulate CNP) it will be the net production or sedimentation respectively. From all presented derivation curves it follows that most of the chemical changes take place in the summer during the algal collapses, whereas the winter changes are much slower. Both nutrients show a decrease of 21.4 % for ammonia and 21.8 % for phosphate which might indicate a nutrient deficiency as a possible trigger for algal collapses (the same applies for PO_4-P in L. 154; D = 15.7 %). However, in the other three lakes cancellation of positive and negative values shows that all N and P in an available form is completely regenerated, i.e., transformed from an organic form into an inorganic one. This cycle is completed within one year or less regardless when it initiates. Discussion Since the pothole lakes have no surface inflow during most of the year, and the groundwater movement in isolated basins is not expected to be significant, the question of the source of the plant nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, arises, and it is natural to look for it in the lakes themselves. According to widely accepted theories by EINSELE (1938), OHLE (1938), MORTIMER (1941, 1942), and HUTCHINSON (1957), phosphorus is found in the form of an insoluble ferric salt in the lake bottom if the redox conditions are favorable, and is released into water column when iron is reduced to the ferro state in anoxic conditions of a lake hypolimnion. This concept has been further elaborated in recent years and shifted from a simple ferric-ferro model to more complex physical-adsorption approaches taking into account various mineral fractions of the lake sediments and their P-binding capacity (STUMM & LECKIE 1970; GOLTERMAN et al. 1969). LEE (1969) pointed out that knowledge is particularly lacking on the role of the lake sediments in maintaining phosphate levels in water. It is not known whether the sediments act as a sink in which the majority of nutrients is refractory, not available for exchange (HAYES 1964; LATTERELL et al. 1971; SCHINDLER et al. 1971), or whether the sediments act as a buffer in which phosphate concentrations in the overlying water are controlled by sediment-water exchange reactions (OHLE 1964, 1968; SERRUYA & BERNAN 1970; BURNS 1972; TESSENOW 1972; GOLTERMAN 1973). Our data indicate that an important source of nutrients in self-contained shallow lakes are the decomposed algal cells, i.e., the sediments and that the whole nutrient cycle is closed and periodically repeated. This can be characterized by a cycle: ![Diagram showing the nutrient cycle: N & P release from algal cells → N & P uptake, incorporation into particulate form → Die-off, sedimentation → Bacterial decomposition → Refractory N & P in the sediments](page_1012_1342_627_388.png) This cycle does not at this stage depend on external sources of nutrients from the drainage basin (these were however important in earlier stages of lake eutrophication history and over a long period of time — in a geological sense — which brought about the existing high nutrient supply). The absolute amount of the available nutrients in the lakes on a year-to-year basis apparently does not change substantially. These conclusions, although quite in agreement with the classical theories, differ in the geochemical aspect of the problem. Concentrations of Fe- or PO_4-absorbing clay minerals at the enormous production of phytoplankton and limited influx of mineral matter from the drainage basin cause that the sediments are formed mostly by dead algae in the summer and the total PO_4-P far exceeds stoichiometrically the available Fe (Fe/PO_4 meq. ratios are 9.32, 1.97, 2.67 and 1.75 respectively for the maxima (Table 1)). The chemical reactions in sediments may be therefore a result of biological processes as well as geochemical ones. I would rather see an analogy of our lakes as compared to large-scale algal cultures in flasks which are allowed to decompose. Indeed, our conclusions are very similar to those obtained from regeneration experiments performed with algal cultures in laboratory scale (Golterman 1960; Grill & Richards 1964; Foree et al. 1970). Particularly Golterman's (1973) model of P-recycling in shallow lakes, with an emphasis on the internal part of his recycling diagram, and his findings on the high efficiency of mineralization, agrees with the present results. The oscillatory patterns of daily release and uptake rates, presented in this paper, allow, both visual and mathematical assessment of the "normal" conditions of a lake. A lake system is in an equilibrium when dM values approach zero. A sudden collapse of an algal bloom, a rapid oxygen depletion and a take-over by decomposition processes act as a force causing disturbance of this equilibrium. The first amplitude of the released N or P is followed by its uptake. After a series of complete cycles, which takes usually several weeks, relaxation oscillations gradually fade out and the equilibrium is reached again. Since any oscillating matter vibrates above and below a mean equilibrium value (in our case it is zero), the sum of displacements in either direction should cancel out. This actually happens in most instances except for DON and DOP values. It proves a periodicity of the process, its return to the initial stage, and, in fact, the law of conservation of matter in self-contained lakes. In this context there is a basic difference between anoxic conditions in the winter, which occur gradually, and the rapid oxygen depletion following the bloom collapses in the summer. The latter affect the chemical equilibrium in lakes more significantly. Summary Variations in total mass of ammonia-, nitrate and dissolved organic nitrogen, phosphate and dissolved organic phosphorus, as compared with total mass of dissolved oxygen and plankton biomass (expressed as particulate CNP) in four productive shallow lakes in the Erickson area, southwest Manitoba, are described. The lakes are groundwater-fed with no permanent surface inflow or outflow. They belong to a pothole winterkill type, producing heavy algal blooms. The data collected between summer 1971 — spring 1973 are presented as total mass under a unit surface area as well as daily release or uptake rates. There are two distinct patterns in the nutrient regime of these lakes: 1) the major year-to-year cycle, characterized by an initial stage in January—March which represents the substantial part of the nutrient supply. The source of this is the decomposed plankton and the mineralized dissolved extracellular products. This amount is sufficient to support an excessive growth of algae. 2) The initial supply is exhausted sometimes in May, when the first algal blooms reach their maxima. At this point, a series of short-time "minor" cycles starts. The algal blooms die off and a part of the nutrients is released back into solution by bacterial decomposition of algal cells. In the case of aquaculture lakes, fish stocks are killed partially or totally, depending on severity and duration of the oxygen depletion. Oscillatory pattern of distribution of daily release or uptake rates of nutrients and other chemical constituents demonstrates a significant disturbance of the chemical equilibrium of the lakes caused by severe oxygen depletion following a collapse of algal blooms. It also shows that a release of ammonia and phosphate from organic matter occurs also during a relative decrease in dissolved oxygen concentrations and not only during its complete depletion to anoxic conditions. This work is a part of broader studies carried out within the aquaculture program of the Freshwater Institute. Zusammenfassung Die Schwankungen der Gesamtmengen von Ammonium, Nitrat und gelöstem organischem Stickstoff sowie von Phosphat und gelöstem organischen Phosphat werden in vier produktiven Flachseen im Ericksongebiet, Südwest-Manitoba, beschrieben und verglichen mit der Gesamtmenge an gelöstem Sauerstoff und der Planktonbiomasse, ausgedrückt als partikulärer C+N+P. Es handelt sich um Grundwasser-Seen ohne permanenten Oberflächen-Ein- oder Ausfluß. Sie gehören zu einem „pothole“ Typ mit starken Algenblüten und winterlichen Fischsterben. Die Ergebnisse von Sommer 1971 bis Frühjahr 1973 werden sowohl als Gesamtmenge unter einer Oberflächeneinheit als auch als tägliche Freisetzung- und Aufnahme-Raten dargeboten. Zwei verschiedene Zyklen des Nährstoffhaushaltes dieser Seen lassen sich unterscheiden: 1. Der umfangreichere Jahreszyklus, charakterisiert durch ein Anfangsstadium in den Monaten Januar bis März, welches den wesentlichen Teil der Nährstoffauffüllung darstellt. Die Nährstoffquellen sind das zersetzte Plankton und die mineralisierten gelösten extrazellulären Produkte. Diese Nährstoffquellen reichen aus für ein exzessives Algenwachstum. 2. Diese Nährstoffmenge aus der Anfangsphase ist in manchen Fällen im Mai erschöpft, wenn die ersten Algenblüten ihr Maximum erreichen. In diesem Zeitpunkt beginnt eine Serie von kleineren Kurzzeit-Zyklen. Die Algenblüten sterben ab, und ein Teil der Nährstoffe wird durch bakterielle Zersetzung der Algen wieder in Lösung zurückgeführt. In den fischereilich genutzten Seen sterben die Fischbestände teilweise oder total ab, abhängig von der Intensität und Dauer der Sauerstoffzehrung. Periodische Schwankungen des Verhältnisses von täglicher Freisetzung und Wiederaufnahme von Nährstoffen und von anderen chemischen Komponenten zeigen eine signifikante Störung des chemischen Gleichgewichtes der Seen, verursacht durch starke Sauerstoffzehrung, bzw. -entleerung als Folge eines Zusammenbruches der Algenblüten. Es zeigt sich ferner, daß eine Freisetzung von Ammono- nium und Phosphat aus organischer Substanz schon während eines relativen Abfalles der Konzentrationen des gelösten Sauerstoffes eintritt und nicht nur während des völligen Sauerstoffentzugs unter anaeroben Bedingungen. Some Observations on Internal Recycling, Regeneration and Oscillation of Dissolved Nitrogen and Phosphorus in Shallow Self-contained Lakes By Jan Barica, Winnipeg With 15 figures and 3 tables in the text Abstract From the fluctuations in mass of nutrients in the water column of four productive shallow lakes in the Erickson area, southwest Manitoba, it is possible to assume that the decomposing plankton is an important source of ammonia and phosphate. The cycle of these nutrients appears to be essentially internal and periodically repeated. The nutrients were released from decomposing algae during totally or partially anoxic conditions in mid-winter under the ice and during short periods in the summer following the collapses of algal blooms. The ammonia and phosphate was subsequently assimilated by algae, transformed into particulate or dissolved organic form and released again. Oscillatory pattern of rates of chemical changes in the bloom-collapse period was demonstrated. Dissolved organic nitrogen and dissolved organic phosphorus were produced by both living and decomposing algae. The midwestern pothole winterkill lakes are small water bodies located in isolated depressions. They lack any permanent inflow or outflow, and depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for their water supply (Fig. 1). The lakes are usually shallow (2—3 m) with no pronounced thermal stratification. Some of the surrounding land is intensively farmed and the lakes have reached high degrees of eutrophy. Many of the lakes experience noxious algal blooms in the summer. In addition most of them also develop anoxic conditions during the 5—6 month long ice cover period. Hence the name "winterkill" lakes. In spite of this drawback, these lakes represent a great potential for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970). In this paper some observations on internal recycling of dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus are presented. They deal with four representative shallow self-contained lakes, with the objective of determining the mechanism and kinetics of chemical changes taking place during characteristic periods of the annual cycles of the lakes. This work presents a part of broader chemical-limnological studies, currently in progress as a part of the aquaculture program of the Freshwater Institute. Fig. 1. Aerial photograph of a group of pothole winterkill lakes. Lake 885 and surrounding lakes. Study Area and Methods The four lakes discussed in this paper are some of about 50 being used for experiments with rainbow trout farming in midwestern winterkill lakes. They are located near Erickson in southwestern Manitoba, south of the Riding Mountain National Park, at about 50° 30' N, 100° 10' W. The area is characterized by morainal deposits resulting from a series of glaciations during the Pleistocene. Many "potholes", formed by remaining blocks of ice after the general ice-sheet retreat, subsequently became small discrete lakes with neither inflow nor outflow. They depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for the maintenance of their water levels, which fluctuate significantly. Most of the area is cultivated with natural forest remaining on hillsides and lake shores (Sunde et al. 1970). The lakes vary significantly as far as their water quality is concerned: some lakes are clear with no apparent algal blooms in the summer, others experience water blooms without any radical changes in their quality. The most problematic group of lakes are those containing nearly pure cultures of Aphanizomenon flos aquae, reaching in mid-summer noxious levels of 0.5 to 2 ml/liter. The sudden dieoff and decomposition of the algal cells in the "summerkill" lakes can cause a complete depletion of dissolved oxygen (Barica 1973) and death of fish. The rationale for selection of representative lakes for this paper was as follows: 1. Lake 885: a representative example of the most extreme cases of summerkill lakes, with several consecutive blooms and collapses of Aphan. flos-aquae during the year. No fish stocks are able to survive the summer months. 2. Lake 154: a lake with less severe conditions of fish kills, having only one algal bloom collapse in late summer with a partial fish kill. 3. Lake 302: with blooms involving algae other than Aphan. flos-aquae. The collapse of the bloom does not cause a total oxygen depletion and subsequent fish mortalities. 4. Lake 255: A "good" lake in a fish farming and water quality sense, with algal populations evenly distributed throughout the summer and never reaching noxious blooms or bloom collapse conditions. All the above lakes are winterkill lakes, reaching anoxic conditions between December and February. They are re-stocked with fish every spring for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970; Sunde et al. 1970). Morphometry, chemistry and phytoplankton data characterizing selected lakes are presented in Tables 1—2. The lakes are small (2.4 to 17.3 hectares), shallow (2—5 m) and fairly saline (specific conductance 780 to 1750 \( \mu \)mhos/cm). Magnesium and sulphate are the predominant ions. The four lakes were under observation from the middle of summer 1971 until April 1973 with the frequency of sampling adjusted according to the advance of the algal blooms, more frequently in summer (1—7 days) than in winter (1—2 months). The lakes were sampled in the center in a vertical profile (usually 0, 1, 2, 3 m in the upper part and 25—50 cm near the bottom), using a Kemmerer or Friedinger sampling bottle. Dissolved oxygen (DO) was measured at 50 cm vertical intervals in before-noon hours using a Model 4 Y.S.I. oxygen meter which was regularly calibrated by the Winkler method (APHA Standard Methods 1971). Ammonia and phosphate, i.e., soluble reactive phosphate as defined by Strickland & Parsons (1968) expressed as PO\(_4\)-P, were determined spectrophotometrically in the field laboratory at Erickson on a Spectronic 88 colorimeter (Bausch and Lomb). The phenol-hypochlorite (Solórzano 1969) and acid-molybdate-ascorbic acid (Murphy & Riley 1962) methods, respectively, were used. Nitrate was determined by reduction to nitrite with a Cd-Cu couple (Wood et al. 1967). Water samples were filtered using GF/C filters in the field laboratory and analyzed in Winnipeg for particulate C, N and P (Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer for particulate C and N, ignition and acid digestion for particulate P). Part of the filtrate was irradiated by ultraviolet light and analyzed for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP) (Henriksen 1970). Concentrations of dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) and dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) were obtained by subtracting the inorganic forms from total dissolved N and P. Other major and minor constituents were determined by standard procedures of Freshwater Institute Analytical Laboratory (MS). This is in accordance with the results of laboratory experiments performed by Krause (1961, 1964). December and a new start from February left an appreciably higher amount of unmineralized DON and DOP in the lakes. The basic source of ammonia and phosphate is obviously DON and DOP, which is either directly excreted by living algae in the previous productive season (Fogg 1966; LEAN & NALEWAJKO 1973) or liberated from the dead cells by bacteria during their lysis. Mainly DON shows a proportional decrease in its content during the winter period with the increasing ammonia concentration, which indicates that ammonia is produced by deamination of DON. Deamination of various dissolved organic N-compounds reaches its maximum in anaerobic late winter conditions. This applies also to the increase in NO_3-N content at the same time, although there is no evidence that the increase in NO_3-N is not only due to the minimum uptake by algae and the continuous input from groundwater. However, nitrate concentration was usually only a small fraction of the total inorganic nitrogen, as compared with NH_3-N. From among all N- forms present in the systems, DON is the most abundant form (3—6 times higher than NH_3-N). This is quite characteristic for lakes with blue-green algae (Prescott 1959). Following the ice break-up and the first occurrence of algal blooms the spring reserves of ammonia, nitrate, and phosphate are reduced to undetectable limits. This is accompanied by their transformation into the particulate form (see the appropriate lines for particulate CNP) together with photosynthetic production of DO. This state remains unchanged as long as the bloom stays alive. Then, if either a sudden collapse of the bloom or its gradual die-off takes place, ammonia and phosphate are rapidly released again via bacterial decay of dead algae. This decomposition, accompanied by a release of ammonia and phosphate, takes place in both settled algae on the bottom as well as sinking algae passing through the water column. The peaks of ammonia and phosphate release in the bloom-collapse periods correspond always to a sudden decrease in seston concentrations (as particulate CNP) and to a nearly total depletion of DO, reaching anoxic conditions in the whole water column for several days. There is usually a certain time lag between the decrease of DO and responding changes in N, P and seston, varying from 1 to 4 days, however, in some instances the response is faster. This depends presumably on the multiplication rates of bacterial populations decomposing the dead plankton and depleting DO, and the time lag required to reach their exponential phase. This at the same time makes any statistical correlation between DO, seston and various organic and inorganic N and P forms impossible. The released ammonia and phosphate are subsequently taken up by the upcoming new algal blooms, which can occur for several times a year (L. 885). Lake 255, which had no blooms, shows steady conditions in the summer without any significant fluctuations in the discussed chemical parameters and shows an appreciable release of nutrients only under sub-ice anaerobic conditions in the mid-winter. It is noteworthy that the release of ammonia or phosphate occurs even during the relative decrease of DO concentrations and not necessarily its complete depletion to anoxic conditions. With the progressing primary production, DON and DOP gradually increase their content and reach their maxima during the algal bloom collapses. This indicates on the one hand that they are produced by phytoplankton itself and do not enter the lakes from allochtonous sources, and on the other hand that they are released additionally from the dying plankton prior to their deamination (peaks of DON in the summer bloom period precede those of NH_3-N by several days in the blooming lakes). If the chemical parameters are compared with the occurrence and duration of algal bloom periods and algal bloom collapses, with resulting anoxic conditions as shown on the baselines of graphs 2—5, it can be seen that the fluctuations in the nutrient content correspond to blooms and decomposition periods, whether they be in the winter or in the summer. Decrease in DO content indicates subsequent releases of N and P from dissolved or particulate organic matter back into the water column. This supports the classical theories on phosphate and ammonia release during the reductive conditions (see Discussion). As far as cycling in release or uptake of nutrients is concerned, there are two distinct patterns: 1. the major year-to-year cycle, characterized by an initial stage in January—March which represents the substantial part of the nutrient supply (additional supplementary input by spring run-off is negligible and limited to a very short period of time — currently under study). The source of this nutrient supply is primarily the decomposed plankton and the mineralized dissolved extracellular products. This amount, since the further surface input from the trainage basin practically does not exist, must meet the demand of algae for the whole ice-free season. Since this amount is extremely high, it is sufficient to support an excessive growth of algae in all lakes except L. 255, where the initial supply is much lower. The initial supply is exhausted sometimes in mid-May, when the first algal blooms reach their maxima (L. 885, 154 and 302). 2. At this point, a series of short-time "minor" cycles starts. The first non-Aphanizomenon blooms (Table 2) die off (gradually without a depletion of DO) and a part of the nutrients is released back into solution by bacterial decomposition of dead cells. The new succession usually favours occurrence of Aphanizomenon flos aquae (L. 885, 154), which takes over completely, soon reaching densities as high as 1—2 ml/liter in near-shore parts of the lakes. Collapse of this bloom is accompanied by a greater oxygen depletion than the previous time. In the case of aquaculture lakes, fish stocks are killed partially or totally, depending on the severity and duration of the DO depletion. In this stage a new release of ammonia and phosphate takes place, with about 30—60\% of the initial winter supply being released again. These "little" cycles can occur several times during the ice-free season, with the new fraction of nutrients being released again and subsequently taken up by new blooms. In the most productive lakes, the algal blooms can occur under the ice (L. 885, 154). Eventually, the cycles end with the death of the last bloom and its bacterial decomposition, and the release of a new initial supply in the winter which is available for the new algal blooms in the forthcoming ice-free season.
