A range of statistical regression lines was tested for their ability to explain the variance in % near-surface thermoclines. The asymptotic regression model above was found to be the best fit (as determined from \( r^2 \) comparisons). Figure 2. The relationship between frequency of near-surface thermoclines (%, \( \Delta T \geq 0.2^\circ \mathrm{C} \)) and light extinction coefficient (\( K_d \)) for the ELA and NOLSS. The regression is: frequency (%) = 32.2 (\( K_d \)) + 26.4; \( r^2 = 0.45 \) (\( P < 0.0001 \)). than in brown-water lakes, independent of lake size (Salonen and others 1984; Pérez-Fuentetaja and others 1999; Snucins and Gunn 2000). Within individual lakes, thermocline depth increases if the water becomes clearer, as is commonly observed during prolonged periods of drought (Schindler and others 1996a; Dillon and Molot 1997). Because of the greater radiation-absorbing capacity of colored waters, heating is restricted to the surface and multiple thermoclines form more readily (Salonen and others 1984). Mazumder and Taylor (1994) showed that water clarity offered a better explanation for thermocline depth in small lakes (less than 12.5 km\(^2\)) than in larger lakes. Fee and others (1996) also showed that the influence of water clarity on thermocline depth diminished as lake size exceeded 500 ha. However, both mixing depth and transparency were positively correlated with lake size. Thus, the correlation between the development of near-surface thermoclines and transparency (\( K_d \)) could simply reflect the underlying relation with lake size that both variables share (\( P < 0.001, r = 0.49 \)). Temperature-related Density Differences Density differences per unit temperature are greater at warm temperatures. This is potentially important because larger lakes are usually colder in the summer than nearby smaller lakes (Fee and Hecky 1992; Fee and others 1992). As expected, average water stability (N) near the surface of the lake decreased with increasing lake size (Figure 3A). The Brünt-Väisälä frequency was also related to water transparency (Figure 3B, \( r^2 = 0.44, P < 0.001 \)). Interannual Patterns Interannual variations in annual means of daily maximum air temperatures and daily mean wind speed might be related to the development of different annual near-surface thermocline patterns. Since 1970, the average air temperature (Schindler and others 1990, 1996a; Fee and others 1996), wind speed (Figure 4A), and water transparency (Figure 4B) in northwestern Ontario have increased. We hypothesized that the increase in wind would reduce the frequency of near-surface thermoclines at the ELA. In the early 1970s, when ELA lakes were surrounded by dense and mature forests (Schindler 1998), the lakes had a high frequency of near-surface thermoclines (Figure 4C, D). Following two major fires (in June 1974 and June 1980) and clearcutting (in the 1970s and early 1980s), which resulted in the partial removal of vegetation in much of the region surrounding ELA, the average wind increased (Figure 4A) and the frequency of near-surface thermoclines decreased (Figures 4C, D). As expected, the frequency of formation of near-surface thermoclines was inversely related to wind speed (\( r^2 = 0.27; P = 0.0071 \)). However, the variance explained by this relationship is low. It is not surprising that wind explained only 27% of the variation, for several reasons. Compared to lake size and water transparency, wind probably Figure 3. (A) The relationship between the average Brünt-Väisälä frequency (N) and lake size for ELA lakes. N was averaged per lake for the years 1968–94. The regression is N = 0.0256 – 0.0088 (log A_0), \( r^2 = 0.39 \) (\( P = 0.0004 \)). (B) The relationship between N and K_d. The regression is N = 0.0081 (K_d) + 0.0108, \( r^2 = 0.34 \) (\( P = 0.0003 \)). has less potential to explain the variability in near-surface thermoclines that we found. In addition, it has recently been shown that only a small fraction (around 3%) of the turbulent energy flux from wind enters the lake (Wüest and others 2000). Furthermore, solar radiation (solar insolation and general heating) is likely a strong driver of the development of near-surface thermoclines (Imberger 1985), regardless of wind velocity. Air temperature has also been increasing in the ELA area (Schindler and others 1996a), and this may offset the wind forcing on the mechanical development/erosion of near-surface thermoclines. Finally, the ELA experienced a drought in the 1980s, causing an increase in water transparency (Figure 4B) and deeper thermoclines (Schindler and others 1996a). It is possible that near-surface thermoclines were also deeper than 1 m. The annual frequency of near-surface thermoclines was positively related with the annual average K_d in Figure 4B (\( P < 0.05; r^2 = 0.22 \)). Clearly, further studies are needed to assess the relative importance of solar radiation, wind, lake size, and lake clarity. It seems that deforestation will only affect stratification patterns (such as thermocline depth) in small lakes (less than 4 ha) (Rask and others 1993; Figure 4. (C) Yearly average frequency of near-surface thermoclines for all lakes during the ice-free season at the ELA. (D) Yearly average frequency of near-surface thermoclines in L239. Asterisks indicate dates of forest fires in the catchment. Two major fires occurred around the L239 watershed. The first, in late June 1974, burned over 50% of the catchment. The second, in June 1980, burned approximately 70% of the catchment. Steedman and Kushneriuk 2000; Scully and others 2000). Recently, Steedman and Kushneriuk (2000) found that logging does not increase wind reaching the surface of lakes 30–40 ha in size. Although wind measured at the ELA weather station has increased since 1970 (Figure 4A), following the fires and clearcutting, it is difficult to assess whether this translated into wind changes at the lake surface. Available field wind data (compiled after 1990) indicate that average wind speeds at the surface of the ELA lakes increase logarithmically with surface area (Figure 5). These data also show that wind speeds at the lakes’ surface quickly reach an upper limit. This upper limit is similar to the average wind velocity measured at the ELA meteorological station for 1990–94. More data are clearly needed to accurately assess the influence of deforestation on wind exposure in lakes of all sizes. CONCLUSIONS The high frequency of near-surface thermoclines indicates that they can be an important determinant of lake biology and chemistry. Williamson and others (1996) showed that near-surface thermoclines occurred 28% of the time in a range of lakes in the northeastern United States. While these lakes were similar in size to the ELA lakes, the lower frequency of near-surface thermoclines reported by Williamson and others (1996) is a result of the criteria (\( \Delta T > 1^\circ \mathrm{C} \)) used in their determination. Here we have demonstrated that the frequency of near-surface thermoclines can be much higher than 28%. Figure 5. Relationship between average wind at the lake surface (1990–94) and lake size for lakes at the ELA. Inset: relationship between average wind speed at the lake surface and lake size for lakes smaller than 80 ha. The darker regression line does not include the outlier L374. Both regression slopes were found to be significantly equal (\( P > 0.05 \); analysis of covariance). The L374 data point is approximately equivalent to the 1990–94 average wind speed at the ELA meteorological station of 11.4 km h\(^{-1}\). In addition to the near-surface layer, which we emphasize here, more attention to deeper substrata seems important. The intensity of UV radiation and photosynthetically active radiation, the intensity of turbulence, and nutrient conditions can differ among sublayers (Spigel and Imberger 1987; Ivey and Imberger 1991; MacIntyre 1993). Small temperature differences within the epilimnion have usually been ignored by chemists and biologists, although they affect many important ecological processes. For example, Xenopoulos and others (2000) found significant changes in the species composition of the algal community when shallow surface thermoclines and high incident UV co-occurred. Weak and transient as these thermoclines are, they are present very frequently and can have important effects on both species assemblages and ecosystem processes in lakes of all sizes. The impact of three-spined sticklebacks on the zooplankton of a previously fish-free pool D. PONT,* A. J. CRIVELLI† and F. GUILLOT *Université Claude Bernard (Lyon 1), Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Systèmes Fluviaux, 1 rue Parmentier 13200 Arles, France; and † Station Biologique de la Tour du Valat, Le Sambuc, 13200 Arles, France SUMMARY. 1. In the Camargue (southern France), most invertebrates inhabiting temporary shallow oligohaline marshes and pools are large-bodied, conspicuous and defenceless taxa that are restricted to fish-free environments. Management practices, by creating drainage canals, strongly affect the invertebrate community by allowing colonization by fish. 2. Sticklebacks colonizing the study pool were sampled daily and zooplankton sampling was carried out at weekly intervals. From early October until the pool dried in June, 1365 sticklebacks entered and only 139 stickleback’s fry and seven adults left the pool. Zooplankton abundance was high during the whole study period with a mean density of 1360 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\). Larger forms (Daphnia magna, Simocephalus vetulus, Arctodiaptomus wierzejskii) quickly disappeared after the first wave of sticklebacks entered the pool in November. Subsequently, smaller species (Diacyclops bicuspidatus odessanus, Chydorus sphaericus and ostracods) replaced the larger ones until the pool dried. 3. Food selectivity of sticklebacks and daily zooplankton consumption were investigated under experimental conditions within the pool in spring. After introduction of sticklebacks, densities of zooplankton species dropped quickly (D. b. odessanus, C. sphaericus) with the exception of Ostracoda. Estimates of daily zooplankton consumption by adult sticklebacks varied between 2.8 and 10.7% of fish body weight. Examination of gut contents showed that fry mainly ingested Chydorus sphaericus. 4. Given that the stickleback is an annual species in the Camargue, and that few fry are able to leave the pool due to the early drying out, the colonization of such a former fish-free pool is not beneficial for the stickleback population. However, a more serious effect of such colonization is the progressive local extinction of the most typical zooplankton species inhabiting these formerly fish-free environments. Introduction Temporarily flooded, shallow oligohaline marshes and pools are typical habitats in the Mediterranean region. Many of these wetlands are fish free. The invertebrates inhabiting them (e.g. copepods, cladocerans and phyllopods) have developed highly specialized adaptations, such as diapause, to enable them to survive early drying out or high water temperatures (Nourisson & Aguesse, 1961; Champeau, 1970; Elgmork, 1980; Wiggins, Mackay & Smik, 1980). In these temporary pools, invertebrates usually belong to large-bodied, conspicuous and defenceless taxa, restricted in their distribution to fish-free environments (Kerfoot & Lynch, 1987). Management practices such as the creation of drainage canals can allow temporary or longer-term colonization of pools by fish, with major consequences for the invertebrate communities. Such practices enable these pools to be used as spawning grounds by various species of fish, especially those spawning early in the spring such as the three-spined stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus L. (Crivelli, 1981; Crivelli & Britton, 1987). In the Camargue in southern France, Gasterosteus aculeatus is a strictly annual species, colonizing seasonally flooded marshes in late autumn and winter. It spawns in February–March and dies in April. Fry produced in these habitats emigrate from early April to the end of May into permanently flooded drainage canals (Crivelli & Britton, 1987; A.J. Crivelli unpublished data). From here they move to the largest permanent brackish-water body in the Camargue, the Etang de Vaccarès, where they spend the period from summer to early autumn. The diet of the three-spined stickleback has been well studied in various types of habitat and in different geographical regions (Wootton, 1976; Walsh & Fitzgerald, 1984; Bentzen & McPhail, 1984; Dauod, Bolger & Bracken, 1985; Snyder, 1984; O’Hara & Penczak, 1987; Delbeek & Williams, 1987). Chironomid larvae and pupae and zooplankton are generally the main food items, with variations according to the time of year and type of habitat. Surface insects, Gastropoda, Gasterosteus eggs and detritus can be of major importance in the stickleback diet in some habitats. Ostracoda are mostly absent or represent less than 1% of the diet (e.g. at Isle Verte, Quebec; Walsh & Fitzgerald, 1984). Few studies have documented the qualitative and quantitative decline or extinction of invertebrates living in fish-free water bodies following accidental or regular colonization by fish, or after stocking with fish (e.g. Gliwicz, 1980; Gliwicz & Rowan, 1984). The aims of this study were to monitor the colonization of a formerly fish-free temporary pool by three-spined sticklebacks, to study their impact on the zooplankton community in the field and to draw conclusions on the long-term variability of the zooplankton and on the consequences of colonization of these pools by spawning sticklebacks. Materials and Methods The study area known as ‘La Fangouse’ (Fig. 1) is a temporary pool located in the delta of the River Rhône on the Mediterranean coast of France. This pool floods naturally with rainwater in the autumn and dries out in early or late spring (Fig. 2). In the 1986–87 period, the pool was flooded on 24 September and dried out on 10 June. The maximum water depth was about 55 cm. At periods of high water level (especially in winter), the pool was connected to the ‘Egout du Cazeau’ drainage canal by a narrow channel. Vegetation cover around the entire pool perimeter was dominated by Arthrocnemum fruticosum L. MOQ. and Juncus maritimus Lamark. Within the pool, submerged vegetation comprised Callitriche truncata Guss, Ranunculus baudotii Godron, Zannichellia pedunculata Lineus and filamentous algae. Mean surface water temperature was 9.0°C in late autumn, 5.8°C in winter and 13.8°C in spring. The pool and connecting channel to the drainage canal were completely frozen over for 20 days in January 1987. Water conductivity (at 25°C) varied between 2.07 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (= 1 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) and 5.03 mS\(^{-1}\) (= 3.0 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) in autumn and winter, reaching 10.8 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (9 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) the week before drying out. The mean conductivity over the entire period of flooding was 4.53 mS cm\(^{-1}\). In the 1987–88 and 1988–89 periods, the pool was flooded on 5 November and 14 October, and dried out by 6 June and 20 March, respectively. In 1987–88 mean conductivity was 10.4 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (3.1–24.9 mS cm\(^{-1}\)), and in 1988–89 it was 6.1 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (2.1–12.1 mS cm\(^{-1}\)). Fish entering or leaving the pool were sampled daily with a system of fish traps situated on the channel connecting the pool and the drainage canal (Fig. 1). The traps were made of mosquito netting (1-mm mesh) and retained fry as small as 8–10 mm long. The two water bodies are connected only when the water level in the pool exceeds 30 cm. All fish captured were identified to species and measured, but only the Gasterosteus attempting to enter the pool were released into it. In 1986–87, 17941 fish belonging to ten species and 2396 Malacostraca (Crangon crangon L., Paleamon squilla L. were recorded entering the study pool (Table 1). The most abundant fish species in order of importance were: Gambusia affinis Baird and Girard, Gasterosteus aculeatus, Atherina boyeri Risso and Lepomis gibbosus L. Trapping was carried out on 35 days in 1986–87, 46 days in 1987–88 but only 5 days in 1988–89. The mean total length of Gasterosteus aculeatus (± 95% CL) was 32.5 ± 0.6 mm in October, 32.4 ± 0.4 in November, 36.0 mm ± 0.3 in December for both sexes combined, and 38.9 ± 2.4 for males and 46.0 ± 2.2 for females in February, and 39.4 ± 1.7 for males and 47.2 ± 1.3 for females in March. Zooplankton sampling was carried out at weekly intervals with a plexiglass core sampler (30-cm\(^2\) section) during the 1986–87 period. The water column, including the soft mud–water interface, was pumped out and the inside was then rinsed out three times (more than 99% of organisms collected). Organisms were finally filtered through a 50-\(\mu\)m mesh-size net and stored in 4% formaldehyde solution (Pont, 1986). Each sample consisted of 24 cores distributed along the entire length of four transects: 80, 60, 130 and 150 m (Fig. 1). In-situ experiments on sticklebacks foraging on zooplankton were carried out in the spring of 1987. Sticklebacks collected at the pool entrance were measured and released into large cylindrical enclosures (1-m\(^2\) section) made of transluscent fibreglass sheeting embedded into the sediment (Fig. 1). Two series of experiments were conducted at the following stickleback densities. (1) Series A (17–22 March). Two or four adult fish per enclosure (three replicates at each density). Zooplankton sample (eight cores) taken just outside the enclosure were used as controls. (2) Series B (18–22 April). One adult or seven young fish per enclosure (three replicates at each density) and two control enclosures. Zooplankton sampling in the enclosures was carried out just before the introduction of sticklebacks, 2 days after (in the case of experimental plots) and at the end of the experiments (Series A: 5 days; Series B: 4 days). At each time, the area sampled represented 2.4% of the total enclosure area, so correction factors were applied to each of the zooplankton counts before computing prey densities. Previous studies (Pont, 1983) have shown that variability between individual cores can be high, so seven cores in two samples were counted separately. The precision indices D, expressed as the ratio of standard error to the arithmetic mean, were 0.18 and 0.15, a reasonable error in such a sampling procedure (Elliot, 1977). Variability in the mean values of total zooplankton density in replicates and controls before fish introduction was of the same order of magnitude: D = 0.16 in Series A and 0.07 in Series B. Therefore, we assume that the relative error in terms of the 95% confidence limits of the mean obtained at each stickleback density tested (eight cores per enclosure and three replicates at each sampling time) was about 40%. Prey length measurements were made under a microscope for each major taxon (n = 150). The mean lengths of Diacyclops, Chydorus and Ostracoda were 0.58, 0.42 and 0.66 mm, respectively. Dry and fresh weights were estimated from length–weight relationships (Dumont, Van de Velde & Dumont 1975; Pont, 1983) and by assuming that dry weight represented 11% of fresh weight (Bottrell et al., 1976). Sticklebacks were measured before experiments (adults: 42–60 mm in length, young: 12–17 mm) and their weights estimated from length–weight relationships (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). Most previous studies of fish feeding rates are based on rates of gastric evacuation and food consumption (Elliot & Persson, 1978). In this study, calculation of stickleback feeding rates was based on Gauld’s method (Gauld, 1951; Edmonson & Winberg, 1971) with the assumption that predation rate is unaffected by changes in prey densities below a critical level. (i) \( E_t = E_0 \, e^{rt} \) where \( E_0 \) and \( E_t \) are the initial and final prey densities in each experimental enclosure and \( r \) is the real prey population growth rate. Thus, \( r = a - (pn) \), where \( a \) is the intrinsic rate of population growth in the absence of predators, \( p \) is the individual fish predation rate and \( n \) is the number of fish in the enclosure. (ii) In the absence of predators (controls), \( a \) is given by: \( a = [\ln(C_0) - \ln(C_t)]/t \), where \( C_0 \) is the initial prey density in the control enclosure and \( C_t \) is the final prey density in the enclosure at time \( t \) (in days). (iii) When fish are present, \( r \) is given by: \( r = [\ln(E_0) - \ln(E_t)]/t \). The number of each prey item ingested by each stickleback in one day is given by \[ \int_0^t pC_0 \, e^{rt} = \frac{pC_0}{r} (e^{rt} - 1) \] Values were computed for each prey taxon and then added to obtain the total number of prey eaten by sticklebacks in one day. Results Colonization of the pool by sticklebacks The density of sticklebacks observed in the study pool at the peak of the reproductive season in the first week of March in 1987 (1365 sticklebacks in the pool, 0.059 adults m\(^{-2}\)) was the highest ever recorded in the temporary marshes of the Camargue (Table 1). However, the number of fry leaving the pool was very low in 1986–87 (139 young) and none left the pool in 1987–88, although fry were abundant within the pool. This contrasts with the numbers of fry leaving three other temporary marshes being studied (Table 1). Young sticklebacks normally start to leave temporary marshes in the first few days of April, at a length of between 12–16 mm. However, at this time of year the connection between the study pool and the drainage canal will only be functional for a few days even in the wettest years. This accounts for the small number of fry leaving the study pool. Only a very small number of adults leave the marshes (seven adults in 1986–87), the majority dying of exhaustion after the reproductive period (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). Assuming that only 20–30% of males will build an effective nest (Fitzgerald & Whoriskey, 1985), that only 30–35% of the eggs will produce fry (Kynard, 1979), and from calculations of the fecundity of females derived from length–fecundity relationships, the length distribution of females, and assuming that each female will only produce one clutch of eggs (Crivelli & Britton, 1987), the number of eggs produced in the study pool in 1986–87 was 88 344. Fry leaving the study pool therefore only represented 0.16% of the eggs produced. In both 1986–87 and 1987–88 sticklebacks started to colonize the study pool 3 weeks after flooding. In the 1986–87 period the rate of colonization was not regular, but occurred in waves (Fig. 3). Three major colonization peaks occurred: the first in late October, the second in the third week of December and the last in early March. Only two major peaks were recorded in 1987–88: in the first week of January and the first week of February. Zooplankton community Zooplankton were abundant throughout the period, with an overall mean density of 1360 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\). These values are similar to those found by other authors in temporary water bodies in the Camargue (Marazanof, 1963, 1964; Pont, 1983; Pirot & Pont, 1987). Dominant taxa were Chydorus sphaericus O.F. Müller (51 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)), Simocephalus vetulus O.F. Müller (28 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)), Daphnia magna (21 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)), Alona rectangula Sars (19 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)) and Arctodiaptomus wierzejskii (6 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)). A month after the pool was flooded (Fig. 4), the zooplankton community was dominated by the cyclopoid \( D. b. odessanus \) (adult length 1.0–1.6 mm, up to 920 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)) and large-bodied species such as the cladocerans \( D. magna \) (3.0–6.0 mm, up to 204 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)) and \( S. vetulus \) (1.5–3.5 mm, up to 212 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)). The typical calanoid \( A. wierzejskii \) was present (1.8–2.8 mm, up to 47 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)) and a few individuals of the very large Hemidiaptomus roubaui lauterborni Kiefer (5.0–5.5 mm in length, very scarce). Some phyllopods (Branchipus sp.) and Culicidae larvae were also collected 2 weeks after filling. The total number of taxa and total density were high (seven taxa; up to 2106 ind. \( 100 \text{ cm}^{-2} \)). A week after the first wave of sticklebacks colonized the pool (from 31 October to 11 November; 0.01 sticklebacks \( \text{m}^{-2} \)), densities of the two large cladoceran species (\( S. vetulus \) and \( D. magna \)) decreased dramatically from 352 FIG. 4. Numbers of adult sticklebacks entering the pool per week (a) and seasonal variations in abundance (ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)) of the eight dominant zooplankton taxa: (b) large zooplankton species (>2 mm adult length), (c) intermediate species (1–2 mm), (d) small species (<1 mm) and (e) Ostracods (up to 1.6 mm). ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) (6 November) to 71 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) (14 November). Cyclopoid densities also decreased a week later from 876 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) to 397 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\). Smaller species quickly replaced \(D.\) magna and \(S.\) vetulus, reaching high densities by mid-November: \(C.\) sphaericus (0.3–0.6 mm in length, 1102 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)), \(C.\) laticaudata (0.6–1.0 mm, 256 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)) and Ostracoda (up to 1.6 mm length, 827 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). \(S.\) vetulus, \(D.\) magna and \(A.\) wierzejskii had completely disappeared by mid-December. Scapholeberis mucronata was present throughout this period, but at very low densities (0.6–1.2 mm, less than 10 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). A week after the second wave of sticklebacks colonized the pool (from 19 December to 22 December; 0.039 sticklebacks m\(^{-2}\)), the population of C. laticaudata dropped suddenly from 118 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) on 20 December to 13 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) on 30 December. From January through to early March very few fish entered or left the pool. Because predation and mortality were probably low (regular counts of piscivorous birds, the main predators, showed that there very few present during this period), it follows that stickleback densities probably remained stable. Zooplankton richness was very low, with only three taxa: D. b. odessanus (67–184 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)), C. sphaericus (429–733 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)) and Ostracoda (328–621 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). No major change occurred to the zooplankton community during the period of ice cover. From mid-March to the end of April, C. sphaericus and Ostracoda densities remained stable, whereas the population of D. b. odessanus declined (31 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) on 10 April). Some new small species of Chydoridae were collected, but at very low densities: A. rectangula (11 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) on 18 March), Alonella exigua and Pleuroxus aduncus (both less than 1 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). In the 3 weeks before the pool dried up, during which time salinity increased from 5.5 to 9.0 gl\(^{-1}\), the populations of C. sphaericus and Ostracoda declined to low densities. A. rectangula (adult length: 0.3–0.5 mm) became abundant at the end of April (111 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) on 30 April) and the population of D. b. odessanus began to recover only in the first few days of May (208 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). The disappearance of large-bodied forms (adult length more than 1.6 mm) could clearly be related to stickleback colonization (Fig. 4). The density of these large species (mainly Daphniidae) dropped after the first wave of sticklebacks entered the pool and they completely disappeared after the second wave in late December. C. laticaudata, an intermediate-sized form, also seemed to be highly preferred by sticklebacks and its density declined quickly after the second wave of sticklebacks colonized the pool. In contrast, seasonal variation in the abundance of other species such as D. b. odessanus, C. sphaericus and Ostracoda revealed no evidence of whether or not they were an important food resource for fish during winter and spring. In-situ predation experiments The field experiments provided direct evidence that stickleback predation is of potential significance to the chydorid and cyclopoid populations (Fig. 5). At the start of the experiments, total population densities were very similar in all four series of experiments, varying from 1103 to 1293 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) (\(x = 1240\) ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\); SE = 91 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\)). C. sphaericus dominated, accounting for 48–52% of individuals, but because of the progressive change in the zooplankton community, cyclopoids were scarce in the second series of experiments (Series B). The density of C. sphaericus declined in the controls of both A and B, by 47 and 45% respectively. D. b. odessanus density also decreased in Series A controls (55%), whereas Ostracoda density decreased only in the Series B controls (69%). Densities of all taxa except Ostracoda dropped quickly in all four experimental conditions (one, two or four adult, or seven young sticklebacks). C. sphaericus densities 2 days after stickleback introduction declined significantly only in Series B (Mann–Whitney test, \(n = 6\), \(P < 0.05\)), but were significantly lower in both series after 4 days (\(P < 0.01\)), with an 85% reduction in Series A (from 677 to 63 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) for two fish and from 607 to 133 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) for four fish) and a 58% reduction in Series B (from 577 to 240 for one fish and from 497 to 209 for seven young fish). When compared with changes in the controls, however, the decrease of C. sphaericus density under conditions of stickleback predation in Series B did not appear to be as impressive as in Series A. This could be due to the lower fish biomass and predation rate in the second series. In Series A, D. b. odessanus populations declined significantly from the start of the experiment (after 2 days \(P < 0.01\)), and mean densities were only 33 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) (two fish) and 68 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) (four fish) after 5 days (\(P < 0.01\)), compared to 317 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) and 287 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\) at the start of the experiment (83% reduction). Ostracod densities did not change significantly during the course of the Series A experiments (\(P > 0.05\)). Significant changes were noted in Series B (\(P < 0.01\)) with a 51% reduction in ostracod numbers, but the FIG. 5. Zooplankton sampling was carried out before fish introduction (To) and after 2 and 4 or 5 days. reduction in the controls was even higher than in the experimental enclosures (69%). The relative abundance of ostracods compared to other taxa increased in all cases, especially when predation was high: from 30 to 62% (four fish), from 23 to 77% (two fish), from 47 to 56% (one fish) and from 48 to 55% (seven young fish). In the three experiments with adult fish (Table 1), total predation rates (\( p \)) varied between 0.08 and 0.32 per day for \( C. sphaericus \) with a mean value of 0.23 (SE = 0.169, \( n = 9 \) replicates), between 0.11 and 0.27 for \( D. b. sphaericus \) with a mean value of 0.21 (SE = 0.13, \( n = 6 \) replicates) and between -0.16 and 0.02 for ostracods with a mean value of −0.07 (SE = 0.12, \( n = 9 \) replicates). The mean \( p \) values (for the three experiments) differed significantly from zero (\( P < 0.01; n = 9 \) replicates) for both \( C. sphaericus \) and \( D. b. odessanus \), but were not significant in the case of ostracods. The total daily biomass of zooplankton (\( C. sphaericus \) and \( D. b. odessanus \)) ingested by adult fish, expressed as a percentage of fish body weight, was between 2.8% and 10.72% with a mean value of 6.62% (\( n = 9 \) replicates) and differed significantly from zero (\( P < 0.05 \)). Results obtained in experiments with two adult fish were higher than those with one and four fish, but the number of replicates was too low to make valid comparisons. In Series A, the total mean daily number of prey ingested was 2882 for chydorids and 1078 for cyclopoids. In the experiments with young fish, the total predation rate \( p \) on \( C. sphaericus \) was 0.08 per day. The mean daily biomass ingested by young sticklebacks was highly variable, ranging from 0 to 166% of live fish weight, with a mean of 67%. The daily mean number of chydorids ingested was 374. Examination of the gut contents of twenty young fish at the end of the experiment showed clearly that they ingested zooplankton. The diet consisted mainly of chydorids (95% of prey items), but some cyclopoids were present (1.8%). The mean number of chydorids per gut was 55.3 (range 10 to 165; 95% confidence limits = 18.6). No ostracods were recorded in the diet of young sticklebacks. Discussion Because of sampling difficulties there are few published figures on the abundance of three-spined sticklebacks; however, there is no doubt that the densities we recorded in the temporary marshes of the Camargue (range 0.005 to 0.126 fish \( m^{-2} \)) are very low. Walsh & Fitzgerald (1984) found densities in a salt-marsh pool varying from 2.2 to 6.7 fish \( m^{-2} \) whereas O’Hara & Penczak (1987) and Wootton (1985) recorded average densities in rivers of 67 fish \( m^{-2} \) and 16.1 fish \( m^{-2} \), respectively. Thorman & Fladvad (1981) found densities of sticklebacks varying between 0.1 and 28 fish \( m^{-2} \) in the River Broälven (Sweden), depending on the season. The cause of the low densities in the Camargue may be that these populations lie towards the southern extremity of species range where it has to face adverse conditions of high summer temperatures and seasonality of water bodies in the Mediterranean-type climate (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). In addition, there is heavy predation by fish-eating birds. In our experiments only the consumption of zooplankton was taken into account in estimating the daily ration of sticklebacks. However, chironomids might also have been occasionally consumed by fish. The mean density of chironomid larvae in Series A and B was 6 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \) and 19 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \), respectively. These values are low compared to densities of up to 250 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \), respectively. These values are low compared to densities of up to 250 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \) recorded in other marshes and pools during the warm months (May–October) (Tourenq, 1975). In the opinion of Ibrahim & Huntingford (1989b) and Visser (1982), planktonic prey are more important in the diet of sticklebacks than benthic prey. Sticklebacks are visual predators, and Gibson (1980), Milinski (1986) and Myszkowski (1986) have shown that sticklebacks will usually choose the larger prey available, irrespective of absolute size. However, Ibrahim & Huntingford (1989a) were of the opinion that prey size was one of the least important factors in determining the choice of diet in the three-spined stickleback. They and Walsh & Fitzgerald (1984) showed that visual clues determine diet preference in the stickleback, and that colour, movement, shape and size of the prey are also important in the selection made by this species. Our field and experimental studies clearly show that sticklebacks first ingested the largest, most conspicuous zooplankton in the study pool. Later, after the disappearance of these prey, they switched to smaller and less profitable prey (\( D. b. odessanus \) and \( C. sphaericus \)). There is, however, an exception to this pattern: Ostracoda, which are larger than \( D. b. odessanus \) and \( C. sphaericus \), were not eaten. Our field estimates of daily food consumption by adult sticklebacks (Table 2) are similar to those published previously. Rajasilla (1980), using the digestion-rate method, found that a stickleback weighing 1g consumes 24.2–132.8 mg per day, corresponding to 2.4–13.3% of fresh body weight. also found a seasonal effect and estimated from diel samples that the daily food consumption of sticklebacks living in a lake was 6.6−7.8% of their body weight. Wootton (1984) also used diel samples and applied the Winberg method to calculate the daily food consumption of a population of sticklebacks in Wales. He found the daily food consumption to be between 3.0 and 3.3% of body weight. Although the daily ration of fry calculated in this study is highly variable, the average ration is remarkably high, corresponding to 67% of the fry body weight. This high feeding rates might be associated with rapid growth in size by fry at this time. Fish-free pools are increasingly being managed in such a way that they are capable of being colonized by fish in the wettest years. In our case, the study pool has effectively been linked with the permanent drainage canal during 6 years out of the past 12. During these periods, sticklebacks and nine other species of fish and two Malacostraca were able to colonize the pool and feed heavily on the zooplankton community. Fish probably first colonize these pools by being attracted by the abundance and quality (large size) of the zooplankton within the water flowing from the pool to the drainage canal, or because of the good nesting conditions within the marshes. The densities of sticklebacks recorded within the study pool are among the highest noted in the Camargue (Table 1). When sticklebacks reach the pool they find highly favourable feeding conditions and stay there until their death after the reproductive period. Sticklebacks reproduced successfully within the study pool, at exactly the same time as elsewhere in the Camargue. However, the number of fry that were able to leave the pool was negligible because the early drying out of the pool cuts the connection with the permanent drainage canal. By way of a comparison, 71931 fry left the Relongues Sud in the 1987–88 season (Table 1), although this temporary marsh had a similar density of adult fish. This is because the larger temporary marshes are linked to the permanent water bodies by deep ditches, and they dry out only in mid-July, leaving sufficient time for stickleback fry to leave the marsh before the connection is cut. It is therefore extremely disadvantageous for sticklebacks to use the fish-free pool. If too many fish-free pools are connected to permanent water bodies because of management practices, they will attract a large part of the reproductive population of sticklebacks but these will produce almost no recruits. This could be very detrimental to the population of sticklebacks, an annual species in the Camargue. Nevertheless, the most important threat posed by the colonization of fish-free pools by fish concerns the unique zooplankton community of these pools. The consequences of colonization by three-spined sticklebacks on the zooplankton in the pool varies greatly according to the species. In this study, three main kinds of prey response can be identified. Large-bodied forms, such as Anostraca and Notostraca, large calanoid copepods (Mixodiaptomus kupelwieseri Brehm, Diaptomus cyaneus intermedius, Hemidiaptomus roubaui lauterborni and Arctodiaptomus wierzejskii) and Daphnia magna are typical species inhabiting fish-free pools in the Camargue (Nourisson & Aguesse, 1961; Marazanof, 1963; Marazanof, 1964; Champeau, 1966; Pirot & Pont, 1987). They are well adapted to living in temporarily flooded environments by having life-history strategies which include the formation of resting eggs and diapause during the dry season (Champeau, 1971), and most of them were noted in both the autumn and spring periods by the above authors. Within the temporary pool studied in 1986–87, the large calanoid A. wierzejskii was present, but only at low densities and only during the first 2 months after the pool became flooded by rain-fall. D. magna also disappeared in December. This temporary pool was connected with the main drainage canal in 1978 or 1979. A previous study of this pool in 1979–80 (Pirot & Pont, 1987; D. Pont, unpublished data) showed that, in the past, the zooplankton community was dominated by large calanoids all along the flooded period with D. c. intermedius (up to 2.8 mm in length), Hemidiaptomus roubaui lauterborni (up to 5.5 mm in length) and A. wierzejskii (from 54 to 90% of total zooplankton organisms). D. magna was present in both autumn and spring (2% of total organisms). In addition to their large-bodied form, the calanoids in the pool might also be strongly affected by predation from visually feeding fish because of their red pigmentation (Pourriot et al., 1982). Predation pressure on the large D. magna could also be increased due to the preference of this species for swimming in the water column layer free of vegetation (Flössner, 1972). Our results show that fish colonization of temporary pools can produce a progressive local extinction of the most typical species (calanoids) inhabiting these water bodies. These results are in good agreement with the size-selective predation hypothesis (Brooks & Dodson, 1965). O’Neill & Hyatt (1987) showed in experimental studies that the standing crop and mean size of planktonic prey organisms are depressed by the foraging activity of sticklebacks. In contrast to a lake environment, large species in shallow pools cannot escape from predation by the vertical migration adaptation (Zaret & Suffern, 1976) and are quickly eliminated from the water column. Similarly, Kerfoot & Lynch (1987) have shown that ancient branchiopod groups occupied a much broader range of habitats during the Palaeozoic era than nowadays and that they have been progressively restricted to fish-free environments due to the increase in fish predation efficiency. So, temporary, isolated fish-free pools must be considered as the last refuge for these species. We suggest that these temporary habitats are also the last refuge for large calanoid species inhabiting inland waters. A second group of species which are less than 1.5 mm in length (D. b. odessanus, C. sphaericus) are preyed upon heavily by sticklebacks, but predation pressure is not sufficient to effectively reduce the abundance of these prey species. In our field experiment enclosures the density of adult sticklebacks was 17 to 67 times higher than within the pool. In March, chydorid and copepod mean densities were 603 and 95 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\), respectively. Assuming that the young fish of the year were still not able to feed in this month and that all the adults that entered the marsh were still alive, it can be estimated that the mean number of prey consumed by sticklebacks per day represented about 0.2% of the chydorid biomass and 0.5% of the copepod biomass. However, only sticklebacks were allowed to enter the study pool, so that predation pressure will have been even greater if all zooplanktivorous fish, and especially Gambusia affinis, had entered the pool as they normally do (Crivelli & Boy, 1987). The last group is the ostracods. This work did not reveal any predation pressure on them. As a consequence, ostracods became dominant during late winter and spring. The lack of predation on this group is in agreement with previous work. Possible reasons include: (i) ostracods have a bi-articulate calcareous shell which can be a very effective defence against predators such as the stickleback; (ii) aquarium observations show that sticklebacks will at times attack ostracods, but that they nearly always spit them out immediately, sometimes after having crushed the shell (B. Britton, pers. comm.); this may suggest that ostracods have developed a chemical defence against fish predation; (iii) most ostracods live close to or within the mud—water interface under the dense submerged vegetation cover of filamentous algae (Evans & Stewart, 1977; Pont, 1983) and so they can escape more readily from predation pressure. More work is required to test these different hypotheses. Fish-free pools are a unique type of wetland in the Mediterranean region, with a distinct flora and fauna, that are increasingly threatened by management practices. One of the major consequences of such practices, as shown in this study, is colonization by fish with a major impact on the zooplankton community. Such colonization may cause the extinction in the short term of several zooplankton taxa restricted to these pools, thus reducing the biodiversity of Mediterranean wetlands. The impact of three-spined sticklebacks on the zooplankton of a previously fish-free pool D. PONT,* A. J. CRIVELLI† and F. GUILLOT *Université Claude Bernard (Lyon 1), Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Systèmes Fluviaux, 1 rue Parmentier 13200 Arles, France; and † Station Biologique de la Tour du Valat, Le Sambuc, 13200 Arles, France SUMMARY. 1. In the Camargue (southern France), most invertebrates inhabiting temporary shallow oligohaline marshes and pools are large-bodied, conspicuous and defenceless taxa that are restricted to fish-free environments. Management practices, by creating drainage canals, strongly affect the invertebrate community by allowing colonization by fish. 2. Sticklebacks colonizing the study pool were sampled daily and zooplankton sampling was carried out at weekly intervals. From early October until the pool dried in June, 1365 sticklebacks entered and only 139 stickleback’s fry and seven adults left the pool. Zooplankton abundance was high during the whole study period with a mean density of 1360 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\). Larger forms (Daphnia magna, Simocephalus vetulus, Arctodiaptomus wierzejskii) quickly disappeared after the first wave of sticklebacks entered the pool in November. Subsequently, smaller species (Diacyclops bicuspidatus odessanus, Chydorus sphaericus and ostracods) replaced the larger ones until the pool dried. 3. Food selectivity of sticklebacks and daily zooplankton consumption were investigated under experimental conditions within the pool in spring. After introduction of sticklebacks, densities of zooplankton species dropped quickly (D. b. odessanus, C. sphaericus) with the exception of Ostracoda. Estimates of daily zooplankton consumption by adult sticklebacks varied between 2.8 and 10.7% of fish body weight. Examination of gut contents showed that fry mainly ingested Chydorus sphaericus. 4. Given that the stickleback is an annual species in the Camargue, and that few fry are able to leave the pool due to the early drying out, the colonization of such a former fish-free pool is not beneficial for the stickleback population. However, a more serious effect of such colonization is the progressive local extinction of the most typical zooplankton species inhabiting these formerly fish-free environments. Introduction Temporarily flooded, shallow oligohaline marshes and pools are typical habitats in the Mediterranean region. Many of these wetlands are fish free. The invertebrates inhabiting them (e.g. copepods, cladocerans and phyllopods) have developed highly specialized adaptations, such as diapause, to enable them to survive early drying out or high water temperatures (Nourisson & Aguesse, 1961; Champeau, 1970; Elgmork, 1980; Wiggins, Mackay & Smik, 1980). In these temporary pools, invertebrates usually belong to large-bodied, conspicuous and defenceless taxa, restricted in their distribution to fish-free environments (Kerfoot & Lynch, 1987). Management practices such as the creation of drainage canals can allow temporary or longer-term colonization of pools by fish, with major consequences for the invertebrate communities. Such practices enable these pools to be used as spawning grounds by various species of fish, especially those spawning early in the spring such as the three-spined stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus L. (Crivelli, 1981; Crivelli & Britton, 1987). In the Camargue in southern France, Gasterosteus aculeatus is a strictly annual species, colonizing seasonally flooded marshes in late autumn and winter. It spawns in February–March and dies in April. Fry produced in these habitats emigrate from early April to the end of May into permanently flooded drainage canals (Crivelli & Britton, 1987; A.J. Crivelli unpublished data). From here they move to the largest permanent brackish-water body in the Camargue, the Etang de Vaccarès, where they spend the period from summer to early autumn. The diet of the three-spined stickleback has been well studied in various types of habitat and in different geographical regions (Wootton, 1976; Walsh & Fitzgerald, 1984; Bentzen & McPhail, 1984; Dauod, Bolger & Bracken, 1985; Snyder, 1984; O’Hara & Penczak, 1987; Delbeek & Williams, 1987). Chironomid larvae and pupae and zooplankton are generally the main food items, with variations according to the time of year and type of habitat. Surface insects, Gastropoda, Gasterosteus eggs and detritus can be of major importance in the stickleback diet in some habitats. Ostracoda are mostly absent or represent less than 1% of the diet (e.g. at Isle Verte, Quebec; Walsh & Fitzgerald, 1984). Few studies have documented the qualitative and quantitative decline or extinction of invertebrates living in fish-free water bodies following accidental or regular colonization by fish, or after stocking with fish (e.g. Gliwicz, 1980; Gliwicz & Rowan, 1984). The aims of this study were to monitor the colonization of a formerly fish-free temporary pool by three-spined sticklebacks, to study their impact on the zooplankton community in the field and to draw conclusions on the long-term variability of the zooplankton and on the consequences of colonization of these pools by spawning sticklebacks. Materials and Methods The study area known as ‘La Fangouse’ (Fig. 1) is a temporary pool located in the delta of the River Rhône on the Mediterranean coast of France. This pool floods naturally with rainwater in the autumn and dries out in early or late spring (Fig. 2). In the 1986–87 period, the pool was flooded on 24 September and dried out on 10 June. The maximum water depth was about 55 cm. At periods of high water level (especially in winter), the pool was connected to the ‘Egout du Cazeau’ drainage canal by a narrow channel. Vegetation cover around the entire pool perimeter was dominated by Arthrocnemum fruticosum L. MOQ. and Juncus maritimus Lamark. Within the pool, submerged vegetation comprised Callitriche truncata Guss, Ranunculus baudotii Godron, Zannichellia pedunculata Lineus and filamentous algae. Mean surface water temperature was 9.0°C in late autumn, 5.8°C in winter and 13.8°C in spring. The pool and connecting channel to the drainage canal were completely frozen over for 20 days in January 1987. Water conductivity (at 25°C) varied between 2.07 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (= 1 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) and 5.03 mS\(^{-1}\) (= 3.0 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) in autumn and winter, reaching 10.8 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (9 mg l\(^{-1}\) total salinity) the week before drying out. The mean conductivity over the entire period of flooding was 4.53 mS cm\(^{-1}\). In the 1987–88 and 1988–89 periods, the pool was flooded on 5 November and 14 October, and dried out by 6 June and 20 March, respectively. In 1987–88 mean conductivity was 10.4 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (3.1–24.9 mS cm\(^{-1}\)), and in 1988–89 it was 6.1 mS cm\(^{-1}\) (2.1–12.1 mS cm\(^{-1}\)). Fish entering or leaving the pool were sampled daily with a system of fish traps situated on the channel connecting the pool and the drainage canal (Fig. 1). The traps were made of mosquito netting (1-mm mesh) and retained fry as small as 8–10 mm long. The two water bodies are connected only when the water level in the pool exceeds 30 cm. All fish captured were identified to species and measured, but only the Gasterosteus attempting to enter the pool were released into it. In 1986–87, 17941 fish belonging to ten species and 2396 Malacostraca (Crangon crangon L., Paleamon squilla L. were recorded entering the study pool (Table 1). The most abundant fish species in order of importance were: Gambusia affinis Baird and Girard, Gasterosteus aculeatus, Atherina boyeri Risso and Lepomis gibbosus L. Trapping was carried out on 35 days in 1986–87, 46 days in 1987–88 but only 5 days in 1988–89. The mean total length of Gasterosteus aculeatus (± 95% CL) was 32.5 ± 0.6 mm in October, 32.4 ± 0.4 in November, 36.0 mm ± 0.3 in December for both sexes combined, and 38.9 ± 2.4 for males and 46.0 ± 2.2 for females in February, and 39.4 ± 1.7 for males and 47.2 ± 1.3 for females in March. Zooplankton sampling was carried out at weekly intervals with a plexiglass core sampler (30-cm\(^2\) section) during the 1986–87 period. The water column, including the soft mud–water interface, was pumped out and the inside was then rinsed out three times (more than 99% of organisms collected). Organisms were finally filtered through a 50-\(\mu\)m mesh-size net and stored in 4% formaldehyde solution (Pont, 1986). Each sample consisted of 24 cores distributed along the entire length of four transects: 80, 60, 130 and 150 m (Fig. 1). In-situ experiments on sticklebacks foraging on zooplankton were carried out in the spring of 1987. Sticklebacks collected at the pool entrance were measured and released into large cylindrical enclosures (1-m\(^2\) section) made of transluscent fibreglass sheeting embedded into the sediment (Fig. 1). Two series of experiments were conducted at the following stickleback densities. (1) Series A (17–22 March). Two or four adult fish per enclosure (three replicates at each density). Zooplankton sample (eight cores) taken just outside the enclosure were used as controls. (2) Series B (18–22 April). One adult or seven young fish per enclosure (three replicates at each density) and two control enclosures. Zooplankton sampling in the enclosures was carried out just before the introduction of sticklebacks, 2 days after (in the case of experimental plots) and at the end of the experiments (Series A: 5 days; Series B: 4 days). At each time, the area sampled represented 2.4% of the total enclosure area, so correction factors were applied to each of the zooplankton counts before computing prey densities. Previous studies (Pont, 1983) have shown that variability between individual cores can be high, so seven cores in two samples were counted separately. The precision indices D, expressed as the ratio of standard error to the arithmetic mean, were 0.18 and 0.15, a reasonable error in such a sampling procedure (Elliot, 1977). Variability in the mean values of total zooplankton density in replicates and controls before fish introduction was of the same order of magnitude: D = 0.16 in Series A and 0.07 in Series B. Therefore, we assume that the relative error in terms of the 95% confidence limits of the mean obtained at each stickleback density tested (eight cores per enclosure and three replicates at each sampling time) was about 40%. Prey length measurements were made under a microscope for each major taxon (n = 150). The mean lengths of Diacyclops, Chydorus and Ostracoda were 0.58, 0.42 and 0.66 mm, respectively. Dry and fresh weights were estimated from length–weight relationships (Dumont, Van de Velde & Dumont 1975; Pont, 1983) and by assuming that dry weight represented 11% of fresh weight (Bottrell et al., 1976). Sticklebacks were measured before experiments (adults: 42–60 mm in length, young: 12–17 mm) and their weights estimated from length–weight relationships (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). Most previous studies of fish feeding rates are based on rates of gastric evacuation and food consumption (Elliot & Persson, 1978). In this study, calculation of stickleback feeding rates was based on Gauld’s method (Gauld, 1951; Edmonson & Winberg, 1971) with the assumption that predation rate is unaffected by changes in prey densities below a critical level. (i) \( E_t = E_0 \, e^{rt} \) where \( E_0 \) and \( E_t \) are the initial and final prey densities in each experimental enclosure and \( r \) is the real prey population growth rate. Thus, \( r = a - (pn) \), where \( a \) is the intrinsic rate of population growth in the absence of predators, \( p \) is the individual fish predation rate and \( n \) is the number of fish in the enclosure. (ii) In the absence of predators (controls), \( a \) is given by: \( a = [\ln(C_0) - \ln(C_t)]/t \), where \( C_0 \) is the initial prey density in the control enclosure and \( C_t \) is the final prey density in the enclosure at time \( t \) (in days). (iii) When fish are present, \( r \) is given by: \( r = [\ln(E_0) - \ln(E_t)]/t \). The number of each prey item ingested by each stickleback in one day is given by \[ \int_0^t pC_0 \, e^{rt} = \frac{pC_0}{r} (e^{rt} - 1) \] Values were computed for each prey taxon and then added to obtain the total number of prey eaten by sticklebacks in one day. Results Colonization of the pool by sticklebacks The density of sticklebacks observed in the study pool at the peak of the reproductive season in the first week of March in 1987 (1365 sticklebacks in the pool, 0.059 adults m\(^{-2}\)) was the highest ever recorded in the temporary marshes of the Camargue (Table 1). However, the number of fry leaving the pool was very low in 1986–87 (139 young) and none left the pool in 1987–88, although fry were abundant within the pool. This contrasts with the numbers of fry leaving three other temporary marshes being studied (Table 1). Young sticklebacks normally start to leave temporary marshes in the first few days of April, at a length of between 12–16 mm. However, at this time of year the connection between the study pool and the drainage canal will only be functional for a few days even in the wettest years. This accounts for the small number of fry leaving the study pool. Only a very small number of adults leave the marshes (seven adults in 1986–87), the majority dying of exhaustion after the reproductive period (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). Assuming that only 20–30% of males will build an effective nest (Fitzgerald & Whoriskey, 1985), that only 30–35% of the eggs will produce fry (Kynard, 1979), and from calculations of the fecundity of females derived from length–fecundity relationships, the length distribution of females, and assuming that each female will only produce one clutch of eggs (Crivelli & Britton, 1987), the number of eggs produced in the study pool in 1986–87 was 88 344. Fry leaving the study pool therefore only represented 0.16% of the eggs produced. In both 1986–87 and 1987–88 sticklebacks started to colonize the study pool 3 weeks after flooding. In the 1986–87 period the rate of colonization was not regular, but occurred in waves (Fig. 3). Three major colonization peaks occurred: the first in late October, the second in the third week of December and the last in early March. Only two major peaks were recorded in 1987–88: in the first week of January and the first week of February. Discussion Because of sampling difficulties there are few published figures on the abundance of three-spined sticklebacks; however, there is no doubt that the densities we recorded in the temporary marshes of the Camargue (range 0.005 to 0.126 fish \( m^{-2} \)) are very low. Walsh & Fitzgerald (1984) found densities in a salt-marsh pool varying from 2.2 to 6.7 fish \( m^{-2} \) whereas O’Hara & Penczak (1987) and Wootton (1985) recorded average densities in rivers of 67 fish \( m^{-2} \) and 16.1 fish \( m^{-2} \), respectively. Thorman & Fladvad (1981) found densities of sticklebacks varying between 0.1 and 28 fish \( m^{-2} \) in the River Broälven (Sweden), depending on the season. The cause of the low densities in the Camargue may be that these populations lie towards the southern extremity of species range where it has to face adverse conditions of high summer temperatures and seasonality of water bodies in the Mediterranean-type climate (Crivelli & Britton, 1987). In addition, there is heavy predation by fish-eating birds. In our experiments only the consumption of zooplankton was taken into account in estimating the daily ration of sticklebacks. However, chironomids might also have been occasionally consumed by fish. The mean density of chironomid larvae in Series A and B was 6 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \) and 19 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \), respectively. These values are low compared to densities of up to 250 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \), respectively. These values are low compared to densities of up to 250 ind. 100\( \text{cm}^{-2} \) recorded in other marshes and pools during the warm months (May–October) (Tourenq, 1975). In the opinion of Ibrahim & Huntingford (1989b) and Visser (1982), planktonic prey are more important in the diet of sticklebacks than benthic prey. Sticklebacks are visual predators, and Gibson (1980), Milinski (1986) and Myszkowski (1986) have shown that sticklebacks will usually choose the larger prey available, irrespective of absolute size. However, Ibrahim & Huntingford (1989a) were of the opinion that prey size was one of the least important factors in determining the choice of diet in the three-spined stickleback. They and Walsh & Fitzgerald (1984) showed that visual clues determine diet preference in the stickleback, and that colour, movement, shape and size of the prey are also important in the selection made by this species. Our field and experimental studies clearly show that sticklebacks first ingested the largest, most conspicuous zooplankton in the study pool. Later, after the disappearance of these prey, they switched to smaller and less profitable prey (\( D. b. odessanus \) and \( C. sphaericus \)). There is, however, an exception to this pattern: Ostracoda, which are larger than \( D. b. odessanus \) and \( C. sphaericus \), were not eaten. Our field estimates of daily food consumption by adult sticklebacks (Table 2) are similar to those published previously. Rajasilla (1980), using the digestion-rate method, found that a stickleback weighing 1g consumes 24.2–132.8 mg per day, corresponding to 2.4–13.3% of fresh body weight. Wootton (1984) also used diel samples and applied the Winberg method to calculate the daily food consumption of a population of sticklebacks in Wales. He found the daily food consumption to be between 3.0 and 3.3% of body weight. Although the daily ration of fry calculated in this study is highly variable, the average ration is remarkably high, corresponding to 67% of the fry body weight. This high feeding rates might be associated with rapid growth in size by fry at this time. Fish-free pools are increasingly being managed in such a way that they are capable of being colonized by fish in the wettest years. In our case, the study pool has effectively been linked with the permanent drainage canal during 6 years out of the past 12. During these periods, sticklebacks and nine other species of fish and two Malacostraca were able to colonize the pool and feed heavily on the zooplankton community. Fish probably first colonize these pools by being attracted by the abundance and quality (large size) of the zooplankton within the water flowing from the pool to the drainage canal, or because of the good nesting conditions within the marshes. The densities of sticklebacks recorded within the study pool are among the highest noted in the Camargue (Table 1). When sticklebacks reach the pool they find highly favourable feeding conditions and stay there until their death after the reproductive period. Sticklebacks reproduced successfully within the study pool, at exactly the same time as elsewhere in the Camargue. However, the number of fry that were able to leave the pool was negligible because the early drying out of the pool cuts the connection with the permanent drainage canal. By way of a comparison, 71931 fry left the Relongues Sud in the 1987–88 season (Table 1), although this temporary marsh had a similar density of adult fish. This is because the larger temporary marshes are linked to the permanent water bodies by deep ditches, and they dry out only in mid-July, leaving sufficient time for stickleback fry to leave the marsh before the connection is cut. It is therefore extremely disadvantageous for sticklebacks to use the fish-free pool. If too many fish-free pools are connected to permanent water bodies because of management practices, they will attract a large part of the reproductive population of sticklebacks but these will produce almost no recruits. This could be very detrimental to the population of sticklebacks, an annual species in the Camargue. Nevertheless, the most important threat posed by the colonization of fish-free pools by fish concerns the unique zooplankton community of these pools. The consequences of colonization by three-spined sticklebacks on the zooplankton in the pool varies greatly according to the species. In this study, three main kinds of prey response can be identified. Large-bodied forms, such as Anostraca and Notostraca, large calanoid copepods (Mixodiaptomus kupelwieseri Brehm, Diaptomus cyaneus intermedius, Hemidiaptomus roubaui lauterborni and Arctodiaptomus wierzejskii) and Daphnia magna are typical species inhabiting fish-free pools in the Camargue (Nourisson & Aguesse, 1961; Marazanof, 1963; Marazanof, 1964; Champeau, 1966; Pirot & Pont, 1987). They are well adapted to living in temporarily flooded environments by having life-history strategies which include the formation of resting eggs and diapause during the dry season (Champeau, 1971), and most of them were noted in both the autumn and spring periods by the above authors. Within the temporary pool studied in 1986–87, the large calanoid A. wierzejskii was present, but only at low densities and only during the first 2 months after the pool became flooded by rain-fall. D. magna also disappeared in December. This temporary pool was connected with the main drainage canal in 1978 or 1979. A previous study of this pool in 1979–80 (Pirot & Pont, 1987; D. Pont, unpublished data) showed that, in the past, the zooplankton community was dominated by large calanoids all along the flooded period with D. c. intermedius (up to 2.8 mm in length), Hemidiaptomus roubaui lauterborni (up to 5.5 mm in length) and A. wierzejskii (from 54 to 90% of total zooplankton organisms). D. magna was present in both autumn and spring (2% of total organisms). In addition to their large-bodied form, the calanoids in the pool might also be strongly affected by predation from visually feeding fish because of their red pigmentation (Pourriot et al., 1982). Predation pressure on the large D. magna could also be increased due to the preference of this species for swimming in the water column layer free of vegetation (Flössner, 1972). Our results show that fish colonization of temporary pools can produce a progressive local extinction of the most typical species (calanoids) inhabiting these water bodies. These results are in good agreement with the size-selective predation hypothesis (Brooks & Dodson, 1965). O’Neill & Hyatt (1987) showed in experimental studies that the standing crop and mean size of planktonic prey organisms are depressed by the foraging activity of sticklebacks. In contrast to a lake environment, large species in shallow pools cannot escape from predation by the vertical migration adaptation (Zaret & Suffern, 1976) and are quickly eliminated from the water column. Similarly, Kerfoot & Lynch (1987) have shown that ancient branchiopod groups occupied a much broader range of habitats during the Palaeozoic era than nowadays and that they have been progressively restricted to fish-free environments due to the increase in fish predation efficiency. So, temporary, isolated fish-free pools must be considered as the last refuge for these species. We suggest that these temporary habitats are also the last refuge for large calanoid species inhabiting inland waters. A second group of species which are less than 1.5 mm in length (D. b. odessanus, C. sphaericus) are preyed upon heavily by sticklebacks, but predation pressure is not sufficient to effectively reduce the abundance of these prey species. In our field experiment enclosures the density of adult sticklebacks was 17 to 67 times higher than within the pool. In March, chydorid and copepod mean densities were 603 and 95 ind. 100 cm\(^{-2}\), respectively. Assuming that the young fish of the year were still not able to feed in this month and that all the adults that entered the marsh were still alive, it can be estimated that the mean number of prey consumed by sticklebacks per day represented about 0.2% of the chydorid biomass and 0.5% of the copepod biomass. However, only sticklebacks were allowed to enter the study pool, so that predation pressure will have been even greater if all zooplanktivorous fish, and especially Gambusia affinis, had entered the pool as they normally do (Crivelli & Boy, 1987). The last group is the ostracods. This work did not reveal any predation pressure on them. As a consequence, ostracods became dominant during late winter and spring. The lack of predation on this group is in agreement with previous work. Possible reasons include: (i) ostracods have a bi-articulate calcareous shell which can be a very effective defence against predators such as the stickleback; (ii) aquarium observations show that sticklebacks will at times attack ostracods, but that they nearly always spit them out immediately, sometimes after having crushed the shell (B. Britton, pers. comm.); this may suggest that ostracods have developed a chemical defence against fish predation; (iii) most ostracods live close to or within the mud—water interface under the dense submerged vegetation cover of filamentous algae (Evans & Stewart, 1977; Pont, 1983) and so they can escape more readily from predation pressure. More work is required to test these different hypotheses. Fish-free pools are a unique type of wetland in the Mediterranean region, with a distinct flora and fauna, that are increasingly threatened by management practices. One of the major consequences of such practices, as shown in this study, is colonization by fish with a major impact on the zooplankton community. Such colonization may cause the extinction in the short term of several zooplankton taxa restricted to these pools, thus reducing the biodiversity of Mediterranean wetlands. TROPHIC STATUS AND THREATS IN ZINAV LAKE (TOKAT/ TURKEY) Saliha Dirim Buhan1, Nihal Bektaş1, Mehmet Ali T. Koçer2,*, Hakan Mete Doğan3, Ekrem Buhan4 and Fatih Polat5 1Gebze Institute of Technology, Faculty of Engineering, Environmental Engineering Department, Gebze/Kocaeli/Turkey 2Mediterranean Fisheries Research Production and Training Institute, Antalya/Turkey, 3Gaziosmanpaşa University, Agricultural Faculty, Soil Science Department, Tokat/Turkey 4Gaziosmanpaşa University, Agricultural Faculty, Aquaculture and Fisheries Department, Tokat/Turkey 5 Gaziosmanpaşa University, Almus Vocational School, Tokat/Turkey Presented at the 7th International Symposium on Ecology and Environmental Problems (ISEEP2013), December 18-21, 2013, Antalya, Turkey ABSTRACT This study was conducted to determine water quality and trophic state of Zinav Lake, which is located in the Central Black Sea Region of Turkey. Temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, electrical conductivity, total suspended solids, Secchi disc transparency, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, total nitrogen, soluble reactive phosphorus, total phosphorus and chlorophyll a were monitored in water column from January 2012 to June 2013. The study showed that Zinav Lake was a dimictic lake, which circulated in spring and fall, and thermally stratified in summer. Hypo-limnetic oxygen deficit and metalimnetic oxygen minima were the cases. Vertical distribution of dissolved oxygen and pH and ammonia accumulation in hypolimnion represented eutrophic/hypereutrophic conditions. The values and ratios of nutrients and chlorophyll a and Secchi disc transparency clearly classified Zinav Lake as eutrophic/hypereutrophic. Allochthonous loadings of organic matter and nutrients from the catchment and the changes in hydrological cycle by a power plant seem to be the most threatening factors controlling the water quality and trophic state in Zinav Lake. KEYWORDS: Zinav Lake, water quality, nutrients, trophic state, threats 1. INTRODUCTION Although the magnitude and proportion of the sources vary widely among different systems, aquatic ecosystems receive organic matter from primary production within system and from terrestrial loadings from catchment area [1]. Many factors such as location, climate, vegetation and land cover/land use in the catchment area have significant influences on the water quality of small lakes [2, 3], considering they have the high hydrologic and nutrient processing rates [4]. Allochthonous organic matter, however, supplements primary production in small lakes, particularly in forested areas [5]. Therefore, organic matter and nutrient loadings from catchment area result in generally higher productivity of small lakes as compared with large ones [6]. Despite diminished characteristics, small lakes were neglected by ecologists partly due to presuming that ecosystems with a small areal extent cannot play a major role in global processes. However, recent analyses have shown that they play an unexpectedly significant role in global cycles [7]. Zinav Lake is a small lake with a surface area of 0.34 km², located in the Central Black Sea Region of Turkey. There is a lack of data on the lake in spite of the biggest natural lake in Kelkit River Basin. In this context, this study aimed to investigate the vertical and seasonal fluctuations of physicochemical properties and trophic state of Zinav Lake. 2. MATERIAL AND METHODS Zinav Lake as abovementioned is located in the Central Black Sea Region of Turkey. The precise position of study area can be described as between the 37°13’-37°21’ North latitudes and 40°32’-40°23’ East longitudes (Figure 1). The study was carried out between January 2012 and June 2013. Surface water samples were collected from three areas of the lake representing inlet, outlet and mid-point, while vertical samples from 0, 5, 10 meters and deep water at the mid-point. Temperature, pH and electrical conductivity were measured in situ by using YSI-556 MPS multi-parameter measurement instrument (YSI, USA). Total sus- pended solids, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, soluble reactive phosphorus, total nitrogen and phosphorus were determined with suitable methods and test kits using by DR2800 benchtop spectrophotometer (Hach-Lange Germany). Chlorophyll a concentrations were calculated by monochromatic method after extraction with 90% acetone solution and absorbance measurement by the spectrophotometer [8]. ![Map showing the location and topographic features of the study area, including sampling stations and elevation contours](page_320_670_728_484.png) FIGURE 1 - Location and topographic features of the study area Normality was firstly tested for each variable using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Comparisons of sampling sites and non-normally distributed water quality parameters were made using a signed rank test (Wilcoxon) and followed by post hoc test (Tukey’s HSD). Wilcoxon test did not detect significant differences between the three surface water sampling sites in terms of physicochemical variables (P > 0.05). Therefore, water quality of the lake was evaluated according to mid-point measurements. All statistical tests were carried out using JMP 8.0 software package. 3. RESULTS Vertical change of temperature was significantly different (P<0.01), with higher values at surface water than 10 meters and deep water (Table 1). Vertical temperature profile displayed a clear seasonal variation, revealing the periods of mixing and thermal stratification (Figure 2a). In summer, temperature sharply decreased from surface water to bottom, and the greatest thermal discontinuity was observed in July. Temperature of surface water gradually decreased in late summer, and thermal stratification was lost during the fall circulation. Measurements showed that the fall turnover was completed in November, and almost a thermal homogeneity in water column prevailed during winter. Dissolved oxygen sharply decreased in metalimnion during thermal stratification, and the hypolimnetic oxygen deficit was the case (Figure 2b). The large volume of anoxic hypolimnion which was expanded above 5 meters in July resulted in low dissolved oxygen concentrations in entire water column during the fall circulation. Despite low concentrations in deep water, high concentrations of dissolved oxygen in surface layers were observed during winter.
